PREFACE 

The number of decisions involving motor vehicles increases every year, so that today motor vehicle cases comprise the most important litigation in the courts of this Commonwealth. 

Much conflict of opinion has arisen as to the existence of liability under any given set of facts. I offer this volume, not as a comprehensive treatise covering every phase of motor vehicle law, but as an embodiment of all the cases under the respective headings, together with quotations and excerpts from the most important opinions of the Supreme Judicial Court. 

It is my hope that bar and laity alike may receive some benefit herefrom. 

Boston, Mass.

September 1, 1932. 

EDWARD M. DANGEL

SI 

Definitions, Legal Status MOTOR VEHICLES 

In 

MASSACHUSETTS 

By 

EDWARD M. DANGEL CHAPTER I. 

DEFINITIONS, DISTINCTIONS AND LEGAL STATUS. 

A. DEFINITIONS. 

1. Motor Vehicle. 

SECTION 1. 

A motor vehicle is an instrument of conveyance of persons and property propelled by power, other than muscular power, upon roads, except a railroad or railway car or other carriage for travel running only upon rails or tracks. 

A motor vehicle is a self-propelled vehicle that moves on the road, not designed for running on the rails. 

McBoyle v. United States, 283 U. S. 25

SECTION 2. 

2. Other Terms Involving Motor Vehicles. 

By General Laws, Chapter 90, Section 1, (Acts 1923, 

464; 1924, 189; 1928, 316, Sec. 2; 381, Sec. 2; 1929, 203; 

1930, 332, Sec. 1), the following terms have been defined:

$2 

APPLICATION, an application by mail or otherwise to the registrar or any agent designated by him for the purpose, upon a blank provided by the registrar and with which is deposited the fee provided in section thirty-three. 

AUTOMOBILE, any motor vehicle except a motorcycle. 

DEALER, any person who is engaged principally in the business of buying, selling or exchanging motor vehicles. 

DEPARTMENT, the department of public works. 

GARAGE, any place where five or more motor vehicles are stored or housed at any one time for pay, except only such places in which motor vehicles are kept by the owners thereof without payment for storage.

INTERSECTING WAY, any way which joins another at an angle, whether or not it crosses the other. 

MOTORCYCLE, any motor vehicle having but two or three wheels in contact with the ground, and a saddle on which the driver sits astride, or a platform on which he stands, or any bicycle having a motor attached thereto and a driving wheel or wheels in contact with the ground in addition to the wheels of the bicycle itself. 

MOTOR VEHICLES, automobiles, semi-trailer units, motorcycles and all other vehicles propelled by power, other than muscular power, except railroad and railway cars and motor vehicles running only upon rails or tracks. 

NON-RESIDENT, any resident of any state or country who has no regular place of abode or business in the Commonwealth for a period of more than thirty days in the year, provided, that any such resident who owns a commercial motor vehicle which is operated in the Commonwealth for more than thirty days in the year shall not, as to such vehicle, be deemed a non-resident.

NUMBER PLATE, the sign or marker furnished by the registrar on which is displayed the register number or

$3 

Definitions, Legal Status mark of a motor vehicle assigned to such motor vehicle by the registrar.

OPERATOR, any person who operates a motor vehicle 

PERSONS, wherever used in connection with the registration of a motor vehicle, all persons who own or control such vehicles as owners, or for the purpose of sale, or for renting as agents, salesmen or otherwise. 

POLICE OFFICERS or OFFICER, any constable or other officer authorized to make arrest or serve process, provided he is in uniform or displays his badge of office. 

REGISTER NUMBER, the number or mark assigned by the registrar to a motor vehicle, whether or not such number or mark includes a letter or letters; and said number or mark, except on motorcycles, shall always be in separate Arabic numerals at least four inches in height, with strokes not less than one-half of an inch in width. 

REGISTRAR, the registrar of motor vehicles. 

THICKLY SETTLED OR BUSINESS DISTRICT, the territory contiguous to any way which is built up with structures devoted to business, or the territory contiguous to any way where the dwelling houses are situated at such distances as will average less than two hundred feet between them for a distance of a quarter of a mile or over. 

TRAILER, a vehicle used for carrying passengers for hire or commodities in connection with commerce and having no motive power of its own, but which is drawn by a motor vehicle. It shall not include a pair of wheels commonly used as an implement for other purposes than transportation. [TRAVELLED WAY, the macadam is not necessarily the travelled way; the travelled part may extend beyond. 

It is that part of the way which, with the knowledge and acquiescence of the town, is used for public travel within the located limits of the way.]

$3 

WAY, any public highway, private way laid out under authority of statute, way dedicated to public use, or way under the control of park commissioners or body having like powers.

B. DISTINCTIONS. 

SECTION 3. 

1. Between Touring Car and Truck. 

There is a well recognized difference between a touring car and a truck in the ordinary use of those words. 

In the statutes a truck is recognized and referred to as a distinct kind of motor vehicle with special provisions for its registration and equipment. 

Comm. v. Magarosian, 261 Mass. 228, at 229 

G. L., c. 90, ss. 2, 7, 19 and 23, as amended by Acts 

1922, c. 342, s. 2.

SECTION 4. 

2. Between Motor Vehicle and Aircraft. 

A motor vehicle travels on the earth while an aircraft travels in the air. 

McBoyle v. United States, 283 U. S. 25 

(National Motor Vehicle Theft Act does not apply to aircraft)

C. LEGAL STATUS. 

1. As a Carriage. 

a. 

SECTION 5. 

When Determined To Be. 

It is said in Baker v. Fall River, 187 Mass. 53, at pp. 56 and 57: "Plainly an automobile is a vehicle which can carry passengers or inanimate matter, and so is such a carriage

$5 

Definitions, Legal Status 

... that the Legislature had in view in the use of that word in the statute." b. When Determined NOT To Be. 

It was said in Doherty v. Ayer, 197 Mass. 241, at 246: "An automobile is not a carriage within the terms of 

Revised Laws, Chapter 51, Section 1, requiring Cities and 

Towns to keep public highways reasonably safe and convenient at all seasons for travellers 'with their horses, teams and carriages.' 999 But this rule has been changed by General Laws, Chapter 84, Section 1, which provides that: "Highways and town ways shall, unless otherwise provided, be kept in repair at the expense of the town in which they are situated, so that they may be reasonably safe and convenient for travellers, with their horses, teams and carriages at all seasons."

Revised Laws, Chapter 208, Section 55 (G. L. c. 266, s. 64) provides, in part that: ... "Whoever . . . with intent to cheat or defraud the owner, refuses to pay for the use of a carriage. the lawful hack or carriage fare established therefor by any city or town, shall be punished by a fine or by imprisonment.. did not apply to automobiles. 

In Commonwealth v. Goldman, 205 Mass. 400, at 401, the court said: "It is certain that when this statute was originally enacted, the Legislature, in using the word "carriage," had no thought of a vehicle made up in large part of compli cated machinery, and propelled by a powerful engine whose operation is similar to that of locomotive engines on railroads. While such a vehicle may be called a carriage in the broad sense that it is used to carry persons and property, it is not commonly referred to as a carriage, but is

$6 

 distinguished from carriages by another name to designate a vehicle of an entirely different character." 

SECTION 6. 

2. As Dangerous Instrumentality. 

An automobile is not an instrumentality inherently dangerous. 

McGowan v. Longwood, 242 Mass. 337, at 341

But a motor vehicle is itself a dangerous instrumentality, which is bound to become a source of imminent danger to other travellers, unless (1) kept in good repair and (2) equipped with adequate brakes and then (3) driven on public ways with a high degree of care and skill. 

Opinion of Justices, 251 Mass. 569, at 597

It was said in District of Columbia v. Colts, 282 U. S. 

63, at 73, that "an automobile is, potentially, a dangerous instrumentality, as the appalling number of fatalities brought about every day by its operation bear distressing witness." a. 

Characteristics. 

An automobile is a peculiar kind of vehicle which requires unusual care in its management, and the presence of which upon the highways involves more than ordinary risks to other travellers. 

Dudley v. Northampton St. Ry., 202 Mass. 443, at 446 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, 167-172

Referring to motor vehicles the court said in Comm. v. 

Boyd, 188 Mass. 79: "They are capable of being driven and are apt to be driven at such a high rate of speed, and when not properly driven are dangerous."

$7 

Definitions, Legal Status SECTION 7. 

3. As a Vehicle. 

In the concurrent use of public ways an automobile is to be classed as a vehicle. 

Foster v. Curtis, 213 Mass. 79, at 82 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155 

Lynch v. Fisk Rubber Co., 209 Mass. 16

Automobiles are vehicles within the meaning of General 

Laws, Chapter 89 relating to "The Law of the Road." 

Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 393, at 395 

Lynch v. Fisk Rubber Co., 209 Mass. 16, 17 and cases cited 

It was said in Baker v. Fall River, 187 Mass. 53, at 57, that: "The automobile is a vehicle in common use for transporting both persons and merchandise upon public ways."

CHAPTER II. 

GOVERNMENTAL REGULATION. 

A. POWER OF. 

SECTION 8. 

The use of an automobile as an instrument of transportation is peculiarly the subject of government regulation. 

Silver v. Silver, 280 U. S. 117; S. C. 108 Conn. 371; 

65 A. L. R. 939, at 942

A motor vehicle is a peculiar kind of vehicle which requires unusual care in its management, and the presence of which upon the highways involves more than ordinary risk to other travellers.

Dudley v. Northampton Street Railway, 202 Mass. 

443, at 446 

Comm. v. Kingsbury, 199 Mass. 542 

Comm. v. Boyd, 188 Mass. 79

Suits arising from the use of motor vehicles may be the subject of legislation. 

Silver v. Silver, 280 U. S. 117; 65 A. L. R. 939, at 942. 

S. C. 108 Conn. 371; 65 A. L. R. 943, at 952 (Statute may limit liability of Owner or Operator to guest to recklessness)

Governmental Regulation 3. State. 

SECTION 10. 

The power of the General Court to regulate travel over the public ways of the Commonwealth for the general welfare is extensive. It may be exercised in any reasonable manner to conserve the safety of travellers. No one has a right to use streets and other public places as he chooses without regard to the presence of others. It is an underlying conception of streets and highways that they shall at all times be reasonably safe and convenient for public travel and that travellers thereupon in the exercise of due care may be secure from preventable danger. 

Opinion of the Justices, 251 Mass. 569, at 595 

All highways now are laid out and established by public authority. Initial costs of construction and subsequent expenses for care, repair, and replacement are charges against the public treasury. The Commonwealth itself, directly or through its governmental subdivisions of counties, cities, towns and districts, all subject to legislative control, is the owner either of the easement constituting the highway or of the fee, when that has been acquired. 

Opinion of the Justices, 251 Mass. 569, at 595 

The Commonwealth as the sovereign power and the proprietor may do with its own as the General Court may direct, provided its action can be said to be in the public interest and not violative of constitutional guarantees. 

Opinion of the Justices, 251 Mass. 569, at 595 

Treasurer and Receiver General v. Revere Sugar 

Refinery, 247 Mass. 483 

Boston v. Treasurer and Receiver General, 237 Mass. 403, and 414 

Boston Fish Market Corp. v. Boston, 224 Mass. 31

Regulations, pursuant to statute, prohibiting utterly the use of automobiles upon certain highways were held valid in 

Comm. v. Kingsbury, 199 Mass. 542

IO SIO 

Opinion of the Justices, 251 Mass. 569, at 596 

G. L. c. 90, ss. 16 and 18

A license to drive and a registration of motor vehicles have been required as prerequisite to their use on the public ways in this Commonwealth almost from their first appearance. The power to license imports the further power to withhold such license except upon compliance with prescribed conditions. The power to regulate, even to the extent of prohibition of motor vehicles from public ways, includes the lesser power to grant the right to use public ways only upon the observance of prescribed conditions precedent. 

Opinion of the Justices, 251 Mass. 569, at 596

The requirement that every owner before being allowed to register his motor vehicle shall provide security for the discharge of his liability for personal injuries or death resulting from the presence of such motor vehicle on the public ways cannot be pronounced unreasonable.

It furnishes a degree of assurance of compensation to those who rightfully and carefully using the ways are injured by the carelessness of operators of motor vehicles. 

Opinion of the Justices, 251 Mass. 569, at 596

The requirements for security for the payment of legal claims arising from personal injuries caused on highways by motor vehicles is an extension of the police power into a new field, so far as we are aware, but in our opinion it falls within the limits of the constitutional power of the General Court. 

Opinion of the Justices, 251 Mass. 569, at 596

The general principle which sustains a statute is that, when the general welfare of travellers on the highway in the opinion of the Legislature is threatened by, and demands protection against, a specific evil, any rational means may be adopted to remedy the evil. 

Opinion of the Justices, 251 Mass. 569, at 600

§11 

Governmental Regulation 

Comm. v. Strauss, 191 Mass. 545 

John P. Squire & Co., v. Tellier, 185 Mass. 18

It was said in Commonwealth v. Kingsbury, 199 Mass. 

542, at 544, 545 and 546: "Automobiles are vehicles of great speed and power, whose appearance is frightful to most horses that are unaccustomed to them. The use of them introduces a new element of danger to ordinary travellers on the highways, as well as to those riding in the automobiles. In order to protect the public great care should be exercised in the use of them. Statutory regulation of their speed while running on the highways is reasonable and proper for the promotion of the safety of the public. It is the duty of the Legislature, in the exercise of the police power, to consider the risks that arise from the use of new inventions applying the forces of nature in previously unknown ways.

The general principle is too familiar to need discussion. It has been applied to automobiles in different states with the approval of the courts. 

Comm. v. Boyd, 188 Mass. 79 "It seems too plain for discussion that, with a view to the safety of the public, the Legislature may pass laws regulating the speed of such machines when running upon highways. The same principle is applicable to a determination by the Legislature that there are some streets and ways on which such machines should not be allowed at all. "The right of the Legislature, acting under the police power, to prescribe that automobiles shall not pass over certain streets or public ways in a city or town, seems to us well established both upon principle and authority." 

It is proper for the Legislature of this Commonwealth to safeguard persons who are lawfully using the highways from the serious risks of injury by motor vehicles which are operated in defiance of the law, and so may require registration in order that the owners of such

 vehicles shall furnish a means by which they can be identified and be compelled to make proper compensation for the injuries which by their violation of the law, or by their mere negligence they might cause to other travellers.

B. VALIDITY OF. 

SECTION 13. 

"Reasonable classification in the selection of subjects for legislation is always permissible to the lawmaking power. It is only when such classification is arbitrary or irrational that it comes in conflict with the Constitution." 

Opinion of the Justices, 251 Mass. 569, at 600 and 601

§15 

Governmental Regulation SECTION 14. 

2. Discrimination. 

"What shall be included and what shall be excluded from the sweep of any statute demand the exercise of discrimination, insight, and sound judgment. دو 

Opinion of the Justices, 251 Mass. 569, at 600 and 601 a. Operators.

SECTION 15. 

The danger from horse drawn vehicles is so small compared with that from motor vehicles as to afford a sound basis for classification.

The omission of operators from the scope of a statute, when not owners of motor vehicles, is not unlawful discrimination.

It may well be thought that responsibility ought to be fastened upon the owner of the dangerous instrumentality, the motor vehicle. 

Opinion of the Justices, 251 Mass. 569, at 601

The primary object is to afford security to the traveller injured on the public way through the negligent operation of the motor vehicle. 

Opinion of the Justices, 251 Mass. 569, at 601 b. 

SECTION 16. 

Non-Residents. 

A statute is not unconstitutional because it does not apply to non-resident owners or operators of motor vehicles not registered under our laws. The use of such motor vehicles may be found by the Legislature to be small in comparison with that of such vehicles registered in accordance with our laws. The expense of enforcing the law with respect to them may be found to be excessive. It may be that there are other difficulties in the way. Moreover,

§17 

 a classification including only motor vehicles registered under our statutes is not unreasonable.

Non-resident owners of motor vehicles or motor vehicles not registered under our laws doubtless might be included within the law. 

Opinion of the Justices, 251 Mass. 569, at 602 

Kane v. New Jersey, 242 U. S. 160 

Hendrick v. Maryland, 235 U. S. 610. 

This omission would not be fatal to a statute. Legislative classification may rest upon narrow distinctions. 

Opinion of the Justices, 251 Mass. 569, at 602

SECTION 17. 

C. Government Vehicles. 

The exclusion of motor vehicles owned by the Commonwealth, or "by a corporation subject to the supervision and control of the department of public utilities, or by a street railway company under public control," cannot be denounced as arbitrary. It has a reasonable relation to the public safety. It does not destroy equality before the law nor create special privilege. It is a classification which may be thought to rest on sound judgment. 

This classification falls within the authority of Packard v. Banton, 264 U. S. 140. 

Opinion of the Justices, 251 Mass. 569, at 602.

SECTION 18. 

3. Reasonableness.

Statutes, ordinances, regulations and rules concerning the use and operation of motor vehicles must be reasonable in their terms and effect. 

Comm. v. Crowninshield, 187 Mass. 221, at 224 (Park Commissioner's rule as to speed on Commonwealth Avenue, Boston.) 

Comm. v. Stodder, 2 Cush. 562, at 570

In examining and interpreting the statute, by-law, ordinance, regulation or rule, every rational presumption in favor of its validity must be indulged, and it will not be denounced as contrary to the Constitution unless its language is so clear and explicit as to render impossible any other reasonable construction. 

Comm. v. O'Neil, 233 Mass. 535

§26 CHAPTER III. 

REGISTRATION OF THE MOTOR VEHICLE. 

A. PROVISIONS FOR. 

SECTION 26. 

The registration of motor vehicles is provided for in 

General Laws, Chapter 90, Sections 2-5. 

A statute requiring registration is constitutional. 

Comm. v. Boyd, 188 Mass. 79

Registration is intended to safeguard persons who are lawfully using the highways from serious risks of injury by motor vehicles and also so owners can be identified and compelled to make proper compensation for injuries which by their violation of the law, or their mere negligence, they may cause to other drivers. 

Dudley v. Northampton St. Ry., 202 Mass. 443, at 447 The Legislature, by General Laws, Chapters 89 and 90, intended to outlaw unregistered motor vehicles, and to give them, as to persons lawfully using the highways, no other right than that of being exempt from reckless, wanton or wilful injury. 

Dudley v. Northampton St. Ry., 202 Mass. 443, at 447, 448 The owner or operator of an unregistered or an improperly registered motor vehicle is a mere trespasser upon the highway, and is there not only against the right of the owner of the soil, and so liable to an action by him, but also against the rights of all other persons who are lawfully using the highway. Such owner and operator

23 

 are violating the law made for the protection of others against them; accordingly, they are trespassers as to such other persons. 

Dudley v. Northampton St. Ry., 202 Mass. 443, at 448 It follows that third persons, as well as railway com- . panies, lawfully using the highways with their own vehicles, owe to the owner and operator of improperly registered motor vehicles no other or further duty than that which they owe to a third person who is a trespasser on their property, that is, not the duty of ordinary care, as those words are commonly used, but merely the duty to abstain from injuring him by wilfulness, wantonness or recklessness. 

Dudley v. Northampton St. Ry., 202 Mass. 443, at 448 

Sullivan v. Boston El. Ry., 199 Mass. 73, at 76 

Fitzmaurice v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R., 192 Mass. 159, at 162 

Massell v. Boston El. Ry., 191 Mass. 491, at 493

The Legislature intended to put these forbidden and dangerous machines outside the pale of travellers, not merely for the purpose of the criminal law, but as regards all other persons rightfully upon the streets. 

Dudley v. Northampton St. Ry., 202 Mass. 443, at 448 Of course, a third person has no right to run a vehicle into an unregistered machine wilfully, wantonly or recklessly. 

Dudley v. Northampton St. Ry., 202 Mass. 443, at 449 

McKeon v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R., 183 Mass. 271 

Welch v. Wesson, 6 Gray, 505

The statutes relating to the operation within the Commonwealth of motor vehicles or trailers owned by nonresidents have been amended and grouped under Acts of 1931, c. 142. (See: G. L. c. 90, ss. I, 3, 4, 6, 10 and 33)

General Laws, Chapter 90, Secton I (as amended by

General Laws, Chapter 90, Section 3 (as amended by 

Acts of 1931, c. 142), provides that: "A motor vehicle or trailer registered in any other state or country and owned by a non-resident who has complied with the laws relative to motor vehicles and trailers, and the operation thereof of the state or country of registration may be operated on the ways of this Commonwealth without registration under this chapter, to the extent, as to length of time of operation and otherwise, that, as finally determined by the registrar, the state or country of registration grants substantially similar privileges in the case of motor vehicles and trailers duly registered under the laws and owned by residents of this Commonwealth; provided, that no motor vehicle or trailer owned by a non-resident shall be so operated beyond the expiration of a period of thirty days except during such time as the owner thereof maintains in full force a policy of liability insurance nor unless the owner or operator of such motor vehicle or trailer, while operating the same during such additional time, has on his person or in the vehicle in some easily accessible place a permit issued by

$28 

 the registrar which then authorized the operation of such vehicle without registration under this chapter. . "Every such vehicle so operated shall have displayed upon it two number plates. . . of the state or country in which such vehicle is registered. . . ." 

But see: Hanson v. Culton, 269 Mass. 471, at 472 and 

473, where, under the prior statutory definition, a person whose legal residence and domicile was in a foreign state but was employed in this Commonwealth for three months where he had a room which he occupied on an average of three nights each week, was not a non-resident and could not legally operate his motor vehicle unless our statute was complied with. 

(I) Border State Registrations. 

General Laws, Chapter 90, Section 4 provides that: 

"Any person owning a motor vehicle who resides in an adjoining state within fifteen miles of the boundary line of this commonwealth, and who has complied with the laws relative to motor vehicles and the operation thereof in the state where he resides, may, upon application, have such motor vehicle registered and may operate the same upon the ways of this commonwealth within fifteen miles of the boundary line of the state where he resides, provided such state grants similar privileges to residents of this commonwealth. The foregoing privilege shall be in addition to any other rights or privileges granted to nonresidents by this chapter. The registrar shall furnish at his office, without charge, to every person whose motor vehicle is registered as aforesaid, number plates of suitable design with a distinguishing number or mark thereon." 

(II) Non-Compliance By. 

If a non-resident has a place of abode or business in this Commonwealth for a period of more than thirty days

$27 

 in any calendar year and operates his motor vehicle on the public streets of this Commonwealth without a registration by this Commonwealth, or permits it to be so operated, his vehicle is an outlaw and nuisance upon the highway, and he is a trespasser and he cannot recover for the negligence of operators of other vehicles. 

Avila v. DuPont, 1932 A. S. 275, at 278 

Hanson v. Culton, 269 Mass. 471, at 473

Gondek v. Cudahy Packing Co., 233 Mass. 105 

Dudley v. Northampton St. Ry., 202 Mass. 443

But a non-resident corporation which has no regular place of abode or business in this Commonwealth for a period of more than thirty days in the calendar year need not procure registration of its motor vehicle in this Commonwealth. 

Gondek v. Cudahy Packing Co., 233 Mass. 105 

See also Hanson v. Culton, 269 Mass. 471, at 473

A person may have a "place of abode," as those words are used in the statute, apart from the place of his permanent residence or domicil. 

Avila v. DuPont, 1932 A. S. 275, at 278 

Hanson v. Culton, 269 Mass. 471

Although a person can have but one domicil he can have more than one regular place of abode or residence. 

Avila v. DuPont, 1932 A. S. 275, at 278 

Emery v. Emery, 218 Mass. 227, at 229 

Lowell Tr. Co. v. Pratt, 183 Mass. 379, at 381 

Wachusett Nat. Bank v. Fairbrother, 148 Mass. 181, at 185 It is not necessary that the owner of the motor vehicle be physically present in this Commonwealth for a period of thirty days during the calendar year.

The statute relates to the maintenance of a "regular place of abode or business" in the Commonwealth for the stated period, and has no necessary and direct ref-

$28 

 erence to the physical presence of the owner in the Commonwealth for that or any other period of time. 

Avila v. DuPont, 1932 A. S. 275, at 278 

Marlborough v. Lynn, 275 Mass. 394, at 396 

Hanson v. Culton, 269 Mass. 471 

Gondek v. Cudahy Pack. Co., 233 Mass. 105, at 110 

So, in Avila v. DuPont, 1932 A. S. 275, where the owner of the motor vehicle was a resident of a foreign state in which he registered the vehicle, which bore a number plate of that state at the time of the accident, and the owner had a summer home in this Commonwealth for several years which was occupied by him personally and by the members of his family, his servants and his guests, and in the vehicle at the time of the accident were the owner's daughter, who was spending the summer there at his house, and three other persons who were staying there with the owner and his wife, and the house was opened more than thirty days before the accident and some of the owner's family were there then and at that time the owner himself was seen, and the vehicle was seen there continuously at different times from then until the time of the accident (more than thirty days), the court said at pages 278, 279 and 280: "The evidence warranted a finding that the owner of the car in question . . . had maintained a summer home [in this Commonwealth] for himself, his family and guests, which was, in fact, occupied by some members of his family continuously. . . [for more than thirty consecutive days up to the time of the accident], and during a part of this time by himself. And . . . that he had a regular place of abode in this Commonwealth for more than thirty consecutive days before the accident It follows that as this automobile was not registered in this Commonwealth it was an outlaw on the highway; that the owner had no right to permit its opera-

$29 

 tion upon a highway here; and that the defendant is responsible for the injuries caused thereby. "Whether the owner of the automobile operated by the defendant at the time of the accident had a regular place of abode in this Commonwealth for a period of more than thirty days during the year 1928 before August II of that year was a question of fact to be determined by the jury upon the entire evidence." 

In Jenkins v. North Shore Dye House, Inc., 1931 A. S. 

2299, the deceased with his wife resided in Providence in the State of Rhode Island. The apartment previously occupied by them in that city was given up in May, 1917; the deceased occupied a room in a lodging house and the wife went to Wrentham in this Commonwealth. The deceased ended his work in Providence about July 12th, but remained there until about July 19th, and thereafter had no place of abode in Providence; then, with his wife, he visited in Maine until August 18, 1927, when they both went to the house in Wrentham, to which their household effects had earlier been removed. They lived thereafter in that house until the date of the fatal injuries, September 12, 1927. The deceased registered his automobile in March 1927 in the State of Rhode Island and had an operator's license from that State, and he was driving the car on the date of the fatal accident under the Rhode Island registration and operator's license and had no Massachusetts registration. During the period after August 18, 1927 the deceased worked in this Commonwealth. The court held that the deceased, having intended prior to the date of his fatal accident to make Massachusetts his residence, executed that intent by actually residing within the Commonwealth. The automobile should have been registered forthwith in Massachusetts, and the failure of the deceased to have this done made his automobile an outlaw and trespasser upon the highway.

$28 

A non-resident who gives up his place of residence is not entitled to thirty days place of abode within this State before it becomes necessary for him to obtain a Massachusetts registration. If he has no other residence he must get a Massachusetts registration immediately. 

Jenkins v. North Shore Dye House, Inc., 1931 A. S. 2299 The court said in this case at pages 2301 and 2302: "Whatever else may be said concerning the word 'nonresident'. . . it can [not] have been intended to comprehend residents. That would be a contradiction of terms. . . It cannot. rightly be construed to mean that one who has been a non-resident and who has ceased to be a non-resident because he has removed his residence from another State or Country to this Commonwealth is entitled to the immunity extended to a non-resident. The statute is designed to afford to such non-resident the protection of the automobile registration of his home State or country during a temporary sojourn within this Commonwealth not exceeding a period of thirty days. But it does not extend such protection to one who has abandoned his foreign residence and taken up his abode within this Commonwealth. All such persons are governed by the usual laws controlling automobile activities of residents of the Commonwealth."

A person ceases to be a non-resident when he gives up his residence in a foreign State and begins to live in this Commonwealth. "Residence' means in general a personal presence at some place of abode with no present intention of definite and early removal and with a purpose to remain for an undetermined period, not infrequently but not necessarily combined with a design to stay permanently." 

Jenkins v. North Shore Dye House, Inc., 1931 A. S. 2299, at 2302 

Marlborough v. Lynn, 275 Mass. 394, at 396 and 

397 and cases cited

$31 

Martin v. Gardner, 240 Mass. 350 

Briggs v. Rochester, 16 Gray 337

If a person becomes a resident of Massachusetts he is required to have his automobile registered forthwith under the laws of this Commonwealth and is not entitled with respect to that automobile to the rights of a nonresident. 

Jenkins v. North Shore Dye House, Inc., 1931 A. S. 2299, at 2302 and 2303 

Hanson v. Culton, 269 Mass. 471

C. PERSONS REQUIRING REGISTRATION. 

SECTION 29. 

General Laws, Chapter 90, Section 2 requires that a person in whose name a motor vehicle is registered shall be the owner thereof. 

Pierce v. Hutchinson, 241 Mass. 557, at 562

And also that the registration shall be issued in the true name of the owner. 

Fine v. Kahn, 270 Mass. 557, at 558

So, where the name of the owner and operator was "Morris I. Fine" but at times he used and was known as "Murray I. Fine" and the motor vehicle was registered in the latter name, the motor vehicle is not registered in accordance with G. L. c. 90, s. 2, as amended, it is therefore an outlaw on the highway and the plaintiff can recover only when he has sustained injuries or damages on account of reckless, wanton or wilful conduct, so that the plaintiff has no rights against other travellers except to be protected from such conduct.

$33 

Fine v. Kahn, 270 Mass. 557, at 558

Koley v. Williams, 265 Mass. 601 Bacon v. Boston El. Ry., 256 Mass. 30 

Fairbanks v. Kemp, 226 Mass. 75 

Crompton v. Williams, 216 Mass. 184

However, the rule might be different if the plaintiff was commonly known by the name of "Murray I. Fine.” 

Fine v. Kahn, 270 Mass. 557, at 558

But the distinction is that the registrant assumes the name once in a while, in restricted connection on separate, and perhaps rare, occasions being usually or commonly known by the particular name. 

Fine v. Kahn, 270 Mass. 557, at 558 

It was said in Keith v. Maguire, 170 Mass. 210, at 212 that: "the word 'owner' is not a technical term. It is not confined to the person who has the absolute right in a chattel, but it also applies to the person who has the possession and control of it."

Registration in name of part owner who does not operate vehicle is not enough. 

Shufelt v. McCarter, 235 Mass. 122 

2. Corporations. 

SECTION 30. 

Motor vehicles of a corporation must be registered in the corporate name and not in the name of its officers or agents. 3. 

Chase v. N. Y. C. & H. R. R.R., 208 Mass. 137 (Sale to new corporation required new registration)

SECTION 31. 

Executors or Administrators.

An executor or administrator should not register a motor vehicle in the name of the testator or intestate.

832 

Motor Vehicles in 'Massachusetts 

So, where the testator obtained registration in his own name it is improper for the executor to put the number plates on the motor vehicle and operate it on the highway. 

Fairbanks v. Kemp, 226 Mass. 75

However, General Laws, Chapter 90, Section 2 provides, in part, that: "On the death of the owner of a motor vehicle or trailer its registration shall be deemed continued in force as a valid registration until the end of the year or until the ownership of such motor vehicle or trailer is transferred by the executor or administrator of the estate of such owner, whichever occurs first."

But where an executor or administrator sells the motor vehicle and fails to turn in the registration certificate neither the executor nor the administrator remain liable for the operation of the motor vehicle by the buyer under the original number plates or registration where the executor or administrator does not participate in the presence of the motor vehicle upon the public way. 

Fulton v. Stahl, 271 Mass. 23, at 25

But the executor or administrator probably would be liable if he furnished the registration or number plates with the anticipation that there should be an appearance of right of the motor vehicle to be upon the highway. 

McDonald v. Dundon, 242 Mass. 229

SECTION 32. 

4. Guardians and Wards.

In the case of a guardian or ward the motor vehicle may be registered in the name of either. 

5. Joint Owners.

SECTION 33. 

It is not necessary that the registration be made in the name of all joint owners. It is sufficient to register a

$33435 

 motor vehicle in the name of one who has contributed to the purchase and has an interest as owner. 

Pearson v. Bara, 263 Mass. 502 

Harlow v. Sinman, 241 Mass. 462, at 463 

Shufelt v. McCartin, 235 Mass. 122 (Non-resident part owner)

SECTION 34. 

6. Married Women. 

As matter of law after her marriage, the legal name of a married woman is that of her husband. 

The wife takes the husband's surname. 

Koley v. Williams, 265 Mass. 601, at 602

Bacon v. Boston El. Ry., 256 Mass. 30 

G. L. c. 208, s. 23

The legal name of the wife upon her marriage is her own Christian name plus the husband's surname. 

Cases just cited above

But a motor vehicle may be registered in the name of the wife as "Mrs. John P. Williams" if the registrant usually signs her name that way or is better known under that name and can be easily identified by such a designation and does not intend to conceal her identity. 

Koley v. Williams, 265 Mass. 601, at 602

So, because General Laws, Chapter 90, Section 2 con templates that a motor vehicle shall be registered in the true name of its owner, a married woman who registers a motor vehicle in her maiden name has caused the motor vehicle to be illegally registered and the vehicle is a nuisance upon the highway, which precludes recovery by its owner and all passengers who knew or had reasonable cause to know of the facts of such registration. 

Bacon v. Boston El. Ry., 256 Mass. 30 

Nichols v. Holyoke St. Ry., 250 Mass. 88 

McDonald v. Dundon, 242 Mass. 229

$34 

Pierce v. Hutchinson, 241 Mass. 557 

Fairbanks v. Kemp, 226 Mass. 75, at 78 

However, a female owner who registers a motor vehicle in her maiden name does not require a new registration when she marries. The motor vehicle is legally registered if it is registered in her true name before her marriage and this registration does not expire upon her marriage.

General Laws, Chapter 90 does not require a new registration when the female owner marries. Section 2 provides that upon a transfer of ownership of a motor vehicle the registration shall expire; but there is no provision that the registration of a motor vehicle shall come to an end if the owner marries and changes her name. The motor vehicle remains her property and is legally registered for the remainder of the calendar year. 

Mussman v. Broderick, 271 Mass. 404, at 405

A husband who remains the real owner cannot legally register a motor vehicle in the name of his wife and if he does so such vehicle is a trespasser and an outlaw on the highway. 

Washburn v. Union Freight R. Co., 247 Mass. 414 

Chase v. N. Y. C. & H. R. R.R., 208 Mass. 137 

Feeley v. Melrose, 205 Mass. 329, at 333 and 334 

Dudley v. Northampton St. Ry., 202 Mass. 443, at 447 

Doherty v. Ayer, 197 Mass. 241

The husband cannot maintain an action for injuries to a motor vehicle so registered in the name of his wife. 

Pearson v. Bara, 263 Mass. 502, at 504 

Harlow v. Sinman, 241 Mass. 462, at 463 

Shufelt v. McCartin, 235 Mass. 122

When operating such vehicle upon the public highway, the husband is a trespasser. He cannot recover from the operators of other vehicles for injuries caused by their mere negligence. Such operators owe him no duty other

$37 

 than to abstain from injuring him by wilfulness, wantonness or recklessness. 

Love v. Worcester C. St. Ry., 213 Mass. 137

But the registration in the name of the wife, who with other members of the family has contributed to the purchase and has an interest as owner, is proper. The motor vehicle is not an outlaw. 

Pearson v. Bara, 263 Mass. 502, at 504 

7. Operators.

SECTION 35. 

It is not necessary that the car be registered in the name of the operator unless he also be the sole owner. 

8. Partnerships.

SECTION 36. 

A motor vehicle belonging to a partnership must be registered in the name of the partnership or all the members of the firm.

Kilduff v. Boston El. Ry., 247 Mass. 453 

If the motor vehicle is registered in the name of one of the partners and is being operated in the absence of such partner by a person not under his control but who is a servant or agent of the partnership, the motor vehicle is illegally upon the highway and no action can be maintained for damages caused to it by the negligence of any third person.

Kilduff v. Boston El. Ry., 247 Mass. 453 

Registration in the name of a partnership, which does not in fact exist, but under which the owner of the motor vehicle is, and has been for several years, doing business and by which he is well known, is legal. 

Crompton v. Williams, 216 Mass. 184

A registration in the name of the partnership or the joint names of the partners terminates with the partnership such as by a transfer of the interest in the firm

$37 

 of one partner to a third person. When a motor vehicle is registered in the name of two partners, a subsequent retirement and transfer of the interest of one partner in the partnership, including the motor vehicle, to a new partner, terminates the registration and the motor vehicle when operated upon the public highway without a new registration is a trespasser. 

Hurnanen v. Nicksa, 228 Mass. 346 

Rolli v. Converse, 227 Mass. 162

SECTION 37. 

9. Sellers and Buyers.

An absolute and unconditional sale, even though the price is wholly or partly unpaid, does not authorize the registration in the name of the seller. 

Murray v. Indursky, 266 Mass. 220, at 223 

Conroy v. Mather, 217 Mass. 91 

Doherty v. Ayer, 197 Mass. 241

So, the buyer to whom possession and control of the vehicle has passed can not legally operate the vehicle upon a public highway if the only number plates upon it are those of the dealer from whom he bought it. 

Liddell v. Middlesex Motor Co. & Another, 275 Mass. 

346, at 350 

Fulton v. Stahl, 271 Mass. 23, at 25 

McDonald v. Dundon, 242 Mass. 229

The dealer's act in permitting his own number plates as dealer to be used upon a motor vehicle is a basis for charging him with responsibility for injury to a third person. 

Liddell v. Middlesex Motor Co. & Another, 275 Mass. 

346, at 351 But a conditional seller who retains the title may properly obtain registration in his own name. 

Murray v. Indursky, 266 Mass. 220, at 223

Temple v. Middlesex & Boston St. Ry., 241 Mass. 

124

$39 

And when operated by the conditional vendee the motor vehicle is duly registered and not a nuisance on the highway.

An agreement that the motor vehicle is to remain in the seller's name is not especially different in its legal effect from an agreement that title shall not pass from him. The intention of the parties respecting the passing of title is a question of fact and must be ascertained from the terms of the agreement as expressed in the language and conduct of the parties and is applied to known usages and the subject matter. 

Murray v. Indursky, 266 Mass. 220, at 223 

However, a motor vehicle registered under G. L. c. 90, s. 2, in the name of the owner, when sold under a contract of conditional sale, may continue to be legally registered in the name of the conditional vendor even though the possession and control pass to the conditional vendee.

Liddell v. Middlesex Motor Co. & Another, 275 Mass. 

346, at 350 

Murray v. Indursky, 266 Mass. 220, at 223

Temple v. Middlesex & Boston St. Ry., 241 Mass. 

124 So, where an automobile is not registered under G. L. c. 90, s. 2, but under G. L. c.. 90, s. 5, the dealer's registration does not protect the motor vehicle after the dealer has sold it and parted with possession and control. 

The word "sold" as used in this section refers not only to absolute sales but to conditional sales. 

Liddell v. Middlesex Motor Co. & Another, 275 Mass. 

346, at 350 

Chase v. N. Y. C. & H. R. R.R., 208 Mass. 137, at 156

Also, where the dealer sold an automobile to an employee with title not to pass until the automobile was paid for in full which was not done and after the sale

$37 

 the dealer permitted his number plates as dealer to remain on the automobile for the reason that the automobile was being used by the employee in the dealer's business and the dealer never had possession of it thereafter, the automobile bearing the dealer's number plates at the time of the accident is illegally registered and a trespasser. 

Liddell v. Middlesex Motor Co. & Another, 275 Mass. 

346, at 351 

MacDonald v. Boston El. Ry., 262 Mass. 475, at 476

Under these circumstances, the dealer who parts with the control of the automobile to the vendee and, without right permits the vendee to use the number plates upon it, cannot escape responsibility for assisting in creating a nuisance on the public way when the automobile is driven by some other person, even though there is no evidence to show that he consented to the use of it by the other person. 

Liddell v. Middlesex Motor Co. & Another, 275 Mass. 

346, at 351 

See: , at 398

The dealer should reasonably anticipate that the purchaser of the automobile might at times permit his wife or someone else to operate it and in this way continue the nuisance which by wrongful loan of his number plates he was responsible for creating.

Liddell v. Middlesex Motor Co. & Another, 275 Mass. 

346, at 351 

In Downey v. Bay State St. Ry., 225 Mass. 281 the court, in referring to the statute, states at page 284: "The provisions of St. 1909, c. 534, s. 4, providing for a distinguishing number or mark to be furnished to manufacturers and dealers, instead of registering each vehicle owned or controlled by them, refers to vehicles which remain in their possession and control as manufacturers or dealers, and not to vehicles which have been sold either

$41 

 conditionally or unconditionally, followed by delivery of possession and unrestricted powers of control."

There is nothing contrary to this in Tripp v. National 

Shawmut Bank, 263 Mass. 505 (See: G. L. c. 106, s. 3 (3):

10. Trade Names. 

SECTION 38. 

An owner of a motor vehicle may register it in the trade name under which he is, and for many years has been, carrying on his business and by which he is well known in the community, in the absence of evidence that such name was adopted or is being used to conceal the owner's real identity. 

Crompton v. Williams, 216 Mass. 184 (“C”—registered under name of "C & Sons")

SECTION 39. 

11. Unincorporated Associations.

A motor vehicle owned in common by a large number of members of an unincorporated association can not be registered in the name of that association. 

Hanley v. American Ry. Express Co., 244 Mass. 248

 D. MANUFACTURERS, DEALERS AND RE- PAIRMEN. 

SECTION 40. 

General Laws, Chapter 90, Section 5 (Acts 1922, 303, s. 2; 1923, 464, s. 2; 1928, 316, s. 4; 1929, 238, s. 1) provides that: "Every manufacturer of or dealer in motor vehicles or trailers or motor vehicle bodies or tops and every person engaged in the business of repairing motor vehicles or trailers, instead of registering each such vehicle owned or controlled by him, may make application for a general distinguishing number or mark, and the registrar, if satisfied of the facts stated in the application, may issue to the applicant a certificate of registration containing the name and business address of the applicant and the general distinguishing number or mark assigned to him, and made in such form and containing such further information as the registrar may determine; and all motor vehicles or trailers owned or controlled by such manufacturer of or dealer in motor vehicles or trailers or motor vehicle bodies or tops, or by such person engaged in the business of repairing motor vehicles or trailers, shall be regarded as registered under such general distinguishing number or mark until sold or let for hire or loaned for a period of five successive days; provided that number plates furnished as hereinafter provided, are properly displayed thereon. The registrar shall, upon payment of the fee provided in section thirty-three, furnish at his office to every manufacturer of or dealer in motor vehicles or trailers or motor vehicle bodies or tops, and to every person engaged in the business of repairing motor vehicles or trailers, whose vehicles are registered in accordance with this section, such number of pairs of number plates as he may request in writing of suitable design having displayed upon them the register number which is assigned

$43 

 to the vehicles of such manufacturer, dealer, or person, with a different letter or letters or mark on each pair of number plates. Number plates furnished hereunder shall, except as provided by section nine, be valid only for the year for which they are issued. Every registration under this section shall expire at midnight on December thirty-first of each year. "The word 'dealer', for the purposes of the registration of motor vehicles or trailers under any provision of this chapter, may include, in the discretion of the registrar, a person whose principal business is financing the purchase of or insuring motor vehicles, but only in respect to such vehicles as such person may take in possession by foreclosure or subrogation of title and all the provisions of this chapter relating to certificates of registration of dealers shall apply to certificates issued to such a person under this provision."

This statute makes it plain that only the owner, or, if a dealer, manufacturer or repairman, the person either owning or in control of a motor vehicle, is entitled to registration. 

Pierce v. Hutchinson, 241 Mass. 557, at 562 

Harlow v. Sinman, 241 Mass. 462 

Shufelt v. McCartin, 235 Mass. 122 

Downey v. Bay State St. Ry., 225 Mass. 281 

 "The statutory definition of the word 'dealer' includes every person who is engaged principally in the business of buying, selling or exchanging motor vehicles, on commission or otherwise, or whose principal business is the renting of motor vehicles." 

Pierce v. Hutchinson, 241 Mass. 557, at 563

It does not refer only to a business that has the required characteristics. 

Pierce v. Hutchinson, 241 Mass. 557, at 562

$40 

But the registration must be issued in the name of the real buyer, the principal, and not his agent or employee. 

So, the registration is illegal when dealer's, manufacturer's or repairman's number plates are issued in the name of a person who is in fact merely the agent or employee of an undisclosed principal. 

By virtue of G. L. c. 90, s. 5, as amended, the number plates of a dealer may be used on motor vehicles owned or controlled by him and when so used the vehicles are regarded as registered until sold or let for hire or loaned for a period of more than five successive days. 

Liddell v. Middlesex Motor Co. & Another, 275 Mass 

346, at 350 

Ducharme v. Coe Motors Inc., 275 Mass. 69, at 73 

De Simone v. Barr, 254 Mass. 79

A dealer's number plates can be used properly upon a motor vehicle to give it a legitimate standing upon a public highway only if the dealer at the time of the accident was in the business of repairing motor vehicles or was a manufacturer or dealer in them within the provision of G. L. c. 90, s. 50, amended by Acts 1923, c. 464, s. 2, and was in control of the car. 

O'Halleron v. Miller, 274 Mass. 508, at 509 (Salesman's use of dealer's plates in endeavoring to sell motor vehicle for third person was improper) 

McDonald v. Dundon, 242 Mass. 229 

G. L. c. 90, ss. 5, 6 and 9, as then amended 

Where the defendant corporation was a dealer in automobiles entitled to hold a distinguishing motor number or mark issued to it as such dealer with the right to permit dealer's plates to be attached to it as dealer's control, such motor vehicle when operated with these number plates attached is by virtue of the statute "regarded as registered

$45 

 under such general distinguishing number or mark until sold or let for hire or loaned for a period of more than five successive days." 

G. L. c. 90, s. 5, as amended by Acts 1923, c. 464, s. 2 (See Acts 1929 c. 238, s. 1) 

Ducharme v. Coe Motors Inc., 275 Mass. 69, at 72 and 73 So, when an automobile has been used in the dealer's business, kept in its garage, and was under its control as a dealer within the meaning of this statute, if so controlled it could be found to be legally registered when operated on a public highway bearing the number plates of the dealer, even if it was owned by its president and sales manager, and on the day in question was being operated by him for purposes of his own. 

Ducharme v. Coe Motors Inc., 275 Mass. 69, at 73 

Koonovsky v. Quellette, 226 Mass. 474, at 477 

Holland v. Boston, 213 Mass. 560, at 562

Because of the terms of the statute a motor vehicle controlled by a dealer and bearing the dealer's number plates does not become an unregistered automobile on the highway when loaned for a single day to be operated for the personal pleasure or convenience of the borrower, whether he be the owner or someone else. 

Ducharme v. Coe Motors Inc., 275 Mass. 69, at 73 

De Simone v. Barr, 254 Mass, 79, at 81 and 82 

Pierce v. Hutchinson, 241 Mass. 557

If the dealer permits the owner of the motor vehicle to use its (the dealer's) number plates on a motor vehicle and the owner takes the vehicle for his own purpose, it does not follow that the dealer thereby assists in creating a nuisance on the highway, with a consequent liability for injuries arising therefrom, without proving negligence. 

Ducharme v. Coe Motors Inc., 275 Mass. 69, at 73 (But see: O'Halleron v. Miller, 274 Mass. 508)

$41 

But where the dealer has made an actual sale to one of his employees the employee cannot thereafter operate the motor vehicle upon the dealer's number plate. 

Liddell v. Middlesex Motor Co., 275 Mass. 346 SECTION 41.

F. PROCURING REGISTRATION. 

SECTION 43. 

General Laws, Chapter 90, Section 2 (Acts 1922, 303; 

1923, 362; s. 64; 1924, 224, 427; 1928, 316, s. 3; 1930, 272, 332, s. 3) provides, in part, that: "Application for the registration of motor vehicles and trailers may be made by the owner thereof. The application shall contain, in addition to such other particulars as may be required by the registrar, a statement of the

$43 

 name, place of residence and address of the applicant, with a brief description of the motor vehicle or trailer, including the name of the maker, the number, if any, affixed by the maker, and, in case of a motor vehicle, the engine number and the character of the motor power. 

The registration fee as required in section thirty-three shall accompany such application.”

What constitutes legal registration. 

Hurnanen v. Nicksa, 228 Mass. 346 

Downey v. Bay State St. Ry., 225 Mass. 281

Formerly registration of a motor vehicle which contained an incorrect maker's number was invalid and made the vehicle a trespasser and nuisance upon the highway. 

Leonard v. Conquest, 274 Mass. 347, at 351 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155 

Dudley v. Northampton St. Ry., 202 Mass. 443

But General Laws, Chapter 90, Section 9 (as amended by Acts of 1927, c. 187) provides that: "A motor vehicle or trailer shall be deemed to be registered in accordance with this chapter notwithstanding any mistake in so much of the description thereof contained in the application for registration or in the certificate required to be filed under section thirty-four B [and 

G. L. c. 175, s. 113 A (5)] as relates to the engine, serial or maker's number thereof." 

So, now, where a registrant gives an incorrect maker's number of the motor vehicle in good faith in his application and registration is issued thereon with the mistaken number, the motor vehicle is not a trespasser and nuisance upon the highway but is operating under lawful registration. 

Leonard v. Conquest, 274 Mass. 347, at 351 

Rosenthal v. Liss, 269 Mass. 373 

Wallace v. New Bedford & Onset St. Ry., 259 Mass. 20

$49 

 De Pasquale v. Bradlee & McIntosh, 258 Mass. 483 

Giving incorrect address, even in good faith, makes registration improper.

Di Cecca v. Bucci, 1932 A. S. 17, at 18 

G. REGISTRATION CERTIFICATES. 

SECTION 44. 

General Laws, Chapter 90, Section 2 provides, in part, that: "The registrar or his duly authorized agents . . . shall thereupon issue to the applicant a certificate of registration. The certificate shall contain the name, place of residence and address of the applicant and the register number or mark and shall be in such form and contain such further information as the registrar may determine." 

H. NUMBER PLATES. 

SECTION 45. 

General Laws, Chapter 90, Section 2 provides, in part, that: "The registrar shall furnish at his office, without charge, to every person whose vehicle is registered under this chapter, two number plates of suitable design, each number plate to have displayed upon it the register number assigned to that vehicle; provided, that number plates assigned to ambulances, fire engines and apparatus, police patrol wagons and other vehicles used by the police department of any city or town or park board solely for the official business of such department or board, road rollers, street sprinklers, power excavators, power graders and concrete mixers may be of a distinctive type or types. The number plates so furnished shall, except as provided by section nine, be valid only for the year for which they are issued."

General Laws, Chapter 90, Section 6 (Acts 1922, 342, s. 1) provides that:

$45 

"Every motor vehicle or trailer operated in or on any way in this Commonwealth shall have its register number displayed conspicuously thereon on the two number plates furnished by the registrar, in accordance with sections two, three, four and five, one number plate to be attached at the front and the other at the rear of said vehicle, so that the said number plates and the register number thereon shall be always plainly visible. The said number plates shall be kept clean and the numbers legible, and during the period when the vehicle is required to display lights the rear register number shall be illuminated so as to be plainly visible at a distance of sixty feet. No number plates other than such as are procured from the registrar or such as may be authorized by him for temporary use, except as provided in section three, shall be displayed on any motor vehicle or trailer so operated; provided, that a motor vehicle or trailer which is commonly operated in this Commonwealth and in an adjoining state may display the register number plates of both states whenever the motor vehicle or trailer is required by law or lawful regulation to be registered in this Commonwealth and also in the adjoining state, if the number plates are displayed as required by law. If any number plate supplied by the registrar is lost or mutilated or if the register number thereon becomes illegible, the owner or person in control of the vehicle for which said number plate was furnished shall make application for a new number plate, and thereupon the registrar shall issue to such applicant a permit allowing him to place a temporary number plate bearing his register number upon said vehicle until a number plate of the regular design is made and delivered to said applicant; provided, that all such temporary number plates and the register numbers thereon shall conform to the regular number plates and be displayed as nearly as may be as herein provided for said regular number plates." 

Shapiro v. Lyon, 254 Mass. 110, at 117 (Need permit from registrar even for a day)

 1. Display of. 

SECTION 46. 

A motor vehicle is a nuisance and trespasser upon the highway which does not have displayed conspicuously thereon the two number plates issued to it as its register number in accordance with G. L. c. 90, s. 2.

Liddell v. Middlesex Motor Co. & Another, 275 Mass. 

346, at 350 

Fulton v. Stahl, 271 Mass. 23, at 25 

McDonald v. Dundon, 242 Mass. 229 

Pierce v. Hutchinson, 241 Mass. 557, at 564 

Evans v. Rice, 238 Mass. 318 

Koonovsky v. Quellette, 226 Mass. 474 

Chase v. N. Y. C. & H. R. R.R., 208 Mass. 137 

Dudley v. Northampton St. Ry., 202 Mass. 443

But the number plates to be displayed must be the ones issued for the particular motor vehicle. 

So, even though the motor vehicle is legally registered in the name of the defendant if at the time of its operation on the highway it does not have its regular number plates displayed conspicuously thereon but has number plates attached which were issued to a person other than the owner, the use of such number plates is not a compliance with the statute. 

Pierce v. Hutchinson, 241 Mass. 557, at 564

So, an owner of a motor vehicle who lends it to a third person and allows that third person to operate the motor vehicle without registration, or without lawful or proper number plates, remains liable for any injury caused by that motor vehicle regardless of whether or not any negligence of the driver contributes to the injury for such a motor vehicle is an outlaw upon the highway. 

Pierce v. Hutchinson, 241 Mass. 557, at 564

Liddell v. Middlesex Motor Co. & Another, 275 Mass. 

346, at 350 

Fulton v. Stahl, 271 Mass. 23, at 26

Koonovsky v. Quellette, 226 Mass. 474

Dudley v. Northampton St. Ry., 202 Mass. 443

Also, the buyer to whom possession and control of the vehicle have passed cannot legally operate the machine upon a public way if the only number plates upon it are those of the dealer from whom he bought it. 

Liddell v. Middlesex Motor Co. & Another, 275 Mass. 

346, at 350 

Fulton v. Stahl, 271 Mass. 23, at 25 

McDonald v. Dundon, 242 Mass. 229

SECTION 46A. 

When a person, with full knowledge that a motor vehicle is not registered, furnishes number plates to be attached to it, in order to give it an appearance of right to be on the highway, he contributes directly and immediately to the nuisance of the trespassing of the machine and is liable for all damage done by it. 

Fulton v. Stahl, 271 Mass. 23, at 25 

McDonald v. Dundon, 242 Mass. 229

J. CONSTRUCTION AND EFFECT OF CERTIFI- CATE OF REGISTRATION. 

SECTION 49. 

While a certificate duly issued creates a presumption that the registrant is lawfully entitled to it, yet it is not conclusive evidence as against a third person such as a pedestrian who is injured by the vehicle. 

Pierce v. Hutchinson, 241 Mass. 557, at 562 and 563 

Koonovsky v. Quellette, 226 Mass. 474 

A motor vehicle which is not legally registered is a nuisance upon the highway, and its driver is a trespasser. 

Pierce v. Hutchinson, 241 Mass. 557, at 563 

Gondek v. Cudahy Packing Co., 223 Mass. 105 

Fairbanks v. Kemp, 226 Mass. 75 

Gould v. Elder, 219 Mass. 396 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155 

Chase v. N. Y. C. & H. R. R.R., 208 Mass. 137 

Dudley v. Northampton St. Ry., 202 Mass. 443

SECTION 50. 

Substitution of One Motor for Another.

Although General Laws, Chapter 90, Section 9 (as amended by Acts of 1928, c., 187, s. 1) countenances mistakes made in good faith in the application for registration

$61 

 yet the substitution of one motor for another is not permitted and the operation of a vehicle after the substitution of a new motor renders it unregistered and an outlaw and trespasser upon the highway. 

Brown v. Robinson, 275 Mass. 55, at 57 and 58 

As was said in the last cited case: "Although they may exist, it is difficult to conceive of cases of the substitution of one motor for another in the ordinary automobile of which the owner, or person having charge of it for him, would not be well aware. If the scope of the legislative intent [of Acts 1928, c. 187, S. I, amending G. L. c. 90, s. 9] be confined so as to exclude from the benefit of the statute those who, being well aware in the change of number arising from replacement of an old engine with a new one, yet innocently overlook making the corresponding change in application for registration, it would fail to accomplish the apparent aim of the statute. "An unconscious forgetfulness of facts which have come to the owner's knowledge and attention resulting in an innocent failure to cause correct registration to be made, is a mistake within the meaning of said c. 187. "This excludes wilful omission, intentional failure or conscious inattention to procure correct registration. It excludes every element of design. It excludes heedless or reckless conduct in view of known facts. It excludes wanton or inexcusable delay in action. It includes only complete honesty of purpose accompanied by blameless oversight or ignorance of facts. "The facts in the group of cases first herein recited would bring them within the scope of said c. 187 as thus interpreted. According to this interpretation the statute becomes a workable piece of legislation affording a shield to the innocent and careful, and to no others. It does not break down the main object of other provisions of the

$51 

 statutes requiring the registration of all motor vehicles and rendering the unregistered vehicle an outlaw on the highway." 

Prior to the effective date of said Acts of 1928, c. 187, an automobile driven which had a motor number different from that stated in the certificate of registration was not properly registered and would have been an outlaw upon the highway. 

Brown v. Robinson, 275 Mass. 55, at 57 

Rosenthal v. Liss, 269 Mass. 373 and cases cited 

Di Franco v. West Boston Gas Co., 262 Mass. 387, at 389 

Wallace v. New Bedford & Onset St. Ry., 259 Mass. 20 

Staley v. Wilbur, 258 Mass. 481

SECTION 51. 

3. Changing Type of Vehicle. 

The owner is not permitted to change the type of vehicle. Such conduct will render the vehicle in effect unregistered. So, the changing of a Ford touring car, which is duly registered, by taking the body off the chassis and putting on a delivery body or a box-like body having six posts and a back board to keep a load from falling off, the vehicle to be used for delivery of goods in the business which the owner carries on, renders the vehicle illegally registered and an outlaw upon the high- way. 

Nichols v. Holyoke St. Ry., 250 Mass. 88 

But the registration of a two and one-half (2-2) ton truck for six (6) tons, which, when loaded, makes the truck overweight, does not invalidate the registration nor create the truck a vehicle different from the truck originally registered. 

Cook v. Cole, 273 Mass. 557

$63 

 K. TRANSFER OF OWNERSHIP. 

SECTION 52. 

General Laws, Chapter 90, Section 2, provides, in part, that: "Upon the transfer of ownership of any motor vehicle or trailer its registration shall expire, and the person in whose name such motor vehicle or trailer is registered shall forthwith return the certificate of registration to the registrar with a written notice containing the date of the transfer of ownership and the name, place of residence and address of the new owner. Even though the seller fails to return the certificate to the Registrar of Motor Vehicles, it cannot be found that such failure is a cause of the wrongful action of the purchaser who operates the automobile without registration or that the act of the seller contributed to the accident. 

The lack of participation on the part of the seller who ceases to be the owner or custodian of the motor vehicle and who is ignorant of status or use thereafter, are the underlying reasons for the lack of liability on his part. 

Fulton v. Stahl, 271 Mass. 23, at 26 

Sales of second hand motor vehicles are regulated by 

G. L. c. 140, ss. 57-69.

Upon a sale by one corporation to another of a business including motor vehicles, the latter must be newly registered. 

Chase v. N. Y. C. & H. R. R.R. Co., 208 Mass. 137

SECTION 53. 

2. From One Vehicle to Another. 

General Laws, Chapter 90, Section 2, provides, in part, that: "A person who transfers the ownership of a registered motor vehicle or trailer owned by him to another or loses

$54 

 possession thereof upon the filing of a new application and payment of the proper substitution fee provided in [G. L. c. 90] section thirty-three, may have registered in his name for the remainder of the calendar year another motor vehicle or trailer.” a. 

SECTION 54. 

Manufacturers, Dealers and Repairmen. 

A dealer in motor vehicles can only use number plates issued to him as a dealer by attaching them to vehicles which he owns or controls. He cannot lawfully loan any of them and if he does and they are attached to another vehicle, the plates offer no protection to the operator of that vehicle, which is a nuisance on the highway and the operator is a trespasser. 

McDonald v. Dundon, 242 Mass. 229, at 231 

The dealer, as lender, is liable for all direct injury caused by the vehicle to which the number plates are attached, even though the operator is not his agent and in fact is not negligent. 

McDonald v. Dundon, 242 Mass. 229, at 231 

SECTION 55. 

3. Rebates of Fees. 

General Laws, Chapter 90, Section 2, provides, in part, that: "A person who, before the first day of August in any year, transfers the ownership or loses possession of any vehicle registered in his name and who does not apply for registration of another vehicle but who, on or before the first day of September in the same year, files in the office of the registrar a written application for a rebate shall be entitled to a rebate of one-half the fee paid for the registration of the vehicle transferred or lost possession of as aforesaid. . . ."

SECTION 59. 

4. Termination by Transfer of Ownership. 

Registration expires on the transfer of ownership of the motor vehicle and if thereafter the motor vehicle bears the number plates of the former owner, unless legally re-registered, it is not lawfully on the highway. 

Fulton v. Stahl, 271 Mass. 23 

Chase v. N. Y. C. & H. R. R.R. Co., 208 Mass. 137 

Feeley v. Melrose, 205 Mass. 329 (See: Section 52, p. 63.)

860 

When the registrant transfers his entire interest in the motor vehicle to another, registration thereafter in the registrant's name is not legal since he has neither a general nor a special property therein, and the motor vehicle can be registered only in the name of the transferee as its new owner. 

Hyland v. Hyland, 1932 A. S. 107, at 112 and 113 

G. L. c. 90, s. 2

See, as to registration of a motor vehicle sold conditionally:

Temple v. Middlesex and Boston St. Ry., 241 Mass. 

124, at 126 

Downey v. Bay State St. Ry., 225 Mass. 281

SECTION 60. 

5. Termination by Death of Registrant. 

Registration in the name of a person who is dead does not protect one who subsequently owns or controls the vehicle. 

Pierce v. Hutchinson, 241 Mass. 557, at 562

So, a widow using an automobile with number plates on it and a certificate of registration issued in the name of, and after the death of, her husband, is a trespasser on the highway. 

Fairbanks v. Kemp, 226 Mass. 75 

But see: G. L. c. 90, s. 2

M. EFFECT OF REGISTRATION. 

SECTION 65. 

Registration record or certificate in name of defendant is sufficient to warrant a finding of ownership. 

G. L. c. 231, s. 85A 

However, it does not show conclusively, but only prima facie, that person operating was agent or servant of defendant. 

McNeil v. Powers, 266 Mass. 446

Trombley v. Stevens-Duryea Co., 206 Mass. 516 

Registration in the name of the defendant is some evidence of ownership by him and such evidence may be rebutted. 

Hyland v. Hyland, 1932 A. S. 107, at 113 

Trombly v. Stevens-Duryea Co., 206 Mass. 516, at 518 It may be found as a fact that such evidence has been rebutted,

866 

Hyland v. Hyland, 1932 A. S. 107, at 113 so the participation of a person in obtaining registration and insurance of the motor vehicle in the defendant's name and his sending a letter to the town tax collector stating that the motor vehicle belonged to the defendant were not conclusive admissions that the defendant retained any interest therein especially where there is evidence warranting an inference to the contrary. 

Hyland v. Hyland, 1932 A. S. 107, at 113 

Leary v. Keith, 256 Mass. 157, at 158 and 159 

Conant v. Evans, 202 Mass. 34, at 38 

Bone v. Holmes, 195 Mass. 495, at 507

N. EFFECT OF FAILURE TO COMPLY WITH LAWS AS TO REGISTRATION. 

SECTION 66. 

Every motor vehicle must be registered in compliance with the statutes of this Commonwealth. 

G. L. chs. 89 and 90

An unregistered automobile cannot lawfully be operated upon the public highways.

It is an outlaw with no other protection than exemption from wilful, wanton or reckless injury or misconduct. 

Farr v. Whitney, 260 Mass. 193, at 195 

Staley v. Wilbur, 258 Mass. 481

The presence of an unregistered motor vehicle on the highways has been outlawed and declared a trespasser and a nuisance. 

Rosenthal v. Liss, 269 Mass. 373, at 377 

Opinion of the Justices, 251 Mass. 569, at 598 

Brown v. Alter, 251 Mass. 223, at 224 

Washburn v. Union Freight Ry., 247 Mass. 414 

McDonald v. Dundon, 242 Mass. 229, at 232 

Pierce v. Hutchinson, 241 Mass. 557

$71 

Gondek v. Cudahy Packing Co., 233 Mass. 105, at 110

Dean v. Boston El. Ry., 217 Mass. 495 Holland v. Boston, 213 Mass. 560 

Feeley v. Melrose, 205 Mass. 329 

Dudley v. Northampton St. Ry., 202 Mass. 443, at 447 

38 A. L. R. 1936 and note

Also its occupants who participate in its operation and who know of its improper registration are declared to be trespassers. 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, at 171 and 172 

Chase v. N. Y. C. & H. R. R.R., 208 Mass. 137, at 158 

Feeley v. Melrose, 205 Mass. 329

As was said in Gondek v. Cudahy Packing Co., 233

The illegality consists in the operation of the improperly registered vehicle. So, the walking with and/or pushing the improperly registered vehicle along the highway does not render the vehicle a trespasser nor create a nuisance.

So, the fact that a bus owner has not a license from the proper authorities to carry passengers does not make his vehicle a trespasser upon the public highway.

The matter of an improper, illegal, or failure of, registration, whether to establish liability or as a defense, places upon the party asserting it the burden of satisfactorily establishing the facts to create that conclusion.

Shepard v. Jacobs, 204 Mass. 110

A person having control of a motor vehicle, without lawful number plates, who loans it to another is liable for injuries caused by that motor vehicle although at the time of the accident the lender was not the owner and the motor vehicle was being operated by the chauffeur of the borrower.

"It would be responsible for injuries caused by the negligent operation of the automobile even though not at the time being used in its business. But, in order to create responsibility upon the owner, it is necessary that he knows or ought to know of the unlawful use of the motor vehicle upon the public highways, so that his acquiescence in such use is either express or implied. 

Gondek v. Cudahy Packing Co., 233 Mass. 105, at 112 (Employee took vehicle without employer's knowledge or consent)

The owner must expressly or impliedly consent to the vehicle being operated upon the public highway. If he does not openly or tacitly approve the operation on the public highway, he is not guilty of creating a nuisance. 

Therefore when an illegally registered motor vehicle is taken by the agent of the owner without authority the owner is not liable for the agent's negligence.

SECTION 68. 

(I) Liability for Death. 

It was said in Di Franco v. West Boston Gas Co., 262 

Mass. 387, at 389 and 390: "As its presence on the highway was in itself unlawful, the defendant was a wrong doer and liable for all direct injury resulting from its use, even though the injury to the intestate could not have been contemplated as the result of the act done. [the above] cited G. L. c. 229, s. 5,

Statute 1922, c. 349 imposes a liability upon one who by his negligence causes the death of another. • • "Within the meaning of this statute the operation of an automobile illegally registered upon the highway was in itself a negligent act for which the plaintiff could recover. "It has been held that the use of such an illegal vehicle is a wrong which gives the injured person a remedy independent of negligence. "But the death of a person upon the highway by an outlaw automobile is caused by negligence under the statute; and the use of such a vehicle upon the public ways makes the owner liable for his conduct and guilty of negligence within the terms of the statute. "The violation of the statute was evidence itself of negligence." b. Operator.

SECTION 69. 

Under General Laws, Chapter 90, Section 9, the oper ator of a motor vehicle which is improperly or not registered is a trespasser upon the public highway. That is, the law requires the operator to know all the facts concerning the registration of the motor vehicle which he operates and binds him to the same extent as if he is the owner of the motor vehicle.

$69 

The act of operating an unregistered or unlawfully registered motor vehicle upon a public highway results in the creation and maintenance of a nuisance thereon. 

McDonald v. Dundon, 242 Mass. 229

So, an operator of an improperly registered motor vehicle cannot recover for personal injuries caused solely by the defendant's negligence in the absence of wilful, wanton or reckless conduct.

(See all other cases cited in this section.)

Downey v. Bay State St. Ry., 225 Mass. 281

It was also said by Knowlton, C. J. in Chase v. N. Y.

The question frequently arises concerning when the act of operation commences and when it terminates.
