 CHAPTER IV. 

LICENSING OF OPERATORS. 

A. REGULATION OF OPERATORS. 

SECTION 73. 

General Laws, Chapter 90, Section 8 (Acts 1921, 403, s. 1; 1923, 464, s. 3; 1925, 283) provides that: "Application for license to operate motor vehicles may be made by any person; but before such a license is granted the applicant shall pass such examination as to his qualifications as the registrar shall require, and no license shall be issued until the registrar or his authorized agent is satisfied that the applicant is a proper person to receive it, and no such license shall be issued to any person under sixteen years of age. To each licensee shall be assigned some distinguishing number or mark, and the licenses shall be in such form as the registrar shall determine. They may contain special restrictions and limitations concerning the type of motor, horse power, design and other features of the motor vehicles which the licensee may operate. They shall contain the distinguishing number or mark assigned to the licensee, his name, place of residence and address, a brief description of him for purposes of identification, and such other information as the registrar shall deem necessary. A person to whom a license to operate motor vehicles has been issued, unless such license contains a special limitation or restriction, may operate any registered motor vehicle. Special licenses shall be issued to operators of motor-propelled fire apparatus who are members of a municipal fire department. 

Every person licensed to operate motor vehicles as aforesaid shall endorse his usual signature on the margin of the license, in the space provided for the purpose, immediately

$85 

Licensing of Operators upon the receipt of said license, and such license shall not be valid until so endorsed. All licenses issued to operators shall be valid for one year only from the date of issue.

Every application for an original license filed under this section shall be sworn to by the applicant before a justice of the peace or notary public." [Oath may be dispensed with if statement is made under penalty of perjury (Acts 1926, c. 

187, s. 2).]

General Laws, Chapter 90, Section 12 (as amended by 

Acts 1923, c. 464, s. 5) provides, in part, that: “No person shall allow a motor vehicle owned by him or under his control to be operated by any person who has no legal right so to do, or in violation of this chapter.” 

These statutes were passed to make the roads more safe and convenient for travellers by preventing unlicensed persons from operating motor vehicles thereon. 

Gordon v. Bedard, 265 Mass. 409, at 412

The purpose of licensing operators of motor vehicles is to make it reasonably certain that the licensee is qualified for the task and a proper person to be licensed (G. L. c. 

90, ss. 8 and 10). Negligent operation of a motor vehicle endangering the safety of other travellers is likely to follow if an unlicensed person is given complete control of its operation. 

Gordon v. Bedard, 265 Mass. 409, at 412

Licensed Operator. 

A person over sixteen years of age riding with or accompanied by a licensed operator, excepting if such person has been licensed and the license is not in force because of revocation or suspension.

Concerning General Laws, Chapter 90, Section 10, the court said, in Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, at 165 and 166: "Evidently it was intended to provide an opportunity for persons to use an automobile by running it under the supervision of a licensed person, and thus acquire skill by practice, without which one never could become skilful. It does not necessarily mean that the unlicensed operator shall be under the legal control of the licensed chauffeur, for the operator might be the owner of the automobile, and the chauffeur, a person hired by him to give instructions under his direction. But the language of the statute undoubtedly contemplated by the words, 'riding with or accompanied by, proximity sufficient to enable the licensed operator to maintain such supervision as might be necessary for safety, and to render assistance, if need be, with reasonable promptness. "In a case like the present, where the unlicensed operator was a person of skill and great experience, whose license had expired only the day before and who was expecting another license within a day or two, the supervision and reasonable proximity required by law would not be as close as in ordinary cases, but we are of opinion that the law contemplates at least knowledge on the part

$75 

of both persons, of the existence of a relation like that of operator without a license, and licensed chauffeur or operator accompanying him, in a position to advise or assist with reasonable promptness, if necessary." 

So, the owner of a properly registered automobile has the right to run it without an operator's license if he has a licensed operator with him.

SECTION 75. 

3. 

Acts Determined to Be Operation. 

The statutory provisions [G. L. c. 90] apply only to actual operation of the motor vehicle. 

However, many acts have been deemed to be operation, such as: 

Delivering Merchandise While Vehicle is 

Stopped.

Soliciting trade or calling for and delivering merchandise while the motor vehicle is stopped on the highway. 

Cook v. Crowell, 273 Mass. 356, at 358

$89 

Licensing of Operators b. Moving Gear Shift.

Moving the gear shift from reverse into neutral in order to lock the transmission causing the vehicle to move about four feet, while the engine was not running. 

Comm. v. Clarke, 254 Mass. 566, at 568 

c. Leaving Vehicle in Public Highway. 

Leaving the motor vehicle in the public highway during the night with all lights extinguished and the engine at rest. 

Comm. v. Henry, 229 Mass. 19

It was said in the last cited case at pp. 22 and 23: "The word 'operator' is not limited to a state of motion produced by the mechanism of the car, but includes at least ordinary stops upon the highway, and said stops are to be regarded as fairly incidental to its operation . . . "The statute must be read with reference to its manifest intent and spirit and cannot be limited to the literal meaning of a single word. It must be construed as a whole and interpreted according to the sense in which the words are employed, regard being had to the plain intention of the Legislature. So considered we cannot doubt that the statute is broad enough to include automobiles at rest, as well as in motion upon the highways." 

In Comm. v. Clarke, 254 Mass. 566, the court said, at 568: "To operate a motor vehicle upon a way in violation of the statute, it is not necessary that the engine should be running. The engine of a motor vehicle may cease to run while it is going down a hill, but the vehicle may remain within the control of the driver and he may operate it, under these conditions. "The statute was passed for the protection of travellers upon the highways and such a vehicle may be operated or standing still."

§76 

For other provisions as to operation, see: 

G. L. c. 90, ss. 9, 10, 11, 12 and 24

All these statutes were enacted to secure fitness to operate and skill in the management of motor vehicles. 

These statutes are penal in the form of positive prohibitions. 

Kenyon v. Hathaway, 274 Mass. 47, at 52 

Comm. v. Clarke, 254 Mass. 566, at 568

Comm. v. Lyseth, 250 Mass. 555 

Comm. v. Henry, 229 Mass. 19 

Dudley v. Northampton St. Ry., 202 Mass. 443 

d. Manipulating Machinery To Put in Motion. 

A person operates a motor vehicle, within the meaning of G. L. c. 90, s. 24, when, in the vehicle, he intentionally does any act or makes use of any mechanical or electrical agency which alone or in sequence will set in motion the motive power of that machine. 

Comm. v. Uski, 263 Mass. 22 e. Examining Vehicle.

The circumstance that a person is upon the road examining his own automobile at the time of his injury does not prevent him from being found to be operating his automobile. 

Jenkins v. North Shore Dye House, Inc., 1931 A. S. 2299, at 2303 

Reynolds v. Murphy, 241 Mass. 225 

Comm. v. Henry, 229 Mass. 19, at 22

SECTION 76. 

4. Qualifications for Licenses. 

a. Age.

The applicant must be over sixteen years of age. 

G. L. c. 90, s. 8 

46 A. L. R. 1067

$91 

Licensing of Operators b. Examination to Determine Ability to

Operate. 

General Laws, Chapter 90, Section 8, provides, in part, that: "before such a license is granted the applicant shall pass such examination as to his qualifications as the registrar shall require, and no license shall be issued until the registrar or his authorized agent is satisfied that the applicant is a proper person to receive it." 

c. Physical Defect. 

The fact that one has a physical defect will not, in itself, prevent him from obtaining a license to operate motor vehicles unless the physical defect renders him incompetent to control the vehicle and keep the necessary look out for its safe operation. 

64 A. L. R. 136

Nor will his failure to disclose a physical incapacity, infirmity or defect render void a license issued to him nor is he a trespasser in operating a motor vehicle upon the highway. 

O'Hare v. Gloag, 221 Mass. 24, at 27 

It was said in the last cited case that: "While the failure of an applicant to make such a disclosure might be a sufficient ground for revoking his license, still, having been regularly issued it is valid unless and until revoked by proper authority."

SECTION 77. 

5. Carrying Licenses.

General Laws, Chapter 90, Section II, (Acts 1929, 101) 

provides that: "Every person operating a motor vehicle shall have the certificate of registration for the vehicle and of the trailers, if any, and his license to operate, upon his person or in the vehicle, in some easily accessible place, except that

$78 

 the certificates of registration of dealers need not so be carried. If for any reason the registrar or his agents are unable to issue promptly to an applicant the certificate of registration or the license applied for, they may issue a receipt for the fee paid, and said receipt shall be carried in lieu of the certificate or license as the case may be, and for the period of thirty days from the date of its issue said receipt shall have the same force and effect given to the certificate or license by this chapter. If, in compliance with a written demand of the registrar or any of his authorized agents, a certificate of registration or license to operate is returned for inspection or for any other purpose, except for suspension or revocation, such written demand shall be carried in lieu of the certificate or license, as the case may be, and for the period of thirty days from its date said demand shall have the same force and effect given to the certificate or license by this chapter." 

6. Construction of License. 

SECTION 78. 

a. Special Restrictions and Limitations. 

A license to operate motor vehicles may contain "special restrictions and limitations concerning the type of motor, horse power, design, and other features of the motor vehicle which the licensee may operate. A person to whom a license to operate motor vehicles has been issued, unless such license contains a special limitation or restriction, may operate any registered motor vehicle." 

Comm. v. Magarosian, 261 Mass. 228, at 229

G. L. c. 90, s. 8 (as amended by Acts 1923, c. 464, s. 3; Acts 1925, 283)

So one who has a license restricted to the operation of a motor vehicle described as a "truck" operates a touring car on a public way, he may be found guilty of operating

$93 

Licensing of Operators an automobile on a public way without a license from the registrar of motor vehicles. 

Comm. v. Magarosian, 261 Mass. 228, at 229

The authority of the registrar to restrict the licensee as to the kind of motor vehicle he may operate is clear, and the defendant has no right to operate any motor vehicle upon a public way unless it is of a kind authorized by his license. 

Comm. v. Magarosian, 261 Mass. 228

SECTION 79. 

7. Suspension or Revocation of License.

General Laws, Chapter 90, Section 22 (Acts 1923, 464, s. 6) provides that: "The registrar may suspend or revoke any certificate of registration or any license issued under this chapter, after due hearing, for any cause which he may deem sufficient, and he may suspend the license of any operator or the certificate of registration of any motorcycle in his discretion and without a hearing, and may order the license or registration certificate to be delivered to him, whenever he has reason to believe that the holder thereof is an improper or incompetent person to operate motor vehicles, or is operating improperly or so as to endanger the public; and neither the certificate of registration nor the license shall be reissued unless upon examination or investigation, or after a hearing, the registrar determines that the operator should again be permitted to operate. 

The registrar, under the same conditions and for the same causes, may also suspend the right of any person to operate motor vehicles in the Commonwealth under section ten until he shall have received a license from the registrar."

 B. EFFECT OF FAILURE TO COMPLY WITH LAW AS TO LICENSING. 

SECTION 80. 

Unlike the rules relating to registration of motor vehicles, the failure to procure a license, or a proper license, does not render the operator a trespasser or outlaw on the highway, nor does it make the motor vehicle a nuisance. 

Comm. v. Magarosian, 261 Mass. 228 

Farr v. Whitney, 260 Mass. 193 

McDonough v. Vozzela, 247 Mass. 552 

McMahon v. Pearlman, 242 Mass. 367 

Walters v. Davis, 237 Mass. 206 

Griffin v. Hustis, 234 Mass. 95, at 100 

Polmatier v. Newbury, 231 Mass. 307 

Pigeon v. Mass. N. E. St. Ry., 230 Mass. 392, at 395 

Conroy v. Mather, 217 Mass. 91 

Holden v. McGillicuddy, 215 Mass. 563 

Holland v. Boston, 213 Mass. 560, at 561 and 562 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, at 171 

Moran v. Dickinson, 204 Mass. 559

The illegal conduct of an owner in personally operating a motor vehicle without a license to do so, or permitting another unlicensed person to operate the motor vehicle, is merely evidence of negligence on the owner's part. It is not conclusive and does not warrant the ordering of a verdict against him. (See cases just cited above) 

The failure to be licensed, or properly licensed, although evidence of negligence, has no bearing upon the rights of the owner, operator or passenger unless it is found as a fact that such illegality connected with the license had a causal connection with the accident. (See cases just cited above)

$95 

Licensing of Operators 

As was said in Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, at 171: "The operating of the automobile in itself is unobjectionable. The illegal element in the act is the failure to have a license. The purpose of the requirement of a license is to secure competency in the operator. If in any case the failure to have a license, looking to those conditions that ordinarily accompany the failure to have it, is a cause contributing directly to an injury, a violator of the law would be legally responsible to another person injured by the failure; or, if he is injured himself, would be precluded from recovery against another person who negligently contributed to the injury. But . . . his failure in that respect is only evidence of negligence in reference to his fitness to operate a car, and to his skill in the actual management of it, unless in the case of the plaintiff. it is shown to be a contributing cause to the injury sued for, in which case it is a bar to recovery. the opera- tion of a car without a license, while it is a punishable act, does not render the operator a trespasser on the highway, but . . . the illegal element in the act is only the failure to have a license while operating it, so that if the operation and movement contributed to the accident with which the want of a license had no connection, except as a mere condition, they would not preclude the operator as a plaintiff from recovery. If the illegal quality of the act had no tendency to cause the accident, the fact that the act is punishable because of the illegality, ought not to preclude one from recovery for harmful results to which, without negligence, the innocent features of the act alone contributed." The question of fact for the jury in each case is whether at the time of the accident the operator was in the exercise of due care and this must be determined by a consideration of the entire evidence. That is, the evidence of the operator's negligence in the management of his motor vehicle as created by the illegality connected

§81 

 with the license together with the consideration of the other evidence bearing upon the operator's negligence in the actual management of the motor vehicle at the time of the accident.

So, evidence should not be introduced that the operator never had a license to run a motor vehicle as tending to show that he was lacking in experience, skill and fitness to properly manage and control the machine at the time of the accident; and therefore at that time he was not in the exercise of due care. 

Polmatier v. Newbury, 231 Mass. 307, at 309

Two rules are established by the decisions: (a.) The violation of the Statute (G. L. c. 90, s. 10) forbidding a person to operate a motor vehicle upon a way unless licensed, is evidence of negligence of the operator to be considered by the jury with other evidence tending to show negligence; and 

 (b.) the violation of the statute (G. L. c. 90, s. 9) forbidding owner to allow an unlicensed person to operate his motor vehicle, is evidence for the consideration of the jury bearing on the negligence of the owner. 

Kenyon v. Hathaway, 274 Mass. 47, at 55 

2. Upon Rights and Liabilities. 

a. Owner.

SECTION 81. 

The illegal conduct of an owner in operating his motor vehicle without a license to do so is merely evidence of negligence on his part. 

McMahon v. Pearlman, 242 Mass. 367, at 370 

Pigeon v. Mass. N. E. St. Ry., 230 Mass. 392, at 395 

Holden v. McGillicuddy, 215 Mass. 563, at 564

$97 

Licensing of Operators 

Holland v. Boston, 213 Mass. 560, at 561 and 562

The fact that the owner operates his motor vehicle without a license and that this act is a crime (G. L. c. 90, ss. 10 and 20) does not render him a trespasser upon the highway. 

McMahon v. Pearlman, 242 Mass. 367, at 370 

As was said in Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, at 169: "The fact that the number of punishable misdemeanors has multiplied many times in recent years, as the relations of men in business and society have grown complex with the increase of population, is a reason why the violation of a criminal statute of slight importance should not affect one's civil rights, except when this violation, viewed in reference to the element of criminality intended to be punished, has had a direct effect upon his cause of action. 

Our decisions seem to have been tending toward the adoption of such a rule.”

It may be determined on the whole evidence in the case that not only was the owner while operating in the exercise of due care but also that his illegal conduct concerning the license to operate did not contribute to the injury for which the action is brought. 

Pigeon v. Mass. N. E. St. Ry., 230 Mass. 392, at 395 

Holden v. McGillicuddy, 215 Mass. 563, at 564 

Under these circumstances the owner's recovery cannot be defeated upon the ground of his illegal conduct connected with the license to operate. 

Pigeon v. Mass. N. E. St. Ry., 230 Mass. 392, at 395 

Holden v. McGillicuddy, 215 Mass. 563, at 564

So, an owner in driving his own automobile without a license to operate it can recover damage for a defect in the highway. His being unlicensed is not necessarily vital to his recovery.. It is merely evidence of his negligence in the management of his motor vehicle, to be

882 

 considered by the jury in connection with the other evidence bearing upon that question. 

Holland v. Boston, 213 Mass. 560, at 561 and 562

In the trial of an action for damages to a motor vehicle, the owner's wrongful conduct in operating without a proper license is evidence of negligence, but does not as matter of law bar his recovery. 

McMahon v. Pearlman, 242 Mass. 367, at 370 

Walters v. Davis, 237 Mass. 206 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155

Even the owner's knowingly allowing the motor vehicle to be driven by a person who has no license so to do does not bar the owner from recovery. (G. L. c. 90, s. 9)

However, this violation of law can be used in considering the evidence of the owner's negligence and if the jury find that the negligence has anything to do with the accident it is then, because the negligence contributes in causing the accident, that the owner is barred from recovery.. 

Gordon v. Bedard, 265 Mass. 408, at 413 

McDonough v. Vozzela, 247 Mass. 552

In a suit against the owner, the fact that the owner was operating his motor vehicle without a proper license so to do is evidence of negligence, but it does not necessarily establish liability as a legal result. 

McMahon v. Pearlman, 242 Mass. 367, at 370 

Walters v. Davis, 237 Mass. 206 

Holden v. McGillicuddy, 215 Mass. 563, at 564 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155 b. Operator.

SECTION 82. 

The operation of a motor vehicle on the public highway by an unlicensed person, or a person with an improper

§99 

Licensing of Operators license, does not make him a trespasser, but such operation is only evidence of negligence on his part with respect to the management of the vehicle at the time of the accident. 

Farr v. Whitney, 260 Mass. 193 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155

The operation of a motor vehicle without a license, or with an improper license, in violation of the statute (G. L. c. 90, s. 10) is merely evidence of negligence. 

Holden v. McGillicuddy, 215 Mass. 563 

However, such illegality does not prevent recovery of damages suffered by the operator when his illegal conduct concerning the license does not contribute to his injury. 

Holden v. McGillicuddy, 215 Mass. 563

Although the failure to have a license is some evidence of an operator's negligence in driving the motor vehicle, it is not conclusive and does not warrant the ordering of a verdict against him. 

Kenyon v. Hathaway, 274 Mass. 47, at 55 

Pigeon v. Mass. N. E. St. Ry., 230 Mass. 392, at 395 

Conroy v. Mather, 217 Mass. 91

An operator whose license has expired and has not been renewed is considered to be unlicensed. 

McMahon v. Pearlman, 242 Mass. 367 

Pigeon v. Mass. N. E. St. Ry., 230 Mass. 392, at 395

Holland v. Boston, 213 Mass. 560 

An operator whose license is restricted to the operation of certain kinds of motor vehicles is considered unlicensed when he drives a motor vehicle of a kind outside of those to which he is restricted. 

Comm. v. Magarosian, 261 Mass. 228

§82 

An operator who violates the conditions under which his license was granted is considered unlicensed. 

Gordon v. Bedard, 265 Mass. 408

However, fraud in obtaining a license does not constitute the operator to be unlicensed. 

O'Hare v. Gloag, 221 Mass. 224 (I) Licensed, Riding with Unlicensed. 

As was said in Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, at 165: "In a case like the present, where the unlicensed operator was a person of skill and great experience, whose license had expired only the day before and who was expecting another license within a day or two, the supervision and reasonable proximity required by law would not be as close as in ordinary cases, but we are of opinion that the law contemplates at least knowledge on the part of both persons, of the existence of a relation like that of operator without a license, and licensed chauffeur or operator accompanying him, in a position to advise or assist with reasonable promptness if necessary." 

Comm. v. Sabean, 275 Mass. 546, at 552 (Licensed operator not responsible where he believed operator to be licensed)

General Laws, Chapter 90, Section 10, provides, in part, that: "6 This section shall not prevent the operation of motor vehicles by unlicensed persons if riding with or accompanied by a licensed operator excepting only persons who have been licensed and whose licenses are not in force because of revocation or suspension, persons whose right to operate has been suspended by the registrar, and persons less than sixteen years of age; but such licensed operators shall be liable for the violation of any provision of this chapter, or any regulation made in accordance herewith, committed by such unlicensed

§IOI 

 operator; provided, that the examiners of operators, in the employ of the registrar, or engaged in other official duty, shall not be liable for the accident of any person being examined." c. Passenger.

SECTION 83. 

A person riding as a passenger with an unlicensed operator is not barred from recovery nor liable for the operator's conduct. But so far as the passenger contributes in the unlawful operation, his act is merely some evidence of negligence. It rarely can be ruled that such negligence directly contributed to injuries received by the passenger, so as to preclude him as matter of law from recovery. 

Griffin v. Hustis, 234 Mass. 95, at 100

So, the employing of an unlicensed operator by a passenger for hire in an automobile is evidence tending to show that the passenger was not in the exercise of due care at the time when the automobile collided with the street car. 

Conroy v. Mather, 217 Mass. 91

The knowledge of the passenger that the operator has not a license is important. Evidence tending to show that the passenger believed the operator to be duly licensed may relieve the passenger from evidence of negligence. 

Comm. v. Sabean, 275 Mass. 546, at 552

 CHAPTER V. 

PERSONAL INJURIES AND DEATH FROM OPERATION OF MOTOR VEHICLES. 

A. RECIPROCAL RIGHTS AND DUTIES ON HIGHWAY. 

SECTION 84. 

1. Between Motor Vehicles and Pedestrians. 

The rights and duties of operators of motor vehicles, pedestrians and drivers of other vehicles on the highway are reciprocal and must be exercised by each so as not to injure the other. Each may rely to some extent upon the due care of the other. 

Hutchinson v. H. E. Shaw Company, 273 Mass. 51, at 52 

Barrett v. Checker Taxi Company, 263 Mass. 252, at 254 

Hepburn v. Walters, 263 Mass. 139 

Di Rienzo v. Goldfarb, 257 Mass. 272, at 280 

Newman v. Hill, 250 Mass. 578 

Gauthier v. Quick, 250 Mass. 258, at 261 

As was said in Emery v. Miller, 231 Mass. 243, at 245: "Neither a pedestrian nor a traveller by automobile has rights superior to those of the other. Each is bound to act with reasonable regard to the presence of the other." 

When a pedestrian and motor vehicle are properly on the public highway each has the right of a traveller thereon. 

Huggon v. Whipple & Company, 214 Mass. 66

The right of a pedestrian to free and unobstructed passage has been somewhat abridged by modern conditions of travel.

$103 

There is no law or principle of law, or of reason, which confines foot passengers to particular crossings. Such a restriction would be very inconvenient and annoying. The street should be kept in such condition that foot passengers may be able to cross, with a reasonable degree of safety, using proper care for themselves, at any and all places. 

The necessity of this might be illustrated very fully by reference to the common and ordinary course of business. 

A person who is left by an omnibus in the middle of the street should be able to go in safety to a sidewalk, at the nearest point, and not be compelled to make his way among the vehicles in the middle of the street till he can reach a place particularly set apart and designated for the purpose of crossing. 

Foster v. Curtis, 213 Mass. 79, at 84 and 85 

Berry v. Newton & Boston St. Ry., 209 Mass. 100 

Mullen v. Boston El. Ry., 209 Mass. 79, 80 and cases cited 

Eustis v. Boston El. Ry., 206 Mass. 143, at 144 

Slayton v. West End St. Ry., 174 Mass. 55 

Raymond v. Lowell, 6 Cush. 524, at 530 and 531

A traveller has a right to pass and repass over the highway, and over all parts of it subject to the duty so to exercise that right as not to injure other travellers in the exercise of a similar right. 

Coates v. Bates, 265 Mass. 444, at 448 

Rice v. Lowell Buick Co., 229 Mass. 53, at 56 and 57 

Johnson v. Shaw, 204 Mass. 165, at 168 

Kerr v. Boston El. Ry., 188 Mass. 434, at 436

Pedestrians are not confined in their rights to specially prepared crosswalks. Sometimes failure to see and avoid a danger in the street may occur under such circumstances as inevitably to indicate a failure to exercise reasonable prudence to protect one's self from peril. 

Wilson v. Charlestown, 8 Allen, 137

$85 

Gilman v. Deerfield, 15 Gray, 577 

Raymond v. Lowell, 6 Cush. 524

But ordinarily there are present such diverting incidents as to make it a question of fact. 

Keith v. Worcester and B. V. St. Ry. Co., 196 Mass. 478, at 482 

SECTION 85. 

2. Between Motor and Other Vehicles. 

The same rule that applies to pedestrians governs the rights and duties of vehicles as between themselves. 

In Fraser v. Flanders, 248 Mass. 62, where a pedestrian sued the operators of two motor vehicles because she was struck, while crossing an intersection, by one vehicle because the other vehicle did not grant the former the right of way, the court said, at page 66: "It could be found that the cars were moving at about equal speed, and, in view of these conditions. . . in the exercise of ordinary prudence the respective drivers ought to have foreseen, that if the speed of either car was not slackened or its direction changed, the cars might ultimately come into collision . . . then [the operator of the car approaching the intersection from the right] could rightly assume that [the other operator] in operating her car would observe the provisions of G. L. c. 89, s. 8, and c. 90, s. I, and grant the right of way at the point of intersection to the [first] car which was approaching on her right. McCarthy v. Beckwith, 246 Mass. 409. "The parties, travellers on a public way, are bound to exercise reasonable care to avoid injury to each other in their respective use of the street." 

A vehicle in this connection is a means of conveyance

$105 

 and the term is not restricted to horse drawn carriages but includes bicycles, motorcycles, automobiles and street cars. 

Foster v. Curtis, 213 Mass. 79, at 84

As between vehicles and pedestrians, and even as between vehicles themselves, neither has a right to assume that the other will keep out of the way at its peril. 

Sutherland v. Caruso, 258 Mass. 513, at 514 and 515 

Foster v. Curtis, 213 Mass. 79, at 84

SECTION 86. 

3. Between Motor Vehicles and Street Cars. 

(See: Chapter XI, "Care as to Street Cars and Per sons Thereon," pages 267 to 283.)

And this rule applies to an electric car even though it has a right to demand that other vehicles shall not obstruct it by unreasonable delay upon the track. 

Foster v. Curtis, 213 Mass. 79, at 84

Eustis v. Boston El. Ry., 206 Mass. 143 

Carroll v. Boston El. Ry., 205 Mass. 429, at 430 

Hatch v. Boston & Northern St. Ry., 205 Mass. 410

Chaput v. Haverhill, G. & D. St. Ry., 194 Mass. 218 

Stubbs v. Boston & Northern St. Ry., 193 Mass. 513 

O'Brien v. Blue Hill St. Ry., 186 Mass. 446 

Mr. Justice Holmes said in White v. Worcester Consolidated Street Railway, 167 Mass. 43, at 44 and 45: "Their tracks are in the highway, where all vehicles have a right, not merely to cross, but to travel. In view of the inability of the cars to leave the tracks, it is the duty of free vehicles not to obstruct them unnecessarily, and to turn to one side when they meet them, but subject to that

§87 

 and to the respective powers of the two, a car and a wagon owe reciprocal duties to use reasonable care on each side to avoid a collision.”

B. THE CARE REQUIRED OF OPERATORS OF MOTOR VEHICLES. 

SECTION 87. 

1. Duty of Reasonable or Ordinary Care. 

The care which the driver of an automobile must exercise is proportionate to that instrumentality or engine which he has in charge.

Speaking with precise technicality, every traveller upon a highway is bound to exercise the care of the ordinary prudent and cautious person under all circumstances. 

The degree of vigilance and continuity of alertness necessary to attain that standard vary with the time and place, surroundings and means of transportation. 

But it would savor too much of refinement to hold that there is any practical inaccuracy in saying that one driving a high-powered automobile must exercise greater care toward others on a state highway than one plodding along a country road with an ox team.

O'Keefe v. United Motors Service, Incorporated, 253 

Mass. 603 

Fraser v. Flanders, 248 Mass. 62 

Regan v. Cummings, 228 Mass. 414 

Newton v. McSweeney, 225 Mass. 402 

Massie v. Barker, 224 Mass. 420, at 423 

Comm. v. Horsfall, 213 Mass. 232, at 235 

Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 392, at 396

$107 

 Chandler v. Matheson Company of Boston, 208 Mass. 

569 

Trombley v. Stevens-Duryea Company, 206 Mass. 

516 

Keith v. Worcester & B. V. St. Ry., 196 Mass. 478 and cases cited 

Sullivan v. Scripture, 3 Allen 564 

Chief Justice Rugg said in Massie v. Barker, 224 Mass. 420, at 423: "The law as to drivers of motor vehicles is not different from that which governs other persons. The standard required is that of a reasonably prudent man under all the circumstances."

The operator of a motor vehicle is required to use sufficient care to avoid injury to any person or property and if he fails to do this, he is guilty of negligence. 

Roberge v. Follette, 261 Mass. 438, at 441 (Child killed on road twenty feet wide by automobile going twelve miles an hour without sounding horn-no other traffic) 

Hicks v. H. B. Church Truck Service Co., 259 Mass. 272 

Leonard v. Fowle, 255 Mass. 531 

Creedon v. Galvin, 226 Mass. 140, at 142 

In going through city streets, the operator must use such care in driving as a reasonably careful person ought to use under like circumstances. 

Dube v. Keogh Storage Co., 236 Mass. 488 (Workman repairing street car struck by motor truck) 

47 A. L. R. 407

The duty of exercising ordinary care to avoid injury to a traveller or travellers who are in plain sight for several

$87 

 hundred feet before they are reached by a motor vehicle, rests upon the driver of that motor vehicle. 

Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 392, at 395

The proper discharge of this duty depends upon the condition by which the driver is confronted. 

Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 392, at 395 and 396

In passing upon the question whether the driver sufficiently performed this duty of exercising ordinary care to avoid injuring a traveller or travellers, the jury may consider the powerful agencies, (motor vehicles) placed under the driver's control, and the disastrous consequences to other travellers if there is mismanagement. 

Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 392, at 396 

Nelson v. Old Colony St. Ry., 208 Mass. 159, at 161 and 162 It is peculiarly a question for the judgment of the jury familiar from observation, and possibly from experiences, with this mode of travel. 

Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 392, at 396

What might be due care in the management of a horse and carriage jogging along a country road, affords no standard for the measurement of the prudence of the driver of a motor car running over the road at a high rate of speed. 

Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 392, at 396

What amounts to the operation of the motor vehicle is usually a question of fact. However, certain acts have been held to amount to operation, such as: 

Stopping in the highway in the ordinary course of travel for soliciting trade or in calling for or delivering merchandise. 

Cook v. Crowell, 273 Mass. 356, at 358 

See also: Comm. v. Clarke, 254 Mass. 566 

Reynolds v. Murphy, 241 Mass. 225, at 227

SECTION 89. 

3. Operator's Reliance on Care of Others.

The operator of a motor vehicle has a right to rely to some extent upon the assumption that other persons in the vicinity of the motor vehicle will exercise reasonable care in regard to their own safety. 

In Sutherland v. Caruso, 258 Mass. 513, where the defendant's motor vehicle collided with a one horse team driven by the plaintiff at the intersection of streets, it was said at pages 514 and 515: 

"Although it is true that a traveller on the highway has a right to rely to some extent on the expectation that other travellers will obey the law and will use reasonable care not to injure him, , 586, Gauthier v. Quick, 250 Mass. 379, 380, yet he still has the duty to use ordinary care and prudence to avoid

$III 

 an injury that might otherwise result from the negligence of another."

Rogers v. Phillips, 206 Mass. 308, 309 

Parker v. Adams, 12 Met. 414, at 419

C. LIABILITY ARISING FROM USE OF MOTOR VEHICLES. 

1. Negligence as Basis of Liability. 

SECTION 90. 

a. General Statement. 

In order for liability to arise from the use of a motor vehicle there must be some negligence on the part of a person concerned with its use. 

Washburn v. R. F. Owens Company, 258 Mass. 446 

Regan v. Cummings, 228 Mass. 414

But proof of ordinary negligence is sufficient to support recovery. 

Even in actions for death caused by motor vehicles, proof of simple negligence is sufficient. 

Dzura v. Phillips, 275 Mass. 283, at 289 

Parker v. Moody, 274 Mass. 100 

Logan v. Reardon, 274 Mass. 83 

Kirby v. Keating, 271 Mass. 390 

McCarron v. Bolduc, 270 Mass. 39 

Blood v. Adams, 269 Mass. 480 

Rog v. Eltis, 269 Mass. 466 

Manning v. Simpson, 261 Mass. 494 

Healy v. O'Riley, 257 Mass. 413 

Flynn v. Lewis, 231 Mass. 550

The mere occurrence of an accident involving a motor vehicle is not in itself evidence of negligence on the part

II891 

 of the operator, owner or other person in control of the motor vehicle. 

Ellis v. Ellison, 275 Mass. 272, at 276 

Pinto v. Brennan, 254 Mass. 298 

Reardon v. Boston El. Ry., 247 Mass. 124, and cases collected at page 126 

Whalen v. Mutrie, 247 Mass. 316 

b. Actionable Negligence. 

SECTION 91. 

(I) 

Elements of. 

To create negligence, whether ordinary or gross, as a basis for liability arising from the use of a motor vehicle, there must be present the following four elements: 

(A) Legal duty of defendant to exercise care toward the plaintiff (See: Sec. 92, page 112) (B) Breach of that legal duty by the defendant (See: Sec. 93, page 113) (C) Injury or damage (See: Sec. 97, page 136) sustained by the plaintiff (D) Proximate cause of the plaintiff's injury or damage was the defendant's breach of duty (See: Sec. 98, page 136)

SECTION 92. 

(II) When Existent. 

Whenever a defendant owes a duty to exercise care toward a plaintiff that care means such precaution and

$113 

 vigilance as are commensurate with the requirements of the circumstances.

To determine the presence or absence of ordinary care the test is whether the defendant's conduct was at least what a reasonably prudent man would have done under similar circumstances. (See: Sec. 93, page 113.)

In ascertaining gross negligence the standard is the conduct of a reasonably prudent man under similar circumstances less some degree of vigilance or precaution or plus some amount of indifference or inattention. (See: Sec. 

94, page 115.) 

Because each case depends upon individual circumstances it usually becomes a question of fact (1) what would have been the conduct of a person of ordinary prudence under like circumstances and (2) did the defendant perform or fail to perform that, or a lesser, degree or amount of care. 

Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 392 

c. Degrees of Negligence. 

(I) Ordinary Negligence. 

(A) 

SECTION 93. 

Definitions. 

Ordinary negligence has been defined as the failure of a responsible person, either by omission or by action, to exercise that degree of care, vigilance and forethought which, in the discharge of the duty then resting on him, the person of ordinary caution and prudence ought to exercise under the particular circumstances. 

Telless v. Gardiner, 266 Mass. 90 

Altman v. Aronson, 231 Mass. 588, at 591

It is a want of diligence commensurate with the requirement of the duty at the moment imposed by the law. 

Altman v. Aronson, 231 Mass. 588, at 591

893 

Ordinary negligence consists in doing or omitting to do an act in violation of a legal duty or obligation due to the person sustaining the injury. 

Bergeron v. Forest, 233 Mass. 392

Negligence is the performance or omission of some act in violation of legal duty. 

Karlowski v. Kissock, 275 Mass. 180, at 183 

Pickett v. Waldorf System, Inc., 241 Mass. 569, at 571 

Bernabeo v. Kaulback, 226 Mass. 128, at 131 

Minor v. Sharon, 112 Mass. 477, 487

It is a breach of some duty which one ought to perform. 

Bernabeo v. Kaulback, 226 Mass. 128, at 131

There can be no negligence when there is no duty. 

Telless v. Gardiner, 266 Mass. 90 

Bernabeo v. Kaulback, 226 Mass. 128, at 130

There must be causal connection between the negligence and the damage sustained by the plaintiff. 

Washburn v. R. F. Owens Company, 258 Mass. 446, at 448 The character of liability involved in the use of motor vehicles may arise from various forms of conduct involving,- Ordinary Negligence Gross Negligence (See: this section as above) (See: Sec. 94, page 115.) (which differs only in degree from ordinary negligence)

 (II) Gross Negligence. 

See: Section 443, page 580.

SECTION 94. 

(A) Definitions. 

Gross negligence is negligence of an aggravated character. It is a substantially greater want of care than that which constitutes ordinary negligence. 

Mason v. Thomas, 274 Mass. 59, at 61

Gross negligence is a heedless and palpable violation of legal duty respecting the rights of others. The element of culpability which characterizes all negligence is in gross negligence magnified to a high degree as compared with that present in ordinary negligence. 

Mason v. Thomas, 274 Mass. 59, at 61 

Altman v. Aronson, 231 Mass. 588, at 591 and 592

Gross negligence is such conduct as results from the addition to ordinary carelessness of an utter disregard of the dictates of prudence, culminating in complete neglect of safety. 

Manning v. Simpson, 261 Mass. 494, at 496 (Increasing speed on slippery road at curve and crossing path of oncoming automobile) 

But see: 

Marcienowski v. Sanders, 252 Mass. 65 

Shriear v. Feigelson, 248 Mass. 432 

Burke v. Cook, 246 Mass. 518

Ordinarily no one element of conduct can be ruled to constitute gross negligence. 

Meaney v. Doyle, 1931 A.S. 1471, at 1471 and 1472 

McKenna v. Smith, 275 Mass. 149

Every act or omission entering into a particular happening must be considered in connection with all the other circumstances before the whole can properly be held to be an instance of gross negligence. 

Meaney v. Doyle, 1931 A.S. 1471, at 1472

$94 

To constitute gross negligence it must appear that the accident was due to something more than simple carelessness, something which has in it elements of “indifference to present legal duty," of "utter forgetfulness of legal obligations so far as other persons may be affected,” of "heedless and palpable violation of legal duty respecting the rights of others,” of “manifestly smaller amount of watchfulness and circumspection than the circumstances require of a person of ordinary prudence," of "the omission of even such diligence as habitually inattentive and careless men do not fail to exercise in avoiding danger to their own person or property." 

Meaney v. Doyle, 1931 A.S. 1471, at 1471 

Dzura v. Phillips, 275 Mass. 283, at 289 

Learned v. Hawthorne, 269 Mass. 554, at 560 

Altman v. Aronson, 231 Mass. 588 "Gross negligence is an act or omission respecting legal duty of an aggravated character as distinguished from a mere failure to exercise ordinary care . . . a manifestly smaller amount of watchfulness and circumspection than the circumstances require of a person of ordinary prudence the omission of even such diligence as habitually inattentive and careless men do not fail to exercise in avoiding danger to their own person or property.” 

Dzura v. Phillips, 275 Mass. 283, at 289 quoting from-Altman v. Aronson, 231 Mass. 588, at 591, 592 and 593 Gross negligence is usually made up by a combination of circumstances. 

Dzura v. Phillips, 275 Mass. 283, at 289 

Different situations existed in: 

Cook v. Cole, 273 Mass. 557 

Clay v. Pope & Cottle Co., 273 Mass. 40 

Cannon v. Bassett, 264 Mass. 383

Gross negligence exists when the conduct of the operator

$117 

 is that of one who recklessly exercises no forethought, no diligence for the safety of his guests or himself, when in a situation which the most inattentive and careless person would recognize as pregnant with imminent peril to life, person or property. 

Learned v. Hawthorne, 269 Mass. 554, at 561. 

In Learned v. Hawthorne, 269 Mass. 554, at 560 an instruction was proper that: "... in determining whether the conduct of the defendant is proper or improper you [the jury] are first to say, What would the ordinary careful and prudent man [do] under those circumstances, how would he perform? And when you have said what his conduct would be, then you compare the conduct of the defendant with that conduct, and by that comparison you say whether the conduct in this particular case was negligent or not.' .. having determined the issue as to whether the conduct was that of negligence 'then you [the jury] analyze the facts, as to whether the conduct, having regard to all the facts and circumstances, was a little worse than negligent; as to whether it found its place somewhere between these two limits.. negligence and wilful, wanton and reckless conduct . . . if if... [the defendant] was negligent and you [the jury] would call his conduct something somewhere between negligence and wilful, wanton and reckless conduct,-you [the jury] don't need to say just where it is, but if it is somewhere between those two points, then it is gross negligence." 

(B) Distinctions. 

Gross negligence is distinguished from ordinary negligence. 

Cook v. Cole, 273 Mass., 557, at 561 

Altman v. Aronson, 231 Mass. 588, at 591 and 593 (See: Learned v. Hawthorne, 269 Mass.. 554)

Gross negligence differs in degree rather than in kind

$94 

 from ordinary negligence and is “materially more want of care than constitutes simple inadvertence," but need not amount to "such reckless disregard of probable consequences as is equivalent to a wilful and intentional wrong." 

Cook v. Cole, 273 Mass. 557, at 561 

Prondecka v. Turners Falls, 241 Mass. 100; S.c. 238 

Mass. 239 

Cotter, Petnr., 237 Mass. 68

This definition does not possess the exactness of a mathematical demonstration. 

Cook v. Cole, 273 Mass. 557, at 561

Gross negligence is substantially and appreciably higher in magnitude than ordinary negligence. It is materially more want of care than constitutes simple inadvertence.

It is an act or omission respecting legal duty of an aggravated character as distinguished from a mere failure to exercise ordinary care. It is very great negligence, or the absence of slight diligence, or the want of even scant care. 

Gross negligence is a manifestly smaller amount of watchfulness and circumspection than the circumstances require of a person of ordinary prudence. 

Rugg. C. J. in Altman v. Aronson, 231 Mass. 588, at 591 and 592 Ordinary and gross negligence differ in degree of inattention, while both differ in kind from wilful and intentional conduct which is or ought to be known to have a tendency to injure. 

Learned v. Hawthorne, 269 Mass. 554

Gross negligence is a degree of negligence much greater than ordinary negligence. It is negligence of greater culpability than lack of due care respecting the rights of others. 

Marcienowski v. Sanders, 252 Mass. 65 (40 miles an hour over rough road going to fire not gross negligence)

$119 

The element of culpability which characterizes all negligence is in gross negligence magnified to a high degree as compared with that present in ordinary negligence. Gross negligence is a manifestly smaller amount of watchfulness and circumspection than the circumstances require of a person of ordinary prudence. But it is something less than wilful, wanton and reckless conduct which renders a defendant who has injured another liable to the latter even though guilty of contributory negligence, or which renders a defendant in rightful possession of real estate liable to a trespasser whom he has injured. It falls short of being such reckless disregard of probable consequences as is equivalent to a wilful and intentional wrong. 

Learned v. Hawthorne, 269 Mass. 554, at 560 and 561

For cases in which the question has been whether there was evidence for the jury of gross negligence, See: 

Shriear v. Feigelson, 248 Mass. 432 

Burke v. Cook, 246 Mass. 518

Adams v. Boston El. Ry., 214 Mass. I

(C) Instances Involving. 

(1) Where Existent. 

Defective Brakes.

So, although the skidding which preceded the collision with the tree, is not of itself evidence of negligence, much less gross negligence, yet when at least one of the reasons for the skidding is defective brakes which had caused the car on the day before the accident to skid to the left when the brakes were applied, and when this condition is known to the driver and could have been remedied before the accident, the finding is justified that the driver was indifferent, to the point of criminality, to every legal obligation which he owed to the plaintiff. 

Logan v. Reardon, 274 Mass. 83, at 86 

Isaacson v. Boston, etc. St. Ry., 1932 A. S. 385

$94 

A driver is grossly negligent when after several requests to go slower he does not slacken speed but continues at 45 miles an hour, and the passenger straightens up in the car in an effort to get out but is pushed back into his seat by the driver, and the brakes on the car are not good but cause the car to skid each time they are applied, which condition the driver knows, and has known that the brakes should have been relined because the day before he skidded from one side of the street to the other, and on the day of the accident the roads are wet and slippery, and at the place of the accident, which is a curve with which the driver is familiar, the vehicle skidded right across the road, and crashed into a tree with great force. 

Logan v. Reardon, 274 Mass. 83, at 85 and 86 

Disregarding or Inattentive to Signal of Operator in

Preceding Vehicle. 

Where the operator, who was familiar with the locality approaching a point on the State road where there were driveways to a hotel and postoffice, followed another automobile at the rate of 35 miles an hour and disregarded or did not see the outstretched hand of the driver in the preceding vehicle who desired to stop at the post office, slowed somewhat, put out his hand to indicate a left turn and drove to his left into a driveway but the defendant operator swung more to the left, ran upon street car tracks and brought up against a tree, the evidence is sufficient to support a finding of gross negligence. 

Dzura v. Phillips, 275 Mass. 283, at 288

Drinking Alcohol on Slippery Road.. 

Where passenger remonstrated; driving at speed of 40 to 45 miles an hour; driving over lawn at detour in road where there were red lights; driver under the influence of liquor. Passenger exclaimed, "Look out for red lights!" 

Automobile tipped over.

One who on an icy road dodged in and out of traffic, skidded once and almost hit another car, disregarding remonstrance, and at an intersection disregarded a stop signal and at high speed attempted to beat out the lights and within the intersection collided with a car coming from the left. 

Parker v. Moody, 274 Mass. 100

So, the act of driving an automobile against the warning of the red traffic light is a reckless disregard of the driver's plain duty to the public, and constitutes gross negligence in that it shows a heedless and palpable violation of legal duty to the passenger in the automobile.

SECTION 95. 

d.

Wilful, Wanton or Reckless Acts or Conduct. 

(I) Definitions. 

To constitute wilful, wanton or reckless acts or conduct, as distinguished from negligence, grave danger to others must have been apparent, and. the defendant must have

$95 

 chosen to run the risk rather than alter his conduct so as to avoid the act or omission which caused the harm. 

Freeman v. United Fruit Company, 223 Mass. 300

The alleged wrongdoer acts wilfully, wantonly and recklessly only when he inflicts the injury intentionally or is so utterly indifferent to the rights of others that he acts as if such rights did not exist. The result is a wilful not a negligent wrong. 

Wentzell v. Boston El. Ry., 230 Mass. 275, at 277 

Freeman v. United Fruit Co., 223 Mass. 300, and cases cited 

Dudley v. Northampton St. Ry. Co., 202 Mass. 443, at 449 Wilful, wanton or reckless acts or conduct are an utter disregard of the rights of others. 

Cotter, Petnr., 237 Mass. 68 

Prondecka v. Turners Falls P. etc., 241 Mass. 100; 

S. C. 238 Mass. 239 

(II) Distinctions. 

Negligence and wilful, wanton or reckless conduct are not equivalents. 

Prondecka v. Turners Falls P. etc., 241 Mass. 100, at 

102; S. C. 238 Mass. 239 at 242

Wilful, wanton and reckless conduct differs in kind from either simple or gross negligence. 

Farr v. Whitney, 260 Mass. 193, at 197 

Altman v. Aronson, 231 Mass. 588, at 592

It is something different from negligence even when the degree may be found under our law to be gross. 

McIntyre v. Converse, 238 Mass. 592, at 594 

Adamowicz v. Newburyport Gas & Elec. Co., 238 

Mass. 244, at 246

$127 

Prondecka v. Turners Falls P. etc., 238 Mass. 239, at 242 

Cotter, Petnr., 237 Mass. 68, at 72 The difference between negligence, whether ordinary or gross, and conduct which is wilful, wanton and in reckless disregard of the rights of others, is a difference in kind and not merely one of degree. In the instance of negligence the wrongdoer is guilty of nothing more than carelessness. In the case of wilful, wanton or reckless acts or conduct, the wrongdoer is guilty of a wilful, intentional wrong. His acts or conduct are criminal or quasi criminal. 

If they result in the death of the injured person he is guilty of manslaughter. 

Hafey v. Dwight Mfg. Co., 240 Mass. 155 

McIntyre v. Converse, 238 Mass. 592, at 594 

Adamowicz v. Newburyport Gas & Elec. Co., 238 

Mass. 244, at 246 

Cotter v. Boston, Revere Beach & Lynn, R. R., 237 

Mass. 68 

Robbins v. Athol Gas & Elec. Co., 236 Mass. 387 

Altman v. Aronson, 231 Mass. 588

Hillman v. Boston El. Ry., 207 Mass. 478 

Bjornquist v. Boston & Albany R.R., 185 Mass. 130 

Aiken v. Holyoke St. Ry., 184 Mass. 269, at 271 

Dillon v. Conn. River R. R., 154 Mass. 478 

Daniels v. N. Y. & N. E. R. R., 154 Mass. 349

It was said in Altman v. Aronson, 231 Mass. 588, at 592: "But it [gross negligence] is something less than the wilful, wanton and reckless conduct which renders a defendant who has injured another liable to the latter even though guilty of contributory negligence, or which renders a defendant in rightful possession of real estate liable to a trespasser whom he has injured. It falls short of being such reckless disregard of probable consequences as is equivalent to a wilful and intentional wrong. Ordinary

$95 

 and gross negligence differ in degree of inattention, while both differ in kind from wilful and intentional conduct which is or ought to be known to have a tendency to injure."

To create negligence there need be nothing more than a lack of ordinary care which causes an injury to another, but to establish wilful, wanton or reckless acts or conduct, there must be wilful, intentional conduct whose tendency to injure is known, or ought to be known, accompanied by a wanton and reckless disregard of the probable harmful consequences from which others are likely to suffer so that the whole conduct together, is of the nature of a wilful, intentional wrong. 

Banks v. Braman, 188 Mass. 367, at 369

A charge which otherwise would be mere negligence becomes by reason of a reckless disregard of probable consequences a wilful wrong.

Romana v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 226 Mass. 532; S. C. 

218 Mass. 76 

Fottler v. Moseley, 185 Mass. 563, at 565 

Aiken v. Holyoke St. Ry., 184 Mass. 269, at 271 

Bigelow on Torts (8th Ed.) C. 3, s. 2

The complete indifference to consequences distinguishes wrongs caused by wantonness and recklessness from torts arising from negligence. 

Freeman v. United Fruit Co., 223 Mass. 300, at 302 

O'Brien v. Union Freight R. R. Co., 209 Mass. 449, at 453 

Comm. v. Byard, 200 Mass. 175, at 177 

Pierce v. Cunard, 153 Mass. 87, at 88 and 89

The essential difference between negligence and wanton or reckless conduct, is this:

If the act or omission of the defendant which caused the harm, in the light of the circumstances, would indicate in an ordinary normal man in the defendant's situation,

$129 

 mere inattention, mere failure to realize danger that should have been clearly understood, or mere failure to use as much care as the law required, the case is one of negligence only, even though the negligence was so extreme as to constitute gross. But if the defendant in fact realized the gravity of the danger, and nevertheless chose to be guilty of the act or omission which caused the harm; or if the standard man in the same situation, by whose normal conduct the law judges the defendant, would have realized the gravity of the danger of the act or omission of which the defendant was guilty and which caused the harm; then, in either case, the defendant in so acting or omitting to act is not guilty of mere negligence, but is guilty of wilful, wanton or reckless conduct. 

Cotter, Petnr., 237 Mass. 68 (A recovery cannot be had on the theory of wilful, wanton or reckless conduct under pleadings charging negligence) 

Bilodeau v. Fitchburg & Leominster St. Ry. Co., 236 

Mass. 526, at 539 (Neither can recovery be had on the theory of negligence under pleadings charging wilful, wanton or reckless conduct) 

Prondecka v. Turners Falls P. etc., 241 Mass. 100; 

S. C. 238 Mass. 239, at 243 (Quaere, whether evidence of wilful, wanton or reckless conduct may justify a finding of negligence) 

See also: 

McIntyre v. Converse, 238 Mass. 592

To constitute such conduct, it is not enough that the act done is intentional and fraught with danger to others, for that is usually or often true in cases of mere negligence. 

Wanton or reckless conduct, like negligence, may consist in a mere omission to act where there is a duty to act.

$95 

But there must be a duty, where either negligence or wanton or reckless conduct is to be found in a mere omission to act.

The fact that the defendant is merely charged with an omission of duty, rather than with an affirmative act, does not show that his conduct may not have been wanton or reckless. 

(III) As Standard of Duty toward Tres passers and Licensees. 

No degree of negligence can make one liable for an injury to a trespasser or mere licensee. 

Wentzel v. Boston El. Ry., 230 Mass. 275, at 277

But a trespasser or licensee has a valid cause of action when suffering injury caused by wilful, wanton or reckless misconduct of the owner of a motor vehicle or by his agents acting within the real or apparent scope of their authority. 

O'Leary v. Fash, 245 Mass. 123 

Prondecka v. Turners Falls P. etc., 241 Mass. 100; 

S. C. 238 Mass. 239, at 242 

Hafey v. Turners Falls P. etc., 240 Mass. 155 

Adamowicz v. Newburyport Gas & Elec. Co., 238 

Mass. 244, at 246 

Robbins v. Athol Gas & Elec. Co., 236 Mass. 387 

Romana v. Boston El. Ry., 218 Mass. 76, at 82 

Dudley v. Northampton St. Ry., 202 Mass. 443 

Banks v. Braman, 188 Mass. 367 

Bjornquist v. Boston & Albany R.R., 185 Mass. 130 

Aiken v. Holyoke St. Ry., 184 Mass. 269 

(IV) Contributory Negligence No Defense. 

When the defendant's acts amount to wilful, wanton or reckless misconduct, the contributory negligence of the plaintiff or his want of due care is not a defense.

$131 

Isaacson v. Boston etc. Ry., 1932 A. S. 385, at 395 

Sieplinski v. Severn, 269 Mass. 261 

Zink v. Foss, 221 Mass. 73, at 75 

Hudson v. Peoples St. Ry. Co., 175 Mass. 23 

See also: cases cited under subdivision (III) of this 

(V) Instances Involving. 

(A) Where Existent. 

When a driver of a motor vehicle takes no precautions to ascertain whether other travellers are using the way, and an accident occurs, it may be found that the accident springs from an indifference on the part of the driver to the safety of other travellers, and this amounts to a wanton disregard of the rights of such travellers. 

The driver of a motor vehicle may be found guilty of wilful, wanton and reckless conduct as well as guilty of an intended wrong, when, being in a moving line of traffic with automobiles ahead for a long way but only three feet apart, with automobiles coming in opposite directions, and the road wide enough only for two lines of traffic, he pulled out of line at a rate of speed about thirty miles an hour and continued to drive on towards the opposite line until he forced the plaintiff's automobile off the road and against a pole. It could be found that the defendant driver rode with death and that no reasonable person would expect to be saved. 

Leonard v. Conquest, 274 Mass. 347, at 352

Several violations of statutes relating to law of the road can be found to have created conduct which was heedless and indifferent to every legal obligation which the driver owed to others. 

Isaacson v. Boston etc. St. Ry., 1932 A. S. 385, at 395

When there was a violation by the driver of a bus of

$95 

 a series of statutes manifestly intended to be observed for the safety of persons upon the highway, coupled with a complete indifference to or reckless disregard of probable consequences, this may be equivalent to a wilful and intentional wrong. 

Isaacson v. Boston etc. St. Ry., 1932 A. S. 385, at 395 

Leonard v. Conquest, 274 Mass. 347 

Comm. v. Arone, 265 Mass. 128 

Freeman v. United Fruit Co., 223 Mass. 300 

Aiken v. Holyoke St. Ry., 184 Mass. 269 

Driving without license at 45 miles an hour and at the same time attempting indecent familiarities with guest is wanton and wilful of the driver. 

Rog v. Eltis, 269 Mass. 466

(B) Where Non-Existent. 

The defendant's illegal registration of his motor vehicle, together with backing it out of a driveway, toward the plaintiff's automobile after the plaintiff blows his horn several times and the defendant pays no attention to it and gives no warning of his approach but backs his car across the road a distance of 20 feet and hits the left front end of the plaintiff's automobile, the windows of the defendant's automobile being closed and the defendant not seeing the plaintiff's automobile although the surface of the road has snow and ice upon it and there is an unobstructed view for 300 feet, shows that the defendant's conduct is negligent, Birch v. Athol and Orange Street Ry., 198 Mass.

The plaintiff and his wife were in an automobile which stalled crossing defendant's tracks. Defendant's street car was approaching at distance of 500 feet. Plaintiff made every effort to start automobile but could not. Defendant's street car, with but slightly diminishing speed, struck the plaintiff's automobile damaging it and injuring

$95 

 the plaintiff's wife. Plaintiff stated he expected motorman would stop street car and plaintiff's wife stated she could have got out of automobile in time, but expected street car would stop. Held that plaintiffs used no care themselves. They trusted everything to the care of the motorman in the expectation that he would realize their predicament and stop. This was the most dangerous course they could have adopted. Even in an emergency one must exercise reasonable care under the circumstances. 

This evidence did not indicate wilful, wanton or reckless conduct of the motorman which entitled the plaintiffs to verdicts in spite of their want of care. 

Lawrence v. Fitchburg etc. St. Ry., 201 Mass. 489

Wilful, wanton or reckless conduct does not arise when the vision of the driver becomes suddenly confused or he makes an error of judgment. 

Isaacson v. Boston, etc. St. Ry., 1932 A. S. 385, at 395 

Austin v. Eastern Mass. St. Ry., 269 Mass. 420, at 424-5 

An insulting remark or profane language is not enough to show wilful, wanton and reckless conduct. 

Farr v. Whitney, 260 Mass. 193, at 197

Nuisance. 

SECTION 96. 

The fact that the motor vehicle is a nuisance has important effects upon the rights of the owner, operator and occupants in their actions for injury inflicted by others. 

Brown v. Alter, 251 Mass. 223

The placing of a motor vehicle upon the public highway so as to become a nuisance, creates liability of the owner and operator for any injury or damage resulting to third persons regardless of whether the operator was or was not negligent or whether he was engaged in the business of the owner at the time of the accident. 

Duggan v. Woodis, 246 Mass. 431 

45 A. L. R. 481

So, when injury is received from a motor vehicle which has become a nuisance it is not necessary for the injured person to prove negligence as against the owner or operator of that motor vehicle nuisance. 

Koonovsky v. Quellette, 226 Mass. 474 (Improper use of dealer's number plates)

In death cases, the fact that the motor vehicle was a nuisance is material to affect damages. The degree of culpability of the owner or operator of the motor vehicle as a nuisance might well be greater if the motor vehicle was wilfully driven as an outlaw on the highway than it would be if all the requirements of law had been scrupulously observed. Larger damages may be assessed if the fact of nuisance should be considered.

897 

Fairbanks v. Kemp, 226 Mass. 75 

(Unlawful registration of Motor Vehicle) 

But even though the defendant's motor vehicle was a nuisance maintained on the public highway, the plaintiff cannot recover for damages caused by that motor vehicle nuisance without showing that his own want to care did not directly contribute to that damage. 

Brown v. Alter, 251 Mass. 223

Sherman v. Fall River Iron Works, 2 Allen 524, at 526 

Parker v. Adams, 12 Met. 415 

Smith v. Smith, 2 Pick. 621

However, the motor vehicle nuisance is considered to be a trespasser and an outlaw and to prevent the effect of contributory negligence in recovery for injuries and damages caused in connection with its use and operation on the highway it is necessary to prove wilful, wanton and reckless conduct of those from whom recovery is sought. 

See: Sec. 95, page 125. 

f. Injury or Damage. 

SECTION 97. 

Unless a party suffers injury or damage from the wrongful conduct of the person responsible for the operation of the motor vehicle, that party has no remedy by an action of tort. 

Des Brisay v. Foss, 264 Mass. 102, at III g. Proximate Cause.

SECTION 98. 

(I) General Statement. 

To establish liability from conduct occurring during the use or operation of a motor vehicle, it is not sufficient that the plaintiff sustained the injury or damage but the de-

$137 

 fendant's negligent conduct must have been the proximate cause of the plaintiff's injury or damage.

Guinan v. Famous Players-L. Corp., 267 Mass. 501 

Slater v. T. C. Baker Co., 261 Mass. 424, at 425 

Washburn v. R. F. Owens Co., 258 Mass. 446

Meech v. Sewall, 232 Mass. 460 

Leahy v. Standard Oil Co. of N. Y., 224 Mass. 352, at 361 

Burke v. Hodge, 217 Mass. 182

Lane v. Atlantic Works, III Mass. 136 

In this connection, the expression "proximate cause" is synonymous with "causal connection," "direct cause," "dominant cause," "efficient cause," "immediate cause," and "natural and probable consequence or result."

The proximate cause referred to in cases involving the negligent use or operation of motor vehicles is said to be the "cause that sets in motion a train of events which brings about [the] result, [injury or damage] without the intervention of any force started and working actively from a new and independent source." 

Slater v. T. C. Baker Co., 261 Mass. 424, at 425

Lynn Gas & Elec. Co. v. Meriden Fire Ins. Co., 158 

Mass. 570, at 575 

So, the plaintiff's injury or damage must be the direct result of the defendant's wrongful conduct but, by direct, it is not meant that the cause or agency which is nearest in time or place to the result is necessarily chosen. 

Guinan v. Famous Players-L. Corp., 267 Mass. 501 Lynn Gas & Elec. Co. v. Meriden Fire Ins. Co., 158 

Mass. 570, at 575 

Freeman v. Merc. Mut. Acci. Assn., 156 Mass. 351

In the leading case of Lane v. Atlantic Works, III 

Mass. 136, at 139 and 140, the rule was laid down that: "In actions of this description, the defendant is liable for the natural and probable consequences of his negligent act or omission. The injury must be the direct result of the misconduct charged; but it will not be considered too

$98 

 remote if, according to the usual experience of mankind, the result ought to have been apprehended. "The act of a third person, intervening and contributing a condition necessary to the injurious effect of the original negligence, will not excuse the first wrongdoer, if such act ought to have been foreseen. The original negligence still remains a culpable and direct cause of the injury. The test is to be found in the probable injurious consequences which were to be anticipated, not in the number of subsequent events and agencies which might arise." 

Regan v. Cummings, 228 Mass. 414 

Oulighan v. Butler, 189 Mass. 287 

For collection of cases following this rule, see: 

Leahy v. Standard Oil Co. of N. Y., 224 Mass. 352, at 360 and 361 The sphere of accountability in connection with the operation and use of motor vehicles is not impracticable or unlimited nor does it extend indefinitely to all possible contingent consequences. 

Milbury v. Turner Ctr. Sys., 274 Mass. 358, at 362

An action can be maintained only when there is shown to be, first, a mis feasance or negligence in some particular as to which there was a duty towards the party injured or the community generally; and, secondly, where it is apparent that the harm to the person or property of another which has actually ensued was reasonably likely to ensue from that act or omission concerning which complaint is made. 

Milbury v. Turner Ctr. Sys., 274 Mass. 358, at 362 

Rea v. Checker Taxi Co., 272 Mass. 510

Guinan v. Famous Players-L. Corp., 267 Mass. 501 

Teasdale v. Beacon Oil Co., 266 Mass. 25 

Gordon v. Bedard, 265 Mass. 408

Dalton v. Gt. Atl. & Pac. Tea Co., 241 Mass. 400 

Leahy v. Standard Oil Co. of N. Y., 224 Mass. 352

$139 

Burke v. Hodge, 217 Mass. 182

Berdos v. Tremont & Suffolk Mills, 209 Mass. 489 Lane v. Atlantic Works, III Mass. 136 

But see distinguished cases:

Falk v. Finkelman, 268 Mass. 524 

Jacobs v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R., 212 Mass. 96 

Glassey v. Worcester C. St. Ry., 185 Mass. 315 

Stone v. Boston & Albany R. R., 171 Mass. 536

Newcomb v. Boston Protective Dept., 146 Mass. 596

Even the failure to perform duties imposed by statute, ordinance or regulation does not create civil liability unless there is a causal connection between that violation and the injury sustained. 

As was said in Milbury v. Turner Center System, 274 Mass. 358, at 362: "The general rule of civil liability for infractions of a penal statute is stated in Berdos v. Tremont & Suffolk 

Mills, 209 Mass. 489, at 492:'. a violation of a duty created by statute, resulting in damage to one of the class for whose benefit the duty was established, confers a right of action upon the injured person. . . It is not enough for a plaintiff to prove a violation of a statute concurrent with his injury, but he must go further and show that a condition to which the statute directly relates has a causal connection with his injury." 

When the plaintiff's injury or damage might have been avoided if the operator of the motor vehicle had done or omitted to do some particular thing or things, which thing or things would not have been done or omitted by a person exercising ordinary care, then the operator's conduct can be said to have been the proximate or probable cause of the plaintiff's injury or damage. 

, and cases cited 

McCrohan v. Davison, 187 Mass. 466, and cases cited

§98 (A) Physical Contact. 

(See: Section 435, page 557.)

To create proximate cause, it is not necessary that there be any physical contact or collision between the motor vehicle and any person, object, or other vehicle. car. 

There need not be physical contact by the defendant's The fact that defendant's car does not collide with the plaintiff's car is immaterial, if the accident was the result in whole or in part of the negligence of the defendant's driver. 

White v. Calcutt, 269 Mass. 252 (Defendant made left turn and plaintiff's auto collided with another auto)

So, where a parked automobile suddenly started and caused the plaintiff's automobile which was passing to collide with a tree, it was immaterial that there was no physical contact or collision between the motor vehicles or the parked motor vehicle and the plaintiff so long as the defendant's negligence was the efficient cause of the plaintiff's injury. 

Golden v. Carnevale, 273 Mass. 159, at 161

When a collision of automobiles is inevitable unless the speed of one of them is slackened, or its direction changed, and the defendant violates a statute giving the right of way to the vehicle approaching on her right and at right angles to the course of her motor car and the collision between the automobiles causes one of them to strike the plaintiff, the defendant's negligence is a question of fact. 

Fraser v. Flanders, 248 Mass. 62, at 66 

Lynn Gas & Elec. Co., v. Meriden Fire Ins. Co., 158 

Mass. 570, at 575 

62 A. L. R. 1186

As matter of law the jury would be justified in finding that the accident would not have happened if first driver had exercised ordinary care, and had obeyed the statute. 

Finnegan v. Winslow Skate Mfg. Co., 189 Mass. 580

$141

62 A. L. R. 1187

In upholding a verdict for the plaintiff, the court said, in Frazer v. Flanders, 248 Mass. 62, at 67: "While the train of events which brought about the result was the active efficient cause of the plaintiff's injuries, the primary cause may be the proximate cause, although it may have operated through successive instruments."

The material facts and the decision of the court, in 

Meech v. Sewall, 232 Mass. 460, at 461, were stated in the opinion as follows: "... the defendant, driving his motor car at great speed, in violation of the law of the road, and without sounding his horn, struck another motor car with such force as to cause the latter to strike and injure the plaintiff, a pedestrian in the exercise of due care. The testimony of the driver of the other car, that he momentarily accelerated its speed to twenty-two miles an hour in a vain effort to escape collision with the defendant, did not require the direction of a verdict in favor of the defendant. . . . Even if the negligence of the driver of the other car contributed to the injury of the plaintiff, that would not exonerate the defendant from the direct result of his own negligence operating in concurrence with that of the other driver." 

62 A. L. R. 1189 (B) Natural and Probable Consequences.

The liability arising from the negligent or other wrongful use or operation of a motor vehicle extends to the natural and probable consequences of such negligence or wrongdoing.

To make out liability on the part of a defendant it is enough to prove that the probable consequence of his acts was that harm of the same general character as that which

$98 

 came to the plaintiff would come to persons who stood in the same general relation to the defendant as the plaintiff.

But it is not necessary in order to make out liability on the part of a defendant that the particular series of events which ended in the injury to the plaintiff were the probable consequence of the defendant's acts. 

Ogden v. Aspinwall, 220 Mass. 100

Nor is it necessary that injury in the precise form in which it in fact resulted should have been foreseen. It is enough that it now appears to have been the underlying and probable consequence. 

Hill v. Winsor, 118 Mass. 251

So it is not essential that an operator of a motor vehicle should or could have foreseen or anticipated the particular result which actually occurs; it is sufficient if the act or omission was such that injury or damage might reasonably have been anticipated to result therefrom. 

Regan v. Cummings, 228 Mass. 414 

Death, five months after accident, of boy struck by motor vehicle may have a causal connection with it. Such as when in the process of healing from fracture and operation some clot "might have been organized causing an embolus or thrombus and then got loose" causing death.

This explanation may be the "probable cause" of death. 

The plaintiff is not required to prove precise organic negligent act and the death. 

Marlow v. Dyke, 269 Mass. 38 and 39 

McNicholas v. N. E. Tel. & Tel., 196 Mass. 138

The plaintiff is not required to prove precise organic changes which took place. 

Marlow v. Dyke, 269 Mass. 38, at 39
