(II) Distinction Between Cause and Condition. 

There is a distinction between negligence or other wrongful conduct in the use or operation of a motor vehicle which is a cause and negligence or such conduct which is a condition in such use or operation. 

Gaffney v. Bay State St. Ry., 221 Mass. 457 

Black v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R. Co., 193 Mass. 448 (Intoxication of passenger not cause but mere condition) 

The wrongful conduct concerning the use or operation of a motor vehicle, such as its position on the highway, its speed, or condition, may or may not be one of the causes of plaintiff's injury or damage.

Anti v. Boston El. Ry., 247 Mass. I

$145 

The mere fact that the plaintiff would not have sustained injury or damage if the motor vehicle had not been operated in the manner claimed or, if it had not been in the place where, and in the order which, it was are mere statements of essential condition and not the cause of the plaintiff's injury or damage. 

Newcomb v. Boston Protective Dept., 146 Mass. 596, at 604 Unlawful parking of a motor vehicle not contributing cause of fire engine colliding with it and pushing it on to the sidewalk where it strikes a pedestrian. 

Falk v. Finkelman, 268 Mass. 524, at 527

The unlawful parking is simply a condition and not a contributing cause. 

Falk v. Finkelman, 268 Mass. 524, at 527 and 528

The distinction is between that which directly and proximately produces, or helps to produce, a result as an efficient cause, and that which is a necessary condition or attendant circumstance of it. 

Walters v. Davis, 237 Mass. 206, at 209 

Rice v. Lowell Buick Co., 229 Mass. 53, at 57 

Newton v. McSweeney, 225 Mass. 402 

Driscoll v. Boston El. Ry., 223 Mass. 533, at 536 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, at 168 

Moran v. Dickinson, 204 Mass. 559, at 562 

McCarthy v. Morse, 197 Mass. 332 

Biggio v. Boston, 179 Mass. 356 

Smith v. Gardner, II Gray 418

The difference is also between the proximate cause of an injury or damage and a mere precedent, contemporaneous or attendant circumstance or condition of it. 

Carter v. Towne, 103 Mass. 507 (Illegal sale of gunpowder to child who delivered it to parents was not cause of explosion after redelivery to child by parents.)

$99 

As was said in Dudley v. Northampton Street Railway, 202 Mass. 443, at 446: "But there is a distinction between an unlawful act which is at least a contributing cause of the accident and one which is merely an attendant circumstance or a condition, though perhaps a necessary condition, of that accident." 

Professor Beale, in 33 Harvard Law Review, 633, at 637, has stated the distinction between cause and condition to be that: "Where the act is the failure merely of a legal duty, causation is established only when the doing of the act would have prevented the result; if the result would have happened just as it did whether the alleged actor had done his duty or not the failure to perform the duty was not a factor in the result, or, in other words, did not cause it." 

Even a violation of a statute, ordinance or regulation does not establish liability unless that violation was the cause of any injury or damage sustained as differentiated from the mere existence of a condition. 

Whipple v. Grandchamp, 261 Mass. 40 

McDonald v. Dundon, 242 Mass. 229

Dalton v. Great Atlantic & Pacific Tea Co., 241 Mass. 

400 

Farrell v. B. F. Sturtevant Co., 194 Mass. 431

Also, an intervening act may be merely a condition and not an independent cause breaking the chain of the causation. 

Burke v. Hodge, 217 Mass. 182

So, the maintenance of an unguarded, unlighted cellar hole at the edge of a parking space is merely a condition to an accident which occurs when an automobile gets out of control and backs into the hole. The maintenance of such hole is not a contribution to the cause of the accident. 

Fielding v. Poli Company, 274 Mass. 20, at 23

If the position of the motor vehicle is such as, in con-

$147 

 nection with ordinary and usual concurring causes, would naturally produce such injury or damage, that indicates that the motor vehicle contributed to such injury or damage. 

Newcomb v. Boston Protective Dept., 146 Mass. 596, at 604 But, even in that case, external causes may have been so exclusive in their operation, and so free from any relation to the position, condition, operation or use of the vehicle, as to have left that a mere condition, without agency in producing the result.

Newcomb v. Boston Protective Dept., 146 Mass. 596, at 604 What is a contributing cause of an accident is usually a question for a jury to be determined by the facts of the particular case.

Newcomb v. Boston Protective Dept., 146 Mass. 596, at 604 

Hall v. Ripley, 119 Mass. 135

Damon v. Scituate, 119 Mass. 66 

Spofford v. Harlow, 3 Allen 176 

Welch v. Wesson, 6 Gray 505 

(III) SECTION 100. 

Concurrent Causes. 

Two or more persons who by concurrent acts of negligence which although disconnected yet operate in combination to inflict injury or damage through the use or operation of a motor vehicle are jointly and severally liable for such injury or damage. The plaintiff, however, can have but one satisfaction in damages. 

Feneff v. Boston & Maine R. R., 196 Mass. 575 

62 A. L. R. 1183

If each contributes to the wrong, the proximate cause is the wrongful act in which they concurrently participate, whether the result causes instantaneous death, or injuries

διοι 

 which the sufferer survives. 

Fraser v. Flanders, 248 Mass. 62 

Bryant v. Boston El. Ry., 212 Mass. 62 

D'Almeida v. Boston & Maine R. R., 209 Mass. 81, at 87 

Feneff v. Boston & Maine R. R., 196 Mass. 575 

Doe v. Boston & Worcester St. Ry., 195 Mass. 168, at 171 

Oulighan v. Butler, 189 Mass. 287, at 293 

In Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 392, the plaintiff could recover from the driver of either of two automobiles which were racing along a road at excessive speed even though the motor vehicle which actually struck the plaintiff was attempting to pass and get out of the way of the other motor vehicle. 

SECTION 101. 

(IV) Intervening Cause. 

A wrongdoer is not liable for the result of separate, independent and intervening acts which break the chain of causation between his wrongful act and the plaintiff's injury or damage. Especially is this true when the intervening act was so improbable that it ordinarily would not have been anticipated. 

King v. Smart, 240 Mass. 174, at 177 

Horan v. Watertown, 217 Mass. 185 

Bellino v. Columbus Construction Co., 188 Mass. 430 

Glassey v. Worcester C. St. Ry. Co., 185 Mass. 315 

Tutein v. Hurley, 98 Mass. 211

An intervening act or cause in this connection is one that interrupts the current of responsible connection between the defendant's negligence or other misconduct and the plaintiff's injury or damage.

In order to be an intervening cause, the intermediate act or omission must entirely supersede the original negli-

SIOI 

 gence or wrongful conduct and must be in itself responsible for the injury or damage, also, it must be of such character that it reasonably would not have been expected to be foreseen or anticipated by the wrongdoer.

The intermediate act or omission must supersede the original negligence or wrongful conduct and be sufficient of itself to stand as cause of the plaintiff's injury, to relieve the original wrongdoer from liability. 

An intervening act or cause is any new force or power which has intervened between the defendant's original wrongful conduct and the plaintiff's injury or damage. If the new force or power is of itself sufficient to cause the plaintiff's injury or damage, the other original misconduct must be considered too remote.

The intervening act or cause which will relieve a defendant from liability for injury or damage must be an independent cause which intervenes between the original wrongful act of the defendant and the injury or damage of the plaintiff, and produces a result which otherwise would not have happened.

But the wrongdoer is liable for intervening acts which were the direct and proximate result of his wrongdoing if he reasonably should have expected them to occur and taken precaution to guard against their effect. 

So, if it required both the defendant's original wrongful conduct and the intermediate act or omission to produce the result, or if both contributed thereto as concurrent forces, the presence and assistance of one will not justify the other, because the original misconduct would still be the efficient cause of the injury. 

Sieplinski v. Severn, 269 Mass. 261

Guinan v. Famous Players-L. Corp., 267 Mass. 501 

Fraser v. Flanders, 248 Mass. 62, at 67 

McDonald v. Dundon, 242 Mass. 229, at 233

διοι

Although a person who commits a wrong in connection with a motor vehicle is liable to every person injured, whose injury is the underlying and probable consequence of the misconduct, the establishment of liability is to be found, not in the number of intervening events or agents, but in their character and in the underlying and probable connection between the wrong done and the injurious consequences. 

McDonald v. Snelling, 14 Allen 290, at 296 

As was said in Milbury v. Turner Center System, 274 

Mass. 358, at 361: "If other happenings cause or contribute toward the injury or intervene between the violation and the injury, the mere circumstance that there have intervened, between the wrongful cause and the injurious consequence, acts produced by the volition of animals or of human beings, does not necessarily make the result so remote that no action can be maintained. The test is to be found, not in the number of intervening events or agents, but in their connection between the wrong done and the injurious consequence. 

So long as it affirmatively appears that the mischief is attributable to the negligence as a result which might reasonably have been foreseen as probable, the legal liability continues."

So having a dog near the operator was a violation of 

G: L. c. 90, s. 13 which requires that nothing shall interfere with the operation of the motor vehicle and consequently the dog's becoming sick should have been anticipated by the operator and guarded against and was not such an intervening act as would break the chain of causation. 

Morse v. Sturgis, 262 Mass. 312 

Wellington v. Downer Kerosene Oil Co., 104 Mass. 64

$102 

The act of a third person intervening and contributing a condition necessary to the injurious effect of the original negligence, will not excuse the first wrongdoer if such act ought to have been foreseen.

Lane v. Atlantic Works, III Mass. 136 

In Slater v. T. C. Baker Co., 261 Mass. 424, where an automobile was left unlocked on a public way with the key in the lock and the brake not pulled up, both in violation of G. L. c. 90, s. 57, the court said, at 425: "The jury undoubtedly could find that if locked the automobile could not have been purloined, set in motion and operated... But the larceny of the automobile and its use by the thief were intervening independent acts which the defendant was not bound to anticipate and to guard against. 

Horan v. Watertown, 217 Mass. 185 at 186. 

Jacobs v. New York etc. Co., 212 Mass. 96, at 99. 

Glassey v. Worcester C. St. Ry., 185 Mass. 315.”

SECTION 102. 

(V) Remote Cause. 

Although there may have been negligent or other unlawful conduct in the operation or use of a motor vehicle, neither the operator nor the owner nor any person responsible for its operation or use is liable for injury or damage resulting therefrom if such negligent or unlawful conduct was merely the remote cause thereof. 

Slater v. T. C. Baker Co., 261 Mass. 424, at 425

A cause is rendered remote when after its origin some new intervening force, acting independently, takes advantage of the original cause and accomplishes the particular injury or damage which would not have been the probable and natural effect of the original cause.

§153 

 SECTION 103. 

(VI) Speculative or Conjectural Cause. 

See: Section 98, page 136. 

Where the cause of the injury for which damages are sought is left to conjecture, surmise, speculation or guesswork, and has no solid foundation in established facts, there can be no recovery. 

Gillis v. Boston, Revere Beach & Lynn R. R., 266 

Mass. 481

Lyford v. Boston & Maine R. R., 227 Mass. IO 

Bigwood v. Boston & Northern St. Ry., 209 Mass 345 

Kansas City S. Ry. Co. v. Jones, 276 U. S. 303 

Chicago, M. & St. P. R. R. Co., v. Coogan, 271 U. S. 472, at 478 

But see: 

McNaughton v. Johnson, 242 U. S. 346

The burden of proof is on the plaintiff to establish that his injury or damage was caused proximately or directly by the defendant's wrongful conduct..

So, to render the defendant responsible the proof must be established by a preponderance of evidence that there is a causal connection between the plaintiff's injury or damage and the defendant's wrongful conduct.

However, if all the evidence in the case leaves the cause of the plaintiff's injury or damage in a state of surmise, conjecture or speculation, then the plaintiff has not sustained the burden of proof and can not recover.

And also, if the entire evidence fails to disclose by a preponderance that there was a causal connection between the plaintiff's injury or damage and the defendant's wrongful conduct or, in other words, that the defendant's wrongful conduct was the proximate cause of the plaintiff's injury or damage, then the plaintiff has not sustained the

§104 

 necessary requisite concerning his burden of proof and can not recover. 

Hirst v. Chevrolet Motor Co., 261 Mass. 155 

Cohen v. Henry Siegel Co., 220 Mass. 215, at 219 

Childs v. American Exp. Co., 197 Mass. 337

SECTION 104. 

h. Unavoidable Occurrences. 

Injury or damage caused by a motor vehicle without any negligent or other wrongful conduct on the part of the operator, owner or person in control is regarded as an unavoidable accident and creates no liability. 

Bolin v. Corliss Co., 262 Mass. 115

This result follows from the rule of law that the operation or use of a motor vehicle does not make the operator, owner or person in control an insurer against injury or damage caused by it and no liability exists unless such injury or damage is caused by actionable negligence.

Such an instance occurs when a portion of the vehicle, such as a tire or a rim, suddenly separates and rolls along the highway. 

Nager v. Reid, 240 Mass. 211 

Regan v. Cummings, 228 Mass. 414

As was said in McAvoy v. Boston Elevated Railway, 275 Mass. 9, at 12: "Cause of the accident has come from the lawful operation by lawful means of an authorized instrumentality, and where any damage or injury that has resulted may have come without any negligence of the defendant, but may have arisen merely as an unavoidable accident from the careful and skilful exercise of its lawful rights in spite of the observance of all proper precautions, there no liability can arise without some affirmative evidence of negli-

$155 

 gence. In such a case the happening of the accident with the resulting injury is as likely to have come without the fault of the defendant as to have been due to its negligence, and the presumption of fact upon which the doctrine res ipsa loquitur is based does not arise; the inference of negligence cannot be drawn without some evidence to support it." 

Sheehan v. Boston El. Ry., 220 Mass. 210 

Carney v. Boston El. Ry., 212 Mass. 179, at 180

Curtin v. Boston El. Ry., 194 Mass. 260 

Unexplained starting of a motor vehicle may come within this rule. 

But see: 

Glaser v. Schroeder, 269 Mass. 337, at 340 (Res ipsa loquitur applied where automobile parked facing up hill on steep grade and rolled backwards down street, crashing into store)

SECTION 105. 

i. Sudden Emergency

Emergency Imminent Startling Danger. 

See: Section 280, page 345. 

Peril - 

A person who is faced with a sudden emergency is not held to the same degree of judgment and presence of mind as would otherwise be required of him under circumstances not indicating sudden peril. 

Austin v. East. Mass. St. Ry., 269 Mass. 420 

Robinson v. Donaldson, 251 Mass. 355, at 357 and 358 

Tuttle v. Conn. Valley St. Ry., 239 Mass. 553 

Neafsey v. Szemeta, 235 Mass. 160 

Emery v. Miller, 231 Mass. 243 

Lemay v. Springfield St. Ry. Co., 210 Mass. 63, at 67

$105 

Steverman v. Boston El. Ry., 205 Mass. 508, at 512 

Hanley v. Boston El. Ry., 201 Mass. 55, at 58 

Gannon v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R. Co., 173 Mass. 40, at 41 and 42 

Hawks v. Locke, 139 Mass. 205, at 209 

Linnehan v. Sampson, 126 Mass. 506

So, the operator of a motor vehicle when confronted with a sudden danger which places him in a position of imminent peril to himself, the occupants of the motor vehicle, or the motor vehicle itself, without sufficient time in which to determine with certainty the best course to pursue, is not held to the same accuracy of judgment as is required of him under ordinary circumstances and he is not liable for injury or damage caused by the motor vehicle, or precluded from recovering for injuries to himself or to the motor vehicle if an accident occurs even though upon after-thought it might be considered that he could have acted more judiciously. 

Chief Justice Rugg said in Massie v. Barker, 224 Mass. 420, at 423: "The law as to drivers of motor vehicles is not different from that which governs other persons. The standard required is that of the reasonably prudent person under all the circumstances. If some unforeseen emergency occurs, which naturally would overpower the judgment of the ordinary careful driver of a motor vehicle, so that momentarily or for a time he is not capable of intelligent action and as a result injury is inflicted upon a third person, the driver is not negligent. The law does not require supernatural poise or self control. But no one safely can drive motor vehicles amid the distractions and dangers likely to be encountered on the modern highway and street who is not reasonably steady of nerve, quick in forming an opinion and calm in executing a design. Whether the conduct of

§157 

 the defendant's agent measured up to the standard of common caution for the driver of a motor vehicle under all the circumstances, was a question of fact. "Whether the surprise occasioned by the sally of the dog from the yard into the highway was such as reasonably to cause the driver of the truck to be governed for the instant by impulse rather than by sound judgment, whether it was a discomposing exigency or a usual peril of the road, was a matter for the jury.”

SECTION 106. 

(I) When Created by Conduct of Person In voking Doctrine. 

But this doctrine does not apply in favor of a person who through his own negligence or wrongful conduct creates the sudden emergency or peril. 

Fogg v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R. Co., 223 Mass. 444

The liability of an operator of a motor vehicle is not limited to negligence at the time an emergency arose if the emergency was created by the antecedent negligence of that operator himself. 

Hennessey v. Moynihan, 272 Mass. 165, at 168 

Tripp v. Taft, 219 Mass. 81, at 84 

Rasmussen v. Whipple, 211 Mass. 546, at 548

But when the defendant claims that he acted under the stress of sudden danger or emergency, the jury is not required to believe this testimony and find such to be the fact. 

Rae v. Checker Taxi Company, 272 Mass. 510, at 513 

Massie v. Barker, 224 Mass. 420 

27 A. L. R. 1197 

6 A. L. R. 676

$107

General Laws Chapter 90, Section 7 (Acts 1921, 189,

Every automobile shall be provided with at least two braking systems, each with separate means of application, each operating directly or indirectly on at least two wheels and each of which shall suffice alone to stop said automobile within a proper distance as defined in said rules and regulations; provided, that if said systems are connected, combined or have any part in common, such systems shall be so constructed that a breaking of any one element thereof will not leave the automobile without brakes acting directly or indirectly on at least two wheels. One braking system shall be so constructed that it can be set to hold the automobile stationary. Every motor cycle shall be provided with at least one brake adequate to stop it within a proper distance as defined as aforesaid. Every motor cycle so operated shall be provided with a muffler or other suitable device to prevent unnecessary noise and with a suitable bell, horn or other means of signalling, and with suitable lamps; and automobiles shall be provided with a lock, a key or other device to prevent such vehicle from being set in motion by unauthorized persons, or otherwise, contrary to the will of the owner or person in charge thereof. 

Every automobile operated during the period from one

 half an hour after sunset to one-half an hour before sunrise shall display at least two white lights, or lights of yellow or amber tint, or if parked within the limits of a way, one white light on the side of the automobile nearer the centre of the way, and every motor cycle so operated at least one white light, or light of yellow or amber tint, and every such motor cycle with a side-car attached, in addition, one such light on the front of the side-car, and every motor truck, trailer and commercial motor vehicle, used solely as such, having a carrying capacity of three tons or over, in addition, a green light attached to the extreme left of the front of such vehicle, so attached and adjusted as to indicate the extreme left lateral extension of the vehicle or load, which shall in all cases aforesaid be visible not less than two hundred feet in the direction toward which the vehicle is proceeding or facing; and every such motor vehicle shall display at least one red light in the reverse direction; provided, that an automobile need display no light when parked within the limits of a way in a space in which unlighted parking is permitted by the rules or regulations of the board or officer having control of such way. General Laws Chapter 90, Section 16, provides that: 

"No person shall operate a motor vehicle nor shall any owner of such vehicle permit it to be operated, in or over any way, public or private, whether laid out under authority of law or otherwise, which motor vehicles are prohibited from using, provided notice of such prohibition is conspicuously posted at the entrance to such a way. No person operating a motor vehicle shall in a thickly settled or business district open the muffler cut-out or sound a bell, horn or other device for signalling so as to make a harsh, objectionable or unreasonable noise, or at any time permit such motor vehicle to make any unnecessary noise, by opening the muffler cut-out, or otherwise, or permit any unreasonable amount of smoke to escape from such vehicle.

Reasonable care in the use, operation and ownership of a motor vehicle requires that the motor vehicle and the equipment attached thereto be in such condition as not to render it unsafe or dangerous either to persons in the motor vehicle or to travellers upon the highway. 

General Laws Chapter 90, Section 13, provides that: 

"No chauffeur or operator, when operating a motor vehicle, shall have or permit. to be on or in such vehicle or on or about his person anything which may interfere

$161 

 with or impede the proper operation of the vehicle or of any of the machinery or appliances by which the vehicle is operated or controlled. No person having control or charge of a motor vehicle shall allow such vehicle to stand in any way and remain unattended without first locking or making it fast or effectively setting the brakes thereon, and stopping the motor of said vehicle."

General Laws Chapter 90, Section 7A (Acts 1929, 

252) provides that: "The registrar shall include in the rules and regulations prepared by him under section thirty-one, rules and regulations providing for the periodic inspection of all motor vehicles and trailers, for the purpose of determining whether they are properly equipped and maintained in good working order, as required by the preceding section." 

But the failure to observe some provision of law relating to the condition of a motor vehicle or its equipment will not deprive that motor vehicle of its rights upon the public highway if it is properly registered. 

Farr v. Whitney, 260 Mass. 193, at 196

Lonergan v. Amer. Ry. Exp. Co.. 250 Mass. 30 

So, the operation of a motor vehicle which tends to zigzag, excessively shaking or wabbling, may constitute negligence and the operator who continues to drive without ascertaining the cause of the irregularity of its motion, and therefrom determining whether it is safe to drive in the condition in which he finds it, is guilty of not exercising proper care. 

Chooljian v. Nahigian, 273 Mass. 396, at 398

Advancing the spark lever to such an extent that it "kicks back" when a person is attempting to crank it is negligence. 

Card v. Turner Centre D. Assn., 224 Mass. 525 

Norris, v. Allen, 217 Mass. 573

§108 

2. Brakes.

SECTION 108. 

The brakes of a motor vehicle should be in such condition as to take hold and stop it whenever the operator so desires in order that he may constantly have the vehicle under control.

Murphy v. New England Transportation Co., 273 

Mass. 275, at 276 

So, brakes which fail to hold because of grease inside the brake bands, and which permit or cause the vehicle to leave the road and injure a person on the sidewalk, are in a negligent and unsafe condition so as to render the owner and operator liable.

Foley v. Wesson Meml. Hospital, 246 Mass. 363 

63 A. L. R. 402

Although the skidding of the vehicle which preceded the collision with the tree is not of itself evidence of negligence, much less of gross negligence, yet the skidding may be found to be part of, or the result from, negligence or gross negligence, when at least one of the reasons for the skidding was defective brakes which caused the vehicle on the day before the accident to skid to the left when the brakes were applied; and this condition of the brakes was known to the driver, and could have been remedied before the trip on which the accident occurred. 

Logan v. Reardon, 274 Mass. 83, at 86

When the application of brakes which the operator knows to be defective cause the motor vehicle to swerve to the left because there is no equalization of brakes on the rear wheels, it can be found that the defective brakes are causally related to the accident. 

Isaacson v. Boston, etc. St. Ry., 1932 A. S. 385, at 393 

3. Chains.

SECTION 109. 

The absence or presence of chains on a motor vehicle upon the highway when that highway is slippery on ac-

S163 

 count of snow, ice, rain or other things, merely presents a question of proper care for the determination of the jury. 

Lonergan v. Amer. Ry. Exp. Co., 250 Mass. 30

So, the operator of a motor vehicle who removes his chains so as to prevent slipping or skidding, and then travels ten miles an hour on a snowy, slippery road without applying his brakes because he thought the vehicle would be held by its motor, merely presents a question of his proper care.

Jones v. Plotkin, 273 Mass. 24 

Whether it is safe to operate a limousine on an icy highway without chains is not for an expert to say but is a question of fact for jury. 

Reed v. Edison Elec. Illg. Co., 225 Mass. 163, at 167

SECTION 111. 

5. Mirror or Reflector.

Although General Laws Chapter 90, Sections 7 and 9, requires a mirror or reflector on a truck or bus, it can not be ruled as matter of law that the failure to comply with the statute is a contributing cause to the injury but it can be found as a fact that if the automobile were equipped with a mirror or reflector, the accident could have been avoided. 

Farr v. Whitney, 260 Mass. 193, at 196

§112 SECTION 112. 

6. Overloading Vehicle. 

Overloading does not effect such a material change in the vehicle that it is no longer the vehicle originally registered. 

Cook v. Cole, 273 Mass. 557, at 562 

Wallace v. New Bedford & O. St. Ry., 259 Mass. 20 

Compare: Nichols v. Holyoke St. Ry., 250 Mass. 88

Therefore, the vehicle is not a nuisance on the highway within the principle laid down in 

Cook v. Cole, 273 Mass. 557, at 563 

Brown v. Alter, 251 Mass. 223 

McDonald v. Dundon, 242 Mass. 229

Koonovsky v. Quellette, 226 Mass. 474 

Nor is its operation prohibited within G. L. c. 90, s. 9 as amended by Acts 1922, c. 303, s. 3 (see now Acts 1928, c. 381, s. 3) on any way of an unregistered motor vehicle. 

Cook v. Cole, 273 Mass. 557, at 563

No statute prohibits the operation of a motor truck where the truck and load exceed the aggregate "weight" and maximum carrying capacity for which it was registered, or imposes a penalty therefor unless such operation is in violation of an authorized rule or regulation. 

Cook v. Cole, 273 Mass. 557, at 563 

See: G. L. c. 90, s. 20 (as amended by Acts 1922, c. 

130, s. 31, added by Acts 1924, c. 457) 

7. Projections. 

SECTION 113. 

The mere fact that the running-board of an automobile carries baggage or luggage is not negligence of itself, even if it projects beyond the running-board, so long as it does not unreasonably interfere with the use of the highway by other travellers.

$165 

However, while not in itself negligence, yet the jury may or may not find that because of that fact the operation of the automobile entailed somewhat greater care upon its operator. 

Coates v. Bates, 265 Mass. 444

The operator, however, has a right to assume that other travellers will exercise reasonable care to avoid coming in contact with the automobile or any luggage projecting therefrom. 

Coates v. Bates, 265 Mass. 444 

8. Repairs. 

SECTION 114. 

Where a person strikes an automobile rim with a hammer near a sidewalk and continues to do so knowing that particles of the rim are flying off as high as his head so that one of the particles gets into the eye of a traveller on the sidewalk, the injuries are a probable consequence against which the person hammering should have taken precautions and such consequence was not merely mischance in the course of prudent conduct of that person who was negligent. 

Perlman v. Burrows, 270 Mass. 182

Guinan v. Famous Players-L. Corp., 267 Mass. 501 

Nichols v. Boston El. Ry., 231 Mass. 299, at 300 

Dulligan v. Barber Asphalt Paving Co., 201 Mass. 227, at 231 

Hill v. Winsor, 118 Mass. 251, at 259 

Brown v. Kendall, 6 Cush. 292, at 297

SECTION 115. 

9. Tires and Rims.

The mere separation of a tire and rim so that it comes off and strikes a traveller on the highway does not by

§116 

 itself show negligence or that its condition could be discovered by reasonable inspection. 

Bolin v. Corliss Co., 262 Mass. 115. 

Nager v. Reid, 240 Mass. 211

But, after a tire blows out and the operator continues to travel thereon for twenty feet when he could have stopped almost instantly, the separation of the locking rim so that it strikes a traveller may be found to be negligence. The negligence is constituted by the operator's failure to stop the car soon enough so as to prevent the release of the rim. 

Regan v. Cummings, 228 Mass. 414 

However, excessive speed causing skidding which bursts tire which then hits and kills pedestrian, creates liability. 

Roach v. Hinchcliff, 214 Mass. 267

§171 

 2. Intoxication. 

SECTION 120. 

It does not follow that because an operator of a motor vehicle involved in an accident was drunk that he was necessarily guilty of ordinary or gross negligence. 

Bertera v. Cuneo, 273 Mass. 181, at 183 

So, a passenger in a vehicle of a drunken driver going about 25 or 30 miles an hour swaying from side to side and striking something and turning over because another vehicle in a line of cars going in the opposite direction suddenly left that line and pulled out to the left so as to turn on to the defendant's side of the road, does not raise a question of fact that the drunken driver was grossly negligent. 

Bertera v. Cuneo, 273 Mass. 181, at 183 

In the last cited case, the court says at page 183: "... But however unsafe it may be for a drunken [driver] to operate an automobile especially upon a public highway, some act of negligence must be shown in addition to drunkenness to make out a case of gross negligence. [There must be an indication that the operator was careless.] He was on his right-hand side of the way... he was driving carefully. The possibility of danger is always present when a drunken person attempts to operate a motor vehicle, but if he acts as carefully as a sober man of ordinary prudence under the existing circumstances he is not negligent. The fact that the car of the defendant as he got 'near the place of the accident . . . switched and changed' does not mean that he was careless or negligent. The switching and changing may have been necessary to avoid a collision. A sober and reasonably prudent operator might have acted in the same manner under conditions then existing. It is not shown that the defendant was negligent in running into the parked sedan. He had to turn to the right to avoid a collision with the automobile coming from the north which had left the line of travel and was on

$120 

 the defendant's side of the road. It does not appear how near to the defendant the parked sedan was located when the collision with the automobile moving south was imminent except that the sedan was 'parked off the hardened part of the highway.' It is not shown that the sedan was lighted, that the defendant saw it or could have avoided striking it. [But see] Bryne v. Great Atlantic & Pacific 

Tea Co., 269 Mass. 130, in [which] case a motor truck struck an excavator standing on the highway between eight and ten o'clock of a September morning. [and there was sufficient evidence to justify a finding that the defendant was negligent and the application of the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur.]." 

56 A. L. R. 327

Law of the Road CHAPTER VI. 

LAW OF THE ROAD. 

SECTION 121. 

A. RULES BASED ON CUSTOM. 

The law of the road is applicable to the use and operation of motor vehicles. 

Rice v. Lowell Buick Co., 229 Mass. 53 

Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 392

The rules relating to the law of the road are confined to public highways. But a public highway is not necessarily the exact limits designated by governmental authorities.

So, the macadam is not necessarily the travelled way, the travelled part may extend beyond. It is a question for jury on the evidence. It is that part of the way which with the knowledge and acquiescence of the town is used for public travel within the located limits of the way. B. 

Dupues v. Billerica, 260 Mass. 210 

Weare v. Fitchburg, 110 Mass. 334

SECTION 122. 

GOVERNMENTAL REGULATIONS. 

The law of the road is set forth in General Laws Chapter 89 Sections 1 to 10, inclusive. 

This statute does not apply to pedestrians. 

Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 392, at 395 

Lynch v. Fisk Rubber Co., 209 Mass. 16, at 17 cases cited.

Nor is it applicable to street cars. 

G. L. c. 89, ss. 6 and 6A. 

Under G. L. c. 89, s. 2, a motor vehicle travelling in the same direction as another vehicle is required to pass that

§123 

 other vehicle ahead by driving to the left of the middle of the travelled part of the way. 

Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 392, at 395 

Lynch v. Fisk Rubber Co., 209 Mass. 16, at 17 and cases cited.

The following cases explain the meaning of the words point of intersection as set forth in G. L. c. 89, s. 8.

(See now: Acts 1929, c. 147)

SECTION 124. 

D. ASSUMING OBSERVANCE BY OTHER TRAVELLERS. 

The travelling public act on the assumption that regulations in the use of public streets will be observed; their safety requires that this shall be done.

$175 

Law of the Road 

An operator of a motor vehicle may assume that other operators will not travel over a one way street in the wrong direction in violation of law, and may act according to this assumption. 

E. JUSTIFICATION OR EXCUSE FOR VIOLATION. 

SECTION 125. 

It rarely can be ruled as matter of law that the law of the road has no application and that the defendant in attempting to pass on the right of the vehicle ahead contrary to the statute was prudent under the circumstances. 

Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 392, at 395 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, at 163

SECTION 126. 

2. Directions of Police Officer or Public Official. 

The signal of a traffic officer does not authorize nor justify an operator in so driving a motor vehicle as to collide with a person or another vehicle in the highway. 

Wilson v. Freeman, 271 Mass. 438, at 440

 CHAPTER VII. 

CARE REQUIRED IN OPERATION UNDER PARTICULAR CIRCUMSTANCES. 

A. POSITION ON HIGHWAY. 

SECTION 127. 

1. Right to Use Any Part of Highway. 

Where an accident happens at or near the junction of two streets that run at right angles to each other and the driver of the automobile is turning around so as to go back in an opposite direction upon the same street on which he came, the operator has a right to make that turn and use any part of the street that he is coming into, subject only to the rights of other people who might be there. 

Johnson v. Shaw, 204 Mass. 165, at 168 

Comm. v. Barney, 258 Mass. 609

When two vehicles meet in a street, it is the duty of each of them, as seasonably as they can, to get each on his own right-hand side of the travelled part of that way. 

But that law does not compel a man always to be on the right side. He can use any part of the street, so long as he is not interfering with the rights of other people. 

Johnson v. Shaw, 204 Mass. 165, at 168

SECTION 128. 

2. One Way Street. 

Prior to the enactment of General Laws Chapter 89, Section 10, a vehicle which proceeded in the wrong direction on a one-way street was an outlaw; the operator of a taxicab was liable to a passenger injured through the operator's negligence in proceeding on a one-way street, Rea v. Checker Taxi Company, 272 Mass. 510, at 512;

177 

 and the operator and all the passengers of the motor vehicle were trespassers. 

But now this statute (G. L. c. 89, s. 10-Acts 1930, c. 

57, s. 1) provides that: "The violation by the operator or driver of a motor or other vehicle of any rule, regulation, ordinance or by-law, limiting traffic on any specified way to traffic moving in one direction shall not, in respect to any civil liability render such operator or driver, or such vehicle or other occupant thereof, a trespasser upon such way." 

B. KEEPING LOOK OUT. 

SECTION 129. 

Motor vehicles must be used very much like other vehicles and it is the operator's or driver's duty to look out for persons and other vehicles on the highway. 

Comm. v. Horsfall, 213 Mass. 232, at 235

So, it is negligence for an operator of a motor vehicle to drive upon a sidewalk to enter his own premises without observing children who are crossing the sidewalk and without acting with due care in view of their presence 

Hirrel v. Lacey, 274 Mass. 431, at 435 particularly, when the children on the sidewalk are in plain view of the operator and there is nothing to obstruct his view: 

Hirrel v. Lacey, 274 Mass. 431, at 435 

King v. Weitzman, 267 Mass. 447 

, at 282 and 283

Also it may be negligence on the part of an operator if he allows his vehicle to overtake and strike a woman walking along the right-hand side of a highway on a rainy

$130 

 evening because he does not see her or does not see her soon enough. 

Booth v. Meagher, 224 Mass. 472 

67 A. L. R. 104

Also it may be negligence of an operator in failing to see a pedestrian who is walking at night along the righthand side of a frozen country road and injuring him by approaching without notice from the rear, even though the operator is temporarily blinded by lights from an electric car or because the pedestrian's clothing is very near the color of the road.

Anthony v. Boston and Maine R.R., A.S. 1931 A.S. 

1697 (Failure to see train approaching grade crossing) 

Stone v. Mullen, 257 Mass. 344 (Unlighted truck in road) 

Alpert v. Ellis, 236 Mass. 404 

Booth v. Meagher, 224 Mass. 472 

Rogers v. Phillips, 217 Mass. 52 (Operator looking to left did not see bicyclist approaching from right) 

Comm. v. Horsfall, 213 Mass. 232 

Lynch v. Fisk Rubber Co., 209 Mass. 16 

Gray v. Batchelder, 208 Mass. 441 

67 A. L. R. 104

When there is nothing to obstruct the view of the plaintiff and his speed is slow, which would enable him to stop quickly if he is careful of the safety of others, a collision with the plaintiff pedestrian indicates the defendant's lack of such care. 

Wilson v. Freeman, 271 Mass. 438, at 440

SECTION 130. 

2. Obstruction of View or Interference with Vision. 

The operator should enable himself to have a clear vision of the roadway, other travellers, pedestrians and all things

§ 179 

necessary for reasonably safe operation of the motor vehicle. 

Comm v. Arone, 265 Mass. 128 

Where a driver does not see a pedestrian until after his car has hit the pedestrian and immediately after the accident the windshield wiper is found to be motionless and the windshield glass covered with mist, it may be found that the driver was negligent in failing to see and avoid the pedestrian. 

A jury which views the scene of the accident, the premises, the driveway, the width of the street and its grade, may determine, without other evidence, the extent to which the view of an operator approaching the place would be obscured. 

Brown v. Daley, 273 Mass. 432, at 435 3. Lights. 

SECTION 131. 

General Laws Chapter 85, Section 15, provides that: 

"Every vehicle, whether stationary or in motion, on any public way, shall have attached to it a light or lights which shall be so displayed as to be visible from the front and the rear during the period from one-half an hour after sunset to one-half an hour before sunrise; provided that this section shall not apply to any vehicle which is designed to be propelled by hand, or to any vehicle designed for the transportation, as its principal freight, of hay or straw while loaded with such freight, and that upon the written application of the owner of a vehicle and the presentation of reasons therefor the division may, in writing, in such form and subject to such requirements as it may elect, and without expense to the applicant, exempt said vehicle from the provisions of this section for such period of time as said division may elect."

S131 

"Acting in pursuance of the authority conferred by section 31 of chapter 90 of the General Laws, the rules and regulations relative to lights on motor vehicles made by the Registrar of Motor Vehicles on June 1, 1921, are hereby rescinded, and the following are declared adopted in lieu thereof:- 

"SECTION 1. If and when, during the period when motor vehicles are required to display lights by section 7 of chapter 90 of the General Laws and amendments thereof, there is not sufficient light within the travelled portion of the highway to make clearly visible all vehicles, persons or substantial objects within a distance of at least 160 feet, no automobile shall be operated unless it is equipped with two lighted headlamps of approximately equal candle power which shall throw sufficient light ahead to make clearly visible all vehicles, persons or substantial objects upon the roadway within a distance of 100 feet; and no motorcycle shall be operated unless it is equipped with one headlamp which shall throw sufficient light ahead to make clearly visible all vehicles, persons or substantial objects upon the roadway within a distance of 115 feet. 

"SECTION 2. Every lens or other device designed to prevent glaring rays, the use of which on motor vehicles has been approved by the registrar, as provided in said section 7, shall be arranged, adjusted and operated in accordance with the requirements of the certificate approving the use thereof and so as to avoid dangerous glare or dazzle, and so that no dangerous or dazzling light, when measured twenty-five feet or more ahead of the lamp on a surface of uniform grade, shall rise to a greater height above such uniform grade than the centers of the lamps, providing that in no case shall dangerous or dazzling light rise to a greater height than forty-two inches above such grade at a distance of seventy-five feet or more ahead of such vehicle. Every lamp, bulb or light used

$181 

 in any headlamp on a motor vehicle shall be of such candle power as may be specified for the approved device in the certificate approving the use thereof. Every reflector which is used as a part of such headlamp, shall have a highly polished reflecting surface of silver, glass, or such other material as shall be approved by the registrar after satisfactory tests have been made, and every such reflecting surface shall be free from dents, rust, and other imperfections. 

"SECTION 3. The operator of every motor vehicle shall permit any police officer or motor vehicle investigator and examiner to inspect the headlighting equipment of such motor vehicle and to make such tests as may be necessary to determine whether the provisions of section 2 are being complied with."

SECTION 132. 

4. Traffic Signs and Lights. 

The erection of signs and traffic lights is provided for by General Laws Chapter 85, Section 1 and 2. 

SECTION 133. 

5. Look Out to Side and Rear. 

Testimony of a driver that he looked back several times before he turned but did not observe the plaintiff's car although his view was unobstructed, warrants a finding either that the driver did not in fact look behind him, or, if he did so, that his failure to see the plaintiff was due to carelessness on his part. 

Clay v. Pope & Cottle Co., 273 Mass. 40, at 45 

Gibb v. Hardwick, 241 Mass. 546, at 548

Haynes v. Boston El. Ry., 204 Mass. 249

$134 

 C. SIGNALS AND WARNING OF APPROACH. 

SECTION 134. 

No rule of law prescribes the form of signal. 

Kane v. Metropolitan Coal Co., 274 Mass. 63, at 65

Negligence may be predicated on the failure to give any signal or upon the failure to give a timely signal. 

Kane v. Metropolitan Coal Co., 274 Mass. 63, at 65 (Turning in front of other traffic)

Clay v. Pope & Cottle Co., 273 Mass. 40 White v. Calcutt, 269 Mass. 252 

Di Rienzo v. Goldfarb, 257 Mass. 272

The question of negligence of the operator in injuring a pedestrian walking along a highway as affected by the failure to give timely signal or warning of approach of motor vehicle is usually one for the jury to consider in connection with all the existing circumstances. 

Alpert v. Ellis, 236 Mass. 40 

Gifford v. Jennings, 190 Mass. 54 67 A. L. R. IOI 

So, in determining whether to direct a verdict for the defendant the trial judge is bound to assume that the defendant did not blow his horn if that question is in issue. 

Dzura v. Phillips, 275 Mass. 283, at 288

The evidence must be affirmative that no horn or other signal was sounded. It is not enough that the evidence is negative and of no value to show that a horn was not blown. 

Jean v. Nester, 261 Mass. 442, at 445 

Gibb v. Hardwick, 241 Mass. 546

But testimony by nearby witnesses that they heard no horn sounded is evidence that it was not sounded and in some circumstances raises the inference that if the

183 

 horn had been sounded the attention of the witnesses would have been attracted and they would have heard it. 

Hough v. Boston El. Ry., 262 Mass. 91, at 94 

Doherty v. Boston & Northern St. Ry., 207 Mass. 27 

Menard v. Boston and Maine R.R., 150 Mass. 386, at 387 and 388 So the fact that a witness who watched the defendant's vehicle approaching heard no signal sounded is evidence that no signal was sounded. 

Shepherd v. Nirenstein, 273 Mass. 7 

Pawloski v. Hess, 253 Mass. 478 (Effect of failure to give signal) 

Kaminski v. Fournier, 235 Mass. 51 

Creedon v. Galvin, 226 Mass. 140 (Time to give signal)

SECTION 135. 

2. Hand Signal.

The hand signal is proper and is the form in frequent use. 

Kane v. Metropolitan Coal Co., 274 Mass. 63, at 65

So, a driver who gives a hand signal of his intent to make a turn is not responsible because the signal is misinterpreted by other operators or pedestrians. 

Kane v. Metropolitan Coal Co., 274 Mass. 63, at 65

The failure to give a hand signal may be considered as evidence of negligence. 

Clay v. Pope & Cottle Co., 273 Mass. 40, at 44 (Left turn) 

Di Rienzo v. Goldfarb, 257 Mass. 272, at 281

Even though there is no contact where damage is caused as the result of a collision with a third car due perhaps, in part, to the defendant turning across the road without

§136 

 putting his hand out in warning thus obstructing view of other car, there is evidence of negligence. 

White v. Calcutt, 269 Mass. 252

SECTION 136. 

3. Duty to Signal as Dependent Upon Circum stances. 

Approaching intersection of ways at a speed faster than the prima facie rate, mentioned in General Laws Chapter 90, Section 17, where a group of children is assembled creates negligence on the part of the operator if he fails to give proper signal of his approach. 

Linnane v. Millman, 261 Mass. 491 

Shipelis v. Cody, 214 Mass. 452 (Driving swiftly into street where there are five to ten children) 

Ayers v. Ratshesky, 213 Mass. 589 (Eighteen miles an hour at dusk on narrow obstructed street where there are children may require signal)

Failure to give a timely signal must have a causal connection with the plaintiff's injury. 

So, there is no negligence for failure to blow a horn when a pedestrian who is walking towards the side of the motor vehicle stumbles and falls against it. 

Engel v. Checker Taxi Co., 275 Mass. 471, at 476

Also there is no evidence of negligence when the defendant, about to make a turn into a side street, signals with his left hand and the driver of an ambulance, thinking that the signal meant the defendant intended to stop, swings to the left and, seeing the defendant turning to the right, travels further to the left and skids on to the sidewalk injuring the plaintiff. 

Kane v. Metropolitan Coal Co., 274 Mass. 63, at 65

$185 

No signal given while plaintiff, after alighting from street car, was crossing street. 

Hepburn v. Walters, 263 Mass. 139, at 140 

Linnane v. Millman, 261 Mass. 491, at 493 

Roberge v. Follette, 261 Mass. 438, at 440

SECTION 137. 

4. Effect of Failure to Hear or See Signal.

The failure to hear the sounding of a gong on an ambulance which is travelling at a fast speed in the rear of the defendant's vehicle is not, as matter of law, negligence. 

Kane v. Metropolitan Coal Co., 274 Mass. 63, at 65 (Truck driver gave hand signal for left turn, partially made same when ambulance in rear travelling at fast speed skidded on the sidewalk and injured the plaintiff-not negligent.)

D. SPEED AND CONTROL. 

SECTION 138. 

Regardless of statutory provisions, ordinances, regulations, or by-laws, the operator of a motor vehicle must not travel at a rate of speed greater than is reasonable and proper with due regard to all the surrounding circumstances existing at the time. 

Evidence that defendant was travelling at a speed prima facie greater than reasonable is not proof of negligence unless it appears that speed contributed to collision. 

Ellis v. Ellison, 275 Mass. 272, at 274

Though the mere fact that a motor vehicle skidded is not evidence of negligence, Hennessey v. Moynihan, 272 Mass. 165, at 167 

Lonergan v. American Ry. Exp., 250 Mass. 30, at 35 

Lambert v. Eastern Mass. St. Ry., 240 Mass. 495, at 499

§138 

 yet when the skidding results from the operation of the motor vehicle at a rate of speed which is excessive (under the circumstances), the skidding is the proximate result of the excessive speed and any injury suffered by the plaintiff through the skidding may be attributed to the speed which was the primary cause. 

Hennessey v. Moynihan, 272 Mass. 165, at 168 (Where, going 15 to 18 miles an hour in a crowded square which was wet and slippery, driver knew that sudden application of brakes might cause truck to skid, and if he had been going slower he would have stopped it, truck skidded 18 feet and struck plaintiff) 

Jabbour v. Central Constr. Co., 238 Mass. 453 

Griffin v. Hustis, 234 Mass. 95 

Williams v. Holbrook, 216 Mass. 239 (Increased speed in car track) 

Roach v. Hinchcliff, 214 Mass. 267 (Tire burst, hit and killed pedestrian)

Even when the operator is driving at a rate of speed greater than is reasonable, that speed must be causally related to the accident. 

Ellis v. Ellison, 275 Mass. 272, at 274 

Rizzittelli v. Vestine, 246 Mass. 391 

Jabbour v. Central Constr. Co., 238 Mass. 453, at 455 

Comm. v. Buxton, 205 Mass. 49 

So, when the operator strikes a bicycle rider who has been travelling in the opposite direction, and who suddenly turns and rides to his left of the center of the road so that the defendant operator can not see him until it is too late to avoid a collision, the excessive speed of the operator as matter of law does not causally 'relate to the collision. 

Ellis v. Ellison, 275 Mass. 272, at 274

Where the evidence showed that a street was wide,

§187 

 straight, level and dry with no other vehicle in sight, that the automobile of the defendant was going from 18 to 25 miles an hour and that after running upon the sidewalk it ran 30 to 40 feet before hitting the plaintiff without diminishing the speed, the question of the defendant's negligence is for the jury. The jury could find that if the car had been under proper control it could have been stopped after the tires exploded and before it reached the deceased. 

Roach v. Hinchcliff, 214 Mass. 267 

Commonwealth v. Newhall, 205 Mass. 344, contains a review by Mr. Justice Hammond of the various statutes regulating the speed, operation and use of automobiles in public highways and authorizing regulations by local authorities. 

Linnane v. Millman, 261 Mass. 491, at 493 

Bogert v. Corcoran, 260 Mass. 206 (Intersection of two streets) 

Woodman v. Powers, 242 Mass. 219 

Creedon v. Galvin, 226 Mass. 140 

Clark v. Blair, 217 Mass. 179

While excessive speed is evidence of negligence on the part of the operator it usually is not conclusive evidence thereof. 

Gallup v. Lazott, 271 Mass. 406, at 409

Also there may be negligence even though the vehicle is operated within the speed made prima facie reasonable. 

Rasmussen v. Whipple, 211 Mass. 546

As to when vehicle is under control, See: 28 A. L. R. 952 

Pawloski v. Hess, 253 Mass. 478 

Burke v. Cook, 246 Mass. 518 

Woodman v. Powers, 242 Mass. 219 

Walters v. Davis, 237 Mass. 206 

Newton v. McSweeney, 225 Mass. 402 

Rasmussen v. Whipple, 211 Mass. 546

$139 

 SECTION 139. 

2. Governmental Regulations. 

General Laws Chapter 90, Section 17 (Acts 1930, c. 

201) provides that: "No person operating a motor vehicle on any way shall run it at a rate of speed greater than is reasonable and proper, having regard to traffic and the use of the way and safety of the public. It shall be prima facie evidence of a rate of speed greater than is reasonable and proper as aforesaid if a motor vehicle is operated on any way outside of a thickly settled or business district at a rate of speed exceeding thirty miles per hour for the distance of a quarter of a mile, or inside a thickly settled or business district at a rate of speed exceeding twenty miles per hour for the distance of one-eighth of a mile, or in any place where the operator's view of the road traffic is obstructed either upon approaching an intersecting way, or in traversing a crossing or intersection of ways, or in going around a corner or a curve in a way, at a rate of speed exceeding fifteen miles per hour."

General Laws Chapter 90, Section 18 (Acts 1928, 357, s. 8) provides that: "The city council or the selectmen and park commissioners, on ways within their control, may make special regulations as to the speed of motor vehicles and as to the use of such vehicles upon particular ways, and may prohibit the use of such vehicles altogether on certain ways; provided, that no such special regulation shall be effective unless it shall have been published in one or more newspapers, if there be any, published in the town in which the way is situated, otherwise in one or more newspapers published in the county in which the town is situated; nor unless notice of the same is posted conspicuously by the town or park commissioners making the regulations at points where any way affected thereby joins other ways; nor until after the department of public works shall have

$189 

 certified in writing, after a public hearing, that such regulation is consistent with the public interests; and no regulation shall be valid which excludes motor vehicles from any state highway or from any main highway leading from any town to another provided, that nothing herein contained shall be construed as affecting the right of the metropolitan district commission to make rules and regulations governing the use and operation of motor vehicles on lands, roadways and parkways under its care and control. 

The aldermen or the selectmen may, after a public hearing, upon special occasions and subject to such regulations concerning the closing, use and control of the way as they deem necessary for public convenience and safety grant permits to persons to drive motor vehicles in hill-climbing contests during a specified time and upon specified parts of a public way at any rate of speed."

SECTION 140. 

3. Reasonable and Proper Speed as Dependent Upon Circumstances. 

What is a proper speed is dependent upon circumstances existing at the time. So there may be negligence in driving at a high rate of speed on a boulevard of a public parkway where there are many children. 

Clark v. Blair, 217 Mass. 179 

In Clark v. Martin, 261 Mass. 60, at 63: "Many people came out of the casino with the intestate ... and were crossing the street, some from the driveway and some at the crosswalk. There were adults and 'about a hundred children. The automobile.. was running twenty-five miles an hour. . . [and it raises the question whether] the automobile was operated immediately preceding the collision at a rate of speed greater than was reasonable and proper, having regard to the traffic and the use of the way at the time of the accident. G. L. c. 90, S. 17."

§141 

A speed of 15 to 20 miles an hour, at night, on a bridge where the street car track changes from the center of the roadway to the right of the bridge leaving room for two automobiles, and at a place where pedestrians usually cross at the end of the bridge, might be found to be greater than was reasonably proper. 

Walsh v. Gillis, 1931 A.S. 1363, at 1366

Although five to seven miles an hour under ordinary circumstances is not unreasonable or excessive yet when combined with other negligent acts, such as not sounding horn or giving any warning of approach, or taking any precautions to ascertain whether any one on a sidewalk is about to cross an alley from which the vehicle is emerging, it may warrant a finding of negligence. 

Woodman v. Powers, 242 Mass. 219 

Buoniconti v. Lee, 234 Mass. 73 

Creedon v. Galvin, 226 Mass. 140 

Clark v. Blair, 217 Mass. 179

SECTION 141. 

4. Duty to Reduce Speed or Stop. 

Circumstances might require the operator to reduce speed or stop.

So, approaching a group of children requires extra precaution, sometimes to the extent of stopping. 

Linnane v. Millman, 261 Mass. 491, at 493

Travelling on a bridge at a point where pedestrians usually cross requires a reduction of speed. 

Walsh v. Gillis, 1931 A.S. 1363, at 1366

So also, travelling at 26 miles an hour and overtaking a pedestrian leading horses and running into him may be negligence due to excessive speed. 

Powers v. Loring, 231 Mass. 458 

67 A. L. R. 107

The fact that one motor vehicle has nearly cleared a cross street before the rear end is struck and the speed

$191 

 of the other vehicle is not at all diminished before the collision, are circumstances bearing both upon the former's due care and the latter's negligence.

Payson v. Checker Taxi Co., 262 Mass. 22, at 26 

(Taxi and motorcycle) Where a pedestrian is within view of the driver of a vehicle which is emerging from an alley, before the vehicle reaches the sidewalk, it usually is his (the driver's) duty to come to a stop before crossing the sidewalk and his failure to do so is negligence. 

Slora v. Streeter, 264 Mass. 586 

Tenney v. Reed, 262 Mass. 335 

Ayers v. Ratshesky, 213 Mass. 589 

Dowd v. Tighe, 209 Mass. 464 

Beale v. Old Colony St. Ry., 196 Mass. 119, at 123 

, at 587

SECTION 142. 

5. Ability to Stop-Out of Control. 

When a motor vehicle is travelling at such velocity as to threaten instant disaster to all who are in its path, it may be found to be out of the control of its driver. 6. 

Murphy v. N. E. Transp. Co., 273 Mass. 275, at 276 (Rear bus collided with one in front)

 b. Mist.

Held that while skidding is not evidence of negligence it was for the jury to say whether it was due

SECTION 151. 

3. Precautions in Backing. 

Drivers of automobiles have equal rights in using the streets with drivers of other vehicles and pedestrians, the duty resting on all alike to exercise reasonable care. 

What amounts to an exercise of such care of course depends primarily upon the surrounding circumstances in each case. 

67 A. L. R. 647

The question of negligence was held for the jury and a finding against the defendant was sustained where there was evidence for the plaintiff that the defendant's auto-

$ 

195 mobile was backed at an intersection of streets, without warning, and struck the plaintiff, who was standing in the street near the sidewalk, conversing with a friend, and there was evidence for the defendant tending to show that the driver exercised proper care in backing the car. 

Millay v. Town Taxi, 242 Mass. 314

The operator may be found to be negligent in backing on to a railroad track at a grade-crossing. 

Chase v. N. Y. C. & H. R. R.R., 208 Mass. 137

So, backing into a boy behind who could assume the vehicle would continue or that horn would be blown.

F. VEHICLES TRAVELLING IN IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS. 

SECTION 153. 

General Laws Chapter 89, Section 1, requires persons travelling with vehicles when they meet on a way to each seasonably drive his vehicle to the right of the middle of the travelled part thereof so that the vehicles may pass without interference. 

Kenyon v. Hathaway, 274 Mass. 47, at 49 

Coates v. Bates, 265 Mass. 444 

Rice v. Lowell Buick Co., 229 Mass. 53 

Johnson v. Shaw, 204 Mass. 165

Where a motorcycle, in passing a vehicle on its left going in the same direction, collided with the left front of the vehicle coming in the opposite direction, it is proper

$153 

 for the judge in his charge to direct the attention of the jury to the law of the road, G. L. c. 89, and refer to section 2, which reads: "The driver of a vehicle passing another vehicle travelling in the same direction shall drive to the left of the middle of the travelled part of the way; and, if it is of sufficient width for the two vehicles to pass, the driver of the leading one shall not wilfully obstruct the other." 

Anzoni v. Gosse, 274 Mass. 522, at 524

It is impossible to observe the law of the road by going between two cars that are passing each other when the way is not wide enough to allow the passing vehicle to travel without going beyond the center of the way, because as to onc, the operator must keep to the left of the middle of the road, and if there is another vehicle coming in the opposite direction that is passing the first vehicle, the operator of the passing vehicle cannot do both and observe the law. 

Anzoni v. Gosse, 274 Mass. 522, at 524

A driver who so operates his vehicle as to reasonably lead the operator of the vehicle coming in the opposite direction to believe that it is necessary for the latter to drive away over on his right side to avoid being struck by the defendant, makes the defendant liable for any injury or damages suffered by the second driver in his effort to avoid being struck by the defendant even though there is no physical contact between the two vehicles. 

Harrington v. Cudahy Packing Co., 273 Mass. 15 (Plaintiff struck tree)

The question of whether violation of the law of the road contributed to the plaintiff's injury should be considered, and although the operator was violating the law of the road, if he was in a safer position as to the plaintiff than if he, the operator, had been observing the law of the road, then even in spite of such violation of the law

$197 

 of the road it may be found that the operator was acting in a reasonably careful manner. 

Anzoni v. Gosse, 274 Mass. 522, at 524 (Motor vehicle ran into left front of automobile travelling in opposite direction)

But if the operator's violation of the law of the road contributed to the plaintiff's injuries such violation may be considered by the jury. 

Ordinarily when a collision occurs between motor vehicles upon a public way, the issues of due care on the part of the plaintiff and negligence of the defendant are for the jury. 

Minnehan v. Hyland, 1932 A. S. 543, at 546 

White v. Calcutt, 269 Mass. 252, at 255

Although the plaintiff may have acted contrary to the provision of some statute relative to speed or position on the highway, yet this will not prevent his recovery if it can be found that such violation did not contribute to his injury or damage. That is, if such violation did not contribute to his injury or damage but was merely an attendant circumstance, he is not precluded from recovery solely because of such violation. 

Minnehan v. Hyland, 1932 A. S. 543, at 546 and 

547 and cases collected

Particularly is this so if the plaintiff's violation was committed in order to avoid a more serious accident. 

Minnehan v. Hyland, 1932 A. S. 543, at 547

When the defendant, without giving any warning signal, suddenly turned out of line into the path of the plaintiff's truck about 20 feet away from it and then stopped within 7 feet of a signal light at a place where a head-on collision between the plaintiff's truck and the defendant's automobile would have been unavoidable if the driver of the truck had not turned quickly to his right, it can be found that the defendant was negligent. 

Minnehan v. Hyland, 1932 A. S. 543, at 546

$154 

 SECTION 154. 

2. Position on Highway. 

Where an operator of a motor vehicle sees two automobiles abreast coming toward him "very fast," pulls to the right side of the road out of a stream of very heavy traffic and stops a foot from a street car track, while attempting to get back into the stream of traffic is struck head-on by a street car whose track occupies the right side within the limits of the way, the space between the rails being filled with gravel and reasonably smooth, the operator is in the exercise of due care and the motorman is negligent.

Austin v. Eastern Mass. Ry. Co., 269 Mass 420 SECTION 155. 

3. Reliance on Care In Operation of Approaching Vehicle. 

The plaintiff had a right to rely to some extent on the expectation that the defendant's truck, in passing, would be to the right of the center of the road. 

Murray v. Indursky, 266 Mass. 220, at 223 and 224

Upon the questions of due care and negligence each party has a right to rely to some extent upon the exercise of due care by the other, but neither could wholly rely upon it. 

Coates v. Bates, 265 Mass 444, at 449

SECTION 156. 

4. Violating Law of Road as Negligence. 

Violation of the statute relating to the law of the road is actionable negligence when it becomes the direct and proximate cause of a collision. 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, at 163 and 166

Newcomb v. Boston Protective Dept., 146 Mass. 596 

So, driving on the right of the middle of the travelled part of the way is evidence of the exercise of due care, but

$199 

 driving in an opposite direction and colliding with the first vehicle is in violation of G. L. c. 89, s. 1, requiring him to drive to the right of the middle part of the road and, unexplained, indicates negligence on the part of that driver. 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, at 163 and 164 

Perlstein v. American Express Co., 177 Mass. 530

The driving of a vehicle on the left side of the road in violation of General Laws Chapter 89, Section 1, is evidence of negligence but is not conclusive. 

Coates v. Bates, 265 Mass. 444, at 449 

Rice v. Lowell Buick Co., 229 Mass. 53 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155 

Johnson v. Shaw, 204 Mass. 165 

Perlstein v. American, 177 Mass. 530, at 531 

Newcomb v. Boston Protective Dept., 146 Mass. 596, at 600 When an accident happens and there has been a violation of the law of the road, the due care of the owner and driver of the motor vehicle is usually in issue. 

Bailey v. Worcester Cons. St. Ry., 228 Mass. 477

So also, a collision of two motor vehicles at or near the intersecting road requires the application of the law of the road. 

Rice v. Lowell Buick Co., 229 Mass. 53 

So, there can be no recovery where the negligence of the driver contributed to his own injury or when he was unlawfully on the highway.

SECTION 157. 

General Laws Chapter 89, Section 2, was enacted for

$157 

 the benefit of the driver of the vehicle overtaken by the vehicle coming from the rear. 

The law of the road as to vehicles passing each other while going in the same direction is not to be so construed as to prevent in all circumstances one vehicle passing another from remaining on the right side. What is reasonably safe and prudent to be done is to be taken into account including the width of the road, the amount of traffic and other circumstances, and the question of what is reasonably safe under the circumstances is a question of fact. 

Anzoni v. Gosse, 274 Mass. 522, at 525 

Smith v. Conway, 121 Mass. 216

A vehicle which has just passed another vehicle travelling in the same direction may have been operated in such a negligent manner as to be the cause of a collision between the overtaken vehicle and a third vehicle. 

Avila v. DuPont, 1932 A. S. 275

In the last cited case, the defendant operated a touring car on the highway, and, after passing an automobile proceeding in the same direction, operated by one D, the left front wheel of the defendant's car collided with the left front wheel of an automobile approaching in the opposite direction, causing the latter automobile to cross part of the road to its left and strike almost head on the D automobile, in which the plaintiff's intestate was riding as a passenger. It was held that the jury could properly find that the defendant drove in a negligent manner so as to cause or contribute to the injuries of the plaintiff's intestate. 

SECTION 158. 

2. Duties of Preceding Vehicle. 

The driver of a motor vehicle on a narrow one way street may be found negligent in failing to proceed in a

$201 

 straight direction while another car is attempting to pass. 

Seymour v. Dunville, 265 Mass. 78

SECTION 159. 

3. Duties of Vehicle in Rear. 

The mere happening of a rear-end collision does not prove negligence; however, uncontradicted evidence showing a broad, smooth highway, with only the plaintiff's wagon at the extreme right and one, possibly two, trucks moving at a reasonable speed behind it, with the road open and free from vehicles for a long distance in front and further showing that a truck struck a wagon from behind, justifies a conclusion that someone was negligent. 

In other words, a situation is presented where an explanation is due if something other than negligence is the cause of the accident, and it relieves the plaintiff from showing the particular act of carelessness. 

Washburn v. R. F. Owens Co., 252 Mass. 47, at 54 and 55 

Reardon v. Boston El. Ry., 247 Mass. 124 

(Street car) 

Sandler v. Boston El. Ry., 238 Mass. 148 (Street car) 

47 A. L. R. 719

A passenger in a coach which was struck from behind by the defendant's coach was entitled to recover. 

Murphy v. New England Trans. Co., 273 Mass. 275, at 277 The operator of a coach which came in contact with the coach in which the plaintiff was riding failed to exercise ordinary care by operating his coach at such a speed and at such distance from the coach immediately in front that he was unable to stop and thus avoid a collision when he knew or ought to have anticipated that the coach directly

$160 

 in front had stopped or might stop, and that such negligence was the proximate cause of the injury to the plaintiff.

Murphy v. New England Trans. Co., 273 Mass. 275.

Murphy v. New England Trans. Co., 273 Mass. 275, at 277

The attempt of the operator of a motor vehicle on the highway to pass on the right of another vehicle proceeding in the same direction in violation of the law of the road is evidence of negligence to be considered in an action by pedestrian who was run into by second vehicle, which attempted to pass the other on the left.

 H. AT INTERSECTIONS OR CROSSINGS.

(See: Chapter VI, "Law of the Road," pages 173 to

General Laws Chapter 90, Section 14 (Acts 1925, c. 

305; Acts 1928, c. 166) provides in part that: "The person operating a motor vehicle on any way approaching an intersecting way or a curve or a corner in said way where his view is obstructed shall slow down and upon approaching any junction of said way with an intersecting way before turning into the same shall slow down and keep to the right of the intersection of the center lines of both ways or extensions thereof, when turning to the right, and shall pass to the right of the intersection of the center lines of said ways or extensions thereof before turning to the left."

General Laws Chapter 89, Section 8 (as amended by 

Acts 1929, c. 147) provides that: "Every driver of a motor or other vehicle approaching an intersection of any ways, which for the purposes hereof shall mean the area embraced within the extensions of the lateral curb lines, or, if none, then the lateral boundary lines, of intersecting ways as defined in section one of chapter ninety, shall grant the right of way to a vehicle which has already entered such intersection, and every driver of a vehicle entering such an intersection shall grant the right of way to a vehicle so entering from his right at approximately the same instant; but the foregoing provisions of this section shall not apply at any intersection of ways when a driver is otherwise directed by a police officer, or by a lawful traffic regulating sign, device or signal maintained by or with the written approval of the department of public works and while said approval is in effect or otherwise lawfully maintained."

SECTION 162. 

2. What Constitutes an Intersection. 

In Fournier v. Zinn, 257 Mass. 575, at pages 578 and 579: . . . By s. I of c. 90 an intersecting way is one which joins another at an angle 'whether or not it crosses the other.' G. L. c. 89, s. 8, established a law of the road at intersecting streets. . . . This 'point of intersection' was determined and fixed by the statute; it was the space common to Packard Street and Lincoln Street where they crossed each other, the area within that rectangle was the intersecting point mentioned in the statute. It was this point of intersection of the two ways and not the point where the paths of the two automobiles would cross each other that the statute established as the point of intersection, at which point the vehicle on the plaintiff's right had the right of way... It ordained a fixed point of intersection. It did not intend to leave this point to the uncertain estimate of every operator. . . . The statute applies to all

§163 

 intersecting ways whether they do or do not cross each. other." 

Keyes v. Checker Taxi Co., 275 Mass. 461, at 468

Mahoney v. Boston El. Ry., 271 Mass. 274

SECTION 164. 

4. Signals and Warnings of Approach. 

The statutes (G. L. c. 90, ss. 7 and 16) relating to horn, bell or signalling device and sounding same are for the protection of persons lawfully using the highway. They require that one approaching an intersection of ways shall exercise due care and give warning of his approach if necessary; also that he must have his car under control. 

These requirements are explicit and absolute; 

Newton v. McSweeney, 225 Mass. 402 although G. L. c. 90, s. 16, prohibits unreasonable sounding of horn, bell or signalling device.

$207 

In Creedon v. Galvin, 226 Mass. 140, the defendant was held to have violated the statute in not giving a timely signal of his approach.

SECTION 165. 

5. Position on Highway.

When due to excessive speed in order to avoid a collision the operator goes to the left or wrong side of road and strikes a pedestrian, this is evidence of gross negligence. 

Manning v. Simpson, 261 Mass. 494 

G. L. c. 90, s. 14, requires a vehicle in entering a highway at an intersection to pass to the right of the intersection.

Whether the violation of this statute contributes to an accident as a cause, or merely as an attending circumstance or condition, is usually a question of fact for the jury. 

Bogert v. Thompson, 260 Mass. *206 

Daris v. Middlesex, etc., Ry., 241 Mass. 580 

Walters v. Davis, 237 Mass. 206, at 209
