SECTION 166. 

6. Speed and Control. 

By General Laws Chapter 90, Section 17, it is prima facie evidence of a rate of speed greater than is reasonable and proper if a motor vehicle is propelled . . . in traversing a crossing or intersection of ways at a rate of speed exceeding eight miles per hour. 

Bogert v. Corcoran, 260 Mass. 206, at 208 

Bengle v. Cooney, 243 Mass. IO 

Woodman v. Powers, 242 Mass. 219 

Griffin v. Hustis, 234 Mass. 95 

Newton v. McSweeney, 225 Mass. 402

$167 

The general rule is that when a collision between two motor vehicles occurs at intersecting streets, the issues of the defendant's negligence and of the plaintiff's due care and contributory negligence ordinarily present questions of fact and cannot be ruled as matters of law. 

Palombella v. Foss, 1931 A.S., 2049, at 2050 

Clay v. Pope & Cottle Co., 273 Mass. 40, at 44 

Dillon v. Plimpton, 239 Mass. 588

This rule is applicable when the plaintiff, nearing the intersection at a rate of speed of eight or nine miles an hour, looks in both directions for approaching vehicles but does not see the automobile of the defendant, which is going about forty miles an hour, and the plaintiff's motor vehicle is struck broadside by that of the defendant and overturned.

Palombella v. Foss, 1931 A.S. 2049 SECTION 167. 

7. Obeying Traffic Officers and Traffic Signals. 

See: Section 279, page 344.

An operator has a duty to perform for the safety of pedestrians and other travellers in the street even though the operator is proceeding in obedience to the orders of a traffic officer or traffic signal or lights.

Margeson v. Town Taxi, Inc., 266 Mass. 192 

(Driver saw pedestrian 5 feet from him while vehicle was stationary, but struck pedestrian) 

Donovan v. Mutrie, 265 Mass. 472

So, an operator who starts up on a traffic officer's signal and strikes a pedestrian crossing the street is negligent. 

Wilson v. Freeman, 271 Mass. 438

SECTION 168. 

8. Reliance on Care of Other Travellers. 

An operator of a motor vehicle may rely to some extent on the expectation that the driver of another vehicle will

$ 

209 comply with the law when approaching an intersection of streets.

Payson v. Checker Taxi Co., 262 Mass. 22, at 25 

Sutherland v. Caruso, 258 Mass. 513, at 514

So also, the operator may rely to some extent upon the expectation that pedestrians will exercise reasonable care and diligence for their own safety.

SECTION 169. 

9. Right of Way Between Vehicles. 

The right of way possessed by a motor vehicle entitled thereto at an intersection covers the entire common area and not merely the half of the way occupied by it. 

Cunningham v. N. E. Transp. Co., 267 Mass. 238 

Each operator is required to see the other vehicle in time to grant or assume the right of way and not wait until the moment of impact to observe the other vehicle. 

Stickel v. Cassasa, 268 Mass. 59 

Fournier v. Zinn, 257 Mass. 575

A driver has a duty to perform for the safety of pedestrians and others on the highway even if he has the right of way.

Cunningham v. N. E. Transp. Co., 267 Mass. 238 

Stickel v. Cassasa, 268 Mass. 59 

246 Mass. 409

Margeson v. Town Taxi, Inc., 266 Mass. 192 

(Obeying traffic signal) 

Donovan v. Mutrie, 265 Mass. 472 (Police officer directed vehicular traffic to go) 

Fournier v. Zinn, 257 Mass. 575 (Leading case-point of intersection is area common to both intersecting ways)

However, a motor vehicle approaching from the right of another vehicle, but travelling the wrong way on a

§170 

 one way street, is not entitled to the protection afforded by G. L. c. 89, s. 8, which provides that every driver of a vehicle approaching an intersecting way shall grant the right of way to vehicles approaching from his right. 

Labay v. Leiken, 252 Mass. 579 

It is not negligence as matter of law for an operator to drive to the left of triangular grass plot for he is not required to travel to the right and take the right-hand roadway so as to approach the intersecting ways which were at the extreme end of the triangular plot. 

Falk v. Carlton, 270 Mass. 213 

G. L. c. 90, s. 14 (as amended by Acts 1925, c. 305)

SECTION 170. 

10. Turning Into Intersecting Way. 

After entering the intersection, which is the area common to adjoining ways, the operator must use due and reasonable care in entering any of the ways which lead from such point of intersection. He is entitled to and should make reasonable preparation for turning into such way.

So, a slight swing one way preparatory to a broader swing in the other direction does not constitute negligence, especially where the signal indicating the real intent has first been given. 

Kane v. Metropolitan Coal Co., 274 Mass. 63, at 65

There is no different measure of care for a turn into an unaccepted way from that applicable to a turn into an accepted way. 

Mahoney v. Boston El. Ry., 271 Mass. 274, at 278

SECTION 171. 

a. Turning to Right.

The operator of a motor vehicle ordinarily has a right to make a turn and in so doing he has the right to use any

$ 

211 part of the street that he is coming to, subject only to the rights of other people who may be there.

If two vehicles meet in a street, it is the duty of each of them, as seasonably as they can, to get each on his own right-hand side of the travelled way of that street. 

But the law does not compel a man always to be on the right side. He can use any part of the street, so long as he is not interfering with the rights of other people. 

The operator's negligence is to be determined from all the circumstances, whether he was doing anything he ought not to have done that an ordinarily reasonable and prudent man would not have done. 

Johnson v. Shaw, 204 Mass. 165, at 168 bottom and 169 top 

(I) Vehicles Proceeding in Same Direction. 

SECTION 172. 

(A) Forward Vehicle Making Left Turn. 

A driver of the forward vehicle is negligent when the sole cause of the accident is the sudden turning of his vehicle to the left toward an intersecting way without the giving of any signal by the driver, by holding out his hand or otherwise. 

Clay v. Pope & Cottle Co., 273 Mass. 40, at 44 

Di Rienzo v. Goldfarb, 257 Mass. 272, at 281

A driver of a coal truck who is on a public highway, where he has a right to be, and gives a hand signal of his intention to make a left turn into an intersecting street is not responsible that the signal is misinterpreted, and is not negligent. 

Kane v. Metropolitan Coal Co., 274 Mass. 63, at 65 (Where ambulance behind truck at a speed of 35 miles an hour attempted to pass on the left as truck was making left turn and skidded on to the sidewalk striking plaintiff)

$173 

A turn to the right by the forward vehicle preparatory to making a swing to the left is not negligence on the part of the driver of that vehicle, especially when the driver in the rear does or should immediately know of the swing to be made to the left in time to act. 

Kane v. Metropolitan Coal Co., 274 Mass. 63, at 65

I. VEHICLES STANDING IN HIGHWAY PARKING. 

SECTION 173. 

1. Right to Stop or Park. 

(See: Sec. 284, page 353.) 

Milbury v. Turner Center System, 274 Mass. 358, at 362 

Falk v. Finkelman, 268 Mass. 524 2. Place of Stopping or Parking; Obstruction of 

Highway.

SECTION 174. 

a. General Statement. 

Leaving a truck unattended without lights at a place on the portion of a hill used for travel where the operator of a motor vehicle, travelling in the same direction at a reasonable rate of speed, could not see the truck in time to avoid it, may be found to be negligence. 

Rotefsky v. Bova, 274 Mass. 23, at 26 

But see: 

Stone v. Mullen, 257 Mass. 344

SECTION 175. 

b. On Hill or Grade.

Parking a motor vehicle upon a hill or grade usually requires precaution of some kind to prevent the motor vehicle from starting.

$213 

In the ordinary case of a motor vehicle starting after being parked upon a steep grade or hill the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur has been held to apply even without the interference of a third person or other intervening act. 

In one case where there was no express evidence of the operator's negligence, the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur was held inapplicable when the only evidence was that before leaving the motor vehicle on the grade, the operator stopped it with the front wheel on the right-hand side up against the curbing, shut off the motor and set the emergency brakes although shortly thereafter the motor vehicle started downgrade when no one was near it. 

However, a finding was sustained for the plaintiff because there was evidence that the brakes were not in good condition which accounted for the vehicle starting and that if the mechanism of the vehicle had been in good condition, the right front wheel turned into the curbing and the emergency brake set, the vehicle could not have run down the hill. 

Dorne v. Adams, 243 Mass. 438 

66 A.L.R. 443

But the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur was held applicable where the defendant parked his automobile on a grade in a city with engine stopped, and left it, and shortly afterwards, after two companions had returned and seated themselves on the rear seat, the car started and rolled backwards and struck the plaintiff's store. 

The court said in Glaser v. Schroeder, 269 Mass. 337, at 339: "The unexplained automatic starting of a machine from a state of rest into motion, when, according to its mechanical construction, it ought to remain still, is evidence not only of some defect or want of repair in the machine, but also of negligence in failing to discover and remedy such defect or want of repair, even though the details of such defect or want of repair may not be shown by the evidence.

§176 

To this extent the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur has been established with respect to the relation of master and servant at common law. 

66 A.L.R. 443 

SECTION 176. 

3. Position of Vehicle. 

A person who places a vehicle on the highway at the junction of two streets at a point nearer one street than is permitted by the city ordinances, may be found to be negligent, and such negligence may be the proximate cause of injury to a boy who is struck by another automobile because his view is obstructed by the improper position of the first vehicle. 4. 

Milbury v. Turner Center System, 274 Mass. 358 

But see: Falk v. Finkleman, 268 Mass. 524

Precautions Against Starting of Vehicle. 

SECTION 177. 

a. General Statement. 

General Laws Chapter 90, Section 13 provides, in part, that: "No person having control or charge of a motor vehicle shall allow such vehicle to stand in any way and remain unattended without first locking or making it fast or effectively setting the brakes thereon, and stopping the motor of said vehicle."

So, leaving a motor vehicle with the brakes set, the spark lever off, the engine shut off but with the ignition key in the lock may be found to be negligence when the vehicle moves from the place where it has been left and travels upgrade unoccupied at a great speed with the ignition key in the lock and the spark and gas levers turned on even though the clutch is in neutral, slightly inclined forward. 

Zandan v. Radner, 242 Mass. 503 

66 A.L.R. 443

§ 215 SECTION 178. 

b. Stopping Without Lights.

Leaving a truck on a dark night without light, unattended, within the travelled part of the public highway, on a hill where it cannot be seen in time to avoid it, so that the truck is not visible to the operators of other vehicles going in the same direction until such vehicles reach the top of the hill, and the distance between such other vehicles and the unattended truck is such that the other vehicles cannot be stopped, or turned aside in season to avoid collision with the unattended truck, may be found to be negligence. 

Rotefsky v. Bova, 274 Mass. 23, at 26 

But see: 

Stone v. Mullen, 257 Mass. 344 where the unattended vehicle was left at a place that could readily be seen by use of headlights as required by law. 

47 A.L.R. 709

But striking an unlighted vehicle at night is not negligence by itself. 

Bertera v. Cuneo, 273 Mass. 181, at 182

It is not negligence to collide with a truck which is standing unlighted in the highway where the operator of the motor vehicle can see objects in the road 100 yards away but comes within 15 feet of the standing truck before he sees it, going at a rate of 20 to 25 miles an hour when the truck could be seen for about 100 or more feet away. 

Stone v. Mullen, 257 Mass. 344

SECTION 179. 

5. Starting of Parked Vehicle. 

A driver who starts his automobile towards the center of the street without any warning, after the same has been parked on the right hand curb may be found to be negligent. 

Golden v. Carnevale, 273 Mass. 159, at 161

§180 

The driver's negligence is a question of fact. So, when the defendant's car is facing in one direction and the plaintiff's car is moving in that direction, and suddenly the defendant turns his car towards the center of the street in front of the plaintiff without giving a signal or warning, by hand or otherwise, that he intends to take this course, his conduct can be found to be a negligent act. 

Golden v. Carnevale, 273 Mass. 159, at 161 

White v. Calcutt, 269 Mass. 252 

Dorne v. Adams, 243 Mass. 438 

Zandan v. Radner, 242 Mass. 503

The driver of an automobile may be found to be negligent where his car is parked near the curb, and the plaintiff is operating his automobile about 20 or 25 miles an hour headed in the direction where the parked automobile is facing, and as the plaintiff gets almost abreast of the parked car, the driver of the latter suddenly starts and turns towards the side of the road on which the plaintiff is travelling so that there are not more than 3 or 4 feet between the plaintiff's car and the parked machine as the plaintiff's car passes the latter, and thereafter the plaintiff turns to the right and applies his brakes, and then to avoid hitting a pole in front of him turned to the left coming in collision with a tree and a pole on that side of the road. 

Golden v. Carnevale, 273 Mass. 159

The fact that there was no collision of the motor vehicles is immaterial. 

Golden v. Carnevale, 273 Mass. 159, at 161 

White v. Calcutt, 269 Mass. 252

L. ENTERING OR LEAVING PRIVATE PREMISES. 

SECTION 182. 

1. Turning In From Highway. 

A traveller on a sidewalk has a right to rely to some extent upon the assumption that a motor vehicle will not be driven onto a highway at a time when persons are likely to be passing without some signal being given of its approach. 

, at 282 (Boy on sidewalk, auto coming from alley)

It may be found to be negligence on the part of the operator of a truck to drive upon a sidewalk to enter his own premises without observing children who are crossing the sidewalk, and without acting with due care in view of their presence. 

Hirrel v. Lacey, 274 Mass. 431, at 435 

Particularly when the children on the sidewalk are in plain view of the operator and there is nothing to obstruct his view. 

Hirrel v. Lacey, 274 Mass. 431, at 435

$182 

King v. Weitzman, 267 Mass. 447 

, at 282 and 283

The driver of a truck was negligent where a boy 6½ years of age, together with his sister about 8½ years old, at half-past seven on an April morning, were walking along a dirt and gravel sidewalk on a public highway, and came to a driveway leading across the sidewalk into the defendant's place of business, the sister being on the outside of the sidewalk and the boy at her right hand side, and the defendant's truck was about 100 feet away travelling in the opposite direction and turned into the driveway, when the sister let go of her brother's hand, and stepped back to save herself, because if she had tried to save her brother, they would both have been killed, and the boy did not see the truck, and the middle of the front of the radiator of the truck hit the boy, and the right front wheel went over his body, and neither the owner nor the driver of the truck saw the children on the sidewalk but first knew of the accident when the boy was run over, and the sister screamed. 

Hirrel v. Lacey, 274 Mass. 431, at 434

And a finding was warranted that the boy was struck by the defendant's truck on the sidewalk and not on the defendant's land, notwithstanding that when the truck came to a stop, the boy's body was six or eight feet inside the property line of the defendant. 

Hirrel v. Lacey, 274 Mass. 431, at 435 

A boy 6½ years of age walking on the sidewalk with his sister 8½ years old, where the boy has a right to be, justly might rely to a considerable extent on the expectation that no one would drive a motor vehicle across that sidewalk, even at a private driveway, without giving seasonable warning and stopping if necessary in order to avoid a collision. 

Hirrel v. Lacey, 274 Mass. 431, at 435

§219 

2. Emerging Onto Highway.

SECTION 183. 

a. Backing Out. 

In Noonan v. Levitt Co., 238 Mass. 481, a watchman was struck by the defendant's vehicle backing into him. 

67 A.L.R. 652

SECTION 184. 

M. ARTICLES PROJECTING, FALLING THROWN FROM VEHICLES. 

OR The carrying of articles which project from the motor vehicle, contrary to law, may be evidence of negligence. 

Murray v. Indursky, 266 Mass. 220 

But, a trailer attached to an express truck which strikes a theatre marquee and signs which extend into the highway does not necessitate a finding of the truck driver's negligence. 

Theatres Co. of Boston v. American Express Co., 267 Mass. 178 :.

CHAPTER VIII. 

CARE AS TO PERSONS. 

A. PEDESTRIANS. 

SECTION 185. 

1. General Duties of Motor Vehicle Operator. 

The operator of a motor vehicle owes to pedestrians walking along the street or highway the duty to exercise reasonable or ordinary care to avoid injuring them. 

Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 392

The rights and duties of a pedestrian and vehicle operator are reciprocal and must be so exercised by each as not to injure the other and each may rely to some extent upon the due care of the other. 

Hutchinson v. H. E. Shaw Co., 273 Mass. 51, at 52 

Barrett v. Checker Taxi Co., 263 Mass. 252 

Hepburn v. Walters, 263 Mass. 139 

DiRienzo v. Goldfarb, 257 Mass. 272, at 280 

Newman v. Hill, 250 Mass. 578 

Gauthier v. Quick, 250 Mass. 258 

But see:

Murphy v. Boston El. Ry., 262 Mass. 485 Will v. Boston El. Ry., 247 Mass. 250 

Bagnell v. Boston El. Ry., 247 Mass. 235 

Sullivan v. Chadwick, 236 Mass. 130 

Emery v. Miller, 231 Mass. 243 

Swetzoff v. O'Brien, 226 Mass. 438 

Booth v. Meagher, 224 Mass. 472 

Lynch v. Fisk Rubber Co., 209 Mass. 16

When there is a collision between an automobile and a pedestrian, the usual question of due care on the part of the plaintiff and negligence of the defendant are raised. 

Hennessey v. Taylor, 189 Mass. 583, at 584

§221 

Ordinarily these are issues of fact for the jury.

Durling v. Lamontain, 1931 A. S. 2429 

, at 584 

Purtell v. Jordan, 156 Mass. 573 

See also:

Griffin v. Taxi Service Co., 217 Mass. 293 

(Pedestrian hit by taxicab while crossing street) 

Lynch v. Fisk Rubber Co., 209 Mass. 16 (Liability where person run over while crossing street)

General Laws Chapter 90, Section 44 provides, in part, that: "Upon approaching a pedestrian who is upon the travelled part of any way and not upon the sidewalk, every person operating a motor vehicle shall slow down." 

The law requires of the operator of an automobile the exercise of reasonable care toward pedestrians; he is not, however, an insurer, and, where a pedestrian is standing in a place of safety and apparently sees an approaching automobile, the driver has the right to assume that the pedestrian will remain in the place of safety until the car has passed, and will not suddenly step into a place of danger. 

65 A.L.R. 193

SECTION 186. 

2. Reliance on Care of Pedestrian. 

The operator of a motor vehicle has a right to rely to some extent on the expectation that the conduct of a pedestrian will be that of a reasonably careful man. 

So, the operator has a right to assume that a pedestrian crossing a street, after reaching a place of safety and being outside the path of an approaching motor vehicle, will remain in such place of safety or continue his journey in crossing the street and that he will not suddenly retrace

$187 

 his steps, turn or step backwards, and come within the line of travel of the motor vehicle. 

65 A. L. R. 196

SECTION 187. 

3. Meeting or Passing Pedestrian. 

A pedestrian, whether he sees an automobile or not, has a right to reply to some extent on the expectation that any motor vehicle, approaching him, will (1) slow down and (2) give a timely warning signal, if necessary, and (3) observe the requirements of G. L. c. 90, ss. 14 and 17. 

Barrett v. Checker Taxi Co., 263 Mass. 252, at 254

The question whether the driver of a motor vehicle in the exercise of due care should have seen the pedestrian in time to avoid the accident by stopping or by passing behind him is usually one of fact for the jury. 

Mulroy v. Marinakis, 271 Mass. 421, at 424 

Jean v. Nester, 261 Mass. 442, at 444

Negligence of the driver may also be found when he fails to comply with the statutory requirement (G. L. c. 

90, s. 14) that upon approaching a pedestrian upon a travelled part of the way every person operating a motor vehicle shall slow down, Mulroy v. Marinakis, 271 Mass. 421, at 424 

Creedon v. Galvin, 226 Mass. 140, at 142

See also: 

Hennessey v. Moynihan, 272 Mass. 165, at 167 and 169 (Excessive speed, crowded square and failure to give signal) 

G. L. c. 90, s. 14 and Acts 1928, c. 166

So, when an operator of a motor vehicle sees a pedestrian walking toward the left hand side of his cab four

$223 

 or five feet away and, as the cab passes, the pedestrian slips or stumbles and falls, this shows no negligence on the part of the defendant even in view of the statute (Acts 1925, c. 305) which requires the operator of a motor vehicle approaching a pedestrian on the travelled part of the way, and not upon the sidewalk, to slow down and give warning. 

Engel v. Checker Taxi Co., 275 Mass. 471, at 476 

Hennessey v. Moynihan, 272 Mass. 165, at 168

In such an instance the pedestrian is approaching the automobile from its side and is not being approached by the automobile, and hence there is no violation of the statute. 

Engel v. Checker Taxi Co., 275 Mass. 471, at 476 

4. Position of Pedestrian on Highway. 

a. 

SECTION 188. 

General Statement. 

A pedestrian when crossing or travelling upon a highway is not necessarily required to use crosswalks or sidewalks but the pedestrian's conduct is governed by the standard of reasonable and ordinary care as it should have been exercised under the particular circumstances. 

So, it is negligence for an operator to fail to see a pedestrian who is walking upon the left hand sidewalk and who as she proceeds comes to a place that is barred for passage when she steps into the gutter and is obliged to walk around an object standing there, after which she waits for the defendant's automobile to pass when she is struck by its rear fender. 

Gray v. Batchelder, 208 Mass. 441

Also, in the case of a person who, after alighting from a truck which is in front of the defendant's motor vehicle, proceeds diagonally to cross the highway when the de-

§189 

 fendant strikes and kills her, the pedestrian's due care and the defendant's negligence are questions of fact. 

Buckley v. Sutton, 231 Mass. 504

One travelling on foot in the evening on a public way might be found to have been in the exercise of due care when walking in the roadway because the sidewalk was muddy. It was held that, under the circumstances, the plaintiff had a right to walk in the roadway and that the questions, whether the plaintiff was in the exercise of due care and whether the defendant was negligent, were for the jury. 

Booth v. Meagher, 224 Mass. 472, at 473

There is no absolute rule of law that, to be in the exercise of due care, one about to cross a public street must look and listen for approaching vehicles. 

Robbins v. Springfield St. Ry., 165 Mass. 30

He must do for his safety what ordinarily careful persons are accustomed to do under like circumstances. 

Hall v. West End St. Ry., 168 Mass. 461, at 462 (Plaintiff had good eyesight, but was very deaf)

SECTION 189. 

b. At Intersections of Highways. 

Where an ordinance related directly to the safety of persons using and passing street corners and sought to keep them clear in order that those using either the sidewalk or the way for vehicles might see the existing traffic in an intersecting street as well as in the way that they were using and be able to act with full knowledge of the conditions in the ways, a violation of that ordinance by obstructing the pedestrian's view indicates negligent conduct. 

Milbury v. Turner Center System, 274 Mass. 358, at (Parked truck too near corner) 362

$225 

So it can be found that the leaving of a solid truck ten or twelve feet high close to a corner, cutting off the view of an intersecting street and with the hood blocking from three to five feet of the space generally used as a sidewalk and approach to the street crossing, is a negligent act. 

Milbury v. Turner Center System, 274 Mass. 358, at 362 A collision might well be found to be not something unusual and unlikely to happen as a result of such blocking of a corner-something only remotely and slightly probable-but, rather, a consequence naturally to be expected. 

Milbury v. Turner Center System, 274 Mass. 358, at 363 

But see:

Falk v. Finkelman, 268 Mass. 524 

which is distinguishable as there the parking of the defendant's automobile at the curb was an innocent act, bare of negligence. Allowing it to remain there beyond twenty minutes, in ignorance of the ordinance forbidding parking for a longer time, although it subjected the owner to punishment, had nothing to do with the collision of fire apparatus or with causing the injury for which recovery was sought. 

See also: 

Rea v. Checker Taxi Co., 272 Mass. 510 where it was determined that the violation of a one way street ordinance placed the automobile where a collision could occur, one of the very things which the ordinance sought to prevent, and this could be found to be negligence directly contributing to the accident. 

Milbury v. Turner Center System, 274 Mass. 358, at 363

§190 SECTION 190. 

C. At or Between Crossings. 

Questions whether, in deciding to cross a street and in the method of carrying out the decision, a pedestrian was in the exercise of due care, whether the driver of the automobile was negligent, and generally, whether the accident was attributable to the negligence of either or of both or of neither parties, are usually questions of fact and not of law. 

Gartland v. Freeman, 1931 A. S. 2443 (Plaintiff half way across when he heard the hum of a motor approaching from his right, stopped and saw the defendant's automobile about 30 feet away and it seemed to veer directly toward him and then struck him)

Durling v. Lamontain, 1931 A. S. 2429 

Huggon v. Whipple & Co., 214 Mass. 64 (Pedestrian crossing on crosswalk of city street crowded with traffic)

Gray v. Batchelder, 208 Mass. 441 

Keaveny v. Moran, 208 Mass. 277

This rule was applied where a pedestrian in the daylight was struck and knocked down on a crosswalk when he was two-thirds of the way across a crowded city street where there were four lines of teams, two going south and two going north. The pedestrian worked his way through the two going south when there was a break in the third row going north caused by the moving of a dray to which a frisky horse was attached. Just as the dray moved the pedestrian, who was looking straight ahead to get through, just took one step with his left foot and the defendant's electric automobile came up, ran on the instep of his right leg, held the foot and struck and knocked him flat on his face on the crossing. 

Huggon v. Whipple & Co., 214 Mass. 64, at 65

§227 

Whether an operator was negligent in driving on a misty night, with a clouded windshield, without sounding an alarm, at 10 or 12 miles an hour, within few inches of a curb and in rounding a corner at a crossing which is fifty feet wide, failed to see and avoid a pedestrian on the crossing to the curb, is not a question of law but of fact. 

Moran v. Brodeur, 261 Mass. 120 

Clark v. Martin, 261 Mass. 60 (Child on crosswalk) 

Huffam v. Paquin, 259 Mass. 191 (Due care-stopped and looked) (Negligence-speed, no horn)

SECTION 191. 

(I) At Unusual Place or Diagonally. 

Although the operator must approach a crosswalk designed for pedestrians in a vigilant manner with his vehicle under such control that he can promptly stop it if occasion arises, yet he is not bound to anticipate that a pedestrian may suddenly run out from behind a parked vehicle. 

65 A.L.R. 194

But a pedestrian, although crossing a street diagonally, may recover for injuries sustained by a motor vehicle which made a sharp left turn into the street and struck the pedestrian. Particularly is this so when the motor vehicle failed to pass to the right of and beyond the center of the intersecting street before turning. 

Lowe v. Antonelli, 245 Mass. 237 

Direnski v. Eastern Mass. St. Ry. Co., 244 Mass. 313 (A motor vehicle proceeding at 20 miles an hour near a street intersection, suddenly turned to the left and proceeding diagonally, at middle of street struck a pedestrian, a boy five years of age) 

67 A.L.R. 333 

67 A.L.R. 319 

14 A.L.R. 1176

§192 

SECTION 192. 

(II) Through Procession of Vehicles. 

When there is nothing to indicate that a pedestrian will come in the pathway of a motor vehicle by first passing through a procession of motor vehicles moving on the same street in one direction or the other, there is no negligence on the part of the operator, particularly when the circumstances would not permit him to see the pedestrian for more than an instant, if at all. 

Rizzittelli v. Vestine, 246 Mass. 391

SECTION 193. 

d. On Sidewalk.

Where a pedestrian is on the sidewalk and is run down by an automobile which was run upon the sidewalk, the operator's negligence is usually a question of fact, Meech v. Sewall, 232 Mass. 460 although the unexplained running onto a sidewalk and striking a pedestrian would come within the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur.

So it is negligence to strike a person on a sidewalk with tires which project over the running board of a motor vehicle. 

Murray v. Liebman, 231 Mass. 7

Where the way is sufficiently wide for the vehicle to pass a pedestrian on the sidewalk without striking him, it is evidence of lack of reasonable care when the vehicle does strike the pedestrian. 

Forzley v. Bianchi, 240 Mass. 36 

Williams v. Holbrook, 216 Mass. 239 

Roach v. Hinchcliff, 214 Mass. 267 

, at 518

$229 

The driving onto a private driveway that emerges from a public sidewalk may be found to be negligence. 

Brown v. Daley, 273 Mass. 432, at 435

Lonergan v. American Ry. Exp. Co., 250 Mass. 30 

The pedestrian on the sidewalk may rely to some extent on the expectation that a motor vehicle emerging from an adjacent alley will stop and blow its horn before coming onto the sidewalk. 

SECTION 194. 

e. Stepping Off Sidewalk.

When the pedestrian is in plain sight although some distance from the motor vehicle and shows an indication to step off the sidewalk to cross the street, the operator may be found to be negligent if he strikes the pedestrian by his failure to give any warning of the car's approach, and by not slackening his speed but keeping on under the same momentum particularly when, after striking the pedestrian, the vehicle carries him some distance before coming to a stop. 

French v. Mooar, 226 Mass. 173 

65 A.L.R. 194

SECTION 195. 

f. Stepping Onto Sidewalk.

The operator of a motor vehicle must exercise reasonable care in permitting pedestrians to step onto sidewalks.

SECTION 196. 

g. Crossing Bridge.

Where the intestate was found about three feet from the left hand sidewalk at a place where persons were accustomed to cross at the end of the bridge, the driver is negligent where he should or could have seen the perilous position of the intestate and avoided the collision by stop-

$197 

 ping or changing the direction of his vehicle; and where driving at twenty miles an hour which speed, in the circumstances, was greater than was reasonably proper, he did not slacken. 

Walsh v. Gillis, 1931 A.S. 1363, at 1366 

G. L. c. 90, s. 17

SECTION 197. 

h. Colliding with Side of Vehicle. 

Walsh v. Gillis, 1931 A.S. 1363, at 1366 

G. L. c. 90, s. 17

CARS. 

1. Walking To. 

SECTION 198. 

(See: Section 317, page 385.)

When a pedestrian is seen by the operator of a motor vehicle at some distance and the operator knows that the pedestrian, having signalled a street car, is about to cross the street, and the operator travels on and knocks down the pedestrian, the issue of the operator's negligence is for the jury. 

, at 586 and 587 

Block v. Worcester, 186 Mass. 526 

Stinson v. Kenny, 176 Mass. 429

So, when a pedestrian, who has waited for a number of cars to go by, looks both ways and seeing no cars starts to cross the street and then upon reaching the car tracks is hit by a motor vehicle, the operator's negligence is a question of fact. 

French v. Mooar, 226 Mass. 173

When a person is struck by an automobile while crossing a street to take a street car, the question of negligence

§231 

 may be determined by the statute (G. L. c. 90, s. 14) that requires operators of motor vehicles to give warning of their approach towards street cars which have stopped to take on passengers.

Simonson v. Angel, 256 Mass. 256

Defendant saw deceased when she was one hundred feet from him, his speed was forty miles an hour and he continued at that speed until the accident. No signal was sounded and the point of impact was the left part of the automobile and the vehicle went one hundred feet after striking deceased before it came to a stop when deceased was on ground near left front wheel. The defendant said, "Never mind. I am insured, and I will take care of her mother."

2. Waiting For.

SECTION 199. 

(See: Section 318, page 386.) 

Where a pedestrian, who though seventy-five years of age, had good eyesight and hearing, after standing and conversing near a white pole which indicated a stopping place for street cars and near which others were also standing, started across the street in broad daylight to a white pole on the other side of the street to take a car going in opposite direction from the car which struck him, the street being broad and straight, with a number of motor vehicles going by, and where the pedestrian, before starting to cross the street, looked both ways on the street.

$200 

As the car which struck him approached, it lessened its rate of speed from twenty-five miles per hour, when nine hundred feet away, to twelve to fifteen miles per hour, when forty feet away, and was gradually going slower, the pedestrian being struck as he was crossing the last rail of the track on which the car was approaching, no gong was sounded in the car, a municipal order as to control of street cars when nearing pedestrians was violated, and just before the pedestrian was struck a terrific noise of putting on the brakes was heard, it was held that the contributory negligence of the pedestrian, and the negligence of the motorman were for the jury.

McGrath v. Boston El. Ry., 257 Mass. 541 

Although operator was blinded by lights of approaching street car and does not see pedestrian because his clothing is in color like that of the road, the question of the operator's negligence is one of fact. 

Alpert v. Ellis, 236 Mass. 404, at 405 (Struck pedestrian from back) 

Powers v. Loring, 231 Mass. 458

Person waiting for a street car was struck by skidding automobile which had no chains and had been driven past a trolley car slowing for a stop into the tracks approaching a considerable number of people in readiness to board a trolley car. These facts in conjunction warrant a finding of negligence. 

Spain v. Oikemus, 1932 A. S. 573 at 575 

3. Alighting.

SECTION 200. 

(See: Section 319, page 387.)

General Laws Chapter 90, Section 14 provides, in part, that: "In approaching or passing a car of a street railway which has been stopped to allow passengers to alight from or board the same, the person operating a motor vehicle

$233 

 shall not drive such vehicle within eight feet of the running board or lowest step of the car then in use by passengers for the purpose of alighting or boarding, except by the express direction of a traffic officer or except at points where passengers are protected by safety zones." 

A person alighting from a street car and following other passengers in crossing in front of it may rely to some extent on the expectation that the driver of a motor vehicle will not run into him, even though it is going thirty-five miles an hour and no signal is given, both of which facts are evidence of negligence. 

Hepburn v. Walters, 263 Mass. 139, at 141 

Pawloski v. Hess, 253 Mass. 478 

Kaminski v. Fournier, 235 Mass. 51 

Emery v. Miller, 231 Mass. 243 

In Hartnett v. Tripp, 231 Mass. 382, at 384 the court said: "If the jury was satisfied... that the [street] car stopped to allow the plaintiff to alight, and the defendant knew it, or in the exercise of reasonable care ought to have known it, there was evidence that he violated [G. L. c. 90, s. 14] .. in approaching or passing a car of a street railway which has been stopped to allow passengers to alight or embark... and if the defendant violated this provision of the statute it was evidence of negligence." 

And in McGourty v. DeMarco, 200 Mass. 57, at 60, where the plaintiff in alighting from a street car was run into from behind by a team owned by the defendant and driven by his son, it was said: 

"If the defendant was attempting to pass the [street] car from behind on his right hand in violation of [G. L. c. 90, s. 14] the jury might find that this, under the circumstances, was negligence on the driver's part such as [the plaintiff] was not called upon to anticipate."

§201 

See also: 

Foster v. Curtis, 213 Mass. 79, at 82 

Keeney v. Springfield St. Ry., 210 Mass. 44, at 48

The relative rights of the general public to use the highway through which a street railway runs were defined some fifty years ago by Chief Justice Shaw in Commonwealth v. Temple, 14 Gray 69, at 75, as being equal “in the absence of any special regulation by law." 

Foster v. Curtis, 213 Mass. 79, at 83

It is common knowledge that passengers generally leave street cars from the right hand side, whether the cars run on single or double tracks, which in cities and large villages usually are located in the center of thoroughfares where travel is most frequent. 

Shepherd v. Nirenstein, 273 Mass. 7 

Dennison v. Swerdlove, 250 Mass. 507, at 508

SECTION 201. 

(See: Section 320, page 388.)

SECTION 202. 

C. PERSONS LEADING ANIMALS. 

See: Section 354, page 441.

General Laws Chapter 90, Section 14 provides, in part, that: "Every person operating a motor vehicle shall bring the motor vehicle and the motor propelling it immediately to a stop on approaching a horse or other draft animal being led, ridden or driven, if such animal appears to be frightened and if the person in charge thereof shall signal so to do; and if travelling in the opposite direction to that in which such animal is proceeding, said vehicle shall remain stationary so long as may be reasonable to allow such animal to pass; or, if travelling in the same direction, the person so operating shall use reasonable caution in thereafter passing such animal.”

So, one driving an automobile at night, at the rate of twenty-six miles an hour, overtaking a pedestrian leading horses along the right-hand side of the highway, may be

E. PERSONS WORKING IN OR ON HIGHWAYS. 

An operator of a motor vehicle should use such care in driving as a reasonably careful operator ought to use in going through the particular locality so as to avoid injury to workmen making repairs on the highway, street railway tracks, other motor vehicles and other things which are incident to the use of the road.

SECTION 211. 

L. PERSONS WITH PHYSICAL DISABILITIES. 

See: Section 323, page 394.

In determining the standard of reasonable care exercised by the operator, consideration should be given to the operator's duty to remember that the travelling public is made up of persons of all kinds, including some who have physical disabilities, mental impairments and other ailments.

So, part of the operator's duty is to remember that there are deaf, blind, dumb, crippled and other pedestrians upon the public highways. 

Brereton v. Milford etc. St. Ry. Co., 223 Mass. 130, at 133

M. INTOXICATED PERSONS. 

See: Section 300, page 373. 

See: Section 324, page 396.

If the operator of a motor vehicle does or reasonably should observe that a pedestrian is intoxicated or is under the influence of intoxicating liquor, the operator should increase his degree of caution or care so as to avoid injury to the pedestrian. 

Black v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R.R. Co., 193 Mass. 448

N. CHILDREN. 

See: Section 325, page 397.

SECTION 213. 

The operator of a motor vehicle is bound to exercise sufficient care to prevent injury to children who are on or near the highway. 

Direnski v. Eastern Mass. St. Ry. Co., 244 Mass. 313

$241 

Nelligan v. Fontaine, 225 Mass. 329 (Child around ice wagon, run over and killed-no signal)

Belleveau v. S. C. Lowe Sup. Co., 200 Mass. 237 

65 A.L.R. 198

But the operator is not bound to anticipate that children will unexpectedly run in front of the motor vehicle or otherwise expose themselves to danger. 

West v. Medford, 255 Mass. 266 (Plaintiff, 7 years old, saw defendant's truck 100 feet distant on road and trolley car on left and ran in front of defendant's truck without looking-defendant not negligent)

But it may be found to be negligence on the part of an operator of a truck to drive upon the sidewalk to enter his own premises without observing children who are crossing the sidewalk, and without acting with due care in view of their presence. 

Hirrel v. Lacey, 274 Mass. 431, at 435 

Particularly when the children on the sidewalk are in plain view of the operator and there is nothing to obstruct his view. 

Hirrel v. Lacey, 274 Mass. 431, at 435 

King v. Weitzman, 267 Mass. 447 

, at 282 and 283 

There is no negligence, however, where boy suddenly runs out from sidewalk. 

Lovett v. Scott, 232 Mass. 541

4. Playing in Highway.

SECTION 217. 

5. Alighting From or Coming From Behind or Around Another Vehicle. 

When under the particular circumstances a person could not reasonably foresee the presence of children in the path of an automobile or prevent a collision, there is no negligence on the part of the operator of the motor vehicle such as is usually the case when without warning a child walks or runs into the street from behind or around another vehicle without stopping and giving the operator an opportunity to observe the presence of the child on the highway. 

So, the driver of a truck is not negligent when, upon approaching a wagon standing near the curb, he turns to the left to pass it and after passing as closely as he can, and going at a moderate speed although not blowing his horn, he turns toward the sidewalk on the right side at the very moment that a boy eight years of age leaves the sidewalk near the standing wagon and walks or runs into the street five or six steps when he is hit by the right side of the truck.

Lovett v. Scott, 232 Mass. 541 

65 A.L.R. 200

The question of negligence is for the jury in an action for an injury to a child who crossed the street in front of a parked automobile and when about in the center of the street stopped and waited for another automobile to pass and after taking several steps was struck by the defendant's automobile, going in an opposite direction, where the defendant could have seen the child if he had looked properly. 

Jean v. Nester, 261 Mass. 442 65 A.L.R. 201

 O. PERSONS IN OR ON MOTOR VEHICLES. 

See: Sections 330-343, pages 406-416. 

SECTION 218. 

A person responsible for the control of a motor vehicle is required to use some care towards persons in or on the vehicle. 

The degree of care which measures the standard of his duty depends upon whether the persons in or on the vehicle are gratuitous or paid passengers. 

For full discussion, see: 

Massaletti v. Fitzroy, 228 Mass. 487.

In the last cited case, it was said at page 510: "Justice requires that one who undertakes to perform a duty gratuitously should not be under the same measure of obligation as one who enters upon the same undertaking for pay. There is an inherent difficulty in stating the difference between the measure of duty which is assumed in the two cases. But justice requires that to make out liability in case of a gratuitous undertaking, the plaintiff ought to prove a materially greater degree of negligence than he has to prove where the defendant is to be paid for the same thing."

So, one who is travelling gratuitously in a motor vehicle by the owner's invitation and is injured by reason of the negligence of the operator cannot maintain an action against such owner or operator for his injuries unless he can show gross negligence on the part of the person whom he seeks to charge. 

Massaletti v. Fitzroy, 228 Mass. 487, at 508

Although a jounce may be some evidence of negligence when taken in connection with other evidence, as of excessive speed, failure by the driver to maintain a proper lookout, of careless handling of the machine when it stands alone, it is not enough to sustain a finding of negligence.

$245 

Broderick v. Lyons, 266 Mass. 184 

Labatte v. Lavallee, 258 Mass. 527

Terlizzi v. Marsh, 258 Mass. 156 

Marcienowski v. Sanders, 252 Mass. 65 

44 A.L.R. 785

When a person is riding in a vehicle under an agreement, consent or request of a person other than the owner of the vehicle, he must prove that the person making such agreement, giving such consent, or making such request had authority so to do.

An ordinary operator has no implied or ostensible authority to invite other persons to ride with him or to hire such persons in the owner's service. 

Broitman v. Silver, 270 Mass. 24, at 25

So, one who is hired to drive a truck to deliver merchandise has no further authority and when he permits another person to ride on the vehicle, the driver is not acting within the real or apparent scope of his employment. 

Broitman v. Silver, 270 Mass. 24, at 28

However, the result is otherwise if the employer expressly or impliedly assents to assume any duty toward such other person, or ratifies the acts of the driver, or an emergency exists requiring additional assistance for the driver. 

Broitman v. Silver, 270 Mass. 24, at 28 

Murphy v. Barry, 264 Mass. 557 

Butler v. Mechanics' Iron Fdry. Co., 259 Mass. 560, at 563 

Stone v. Commonwealth Coal Co., 259 Mass. 360 

O'Leary v. Fash, 245 Mass. 123, at 127 

Bowler v. O'Connell, 162 Mass. 319, at 320 

Powers v. B. & M. R.R., 153 Mass. 188, at 190 

But see Lyttle v. Monto, 248 Mass. 340, where driver, who was owner of the truck, asked to be directed to a place and invited other person to accompany him and show the way.

$219 

The result may be different if person was invited by anyone who had the authority so to do, such as a manager. 

Broitman v. Silver, 270 Mass. 24, at 28

Making no remonstrance when driver turned to left of road (in violation of General Laws Chapter 89, Section 

4) to pass another car, as matter of law is not due care.

Thorpe v. Boston El. Ry., 259 Mass. 415 

Morel v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R.R., 238 Mass. 392

Distinguished from: 

Chadbourne v. Springfield St. Ry. Co., 199 Mass. 574

SECTION 219. 

2. Passengers for Hire.

Where an occupant gives good and sufficient legal consideration to the owner for the transportation, he is not a guest but a passenger for hire. 

Chooljian v. Nahigian, 273 Mass. 396, at 398

So, where a contract is established between the occupant and the owner of the motor vehicle, whereby, for a sufficient legal consideration, the occupant agrees to give to the owner the use of a garage for a reasonable time without the payment of rent, and the owner, in consideration of such agreement and use, promises to take the occupant and her husband to ride on Sundays, evenings and holidays, as the occupant and the owner might reasonably agree upon during the owner's use of the garage: 

Chooljian v. Nahigian, 273 Mass. 396, at 398 

Evers v. Gilfoil, 247 Mass. 219, at 224 

Proctor v. Union Coal Co., 243 Mass. 428, at 432 

Sherman v. Pfefferkorn, 241 Mass. 468, at 473 

Carnig v. Carr, 167 Mass. 544

$247 

 when the automobile is zigzagging, shaking and wobbling and the occupant calls the operator's attention to such fact, it may be found to be negligence for the operator to continue to operate the car without ascertaining the cause of the irregularity of its motion and therefrom determining whether it is safe to drive the car in the condition in which it is. 

Chooljian v. Nahigian, 273 Mass. 396, at 398 (Where car tipped over)

A company that operates a bus owes and is obliged to treat a passenger with a high degree of care, and to permit such passenger to reach a place of safety within the body of the vehicle before starting. 

Coyle v. Worcester C. St. Ry. Co., 273 Mass. 475, and cases cited

So, when a bus starts before the passenger has safely reached a position within the body of the bus, there is a basis for the finding of negligence on the part of the operator of the bus. 

Coyle v. Worcester C. St. Ry. Co., 273 Mass. 475, at 476 It is negligent operation to cause injuries to a passenger, where a bus is standing by the side of the road in a slanting position, and the passenger has to stoop down and walk sideways to reach her seat, when the operator puts out the lights and starts the bus "with a jump ahead and then backwards again" so that the passenger is taken off her feet, unable to maintain her balance, cannot see anything to seize hold of because of the darkness, and then is thrown down, her shoulder striking on the corner of a seat so that when she attempts to leave the bus she is unable to raise her hand and take hold of the seat in front of her. 

Dorman v. Worcester Cons. St. Ry., 1931 A.S. 1967, at 1968 One in the taxi business is a carrier of passengers for hire and is liable for negligence to the plaintiff, who, as the

$219 defendant said, "hopped" into his cab, which had been hired by another, with the owner's knowledge and consent and without objection. As a matter of law, a contract for conveyance as a passenger for hire was made out. 

Dion v. Drapeau, 254 Mass. 186

Even though the plaintiff is carried gratuitously, he can recover because having accepted the plaintiff as a passenger, the defendant is bound to exercise a degree of care consistent with the nature of the business in which he is engaged. 

Dion v. Drapeau, 254 Mass. 186

A passenger may recover from a taxi cab company for the negligence of its driver in proceeding down a one way street in a direction which is in violation of the Park Department rule when the passenger is injured by a collision with an automobile coming in the opposite direction. 

Rea v. Checker Taxi Company, 272 Mass. 510

The violation of the rule of the Park Department by the driver of the taxi is not only in itself a wrongful act, apart from negligence, rendering him a trespasser on the one way street as to other persons using it lawfully: 

Rea v. Checker Taxi Company, 272 Mass. 510, at 512 

MacDonald v. Boston El. Ry., 262 Mass. 475, at 476 

See also: 

Dudley v. Northampton St. Ry., 202 Mass. 443, at 448 and 449 but the violation of the rule by the driver of the taxi cab can be found to be a contributing cause of the accident and not merely an attendant circumstance or condition though perhaps a necessary condition thereof. 

Rea v. Checker Taxi Company, 272 Mass. 510, at 512 

Widronak v. Lord, 269 Mass. 238 

Loftus v. Pelletier, 223 Mass. 63 

Hinds v. Steere, 209 Mass. 442, at 444 

Dudley v. Northampton St. Ry., 202 Mass. 443, at 446

$249 

A person riding in a motor vehicle is not a passenger for hire just because he has agreed to pay part of the expenses of gasoline, oil and garage on a fishing trip, for the vehicle is not being operated under a contract express or implied that the owner should be paid for transportation as a separate and distinct charge. 

Askowith v. Massell, 260 Mass. 202, at 205

The owner of a sightseeing automobile carrying passengers for hire is obliged to use the highest degree of care consistent with the proper transaction of the business. 

Hinds v. Steere, 209 Mass. 442 

3. Invited Guests.

SECTION 220. 

An invited guest whose passage is gratuitous cannot recover for ordinary negligence but can recover only if the defendant was guilty of gross negligence or wilful, wanton and reckless conduct.

Meaney v. Doyle, 1931 A.S. 1471 

Bank v. Satran, 266 Mass. 253 

Manning v. Simpson, 261 Mass. 494, at 495 

Gaboury v. Tisdell, 261 Mass. 147, at 148 

Flynn v. Lewis, 231 Mass. 550 

Massaletti v. Fitzroy, 228 Mass. 487

In accordance with this rule, the operator or owner of an automobile must be guilty at least of gross negligence before a guest or gratuitous passenger may recover for injuries sustained while riding with him. 

Terlizzi v. Marsh, 258 Mass. 156 

51 A.L.R. 582 and 583

A person may be found to be a guest of the operator although apparently he was driving that person in the motor vehicle to places where that person desired to go. 

Notwithstanding that circumstance, the operator, or person

$220 

 in control of the vehicle, is liable to the guest for injuries caused by the operator's gross negligence. 

Smiddy v. O'Neil, 1931 A.S. 1963, at 1965 

O'Leary v. Fash, 245 Mass. 123, at 124 

Altman v. Aronson, 231 Mass. 588, at 591 

Massaletti v. Fitzroy, 228 Mass. 487, at 489, 508 and 510 

West v. Poor, 196 Mass. 183

The fact that the injured person is especially invited by the defendant, who urges and desires to have the injured person accompany him so all could have a better time and everything would be all right does not change the injured person to any other status than a gratuitous guest. 

Gaboury v. Tisdell, 261 Mass. 147, at 149

However, if the injured person is in the employment of, or is performing a service for, the defendant such person is not classified as a guest. 

Gaboury v. Tisdell, 261 Mass. 147, at 148 

Labatte v. Lavallee, 258 Mass. 527 

Jackson v. Queen, 257 Mass. 515 

Lyttle v. Monto, 248 Mass. 340

The invitor is liable to the invitee if the latter is in the exercise of due care and his injuries are the result of gross negligence on the part of the invitor.

Marcienowski v. Sanders, 252 Mass. 65 (No. G. N.) 

O'Leary v. Fash, 245 Mass. 123 

Barry v. Harding, 244 Mass. 588 

Flynn v. Lewis, 231 Mass. 550

The fact of the passenger's request that the operator let him off the vehicle and that the operator told the passenger that he would be all right does not create gross negligence. 

Cook v. Cole, 273 Mass. 557, at 562 

Bertelli v. Tronconi, 264 Mass. 235 

Burke v. Cook, 246 Mass. 518

The rule is that the operator of a motor vehicle, by

251 

 analogy to the liability of a gratuitous bailee, is liable for injuries resulting from his gross negligence to an invited person whom he is transporting gratuitously. 

Cook v. Cole, 273 Mass. 557, at 559

Rog v. Eltis, 269 Mass. 466 

Manning v. Simpson, 261 Mass. 494 

Marcienowski v. Sanders, 252 Mass. 65, at 67 

Burke v. Cook, 246 Mass. 518 

Flynn v. Lewis, 231 Mass. 550, at 554 

Massaletti v. Fitzroy, 228 Mass. 487 2 A.L.R. 896 

Mere acquiescence by the operator in the passenger's presence on the vehicle does not create an invitation, but makes the passenger a self-invited guest. 

Cook v. Cole, 273 Mass. 557, at 559 

West v. Poor, 196 Mass. 183, at 185

Even if the passenger is riding on the vehicle solely for his own purposes, it does not follow necessarily that he is not an invited person within the meaning of the rule. 

Cook v. Cole, 273 Mass. 557, at 559 and 560

One, a stranger to defendant, who accepts an invitation to ride warrants a finding that he is a guest. 

Cook v. Cole, 273 Mass. 557

Where plaintiff, who has been invited to ride by defendant's servant on wagon, alights to see a number and, telling this to servant, turns away to go home and is struck by a wheel when wagon starts, the defendant is liable as it may be found that the unauthorized ride was at an end and plaintiff was a traveller. 

Conley v. Rosenfield, 271 Mass. 433

(II) Actions for Injuries Received in For eign States.

The rule requiring a guest in a motor vehicle to show that the operator was guilty of gross negligence does not apply to an action brought to recover for injuries received in an accident in a foreign state or jurisdiction by the law of which a guest may recover upon showing only ordinary negligence on the part of the operator. 

Askowith v. Massell, 260 Mass. 202 

51 A.L.R. 583

But a suit may be maintained in this Commonwealth for negligently rendering a highway in a foreign state so dangerous as to cause injury to the plaintiff there, although the defendant was acting under the control of the highway commission of that state.

Licensees-Permissive Guests. 

A person who is merely a licensee or is permitted to remain upon a motor vehicle without an invitation, express or implied, can recover only in the event of wilful, wanton and reckless conduct on the part of the operator or owner. 

Prondecka v. Turner Falls etc. Co., 241 Mass. 100; 

S. C. 238 Mass. 239

$224 

So, where a girl five years of age, in the absence of defendant, climbed onto his wagon and the defendant drove her a short distance but while she was alighting, although the defendant was helping her, she was thrown to the ground and hurt, the court held that in order to be liable the defendant must have been guilty of culpable negligence which in effect is wilful, wanton and reckless conduct. 

West v. Poor, 196 Mass. 183

SECTION 224. 

5. Trespassers.

The duty owed to a trespasser is to refrain from wilful, wanton and reckless conduct.

A trespasser can not recover for acts of the defendant. which were either ordinary or gross negligence. He must further and show conduct of a different character which was wilful, wanton or reckless. go So, a trespasser on the defendant's vehicle who is ordered off by the driver cannot recover for injuries received when alighting unless there was an intentional purpose to injure the trespasser or to proceed regardless of the trespasser's position. 

Gallagher v. O'Riorden, 208 Mass. 275

Also, an employee of an automobile dealer who, after the close of his day's work and in violation of a rule established by his employer, rode in an automobile driven by a fellow employee, who had no authority to invite him, can not recover from his employer for injury suffered in a

$255 

 collision with another vehicle.

He was a trespasser to whom the employer owed no duty of care. 

Walker v. Fuller, 223 Mass. 566

SECTION 225. 

P. PERSONS HOLDING ON TO MOTOR VE- HICLES. 

Persons holding on to motor vehicles may come within the category of passengers for hire, invited guests, licensees, permissive guests or trespassers, depending upon the circumstances.

As to a chauffeur within the course of his employment, the owner owes the duty of refraining from ordinary negligence. 

So, if the owner shifts levers without the knowledge of the chauffeur while the latter is cranking the motor vehicle, thereby causing the engine to "back-fire" and break the chauffeur's wrist, the owner has been guilty of negligence. 

Norris v. Allen, 217 Mass. 573 

Gross negligence may be found where a child of seven and one-half years of age is invited by the defendant to ride standing on the running board and then, travelling at an excessive speed on a rough road the defendant turns his car so that the child is thrown off. 

Terlizzi v. Marsh, 258 Mass. 156 

25 A.L.R. 1513

CHAPTER IX. 

CARE AS TO ANIMALS. 

SECTION 226. 

A. INJURING ANIMALS. 

General Laws Chapter 90, Section 14 (Acts 1925, 305; 

1928, 166) provides, in part, that: "Every person operating a motor vehicle shall bring the vehicle and the motor propelling it immediately to a stop when approaching a horse or other draft animal being led, ridden or driven, if such animal appears to be frightened and if the person in charge thereof shall signal so to do; and, if traveling in the opposite direction to that in which such animal is proceeding, said vehicle shall remain stationary so long as may be reasonable to allow such animal to pass; or, if traveling in the same direction, the person operating shall use reasonable caution in thereafter passing such animal.”

An operator of a motor vehicle must refrain from negligently injuring animals that may be in the highway which are attended or unattended. 

Lacker v. Strauss, 226 Mass. 579 (Dog run over)

II A.L.R. 1402 

Even animals straying on the highway must not be injured through the negligent operation of a motor vehicle. 

So, a bull which is at large upon a highway without fault of its owner, though subject to be impounded under G. L. c. 49, s. 24, is not a trespasser in the highway and the operator of a motor vehicle is liable to the owner of the bull for negligently injuring it. 

Carrington v. Worcester Cons. St. Ry., 222 Mass. 119

257 

Care as to Animals

B. FRIGHTENING ANIMALS. 

An operator of a motor vehicle may be negligent in not sounding a horn or giving signal when approaching a horse, or other animal, whether led, ridden or attached to a wagon.

(Excessive speed-vehicle should have stopped)

A speed of 35 miles an hour upon a straight and level road in approaching a vehicle drawn by a horse which shows no sign of alarm, travelling on the opposite side of the center of the way, is not negligent. 

Boyd v. Mills, 1932 A. S. 115, at 116 

Hicks v. H. B. Church Truck Service Co., 259 Mass. 272, at 275

Travellers can not entirely rely on signals and the performance of duty by the train employees.

The true rule, in the absence of a statutory or municipal regulation governing the situation, is indicated by the frequently repeated declarations by the courts of the obvious truth that a railroad track is in itself a signal of danger. 

Whatever difference of opinion there may be on the question of stopping an automobile before crossing the tracks, it is practically agreed that the driver is guilty of contributory negligence as a matter of law if he does not look and listen, for approaching trains before venturing on the tracks.

So, one about to pass over a railroad crossing who sees a train approaching, as a general proposition, has a duty to stop the machine and permit the train to pass. 

Absence of proper warning will not carry the question of contributory negligence to the jury but the matter will be disposed of as a question of law. 

If the driver looked, he either saw the approaching train or he did not see it. If he saw it, he might be found guilty of negligence in taking the chance of beating the train over the crossing.

The rule releasing one from careless acts committed in an emergency cannot be invoked in behalf of one who has placed himself in such a position through his own lack of care.

Not negligent in failing to give warning by lights, flagmen or otherwise of the presence of such a train, unless the circumstances are such as to charge the employees of the railroad company with knowledge that travellers are likely to collide with it.

Where an automobilist, injured by running into a freight train on a crossing with which he was familiar, drove at top speed onto such crossing, on a stormy night, with the windshield up and all curtains down, he was guilty of contributory negligence. 

No recovery because of lack of due care. Reasonable care requires that the driver of a motor vehicle have the machine under such control at a railroad crossing that it may be stopped if necessary to avoid the train.

Motorist driving machine to within about 15 feet of crossing with which he was familiar and where he knew train might come from either direction at any moment and then saw an approaching train which struck him when he attempted to cross. 

His negligence precluded recovery although the railroad company was negligent in running the train at a high rate of speed and in failing to give crossing signals. 

Under the Massachusetts doctrine a person riding in an unregistered automobile does not have the rights of a traveller and a person so riding cannot invoke the statute.

Care as to Street Cars CHAPTER XI. 

CARE AS TO STREET CARS AND PERSONS THEREON SECTION 229. 

See: Sections 290-295, pages 362-365.

The rule as to ordinary reasonable care, which measures the duty of the operator of a motor vehicle towards other vehicles and persons, prevails in the same degree in measuring his obligation toward street cars and persons thereon. 

The operator of a motor vehicle, either in approaching toward or travelling alongside of street railway tracks, is not usually required to constantly watch out for street cars. The operator should not give all his attention to one direction but should be alert to, and anticipate the possibility of, danger from any direction.

It may constitute negligence for the operator to devote his observation solely to street cars while he is required to exercise care towards other vehicles as well as pedestrians and persons on the highway. The operator should apportion his faculties and attention among all vehicles and travellers. If he fails to see an approaching pedestrian because his attention is devoted exclusively to street cars, he may be negligent, and vice versa.

The operator of a motor vehicle has a right to rely to a certain extent upon the exercise of reasonable care by the motormen of street cars. Both operator and motorman have a right to rely on each other to a certain extent that each will exercise diligence to avoid collision. 

A street car company has not the exclusive right to travel upon its tracks either in the highway or at crossings and intersections.

The motor vehicle operator has an equal right to use the highway and street crossings and intersections.

$229 

So, when the motor vehicle reaches an intersection or crossing in advance of a street car, the operator may properly assume that the motorman will give the operator of the motor vehicle the right of way if he is entitled to it under G. L. c. 89, ss. 8 and 9, reduce the speed of the street car and do other acts necessary to avoid a collision. 

At crossings and intersecting ways both the operator of the motor vehicle and the motorman of the street car must exercise reasonable care to avoid a collision and neither can continue to travel without regard to the other and upon the assumption that the other will stop his vehicle or permit the other to pass. 

However, under G. L. c. 89, ss. 8 and 9, the vehicle reaching the intersection in advance of the other is entitled to priority but, even with such right of way, the operator of that vehicle can not heedlessly proceed on the assumption that the other will do nothing to interfere with his right of way.

But the motor vehicle operator is not required to assume that the street car will travel at an unreasonable or improper speed, will not grant the right of way or will otherwise violate the law.

The motor vehicle operator is not usually required to stop his machine before crossing a street railway track and if the operator, after prudent observation, believes that he has sufficient time to cross the track in safety, he is not negligent in attempting so to do. 

However, the street car operating upon rails, going forward and back, has not the same opportunity to avoid a collision as has the motor vehicle because of the latter's ability to turn in and out.

A motor vehicle operator may be guilty of contributory negligence in approaching a street car or crossing ahead of it either at an intersecting way or while travelling in the same or opposite direction, such contributory negli-

$269 

Care as to Street Cars gence depending upon the circumstances, the speed, distance, condition of highway, presence of other vehicles and every condition entering into the determination of the reasonableness of the conduct of both the motor vehicle operator and the motorman. As to whether either should stop or proceed depends upon existing conditions. 

The street railway company is not an insurer of the safety of persons travelling in a motor vehicle. The company is responsible only for injury and damage caused by its negligence. 

Improper conduct of persons in a motor vehicle may not deprive them of recovery from a street railway company unless that conduct was a proximate contributing cause of the accident.

Passengers of both motor vehicle and street car usually have greater rights than do the operators thereof as against the street railway company. Passengers may recover for concurrent negligence of the motorman and the motor vehicle operator. 

When a motorman discovers that a motor vehicle is in a position of danger at, on or near the street railway tracks, the motorman may be negligent in failing to avoid damage to it or its occupants even though the motor vehicle was improperly placed in its position.

A motorman is required to have the street car under control, operate at a reasonable rate of speed, give necessary warnings of approach, particularly at street crossings, congested areas and places where travellers are likely to be 

Under the sudden danger doctrine both the motorman and the motor vehicle operator are not required to exercise the same degree of thought and caution as they would under ordinary circumstances. However, each must think and act as a reasonable person would in such an emergency, taking into consideration the lack of opportunity for deliberate judgment and the necessity for quick action.

COLLECTION OF CASES Falkner v. Eastern Mass. St. Ry. Co., 1931 A. S. 2261 

Collision between a street car of the defendant and the automobile in which the deceased was riding as a guest; the accident occurring at night. The atmosphere was foggy and misty and the road surface wet. The concrete part of the road was 192 feet wide with a graveled shoulder on either side 3 feet 3 inches wide; upon one side of the street and within the limits of the highway was the single track of the defendant. The top of the rail was flush with the surface of the street but there was a drop of 5 inches to the crushed stones between the ties. The defendant's street car was going in the opposite direction from that of the automobile which was moving at a speed of 10 to 15 miles an hour, and as it approached the point of the accident the operator saw a headlight 100 to 150 yards away. He was traveling on the right hand side of the road and thought the headlight was upon an automobile with one light and accordingly veered slightly to the right and dropped into the street car track and then travelled 10 to 20 feet while he was trying to get out. The automobile came to a stop. 

The rail was wet and slippery and before the accident both headlights of the automobile were on; no gong or whistle from the street car which was going 40 miles an hour. The street car pushed the automobile more than 60 feet and came to a stop more than 200 feet from the place where the emergency brakes were applied. Following the collision one wheel of the automobile was missing and the engine was pushed back toward the front or side. 

The damage was to the front right part of the automobile and the front right part of the street car. 

The court said at page 2264: "This evidence brings the case within the principle stated in Austin v. Eastern Massachusetts Street Railway, 

269 Mass. 420, where the motorman should have · • ·
