The fact that plaintiff looked and failed to discern the approaching car will not relieve him from charge of negligence. 

Finn v. East. Mass. St. Ry., 1932 A. S. 827 

Plaintiff backed from private driveway onto track, stopped to allow passing of other vehicle, struck by street car.

$230 

 CHAPTER XII. 

PERSONS LIABLE FOR INJURY A. OPERATOR. 

SECTION 230. 

The operator of a motor vehicle is liable for his own negligence irrespective of whether the owner, person in control, or others may also be liable.

But the operator is liable only for the injuries of which his negligence is the proximate cause.

So, leaving an automobile unlocked contrary to the statute is not the proximate cause of a collision due to the theft of that automobile when the thief causes injury by his negligent operation of the vehicle. 

Slater v. Baker, 261 Mass. 424 

B. OWNER (See Sec. 244, page 296 et seq.)

SECTION 231. 

General Laws Chapter 231, Section 85A (Acts 1928, 

317, s. 1) provides that: "In all actions to recover damages for injuries to the person or to property or for the death of a person, arising out of an accident or collision in which a motor vehicle was involved, evidence that at the time of such accident or collision it was registered in the name of the defendant as owner shall be prima facie evidence that it was then being operated by and under the control of a person for whose conduct the defendant was legally responsible, and absence of such responsibility shall be an affirmative defence to be set up in the answer and proved by the defendant."

285 

This statute merely creates prima facie evidence which may be rebutted and controlled by other evidence. 

General Laws Chapter 229, Section 5 (Acts 1922, 439; 

1925, 346, s. 9) provides that: "Except as provided in sections one, two and three, a person who by his negligence or by his wilful, wanton or reckless act, or by the negligence or wilful, wanton or reckless act of his agents or servants while engaged in his business, causes the death of a person in the exercise of due care, shall be liable in damages in the sum of not less than five hundred nor more than ten thousand dollars, to be assessed with reference to the degree of his culpability or of that of his agents or servants, to be recovered in an action of tort, commenced, except as provided by section four of chapter two hundred and sixty, within two years after the injury which caused the death by the executor or administrator of the deceased, to be distributed as provided in section one."

Proof that the defendant owned the automobile is not in itself sufficient to entitle the plaintiff to go to the jury. 

There must be satisfactory evidence that he was in control or driver was his servant. 

Phillips v. Gookin, 231 Mass. 250

Proof of ownership of a car by the defendant and that the driver was in his general employ are not sufficient to establish liability for the negligence of the driver. Plaintiff must go further and offer evidence from which it can be found that the driver was engaged in business of his employer. 

Lekarczyk v. Dupre, 265 Mass. 33 

Arnold v. Brereton, 261 Mass. 238 

Kwedares v. Knoel, 261 Mass. 91 

Rosenberg v. Karas, 259 Mass. 568 

Washburn v. R. F. Owens Co., 252 Mass. 47 

McDonough v. Vozzela, 247 Mass. 552 and cases collected

§231 

Moquin v. Kalicka, 247 Mass. 476, at 478

Porcino v. De Stefano, 243 Mass. 398 

O'Rourke v. A-G Co., Inc., 232 Mass. 129 

Gardner v. Farnum, 230 Mass. 193 

Melchionda v. American Locomotive Co., 229 Mass. 202, at 204 

Robinson v. Doe, 224 Mass. 319, at 321 

Heywood v. Ogasapian, 224 Mass. 203 

Hartnett v. Gryzmish, 218 Mass. 258 

Perkins v. Rice, 187 Mass. 28

But rule is different if owner permits unlicensed driver to operate. (See: Section 236, page 289.) · 

Under the common law of this Commonwealth mere ownership of a motor vehicle without evidence that it is being driven by his servant is not enough to fasten on the owner liability for its negligent operation. 

Opinion of the Justices, 251 Mass. 569, at 599 

Phillips v. Gookin, 231 Mass. 250

Such a rule of the common law may be changed by statute. 

Opinion of the Justices, 251 Mass. 569, at 599 

Duggan v. Bay State St. Ry., 230 Mass. 370, at 380

The liability for the negligent use of an automobile by one other than the owner can not be predicated against the owner merely because of his ownership of the car. 

See: Opinion of the Justices, 251 Mass. 569, at 599 

Owner is not liable for negligence of chauffeur unless latter is his servant and at time is acting within the scope of his employment. Mere proof of ownership of car does not make out prima facie case. 

Hartnett v. Gryzmish, 218 Mass. 258

The extension of liability of the owner of a motor vehicle under a policy with an omnibus clause so as to in-

287 

 clude personal injury caused by the motor vehicle while being negligently operated by the owner's express or implied consent, does not render the owner liable for damages caused by negligence of one not his servant or agent. 

Hobbs v. Cunningham, 273 Mass. 529, at 532 

McNeil v. Powers, 266 Mass. 446 

Opinion of the Justices, 251 Mass. 569, at 599 

A manufacturer of automobiles who sold and delivered under a conditional sale contract is not liable to one injured by a collision in New Hampshire because the automobile was of unlawful width; car being driven by purchaser. 

Sanders v. Worcester Lunch Car etc. Co., 272 Mass. 180 

SECTION 232. 

2. Personal Negligence. 

An owner is responsible for his own negligence while personally operating a motor vehicle. 

Pigeon v. Mass. etc. St. Ry. Co., 230 Mass. 392 (Owner operating after failure to renew licenseevidence of his negligence not conclusive)

SECTION 233. 

3. Permitting Operation of Vehicle Not Lawfully 

Registered.

The operation on the public highway of a motor vehicle not lawfully registered being a nuisance, recovery may be had against any person who assists in the maintenance of such a nuisance, such as an owner who allows it to be operated. 

Ducharme v. Coe Motors, Inc., 275 Mass. 69, at 72 

But it does not follow that, because a dealer permits the owner to use the dealer's number plates for a single

$234 

 day on the motor vehicle issued under G. L. c. 90, s. 5, as amended by Acts 1923, c. 464, s. 2 (See: Acts 1929, c. 238, s. I) that, when the owner takes the motor vehicle for his own purposes, the dealer thereby assists in creating a nuisance on the highway with the consequent liability for injuries arising therefrom. 

Ducharme v. Coe Motors, Inc., 275 Mass. 69, at 72 

But see: 

O'Halleron v. Miller, 274 Mass. 508 

However, when the dealer permits his son to operate a car not properly registered he is liable whether the car was used for his own business or the son's purposes. 

A person who has control of an automobile without lawful number plates and who loans it to another person is liable for injuries caused by the automobile although at the time of the accident it was being operated by the chauffeur of the person to whom it was loaned. 

Liddell v. Middlesex Motor Co., 275 Mass. 346, at 352 

Pierce v. Hutchinson, 241 Mass. 557, at 564 

Goldrick v. Lacombe, 231 Mass. 397 (Husband liable because only nominal title in name of wife)

SECTION 234. 

4. Permitting Operation of Defective Vehicle. 

An owner is liable if he permits the operation of a vehicle so defective that the operation of it creates danger. 

SECTION 235. 

5. Permitting Operation by Incompetent Operator. 

The owner is liable for injuries caused through the operation of a motor vehicle by a person whom he knows

289 

 to be incompetent to operate the same even though such person has a license to operate.

SECTION 236. 

6. Permitting Operation by Unlicensed Person. 

General Laws Chapter 90, Section 9 provides that no person shall allow a motor vehicle owned by him or under his control to be operated by any person who has no legal right to do so.

See also: G. L. c. 90, s. 1O. 

The operation of the motor vehicle in itself is unobjectionable, the illegal element in the act is the failure to have a license. The purpose of the requirement of a license is to secure competency in the operator. 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155

The operator's failure to have a license is only evidence of the owner's negligence. 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, at 172

As was held in Gordon v. Bedard, 265 Mass. 408, the owner of a truck was not relieved from liability, as matter of law, for its negligent operation by his son, where the owner knew that the son's license had been revoked for driving while intoxicated. It properly could be found that the owner's violation of the law in permitting his son to drive was the cause of the son being in a position to cause the injury or damage, since, under the circumstances, negligence on the part of the son should reasonably have been anticipated as likely to occur.

But if in any case the failure to have a license, looking to those conditions that ordinarily accompany failure to have it, is a cause contributing directly to an injury, a violator of the law, the owner, would be legally responsible to another person injured by the failure; so if he is injured himself would be precluded from recovery against

8236 

⚫ another person who negligently, and not wilfully, wantonly or recklessly, contributed to the injury. 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, at 171

But the owner's failure in ascertaining whether the operator is duly licensed, or in intrusting the motor vehicle to one whom the owner knows to be unlicensed, is only evidence of negligence in reference to the operator's fitness to operate the motor vehicle and to his skill in the actual management of it and, unless such failure is shown to be a contributing cause to the injuries sued for, it is immaterial. 

The permission of the operation of a motor vehicle without a license, while a punishable act, does not render the owner, operator or vehicle a trespasser on the highway but the illegal element in the act is only the failure of the operator to have a license while operating it, so if the operation and movement contribute to the accident with which the want of a license had any connection, except as a mere condition, that would not preclude the operator or owner as plaintiffs from recovery. 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, at 171

If the illegal quality of the act had no tendency to cause the accident, the fact that the act is punishable because of the illegality, ought not to preclude one from recovery for harmful results to which, without negligence, the innocent features of the act alone contributed. 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, at 171

The wrongful act in allowing an unlicensed person to operate a motor vehicle continues to be an active force at every instant of time when the person is operating it. Because of the permission, the person is placed where he can cause the injuries to other persons. 

Gordon v. Bedard, 265 Mass. 408

But the fact that the operator is unlicensed does not make the motor vehicle a nuisance or trespasser. 

McMahon v. Pearlman, 242 Mass. 367

291 

 SECTION 237. 

7. Intrusting Vehicle to Guest. 

Ordinarily the owner is not liable for merely intrusting his motor vehicle to his guest but there are instances where the guest may be considered the agent of the owner, such as- 

Campbell v. Arnold, 219 Mass. 160 where the owner of an automobile, who had two men and two women as guests at his summer cottage, yielding reluctantly to the entreaties of the women to give them an automobile ride, said, "Well, you can go if you want to, but don't be gone very long," and threw down the key which was necessary to unlock the switch of the automobile, and where one of the men guests, who held a chauffeur's license and knew how to operate this automobile and who until a day or two before had been employed by a firm of which the owner of the automobile was a member, thereupon took the key and prepared the automobile for starting and in the owner's presence drove off for a pleasure drive with the two women guests and negligently ran into a horse driven by a traveller on the highway, injuring the traveller and his property, in an action by the traveller against the owner of the automobile for the injuries thus sustained, these facts were held to be evidence for the jury that the driver of the automobile was acting as the agent of the defendant at the time of the plaintiff's injuries. 

8. Acts of Members of Family. 

SECTION 238. 

a. "Family Use" Doctrine. 

The owner who keeps a motor vehicle for the use, pleasure and convenience of himself and his family is not liable for the acts of persons operating that motor vehicle for their own purposes even though such persons be mem-

$238 

 bers of the owner's family and are using the motor vehicle for their own pleasure and convenience which is the very purpose and object for which the owner keeps the vehicle. 

Field v. Evans, 262 Mass. 315 

Dennis v. Glynn, 262 Mass. 233 

Haskell v. Albiani, 245 Mass. 233 (Negligent operation by adult son who had defendant's permission to use the vehicle and who went with his brother to call on cousins) 

McGowan v. Longwood, 242 Mass. 337 (Father not liable for son's use of vehicle maintained for family use) 

Smith v. Jordan, 211 Mass. 269 (Son not father's agent in driving mother) 

64 A.L.R. 848, 855 and 856 

23 A.L.R. 617 

But see: 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155

The "family use" doctrine does not prevail in Massachusetts. 

See: Cases just cited above. 

However, a parent may be responsible for the tortious acts of his children, or the owner for the tortious acts of members of his family when there exists some authority or ratification and adoption of the acts of the persons operating the motor vehicle. This authority, ratification or adoption may be expressed or implied from the circumstances. 

It may be found in the actual presence of the parent or owner, or in an express or implied direction, or in a precedent course of conduct. If the act is within the general scope of authority conferred by the parent or owner, or in carrying out the enterprise for which the child or member of the family has been commissioned, then the parent or owner may be liable even though he had no knowledge

$293 

 of the specific conduct in question and it was contrary to his direction. 

DuBois v. Powdrell, 271 Mass. 394, at 396 

Smith v. Jordan, 211 Mass. 269

If the act is not done by the child or member of the family in furtherance of the business of the parent or owner, but in the performance of some independent design of the operator's own, the parent or owner is not liable. 

This is an instance of a mere permissive use of the vehicle by an operator for his own pleasure. 

Smith v. Jordan, 211 Mass. 269

The relation of husband and wife is such that when the former purchases a motor vehicle for "family use," a ride by the wife in it with the husband's general permission is not as matter of law business of the wife nor the creation of an agency of the wife for the husband. 

Smith v. Jordan, 211 Mass. 269 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155

Although the "family use" doctrine does not prevail the doctrine of respondeat superior does prevail. 

SECTION 239. 

b. Loaning Vehicle to Member of Family. 

The owner of a motor vehicle is not liable in the absence of an agency relation for the negligent use of the motor vehicle by members of his family who have borrowed it, where the person to whom the machine is loaned is a competent driver. 

McNeil v. Powers, 266 Mass. 446 

Kindell v. Ayles, 263 Mass. 244 

Field v. Evans, 262 Mass. 315 

Dennis v. Glynn, 262 Mass. 233 

But see: 

Smith v. Jordan, 211 Mass. 269 (Vehicle operated by owner's minor son)

$240 

Even though under the compulsory insurance law [G. 

L. c. 90, s. 34A] the insurance company is liable for the acts of every person operating the motor vehicle with the express or implied consent of the owner, and even though by G. L. c. 231, s. 85A the registrant is prima facie responsible for the conduct of the person operating the motor vehicle and the absence of such responsibility is an affirmative defense, the owner of a motor vehicle is not responsible for the negligent operation by a member of his family, not his servant or agent, although such person was operating the vehicle with the owner's knowledge and consent. 

An owner is not liable for the negligent operation by his eighteen year old son merely because of the ownership of the vehicle. 

Field v. Evans, 262 Mass. 315 

Dennis v. Glynn, 262 Mass. 233

C. Acts of Particular Members of Family. 

(I) Children.

SECTION 240. 

Haskell v. Albiani, 245 Mass. 233 

McGovern v. Longwood, 242 Mass. 337

SECTION 241. 

(A) As Agent of Parent. 

Where a child regularly acts as chauffeur for his parent and at the time of the accident is using the car with his parent's permission and the persons whom he is conveying were brought to a dance in the evening and carried home just before the accident and where, in the presence of the parent and the family at the dance so that the parent saw the child start to take such persons home from the dance

$295 

 and told the child to light the headlights, the evidence is proper consideration for the jury as to whether the child was representing his parent in running the motor vehicle at the time of the accident. 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155 

As to other cases, see: 

Haskell v. Albiani, 245 Mass. 233 

McGowan v. Longwood, 242 Mass. 337 

Flynn v. Lewis, 231 Mass. 550 

Smith v. Jordan, 211 Mass. 269 

23 A.L.R. 687

A child may be the agent of his mother engaged in her business or acting under her direction. 

DuBois v. Powdrell, 271 Mass. 394, at 396

But because the mother is the owner of the automobile and the child is in the habit of using it to drive down town to do her errands and uses it on an errand for the mother at noon on the day of the accident, is not by itself sufficient to warrant a finding that the child is acting for the mother in the afternoon of that day. 

DuBois v. Powdrell, 271 Mass. 394, at 396

However, when without objection evidence is introduced that immediately after the accident, in reply to charges that he was driving fast the child says, "My mother sent me to the telephone office to telephone to my father," this evidence tends to prove that the child was driving the automobile for his mother and is sufficient to carry the case to the jury on the question of agency. 

DuBois v. Powdrell, 271 Mass. 394, at 397 

O'Leary v. Fash, 245 Mass. 123 

Walker v. Fuller, 223 Mass. 566

Where an automobile is driven by one not strictly A's servant, A may also be liable because helping to direct or participating in driving. 

Hutchings v. Vacca, 224 Mass. 269, at 270 (Telling son to look out)

8242 

Mere relationship of father and daughter does not prove agency. 

Doyle v. Peerless Motor Car Co. of N. E., 226 Mass. 561, at 570 

Poirier v. Terceiro, 224 Mass. 435 

(Son driving father's vehicle, not enough to prove agency) 

SECTION 242. 

(1) Ratification or Adoption of Children's Acts. 

A parent may ratify or adopt the act of a child even to the extent of including the negligent operation of a motor vehicle. 

Smith v. Jordan, 211 Mass. 269

C. EMPLOYER. 

SECTION 243. 

An employer is responsible to his employees under the 

Workmen's Compensation Act (if insured) or at common law (if not insured) to his employees for the negligent operation of anyone operating the employer's motor vehicle in transporting his employees to or from their work. 

But an employer who pays part of the fare of his employees to the owner of a motor conveyance, who is an independent contractor, is not liable for injury to an employee while a passenger in such motor conveyance. 

Neelon v. Hirsh & Renner, Inc., 255 Mass. 285

D. LIABILITY FOR CONDUCT OF OF AGENT OR SERVANT OR DOCTRINE RESPONDEAT SUPERIOR. 

SECTION 244. 

(See: Section 231, page 284.)

OF The doctrine of respondeat superior makes the principal liable for the acts of his agent and the master responsible for the conduct of his servant.

$297 

Fleischner v. Durgin, 207 Mass. 435

Shepard v. Jacobs, 204 Mass. IIO (Loaned operator) 

2 R.C.L. 1200 

Since the enactment of G. L. c. 231, s. 85A, it rarely can be found that the registrant of a motor vehicle was not responsible for the acts of the operator because of the prima facie evidence.created by this statute. 

Leonard v. Conquest, 274 Mass. 347, at 351

Thomas v. The Meyer Stores, Inc., 268 Mass. 587 

But even with the prima facie evidence created by this statute (G. L. c. 231, s. 85A) and the provisions of the

Compulsory Insurance chapter (G. L. c. 90, s. 34A) it is still necessary for the plaintiff to maintain the burden of proof as to the defendant's control and responsibility for the acts of the operator of the motor vehicle as the defendant's agent or servant. 

McNeil v. Powers, 266 Mass. 446

So, where several children sitting in a wagon were struck by a motor truck on a public highway and the only question at issue was whether the defendant who owned the truck which was registered in his name at the time of the accident, was legally responsible for the conduct of the operator, who at the time of the accident was one of his employees, the Court said: "As the trial took place after September 1, 1928, G. L. c. 231, s. 85A (St. 1928, c. 317, s. 1) was applicable; see

S. 3." 

Ferreira v. Franco et ali, 273 Mass. 272, at 273 

Wilson v. Grace, 273 Mass. 146 

Smith v. Freedman, 268 Mass. 38

The defendants set up in the answer in each case, as an affirmative defense, the absence of such responsibility. By force of the statute, the defendants' admission that at the time of the accident the motor truck was owned by them, registered in their names and operated by C, their em-

$244 

 ployee, was prima facie evidence that they were legally responsible for his conduct, and the burden of proving the contrary rested upon them. They introduced evidence tending to show that C had no license to operate motor vehicles and that when the accident occurred, though he was their employee, he was not acting within the scope of his employment. If believed, this evidence warranted a finding that the prima facie evidence was overcome and the affirmative defense established. But the evidence was oral and even if contradicted only by the prima facie evidence might be disbelieved by the jury. 

Ferreira v. Franco et ali, 273 Mass. 272, at 274

Thomas v. The Meyer Stores, Inc., 268 Mass. 587 

Fleischner v. Durgin, 207 Mass. 435

It is usually a question of fact whether at the time of the accident, the operator of the motor vehicle was engaged in the owner's business and acting within the scope of such agency. 

Heywood v. Ogasapian, 224 Mass. 203 (Driver was agent, acting within scope of employment at time of striking pedestrian) 

Ouimette v. Harris, 219 Mass. 466

An operator may be the agent or servant of the owner in some matters or during part of the time of his operation and not the agent or servant in other matters. 

Wescott v. Henshaw Motor Co., 275 Mass. 82, at 87 

Child's Case, 274 Mass. 97 

Hardaker's Case, 274 Mass. 7

A public officer undoubtedly is liable for personal acts of misfeasance. But a Chief of a Fire Department in which the driver is a subordinate, although they are riding to the fire in an automobile driven by the subordinate, is not responsible for that subordinate's loss of control of the car through excessive speed unless the subordinate was acting under the personal direction or orders

$299 

 of his Chief and the doctrine of respondeat superior is inapplicable. 

Skerry v. Rich, 228 Mass. 462, at 463

It is settled law that a master is not responsible for the acts of a servant who is acting without authority from him. 

Bruce v. Hanks, 1931 A. S. 2249, at 2250

Hobbs v. Cunningham, 273 Mass. 529 

Ciarmataro v. Adams, 1931 A. S. 1231, at 1236 

Simmons v. Rabinowitz, 266 Mass. 109 

Dubois v. Powdrell, 271 Mass. 394

It is indispensable for recovery against the defendant to find that the driver was acting by the defendant's authority. 

Bruce v. Hanks, 1931 A. S. 2249, at 2251 

2. Agency Relationship. 

SECTION 245. 

a. As a Requirement.

In order to create responsibility of one person for the negligent operation of a motor vehicle by another, it is necessary that there shall be a relationship between them such as creates the latter person the agent or servant of the former. 

Chute v. Morey, 234 Mass. 387 

Santoro v. Bickford, 229 Mass. 357 (Assistant manager, using auto owned by general manager in business of corporation, was not agent of owner) 

Melchionda v. Amer. Locomotive Co., 229 Mass. 202.

So, the lending of a motor vehicle and an operator to an employee in order that he might take his friends for a ride will not render the employer responsible for the acts of the operator. 

Kennedy v. R. & L. Co., 224 Mass. 207

$246 

SECTION 246. 

b. Sufficiency In Existence Of. 

When a person is riding in a vehicle under an agreement, consent or request of a person other than the owner of the vehicle, he must prove that the person making such agreement, consent or request had authority so to do. An ordinary operator has no implied or ostensible authority to invite other persons to ride with him or have such persons in the owner's service. 

Broitman v. Silver, 270 Mass. 24, at 25

So, one who is hired to drive a truck to deliver merchandise has no further authority and when he permits another person to ride on the vehicle, the driver is not acting within the real or apparent scope of his employment. 

Broitman v. Silver, 270 Mass. 24, at 26

However the result is otherwise if the employer expressly or impliedly assents to assume any duty toward such other person or ratifies the acts of the driver or an emergency exists requiring additional assistance for the driver. 

Broitman v. Silver, 270 Mass. 24, at 28 

Murphy v. Barry, 264 Mass. 557 

Butler v. Mechanics' Iron Fdry. Co., 259 Mass. 560, at 563 

Stone v. Commonwealth Coal Co., 259 Mass. 360 

O'Leary v. Fash, 245 Mass. 123, at 127 

Bowler v. O'Connell, 162 Mass. 319, at 320 

Powers v. B. & M. R.R., 153 Mass. 188, at 190 

But see: Lyttle v. Monto, 248 Mass. 340, where driver who was owner of the truck asked to be directed to a place and invited other person to accompany him and show the way.

The result may be different if person was invited by anyone who had the authority so to do, such as a manager. 

Broitman v. Silver, 270 Mass. 24, at 28

$301 

Where a person is employed by a dealer as a sales supervisor and at the time of the accident is intending to call on a customer for the purpose of selling a truck, and he is driving his own motor vehicle, and an allowance is made by the dealer for expenses for operating his automobile, besides a flat weekly salary which he receives, and although he is subject to the directions of the dealer as to where he should go and what people he should see in reference to the sales of automobiles, but within reasonable limitation the person can go at such times as within his judgment he feels wise, how he goes and what road he pursues in going being entirely in his own judgment, and the manner in which he operates and handles his car on the way is a matter for him in his judgment to make up as he goes along, such person is not an agent of the dealer in operating the automobile and consequently the dealer is not liable for his negligence in such operation. 

Wescott v. Henshaw Motor Co., 275 Mass. 82, at 87 

In this case, the court said: "Young was operating his own motor vehicle, registered in his name. The defendant assumes no responsibility for it. It was under the control of Young and the defendant had no power to direct or control the way in which it was to be operated. The defendant had no right to direct the employee Young in any particular way he should go, the course he should take, the speed of the motor vehicle. 

These were matters for Young to determine." 

Wescott v. Henshaw Motor Co., 275 Mass. 82, at 87 

Child's Case, 274 Mass. 97 

Khoury v. Edison Elec. Illg. Co., 265 Mass. 236, at 238 The method of payment was not important. 

Wescott v. Henshaw Motor Co., 275 Mass. 82, at 87

Hoffman v. Liberty Motors, Inc., 234 Mass. 437

$246 

Cardoza v. Isherwood, 258 Mass. 165, is not in conflict.

In that case the plaintiff was injured while the defendant's agent was engaged in the specific act of demonstrating the performance of an automobile about to be sold. This was the act the servant was hired to do. In the case before us 

Young was hired to sell an automobile and could use his own motor vehicle. 

In Champion v. Shaw, 258 Mass. 9, the manager of the defendant was operating a particular automobile while showing it to a customer. 

Wescott v. Henshaw Motor Co., 275 Mass. 82, at 88 

Oulighan v. Butler, 189 Mass. 287, and Marsh v. Beraldi, 260 Mass. 225, are to be distinguished. 

In Fox v. Pallotta, 274 Mass. 110, at 113, the evidence did not warrant a finding that, at the time of the accident, Beraldi was the agent or servant or employee of the defendant in operating the truck, so that the defendant was responsible for his negligence. Such agency-or employment-was not shown by evidence that Beraldi, by agreement with the defendant, was operating his own truck and transporting stone for the defendant from the ledge and stone crusher in Dracut to the state road in Westford, at a fixed price per ton, without further evidence of actual control or right of control of Beraldi by the defendant.

This leaves Beraldi in the position of an independent contractor, who undertook to accomplish a given result, by the use of his own property under his own control. 

Neelon v. Hirsh & Renner, Inc., 255 Mass. 285, at 291 

Gallagher's Case, 240 Mass. 455 

Eckert's Case, 233 Mass. 577 

Winslow's Case, 232 Mass. 458

Centrello's Case, 232 Mass. 456 

The evidence that the truck was loaded sometimes by Beraldi, sometimes by him with the help of the defendant's

$303 

 employees (Gallagher's Case, 240 Mass. 455, see also 

Winslow's Case, 232 Mass. 458), and sometimes by them 

(Centrello's Case, 232 Mass. 456; Eckert's Case, 233 

Mass. 577) did not tend to show that the operation of the truck on the highway was under the control of the defendant. Nor did the evidence that the defendant's foreman directed Beraldi where to dump the stone (Centrello's 

Case, 232 Mass. 456, see also Peach v. Bruno, 224 Mass. 

447) nor the evidence that a record of the weights of the loads was kept for the defendant by his daughter who sometimes did the weighing so tend. Unlike the case of 

Marsh v. Beraldi, 260 Mass. 225, at 231, only one conclusion could be drawn from the evidence. 

Furthermore, even if it could have been found that the plaintiff's injuries resulted from overloading Beraldi's truck it would not follow that the defendant was liable therefor, since the evidence did not warrant a finding that he was responsible for such overloading. 

Where H, who was manager for the W. Co., had sold a motor car to B a year before the accident, and had had it occasionally for repairs and testing and on the morning of the accident B asked H to drive car to determine what was the trouble and expected to pay the W. Co., it was for the jury to say whether H was acting for the W. Co. 

Roach v. Hinchcliff, 214 Mass. 267

The plaintiff's intestate upon a motorcycle collided with the defendant's auto and was killed. The latter was being operated by A under the instruction of B, both employees of the defendant. The auto being operated by the defendant's servants, it was held that a finding was warranted that they were engaged in its business under Acts 

1907, C. 375. 

Winslow v. N. E. Co-op. Soc., 225 Mass. 576

Plaintiff injured by automobile of defendant, driven by one T who had been employee of defendant shortly before. 

Defendant entertaining two women at summer cottage who

$247 

 wished to go riding. He had refused for some time but finally assented reluctantly, and threw down the key of the automobile, which T picked up. Defendant stated he knew T would drive them around a little and bring them back. It was a question for the jury whether T was acting as agent for defendant. Women were defendant's guests.

There was evidence the relation of host and guest did end with their departure but that defendant expected they would return soon. By laying down the key, the jury might find the defendant impliedly empowered T to take his car for the purpose of gratifying the desires of his guests for a ride. 

Campbell v. Arnold, 219 Mass. 160

Even if the defendant's wife is in the car the driver must be the defendant's agent acting within the scope of his employment. The driver must be on business of the defendant or have been requested to take wife on the ride. 

The burden rests upon the plaintiff to prove that the driver while operating the car was the servant of the defendant, acting within the scope of his employment rather than for his own private purposes. 

Kwedares v. Knoel, 261 Mass. 91, at 93

There is no ostensible authority to use the defendant's automobile after hours and for his own pleasure. 

Vallavanti v. Armour & Co., 260 Mass. 417, at 420

But a chauffeur employed in family and liable to be called upon at all hours for duty may have implied authority to use the vehicle going to and from his necessary places. 

Reynolds v. Denholm, 213 Mass. 576

SECTION 247. 

(I) Vehicle and Operator Hired or Loaned to 

Third Person.

The responsibility of the person who rents or loans a motor vehicle with an operator to a third person depends

$305 

 upon how far the renter or lender retains control over the acts and conduct of the operator or whether he surrenders such control to the hirer or borrower. 

Melchionda v. Amer. Locomotive Co., 229 Mass. 202 (Motor truck driven by agent of hirer) 

Kennedy v. R. & L. Company, 224 Mass. 207

Tornroos v. R. H. White Co., 220 Mass. 336 Shepard v. Jacobs, 204 Mass. IIO 

In the case of Goyette v. Kennedy & Co., Inc., 1931

A. S. 2151, where there was a collision between the plaintiff's automobile and the defendant's trailer, it was held that it would not be ruled as a matter of law that the servant of the defendant became, under the terms of the hiring, the servant of the owner of the propelling truck, because in the absence of clear terms in the contract to that end, it was a question of fact on all the evidence whether the owner of the trailer had surrendered for the time being his control over his servant who was to have general charge of the trailer and was to accompany it until it was returned to the owner, and whether such servant assented to becoming the servant of the owner of the propelling truck while he was in charge of the trailer. 

The issue must be left to the determination of the jury. 

Khoury v. Edison Elec. Ill. Co., 265 Mass. 236, at 239 

Marsh v. Beraldi, 260 Mass. 225 

Pyyny v. Loose-Wiles Biscuit Co., 253 Mass. 574, at 576 

Mahoney v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R., 212 Mass. 102, at 107 

Shepard v. Jacobs, 204 Mass. IIO 

Reagan v. Casey, 160 Mass. 374 Where defendant rented an automobile with a driver to the Fiat Co. to be used by H., one of its employees, for two days at $50.00 a day, he giving orders to driver when and where to drive, defendant contended that Fiat Co.

$247 

 was responsible for negligence of driver and that latter was not at time of accident their servant. Held that if one lets a carriage to another he in no sense places the driver under control of the hirer except that latter may indicate destination he wishes. The safety of machine and need of careful management are so important to owner that it will not be presumed to have given up management when it has sent its own servant for the special purpose of retaining management, in absence of express contract.

Shepard v. Jacobs, 204 Mass. IIO 

Where defendant purchased six cars from the Auto Car

Co., the contract providing latter should furnish chauffeurs for seven days who would drive the cars for the purpose of making deliveries of merchandise, subject to directions where to go, and who would also instruct defendant's employees how to operate and care for the cars. Cars at end of day were kept in Auto Car garage. On day of accident, one of the cars was being driven from Auto Car garage to defendant's stable when it injured plaintiff. Held that 

Auto Car Co. and not the defendant was liable. The particular business at time of accident was the driving of the truck which for the seven day period was exclusively in the control of the Auto Car Co. The car had not reached defendant's stable and the business of delivering goods had not yet commenced.

Toonroos v. R. H. White Co., 220 Mass. 336 

It was said in Mahoney v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R.R., 240 

Mass. 8, at 10, that: "The plaintiff does not controvert that the general rule is that a servant of one master may, with the express or implied assent of that servant, be lent to another for a particular employment with the result that the servant lent or hired while thus employed becomes the fellow servant of the employers of the latter with an assumption of all risks which in law are incident to that relation. He relies upon the exception to the general rule which is well

$247A 

 established in this Commonwealth, that drivers of horses, automobiles, locomotives and perhaps other vehicles of travel, when lent with the vehicles presumptively remain the servants of the general employer and are subject to his control in so far as pertains to the care, management and preservation of the property." 

Owner who loans car to chauffeur to take latter's friend to ride is not liable even though gasoline is his and he pays for repairs. 

Herlihy v. Smith, 116 Mass. 265

SECTION 247A. 

(II) Owner of Vehicle Acting as Agent or Servant of Another. 

(See: Section 259, page 320.)

The test to determine whether the owner while driving his own automobile is acting as proprietor or as servant of another is whether the owner is in control so that he can at any time stop or continue and determine the way in which it shall be used or driven, not merely with reference to the result to be reached but with reference to the method of reaching that result even as to possible small particulars. The vital inquiry concerns the right to control. If that right rests in the owner he is acting as proprietor. 

If that right rests with another person then he is the servant of that other person who becomes responsible as master for the conduct of the owner. 

Reardon v. Coleman Bros., Inc., 1931 A. S. 2205, at 2206 and 2207 

Strong's case, 1931 A. S. 2139 

Bradley's case, 269 Mass. 399, at 401 

Khoury v. Edison Elec. Ill. Co., 265 Mass. 236, at 

Shepard v. Jacobs, 204 Mass. 110, at 112 238

§247A 

So, when the operator owns the automobile which is registered in his name and he is under no duty to use it for the business of the defendant, is using it on his own journey and for his own personal convenience in going from one place of work to another place of work when the defendant has no power of control over the operator as to the route, the speed or the method of operation of the automobile, and pays him no compensation, and the operator receives none for the use of the automobile, the single circumstance that as a matter of accommodation in going on his own business and in his own way to his own place of work, the operator takes other employees and tools and materials of the defendant does not render the defendant liable as master. It is no evidence that the power of domination as to the use of the automobile is vested in the defendant. 

Reardon v. Coleman Bros., Inc., 1931 A. S. 2205, at 2207

 3. Scope of Employment. 

SECTION 248. 

a. General Statement. 

Although one owns a motor vehicle and although the operator is in his employ, the owner is not liable unless, when the accident occurs, the motor vehicle is being used in and the operator is acting within the scope of his employment. 

Vallavanti v. Armour & Co., 260 Mass. 417, at 418 

Stone v. Commonwealth Coal Co., 259 Mass. 360 

O'Leary v. Fash, 245 Mass. 123

Seaboyer v. Director Gen❜l of Railroads, 244 Mass. 122 

Gardner v. Farnum, 230 Mass. 193

The plaintiff, a minor, was injured by defendant's automobile. Auto driven by one A, a chauffeur, in the general employ of the defendant who was a summer resident and had left with his family before the accident. The evidence showed that A and his wife lived in Magnolia after the defendant left at the end of summer and on morning of accident A drove to Gloucester and returned with an expensive toy sail boat in the machine. Defendant had two young children and A had none. It was held there was an entire absence of testimony indicating that A purchased the boat for any child of the defendant or if such was his purpose that the defendant or any member of his family directed it or knew that such purchase was to be made; nor can it be inferred upon any view of the evidence that he was engaged at the time of the accident on any business of the defendant. To deem otherwise would be to reach a conclusion based wholly on speculation and conjecture. 

Gardner v. Farnum, 230 Mass. 193

(One permitted by driver to operate truck not in scope of agency)

 SECTION 249. 

b. What Constitutes. 

Where a night watchman in a coal yard, employed only as such, and to do odd jobs as directed by his superior, without authority or direction, drove the defendant's motor truck for wood for the defendant, it was held that he was acting outside the scope of his employment and that his employer was not liable for his negligence in striking and injuring a pedestrian. 

The court said: "It is not enough, in order to establish liability, to show that the master has an interest in what is being done. It must also be made to appear that the servant whose act is in question has authority from the master to perform the class of service to which the act belongs. If the act is within the class, the master is bound, although the servant is forbidden to perform the particular act." 

Stone v. Commonwealth Coal Co., 259 Mass. 360 

McDonough v. Vozzela, 247 Mass. 552 

Seaboyer v. Director Gen❜l of Railr'ds, 244 Mass. 122 

Stegman v. Sturtevant & H. Beef & Sup. Co., 243 Mass. 269 

Regan v. Kelly Contr. Co., 226 Mass. 58

A travelling salesman employed by a corporation, who is furnished a car for use in the business, is held to be acting within the scope of the business so as to render the corporation liable for an accident which happens while he is taking a carpenter to the residence of the president of the corporation, at the latter's request, even though he intends, in accordance with his frequent practice, to take the latter to the place of business of the corporation. 

Stegman v. Sturtevant & H. Beef & Sup. Co., 243 Mass. 269

SECTION 250. 

(I) Acts for Benefit Of or At Direction of Members of Owner's Family. 

Where a chauffeur lived in the owner's family and took persons to a dance in the evening and carried them home again just before the accident and where, in the presence of the owner and his family at the dance, when the owner saw the chauffeur start to take them home from the dance and told him he had better light the headlights, this is evidence that the chauffeur was representing the owner, although acting under the direction or for the benefit of members of the owner's family, in running the motor vehicle at the time of the accident. 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, at 172 and 173 (II) 

SECTION 251. 

Teaching Person to Operate. 

The permitting of a person not licensed to operate the automobile when accompanied by a licensed operator might in certain instances be found to be a negligent act. 

It is not gross negligence and probably not ordinary negligence to permit an operator who is experienced and duly licensed to teach another person to operate an automobile on the public highway when accompanied by a licensed driver especially where the place is a straight cement road about eighteen feet wide with little traffic. 

Mason v. Thomas, 274 Mass. 59, at 61

This is so even when the unlicensed person becomes confused when a car goes by him and instead of stepping on the brake, as he intends to do, steps on the accelerator and before the operator can render any assistance the automobile goes to the right and turns over. 

Mason v. Thomas, 274 Mass. 59, at 61 

Winslow v. New England Co-Op. Soc., 225 Mass. 576

(III) Permitting Children or Others to Ride. 

A driver of a truck has no right to permit anyone to ride with him and such person cannot recover for injury against owner. 

O'Leary v. Fash, 245 Mass. 123 

Coyne v. Maniatty, 235 Mass. 181, at 186 (Operator has no implied authority to take stranger)

Person.

Master not liable to wife of servant who is injured by her husband's negligence. 

Where plaintiff received damage by reason of a collision with automobile of defendant driven by H, a chauffeur in his employ. It appeared that the chauffeur dined with defendant on evening of the accident and used auto to take for a drive his friends who were possible friends of the

$255 

 defendant, that the defendant knew he was to invite the friends and that the defendant paid for the damage to his automobile. 

Held that these facts would not warrant the inference that H was the servant of the defendant or acting in the scope of his employment at the time of the accident. 

Neither is the making of repairs on his own auto evidence that the defendant adopted or ratified the acts of H. 

This case is distinguished from some other cases by the fact that the use of the automobile at the time of the collision was not an incident of H's employment and that it was not then in use in the entertainment of guests of the defendant. 

Plaintiff was injured by defendant's automobile driven by his chauffeur. Evidence of plaintiff's due care and negligence by defendant's chauffeur. The only evidence of defendant's control was his testimony where he stated that upon the Sunday in question he had permitted the chauffeur to use the car for a pleasure trip and that the latter had used the car for this purpose and was on his way home to the garage when the accident occurred.

Held if this evidence was believed the defendant was not liable, and if not believed, the case was bare of other evidence upon this aspect of the case. 

O'Rourke v. A.-G. Co., Inc., 232 Mass. 129

SECTION 255. 

(VI) Going To or From Work or Meals, or To 

Get Laundry.

In an action to recover for injuries resulting from the negligence of an employee who, with his employer's permission, was driving home in the employer's automobile, it was held that the question whether the driver was acting

$315 

 within the scope of his employment was for the jury. 

Puccia v. Sevigne, 258 Mass. 234

Barney v. Magenis, 241 Mass. 268 

(Chauffeur, after procuring laundry, went to his room, changed his linen, got his mail, and was proceeding to florist's to get flowers for his employer)

Regan v. Cummings, 228 Mass. 414 

(Evidence for the jury that plaintiff's injuries were caused by negligence of owner's servant, the operator of the automobile) 

Hartnett v. Gryzmish, 218 Mass. 258 

68 A.L.R. 1058

Chauffeur of automobile, in driving to and from dinner during time that was his own is not acting as an agent for his master.

Hartnett v. Gryzmish, 218 Mass. 258 

In the case of an automobile with a chauffeur to operate it provided by the defendant for the use of his family, the chauffeur having no fixed hours of service but subject at all times to the directions of the family, sleeping in the house and getting his meals and laundry elsewhere, for which the defendant paid as a part of his wages and allowed or suffered by the family without objection to use the automobile to go to his meals and get his laundry as he found it convenient, and while going for his laundry in the automobile after he had got his supper, ran into and injured the plaintiff, it was held under the circumstances the jury could find that the use of the automobile by the chauffeur was an incident of his employment, expressly or impliedly authorized by the defendant.

It is not a question of actual knowledge or expressed authority on the part of the defendant but whether taking all the circumstances relating to the chauffeur's employment his use of the automobile as and for the purpose for which he was using it at the time of accident was incident to his employment, or was permitted or assented to, either

$256 

 expressly or impliedly by those who were acting under authority received from the defendant. 

Reynolds v. Denholm, 213 Mass. 576

Plaintiff's intestate was killed by defendant's car operated by defendant's chauffeur, K. The latter, called by plaintiff, testified that just before the accident he had taken the car from garage and had then driven to his home and eaten his dinner. After dinner he started for defendant's house. Defendant had never told him to use the car to go to dinner or for similar purposes and had no knowledge the car was put to such a use. 

Held it is not intended that K lived in the family of the defendant or that the latter was to furnish him with dinner. 

The fair inference is that K was to procure his own meals and that the time required for this should be his and not the defendant's. The evidence shows that at time of accident he was driving the car for his own purposes and not for his master's. 

The case is distinguished fromand 

McKeever v. Ratcliffe, 218 Mass. 17

SECTION 256. 

c.

Deviation or Departure as Being Outside 

Scope of Employment. 

The owner of a motor vehicle is not responsible for the operation by his servant when he deviates or departs from his scope of employment.

Where plaintiff was injured by an automobile of the defendant, the latter's servant on the occasion of the accident, while returning from a job, instead of taking the shortest way travelled a route two miles longer because he said he thought that was the best way to go, it was held that in

$317 

 view of the longer way the driver took, whether he was acting for a purpose of his own or was still engaged in his master's work, his intention is important. 

Mathewson v. Edison Elec. Co., 232 Mass. 576

Deviation by a servant from the regular course or travelling by a longer route is not conclusive evidence that he is acting outside the scope of his employment. Automobiles run better on smooth roads and where there is little traffic. 

The jury might have found that in taking the route he did the driver chose the quickest and best way to reach his destination and had not abandoned his master's business. 

Mathewson v. Edison Elec. Co., 232 Mass. 576 

Defendant had directed his chauffeur one M. to hire one

S. and take his car to Swampscott and overhaul it. M. made an appointment with S. at a certain place which the latter failed to keep and M. thereupon decided to abandon the enterprise and with one P. and two women went to a hotel and drank for several hours. Returning to garage

M. was informed S. had telephoned he would meet him at a certain hotel at midnight. M. accordingly went there with his party and waited until 12:15 at which time, S. not appearing, he started, as he said, for Swampscott, intending on way to leave one woman in Cambridge and the other in Somerville.

On his way, before leaving either of the women, he ran over and killed two men. Held there was evidence that M. was engaged in the defendant's business. He testified that he was on his way to Swampscott incidentally intending to leave his two guests at their homes at two places on the direct route to his destination. If it was his intention to go to Swampscott pursuant to instructions, his intention to gratify a private desire by leaving two people at two different places on the route is not material. It was a question for the jury to decide upon the evidence what M. intended. 

It cannot be ruled that M.

once having abandoned his

$256 

 duty could not again resume it without an implied assent by the defendant.

Donahue v. Vorenberg, 227 Mass. I

 SECTION 257. 

d. Return To Scope of Employment. 

Although an agent or servant of the person in control of a motor vehicle has deviated or departed from the scope of employment so during such deviation or departure the owner or person in control is not liable for the acts of the operator, yet the owner or person in control again becomes responsible for the acts of the operator when he returns to the scope of employment.

Cummings v. Republic Truck Co., 241 Mass. 292 Donahue v. Vorenberg, 227 Mass. I 

e. 

SECTION 258. 

Ratification.

The owner or person in control of a motor vehicle may ratify unauthorized acts of an agent or servant and adopt acts committed outside the scope of employment of the

$259 

 agent or servant and even conduct which occurred during a deviation or departure from the scope of employment. 

So, an owner by paying for the necessary repairs on his car does not ratify nor adopt the acts of the chauffeur. 

SECTION 259. 

E. INDEPENDENT CONTRACTOR. 

An independent contractor is liable for his own personal negligence and the negligence of his servants or agents in operating a motor vehicle. 

Whalen v. Sheehan, 237 Mass. 112 

Chute v. Morey, 234 Mass. 387

An owner who hires an independent contractor to assume operation of a motor vehicle is not liable for the acts of such independent contractor.

Whether the operator of a motor vehicle is a servant of the defendant or an independent contractor in its operation depends upon whether the operator personally or the defendant was in control of the vehicle-whether the operator is an independent contractor, not subject to the direction and control of the defendant in driving the vehicle, or is a servant or agent of the defendant, and, as such, subject to his control and direction. 

Marsh v. Beraldi, 260 Mass. 225, at 229

Shepard v. Jacobs, 204 Mass. IIO 

There is no rule of law which renders impossible that an owner may be employed as a servant to handle what he owns. The test of the relation is the location of the power of control. If it rests in the employer, the employed is a servant; if it rests in the employed, he is an independent contractor. 

Marsh v. Beraldi, 260 Mass. 225, at 231 

McAllister's Case, 229 Mass. 193 

Oulighan v. Butler, 189 Mass. 287, at 290 and 291

$321 

Where more than one conclusion is presented by the evidence the jury determines the relationship. But when only one conclusion can be drawn, the court must rule upon the relationship. 

Marsh v. Beraldi, 260 Mass. 225, at 231 

Neelon v. Hirsh & Renner, Inc., 255 Mass. 285 

Pyyny v. Loose-Wiles Biscuit Co., 253 Mass. 574

Centrello's Case, 232 Mass. 456 Scribner's Case, 231 Mass. 132 

When a person working for the defendant obtains the motor vehicle under a lease from the latter and is entitled to its possession and it is in that person's control and operated by him at the time of the accident, he is an independent contractor even if there is an agreement between him and the defendant that the latter shall pay the expenses and assume the liability in connection with the operation of the motor vehicle. This does not give the defendant control of its operation so as to establish the relationship of master and servant between the defendant and that person while the motor vehicle is being operated by that person in his own business. 

Hawker's case, 1932 A. S. 295, at 297 

Hardaker's case, 274 Mass. 7 and cases therein cited 

, at 519 

SECTION 260. 

F. PARTNER OR CO-OWNER. 

One partner or co-owner is liable for the acts of partners or co-owners within the scope of the partnership, joint enterprise or common object for which the motor vehicle is being used. But a partner or co-owner is not liable for acts of other partners or co-owners outside of such scope, purpose or object. 

Shriear v. Feigelson, 248 Mass. 432 

Teague v. Martin, 228 Mass. 458

$261 

 SECTION 261. 

G. JOINT OR COMMON ENTERPRISE. 

Persons engaged in a joint or common enterprise are responsible for the acts of the operator performed during the consummation of that joint or common enterprise.

So, a mother who permits a minor daughter to drive a motor vehicle, and who is present and contributes part of the charge for the same may be found to be engaged in a joint enterprise with the other contributor and the daughter to such an extent that the mother would be responsible for the daughter's acts. 

Adams v. Swift, 172 Mass. 521, at 522

If the mother and daughter and such other person go on an excursion or ride so that the mother is interested and pays part of the expenses, her interest being as one of the parties, and she allows the daughter to drive so that it is the mother's excursion in part, it may fairly be said that the daughter is acting as the mother's servant, or her agent for that purpose and the mother is responsible and liable for the daughter's acts. 

Adams v. Swift, 172 Mass. 521, at 522 

Where the mother contributes to the hiring of the vehicle and allows or lets the daughter drive for her, or the driving is for the mother as well as for the others, and the vehicle is driven without due care by the daughter, then the mother is liable. 

Adams v. Swift, 172 Mass. 521, at 523 and 524

But if the situation is that the third person hires the vehicle and the mother does not contribute and is not interested in the excursion or the vehicle, did not hire it or do anything about it except that she accepted an invitation to ride solely, then the mother would not be liable. 

Adams v. Swift, 172 Mass. 521, at 524

But if the vehicle is driven by the daughter and the mother is present and the driving is countenanced or al-

$323 

 lowed by the mother, and if also the mother is interested in it and pays for the vehicle and the hiring in part, then the mother is liable for the negligence on the part of the daughter. 

Adams v. Swift, 172 Mass. 521, at 524

So, upon such facts the mother of the daughter who is present when the accident happens is an equal promoter and manager, and not a mere guest. If under the mother's control and direction, her daughter, so inexperienced that it might be negligence to allow her to drive, is allowed to drive, the mother is responsible for the daughter's driving carelessly. 

Adams v. Swift, 172 Mass. 521, at 524

One of those engaged in a common enterprise with another cannot sue that other if one of them is injured through the negligence of the other. 

Loftus v. Pelletier, 223 Mass. 63, at 65

H. BAILEE. 

SECTION 262. 

The owner or bailor is not responsible for the acts of his bailee unless such bailee, under special circumstances, is performing a duty as agent or servant of the bailor.

So, acts of the bailee in his own personal interests are not attributable to the bailor. 

Nash v. Lang, 268 Mass. 407 

Phillips v. Gookin, 231 Mass. 250 

Campbell v. Arnold, 219 Mass. 160

Even though this Commonwealth requires compulsory insurance against injuries or damage inflicted by a motor vehicle while being operated on its public highways, the owner of the motor vehicle is not responsible for the negligence of one who is not his servant or agent although

$263 

 operating the owner's motor vehicle with his knowledge or consent. 

McNeil v. Powers, 266 Mass. 446

SECTION 263. 

I. BUYER ON CONDITIONAL SALE. 

Where the manufacturer of a lunch car sells it on conditional sale so that he retains the title and the lunch car is delivered to the buyer at the factory and then a motor truck tows the lunch car over the road, the truckman not being the manufacturer's employee or agent, and the manufacturer does not cause or permit the lunch car to be operated upon the highway at the time and place of the accident, the delivery of the lunch car to the truck driver ends the seller's control over it. The method of transportation is not under the direction of the seller and the seller is in no way responsible for the conduct of the buyer or his truck driver. 

Sanders v. Worcester etc., 272 Mass. 180, at 181

As a seller delivering a lunch car to a conditional sales purchaser, the seller is not responsible for the violation of law or for damage caused by the acts of a carrier in taking the lunch car to the buyer's home or place of business. 

Sanders v. Worcester etc., 272 Mass. 180, at 182

No act of the seller contributes to the plaintiff's injury and damage. 

Sanders v. Worcester etc., 272 Mass. 180, at 182

The seller does not participate in the alleged illegal act; the seller in no way controls the method of transportation or the route to be taken. The entire management of the lunch car and the way of carrying it from the seller's factory to the buyer's place of business are under the direction of the buyer. 

Sanders v. Worcester etc., 272 Mass. 180, at 181

This is not a case where the defendant procures an

$325 

 illegal act to be done or assists in its performance, or actually contributes to it, or sells an article inherently dangerous to health and property. The car was sold in good faith in ignorance that any unlawful act was to be committed in transporting it. 

Sanders v. Worcester etc., 272 Mass. 180, at 182

SECTION 264. 

J. STATUTORY LIABILITY. 

The combined effect of the Compulsory Insurance 

Statute (G. L. c. 90, s. 34A) and G. L. c. 90, s. 85A is to create, in effect, liability upon the registrant of a motor vehicle whenever he expressly or impliedly consents to its operation upon the public highways and during that operation a person is injured or killed. 

Opinion of the Justices, 251 Mass. 569, at 600 

Thomas v. The Meyer Store, Inc., 268 Mass. 587

K. LIABILITY OF PERSONS OTHER THAN OWNER OR OPERATOR. 

SECTION 265. 

To create liability upon a person it is not necessary that he be either the owner or operator of a motor vehicle. It is sufficient if he either was in actual or constructive control of the vehicle at the time of the negligent act. 

It is also sufficient to create his liability if he was responsible for the specific negligence or the acts or conduct of the operator of the motor vehicle. 

Generally, a person is responsible if he creates the particular circumstances which cause the injury or damage sustained. 

Champion v. Shaw, 258 Mass. 9 

Stegman v. Sturtevant & H. Beef & Sup. Co., 243 Mass. 269

$266 

So, a dealer in motor vehicles has no lawful right to permit the use of his number plates on any motor vehicle unless owned or controlled by him. 

Tripp v. National Shawmut Bank, 263 Mass. 505 

McDonald v. Dundon, 242 Mass. 229, at 231 

26 A.L.R. 1243

Through the dealer's act in lending the plates, he furnishes means and facilities for the unlawful operation of the motor vehicle and thereby aids and abets in the creation of a nuisance. He is therefore liable for all direct injury resulting from such operation of the motor vehicle. 

McDonald v. Dundon, 242 Mass. 229, at 231 

Evans v. Rice, 238 Mass. 318 

Fairbanks v. Kemp, 226 Mass. 75 

Under such circumstances it is not necessary for the plaintiff to prove that the operator was acting as the agent of the lender of the number plates or that the operator was negligent. 

McDonald v. Dundon, 242 Mass. 229, at 231 

Gould v. Elder, 219 Mass. 396 (Son driving unlawfully registered car of father)

SECTION 266. 

2. Guest or Occupant of Vehicle. 

Ordinarily neither a guest nor occupant of a motor vehicle is responsible for the negligence of the operator. 

Nor is the negligence of the operator imputed to the guest or occupant. 

Bullard v. Boston El. Ry., 226 Mass. 262

But participation by the guest or occupant in the active management of a motor vehicle by giving directions intended to control or influence the conduct of the operator is sufficient to render the guest or occupant liable as a joint tortfeasor for negligent operation. 

Hutchings v. Vacca, 224 Mass. 269

$327 

 SECTION 267 3. Parent of Owner or Operator. 

(See: Sec. 238, page 291 et seq.) 

Goldrick v. Lacombe, 231 Mass. 397 (Driven by woman's son, killed pedestrian) 

Hutchings v. Vacca, 224 Mass. 269

SECTION 268 4. Administrator or Executor. 

If an operator, at the time of the accident, is operating a vehicle with the implied or express consent of the administrator, then the administrator is liable through the driver as his agent. 

Hobbs v. Cunningham, 273 Mass. 529, at 532

Under an insurance policy which indemnifies against loss not only to the assured but any person operating the motor vehicle with his express or implied consent, a person who is injured by the driver who has the consent of the assured administrator may recover under the insurance policy. 

Hobbs v. Cunningham, 273 Mass. 529, at 532

But not if the title to the vehicle is vested in a legatee before the accident. 

Hobbs v. Cunningham, 273 Mass. 529, at 532

SECTION 269 

5. Heirs or Legatees.

A legatee is not the agent of a deceased so as to make an insurance company liable to a person who is injured through the negligence of a driver who is operating the car with the implied or express consent of the legatee. 

Hobbs v. Cunningham, 273 Mass. 529, at 532

$270 

SECTION 270 6. Principal or Master When Operator Is His Agent or Servant.

An employer is ordinarily liable for the negligence of his employee while engaged in the employer's business if he assumed control of the operation even though the employee is driving his own vehicle or a vehicle belonging to a third person. That is, ownership of the vehicle is not essential to the creation of responsibility for the acts of the operator. 

So, where a sales agent of the defendant while returning from the home of a prospective buyer of one of the defendant's trucks injured the plaintiff, the sales agent was engaged in the course of the defendant's business and the fact that the sales agent was driving the motor vehicle of a third person at the time of the accident is not controlling. 

The means made use of by the sales agent, though not intended or contemplated by the defendant, while the sales agent was acting for the defendant and within the scope of his employment, does not prevent the plaintiff's recovering from defendant. 

Champion v. Shaw, 258 Mass. 9 

57 A.L.R. 743

SECTION 271 7. Lender of Number Plates or Registration. 

A person who lends number plates or registration so that a motor vehicle while ostensibly and lawfully travelling on the highway is in fact a trespasser, outlaw and nuisance is liable to anyone who sustains injury through its operation regardless of the negligence of the operator. 

McDonald v. Dundon, 242 Mass. 229

Due Care and Contributory Negligence 329 CHAPTER XIII. 

DUE CARE AND CONTRIBUTORY 

NEGLIGENCE 

A. DEFINITIONS. 

1. Due Care.

SECTION 272. 

Due care means that care for one's own safety required by law. 

O'Connor v. Hickey, 268 Mass. 454, at 458

Due care consists in reasonable action or restraint in circumstances where there is a duty to act or to avoid action. 

Nolan v. Boston El. Ry., 271 Mass. 375, at 379 

In Fletcher v. Boston & Maine R. R., 1 Allen, 9, at 15, it is said: "Ordinary care is a term that has relation to the situation of the parties and the business in which they are engaged. It is used here and is synonymous with the term 'reasonable care' as used by the courts in England. 'Care and diligence should vary according to the exigencies which require vigilance and attention, conforming in amount and degree to the particular circumstances under which they are to be exercised.'” 

Holly v. Boston Gas Light Co., 8 Gray, 131

Due care is the active, intelligent, energetic attention to safety required of the plaintiff under the circumstances. 

O'Connor v. Hickey, 260 Mass. 110, S. C. 268 Mass. 454 

Bothwell v. Boston El. Ry., 215 Mass. 467, at 470 

Hudson v. Lynn & Boston R. R., 185 Mass. 510, at

Due care is that kind and degree of care that persons of 521

8273 

 ordinary prudence would exercise in the same circumstances. 

O'Connor v. Hickey, 260 Mass. 110, at 112, S. C. 

268 Mass. 454

Failure of plaintiff to exercise due care has been described as negligence. 

O'Connor v. Hickey, 260 Mass. 110, at 112, S. C. 

268 Mass. 454 

May v. Princeton, II Met. 442, at 444

The conventional definition of due care as the kind and degree of care that persons of ordinary prudence would exercise in the same circumstances of place, time and attendant conditions, in its practical application to the trial of cases, is not an abstraction. It is practical, specific, definite; it is descriptive of conduct with reference to the cause of action on trial, not with reference to unrelated matters. 

O'Connor v. Hickey, 268 Mass. 454, at 459

It is conceivable that a plaintiff in an action for negligence might be wanting in due care with respect to an indifferent matter and yet be in the exercise of due care with respect to the cause of the injury inflicted by or through the negligence of the defendant.

Negligence which does not contribute to the injury is immaterial and irrelevant. 

O'Connor v. Hickey, 268 Mass. 454, at 459 

Marble v. Ross, 124 Mass. 44, at 48

SECTION 273. 

2. Contributory Negligence. 

Contributory negligence on the part of a person injured or killed through the negligence of another is want of due care in respect to the cause of the injury or death and is itself conduct having a share in bringing on the harm. 

O'Connor v. Hickey, 268 Mass. 454, at 458

Due Care and Contributory Negligence 331 

Want of due care by the person injured, touching the cause of his injury resulting from the negligence of another, is contributory negligence. 

O'Connor v. Hickey, 268 Mass. 454, at 458

Contributory negligence means violation of the duty to care for one's own safety which exists at least in those cases where a person who has sustained an injury seeks to fasten liability for that injury upon some other person. 

O'Connor v. Hickey, 268 Mass. 454, at 458 

Contributory negligence is an act or omission amounting to want of ordinary care, on the part of a person injured by the actionable negligence of another, combining, concurring or co-operating with the negligent act of that other as a proximate cause or occasion of the injury or damage complained of, without which such injury or damage would not have occurred. 

Contributory negligence must have in it: (1) the want of ordinary care on the part of the person injured or damaged; and (2) the proximate cause and connection between that want of ordinary care and the injury or damage-not the remote cause, but the proximate result from which the accident or injury or damage, in whole or in part, directly and immediately resulted, and but for which, either by itself or by the presence of the negligence of the other person, the injury would not have occurred. Besides these two, there are no other necessary elements. 

The test of contributory negligence is whether or not it contributed in any degree to produce the injury or damage for which complaint is made.

B. 

SECTION 274. 

GENERAL STATEMENT. 

General Laws, Chapter 231, Section 85 provides that: 

"In all actions, civil or criminal, to recover damages for

$274 

 injuries to the person or property or for causing the death of a person, the person injured or killed shall be presumed to have been in the exercise of due care, and contributory negligence on his part shall be an affirmative defence to be set up in the answer and proved by the defendant." 

Due care and contributory negligence on the part of a person killed or injured through the negligence of another are correlative terms; one states his essential positive duty with reference to his own safety and the other his failure in performance of that duty; both imply conduct touching the proximate cause of his injury. They relate to the causal connection between his conduct and his injury, with respect to the tortious conduct of the defendant. 

O'Connor v. Hickey, 268 Mass. 454, at 458

It is the duty of all travellers upon the highway to exercise reasonable care under all circumstances. 

Coates v. Bates, 265 Mass. 444

Negligence of the defendant does not relieve the plaintiff from his duty to exercise reasonable care for his own safety.

Jones v. Plotkin, 273 Mass. 24 

Sutherland v. Caruso, 258 Mass. 513, at 515 

Barry v. Harding, 244 Mass. 588 

Gibb v. Hardwick, 241 Mass. 546 

Cowles v. Springfield Gaslight Co., 234 Mass. 421 

Burns v. Oliver Whyte Company, 231 Mass. 519 

Newton v. McSweeney, 225 Mass. 402

Rogers v. Phillips, 206 Mass. 308

Brown v. Alter, 251 Mass. 223, at 224 

Sherman v. Fall River Iron Works Co., 2 Allen, 524, at 526

1. Causal Connection. 

There must be a causal connection between the plaintiff's negligence and his injury in order to create the conclusion that his negligence contributed to that injury.

F. RELIANCE ON CARE OF PERSON CAUSING INJURY. 

General Laws, Chapter 90 has not provided merely for the protection of travellers in vehicles; pedestrians also are entitled to rely upon the presumption that it will be observed. 

Foster v. Curtis, 213 Mass. 79, at 85 

Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 392

It should receive a construction not only in harmony with what has been declared to be the reciprocal rights and duties of travellers as defined by the authorities cited, but one which will not create an exception where none is necessary to effectuate the legislative intent. 

Foster v. Curtis, 213 Mass. 79, at 85 

A boy, six and one-half years of age, walking on the sidewalk with his sister, eight and one-half years old, where the boy has a right to be, justly might rely to a considerable extent on the expectation that no one would drive a motor vehicle across that sidewalk, even at a private driveway, without giving seasonable warning and stopping if necessary in order to avoid a collision. 

Hirrel v. Lacey, 274 Mass. 431, at 435

A pedestrian has a right to act in part on the theory that the driver of a motor vehicle will exercise reasonable caution with respect to him as a fellow traveller on the way and to assume that such vehicle will not run into him from behind. 

Wilson v. Freeman, 271 Mass. 438, at 440

$278 

Especially is this so if it might be found that even if he had been highly alert in looking out for careless drivers, he probably would not have discovered, until too late to avoid the impact, that the defendant's motor vehicle had been turned at a direct angle and was being driven towards him. 

Wilson v. Freeman, 271 Mass. 438, at 440

A pedestrian, crossing a street when no vehicles are in sight, may assume the operator of any approaching vehicle will slow down and give timely signal of his approach as required by statute (G. L. c. 90, s. 14, as amended by 

Acts 1925, c. 305) and that such operator will not alter his course and turn the vehicle towards the pedestrian plaintiff. 

Martin v. Florin, 273 Mass. 13, at 15 

Seymour v. Dunville, 265 Mass. 78

Barrett v. Checker Taxi Co., 263 Mass. 252 

Gauthier v. Quick, 250 Mass. 258

Gauthier v. Quick, 250 Mass. 258, at 261

Gaulin v. Yagoobian, 261 Mass. 145, at 147 

Davicki v. Flanagan, 250 Mass. 379 

Gauthier v. Quick, 250 Mass. 258 

As is said in Jean v. Nester, 261 Mass. 442, at 445: "It could have been found that she was at or near the

343 center of the street, between the east and west set of tracks, when struck. She might infer that at this point the defendant's automobile coming from the south had room to pass her in safety and would not collide with her and would give warning of its approach by sounding its horn. See Rogers v. Phillips, 206 Mass. 308. Even if it could be said that the evidence that she heard no horn was negative and of no value to show that the horn was not blown, Gibb v. Plaintiff may rely to some extent upon the belief that the operator of the motor vehicle will observe the law. 

McGuiggan v. Atkinson, 1932 A. S. 251 (Pedestrian had right to rely on timely signal and other requirements) 

Pierce v. Hutchinson, 241 Mass. 557, at 564

So, the plaintiff has a right to assume that others using the highway will use it lawfully and that the operator of a motor vehicle will obey the law in reference to slowing down or stopping, if necessary, on approaching a trolley car while it is discharging its passengers. 

Pierce v. Hutchinson, 241 Mass. 557, at 560

But this right thus to assume continues only until the plaintiff either knows or ought to know or realize that the operator of the motor car is not going to obey the law or is not in fact obeying the law, and when that moment arrives, it becomes the duty of the plaintiff pedestrian to do what he reasonably can to escape injury. 

Pierce v. Hutchinson, 241 Mass. 557, at 560

A driver has a right to rely to some extent on the expectation that the operator of another motor vehicle in passing in the opposite direction will be on the right of the center of the road in accordance with the statute (G. L. c. 89). 

Murray v. Indursky, 266 Mass. 220

8278

Payson v. Checker Taxi Co., 262 Mass. 22

A passenger alighting from a street car who does not look to the right or left, but looks straight ahead to the right hand curbing and who takes two steps, when she is struck by a motor vehicle, is not conclusively contributorily negligent for she rightly may assume that the operator will not violate the law (G. L. c. 90, s. 14) requiring the driver to allow street car passengers to alight and not to drive within eight feet, and she may rely to some extent upon the circumstances that other passengers are both preceding and following her in line crossing the street in the direction in which she is going.

A pedestrian is in the exercise of due care who, seeing a car fifty yards away, expects it to slacken its speed and not to continue on its way and collide with him.
