SECTION 280. 

H. ACTS IN SUDDEN EMERGENCY—IMMI- NENT PERIL-STARTLING DANGER. 

See: Section 105, page 155.

If the plaintiff is confronted with or called upon to act in a sudden emergency he is still required to exercise due care. 

Even in an emergency one must exercise reasonable care under the circumstances. 

Lawrence v. Fitchburg etc. Ry., 201 Mass. 489, at 494 The standard of his care, however, is governed by what reasonably careful men would do when confronted with a like emergency. In other words, what would a reasonably careful man do under the circumstances in which the particular plaintiff found himself. 

Pierce v. Hutchinson, 241 Mass. 557, at 559, 560 and 564 

Fitch v. Bay State St. Ry. Co., 237 Mass. 65 

Lemay v. Springfield St. Ry., 210 Mass. 63, at 67

Though in retrospect it may appear that a person's choice of a course of action was mistaken, it is a question of fact, in view of the need for speedy decision and action, whether the choice was prudent under the circumstances of the case. 

Austin v. Eastern Mass. St. Ry., 269 Mass. 420, at 424 

A choice may be mistaken and yet prudent. 

Austin v. Eastern Mass. St. Ry., 269 Mass. 420, at 424 

Fitch v. Bay State St. Ry., 237 Mass. 65, at 68 

Lemay v. Springfield St. Ry., 210 Mass. 63, at 67 

Kane v. Worcester Cons. St. Ry., 182 Mass. 201, at 202 The degree of care decreases in proportion to the suddenness and unexpectedness of the emergency.

$281 

Some allowance has to be made for the effect of fright and the necessity of immediate action in imminent peril. 

Dube v. Keogh Storage Co., 236 Mass. 488 Neafsky v. Szemete, 235 Mass. 160 

If an emergency existed and it can be found that it did not arise until the defendant's driver had turned to the left, then that emergency was created by his own negligent act. One cannot shield himself behind an emergency created by his own unlawful act. 

Isaacson v. Boston, etc. St. Ry., 1931 A. S. 385, at 394 

Tuttle v. Conn. Valley St. Ry., 239 Mass. 553 

Rundgren v. Boston & Northern St. Ry., 201 Mass. 156 

SECTION 281. 

I. VIOLATION OF STATUTE, ORDINANCE, BY- LAW, REGULATION OR RULE. 

"General Laws, Chapter 90, Section 9 provides that violation of the registration law shall not be a defence to actions of tort for injuries to property ‘unless it is shown that the person injured in his person or property or killed was the owner or operator of the motor vehicle the operation of which was in violation of [said provisions] or unless it is shown that the person so injured or killed, or the owner of the property so injured, knew or had reasonable cause to know that said provisions were being violated."

In Carrington v. Worcester Consolidated Street Railway, 222 Mass. 119, it was held that a bull which was at large upon a highway without fault of its owner, though subject to be impounded under General Laws Chapter 49, Section 24, was not a trespasser in the highway in relation to a street railway company, and that the latter was liable to the owner for negligently injuring it.

$347 

Due Care and Contributory Negligence 

The automobile cases are distinguished. 

Boyd v. Ellison, 248 Mass. 250 (Plaintiff coasting in streets in violation of ordinance)

If a motorist is approaching an intersecting street at a speed of thirty to thirty-five miles an hour, he is guilty of a violation of General Laws Chapter 90, Section 17 

and such a violation of the statute is evidence of negligence. 

Regan v. Rosenmark, 272 Mass. 256, at 258

Whether an operator's violation of a statute contributes to the accident as a cause or merely as an attending circumstance or condition is usually a question of fact. 

Bogert v. Corcoran, 260 Mass. 206, at 209 

Daris v. Middlesex etc. St. Ry., 241 Mass. 580 

Walters v. Davis, 237 Mass. 206, at 209 

Newton v. McSweeney, 225 Mass. 402

As is said in Jones v. New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad Company, 275 Mass. 139, at 143: "In an ordinary action of tort at common law to recover compensation for personal injuries, violation of a penal statute by the plaintiff at the moment of injury is a factor to be regarded. Its relation to the rights of the plaintiff was exhaustively considered, with a full review on pertinent authorities, in Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 

155, by Chief Justice Knowlton, who said at page 167: 'It has been established from early times that one who is violating a criminal law cannot recover for an injury to which his criminality was a directly contributing cause.' 

The rule there stated with amplifications is in substance that a plaintiff engaged in a criminal act at the time of sustaining injury through the negligence of another is not thereby necessarily precluded from recovery provided the element of criminality involved in that act and intended to be punished by the law has direct contributory effect in bringing on his injury. He may recover (if the other

$281 

 essentials of liability are established) provided the element of criminality involved in that act and intended to be punished by the law did not have a direct contributory effect in bringing on his injury. The law on its civil side will not aid a violator of the criminal law in seeking relief from the consequences of his own transgression. But it will not deny relief if the illegal factor of a plaintiff's conduct has no causal connection with the injury for which he seeks compensation. The distinction is often said to be between an illegal act which is a mere condition and an illegal act which is a contributing cause. This doctrine has now become firmly fixed and has been followed in numerous decisions." 

Cook v. Crowell, 273 Mass. 356, at 358 

Cannon v. Bassett, 264 Mass. 383, at 385 

Boyd v. Ellison, 248 Mass. 250, at 254 

Walters v. Davis, 237 Mass. 206, at 209 

Berdos v. Tremont & Suffolk Mills, 209 Mass. 489, at 499 If the failure of the operator to observe the law of the road contributed to the operator's injury, this failure may be considered in deciding the question of the operator's contributing negligence. 

So, the question resolves itself down into a matter merely of evidence and the proper inference to be drawn from the facts, to decide whether the operator was acting reasonably under the circumstances at the time. 

Anzoni v. Gosse, 274 Mass. 522, at 525

An operator is not liable unless he is careless in acting in an unreasonable manner and this depends on all the facts. 

Anzoni v. Gosse, 274 Mass. 522, at 525

A plaintiff, driving his vehicle on a public way in a manner forbidden by law or without appliances required by

$Due Care and Contributory Negligence 

349 law, while himself using all due care, when injured by an accident due solely to the negligence of a third person, his own violation not being a contributing cause of the accident but merely one of the conditions existing at the time, cannot be said to be barred from recovery by the mere fact of his violation of the law. 

Dudley v. Northampton St. Ry., 202 Mass. 443, at 446 

The plaintiff's unlawful act will prevent his recovery if it directly contributed to his injury. But there is a distinction between the unlawful act which is at least a contributing cause of the accident and one which is merely an attendant circumstance or condition, though perhaps a necessary condition, of that accident. 

Newcomb v. Boston Protective Dept., 146 Mass. 596 

Dudley v. Northampton St. Ry., 202 Mass. 443, at 445 and 446 

McCarthy v. Morse, 197 Mass. 332 

Black v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R. Co., 193 Mass. 448, at 452 and cases there cited 

Biggio v. Boston, 179 Mass. 356 

It was said in Farr v. Whitney, 260 Mass. 193, at 196: "... the violation of a criminal law does not prevent recovery, unless the violation contributes as a cause to the injury and damage.......if it be assumed, without deciding, that the plaintiff did not have a valid license from the selectmen of Ayer, these facts were a mere condition or circumstance and not, as matter of law, a cause contributing to the collision. A violation of a criminal statute is not a bar to recovery, except in matters to which the statute relates. It is settled law in this Commonwealth that the civil rights of a plaintiff are not affected by the failure to comply with a statute or ordinance, except when the failure to observe the law has a direct effect on his cause of action. The matters aimed at by the statute must be considered, and while criminality as a cause will

$281 

 prevent recovery, criminality which is a mere condition or circumstance will not have this result 

The absence of a license to operate the plaintiff's vehicle for the carriage of passengers did not prevent his recovery, unless it was found that this was a contributing cause to the damage. "What has been said applies to the absence of a mirror or reflector upon the plaintiff's automobile. G. L. c. 90, ss. 

7, 9. An automobile must be registered, and the conditions requisite for a legal registration must be complied with. Staley v. Wilbur, supra [258 Mass. 481]. But if properly registered it has rights upon the highway, although some provision of law relating to its equipment may not have been observed.”

 CHAPTER XIV. 

DUE CARE AND CONTRIBUTORY NEGLIGENCE OF PARTICULAR PERSONS A. OPERATORS OF MOTOR VEHICLES. 

SECTION 282. 

Driving at a speed which by statute is made an unreasonable and improper rate (G. L. c. 90, s. 12) may well be sufficient to create the operator's contributory negligence but this is a matter of fact and the conclusion of the operator's contributory negligence is not required as a matter of law. 

Murray v. Indursky, 266 Mass. 220

It is usually a question of fact whether, under particular circumstances, the operator exercised reasonable care to avoid the accident and the resulting injury or damage.

So, it is a question of fact, not law, whether, in his care to avoid a collision with another vehicle, the plaintiff operator carelessly disregarded the conditions existing on the road at the time. 

Harrington v. Cudahy Packing Co., 273 Mass. 15, at 18 In determining the operator's due care, consideration should be given to the fact that the operator is entitled to some extent to rely upon the expectation that operators of other vehicles will not operate them negligently and will turn into the middle of the road and will do such acts as will enable the plaintiff operator to pass. 

Harrington v. Cudahy Packing Co., 273 Mass. 15, at 18

$283 

(Defendant's truck cut out of line and then proceeded on left hand side of road approaching plaintiff from opposite direction) 

Austin v. Eastern Mass. St. Ry., 269 Mass. 420

The fact that the operator of a registered motor vehicle is not licensed as required by the statute (G. L. c. 90, s. 8) does not render him a trespasser nor is such fact conclusive against a recovery by him, if injured through the fault of another. The lack of such license is evidence of negligence in reference to the operator's fitness to operate and skill in management of the vehicle. 

Conroy v. Mather, 217 Mass. 91 (Passengers for hire were injured by collision between automobile and street car) 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155 (See: Section 81, page 96.)

But the rule is different concerning the operation of a vehicle which is either unregistered or not lawfully registered. (See: Section 66, page 70.)

The operator of an unregistered or improperly registered motor vehicle, even while unloading the same upon the public highway, is guilty of contributory negligence and can recover only in the event that the defendant was guilty of wilful, wanton or reckless conduct. 

Cook v. Crowell, 273 Mass. 356, at 358

The stalling of a motor vehicle may be found to be due either to some defect in the vehicle or in the manner of its operation.

SECTION 284. 

As to Vehicles Standing in Highway. (See: Sections 173-179, pages 212-216.)

An operator is careless, as matter of law, when he runs. into a standing truck parked on the roadside without lights one-half hour before sunset when he does not see it until fifteen feet away, although he has an opportunity of clear vision for at least one hundred yards back. 

Stone v. Mullen, 257 Mass. 344

But, trying to stop the motor vehicle as soon as the operator sees a truck which is unlighted and unattended on a public highway, by putting on his brakes as hard as he can and swinging to the left when he is not more than ten feet from the truck may be found to be due care where a truck is left on the crest of a hill. 

Rotefsky v. Bova, 274 Mass. 23, at 25

The care of an operator in passing a parked car at the rate of twenty to twenty-five miles an hour is a question of fact. 

Golden v. Carnevale, 273 Mass. 159

So, if the operator collides with a tree in an effort to avoid a parked car which suddenly starts toward the center of the road, the question of the operator's contributory negligence is one of fact. 

Golden v. Carnevale, 273 Mass. 159

4. As to Curves and Bends in the Road.

An operator who drives around a curve where his view is obstructed in excess of the statutory speed may well be found guilty of contributory negligence. 

Murray v. Indursky, 266 Mass. 220

 SECTION 286. 

5. As to Vehicles Travelling in Opposite Direction. 

See: Section 153, page 195.

An operator is not guilty of contributory negligence because he drives away over onto the right side, and even off the road, to avoid a reasonable probability of being struck by the defendant's car which is approaching him in the center of the road. 

And the continuing to proceed, when there is reasonable probability of an accident, is not contributory negligence. 

Harrington v. Cudahy Packing Co., 273. Mass. 15

Where the plaintiff voluntarily, and not under any constraint for instant action, goes into the path of obvious danger, he is guilty of contributory negligence. 

Harrington v. Cudahy Packing Co., 273 Mass. 15, at 18 

Sullivan v. Chadwick, 236 Mass. 130, at 137

SECTION 287. 

6. As to Railroad Crossings. 

See: Section 228, page 258; Section 334, page 355.

General Laws Chapter 90, Section 15 provides that: 

"Every person operating a motor vehicle, upon approaching a railroad crossing at grade, shall reduce the speed of the vehicle to a reasonable and proper rate, and shall proceed cautiously over the crossing. Whoever violates any provision of this section shall be punished by a fine of not less than ten nor more than fifty dollars.” 

Violation of this statute, if found as a fact, is something more than mere evidence of negligence; if it has a causal connection with injuries of an operator, it bars him from recovery. 

Jones v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R. Co., 275 Mass. 139, at 144 So, the defendant railroad is entitled to have the jury instructed in substance that if the operator failed to proceed cautiously over the railroad crossing, he was acting in violation of law and if such violation contributed to the accident, the operator is not entitled to recover against the railroad company. 

Jones v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R. Co., 275 Mass. 139, at 144 It is insufficient merely to read the statute to the jury and state that it applied to the operator and that whether the operator was cautious approaching the crossing was to be taken into consideration in determining whether the

$287 

 operator was negligent, for the occurrence of a violation of this statute is pertinent and vital to the issue of the operator's contributory negligence and involves a general principle essential to a correct understanding of the rights of the parties. It relates to specific conduct in the operation of the motor vehicle which, if found by the jury to exist, will be a bar to recovery by the operator and those who relied upon him. 

Jones v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R. Co., 275 Mass. 139, at 142 

Libby v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R. Co., 273 Mass. 522  

IOI (Operator violated statute when, after walking to track and looking for a distance of a thousand feet, he saw nothing to left and drove up slowly to track increasing speed without looking to left for a period of two minutes when he saw train upon him and was struck)

If, in crossing a grade crossing of a railroad, the driver of a motor vehicle has a clear vision for several hundred feet in the direction a train is coming, when he is about five feet from the nearest rail moving at a speed of two or three miles an hour and able to stop his car within a foot, and it is obvious that any train could not strike his car while it is crossing the second line of tracks, a distance of approximately the length of his car, it must be within the driver's vision when he looks from the point five feet from the nearest rails, and evidently if he does not then see the train he must look carelessly. 

Creeley v. Boston & Maine R. R., 263 Mass. 529, at 533

IOI, at 105 It is a rule of public policy designed to promote the general welfare of travellers upon railroads as well as upon ways. It is not satisfied when, as here, one so driving has opportunity to observe the approach of a train for at least two minutes before reaching a crossing, but neglects to look in both directions to make certain no train is drawing near and then goes on the crossing with a train close upon him. At a railroad crossing an operator must use his senses, -look and listen, and govern his conduct accordingly. 

Fogg v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R. Co., 223 Mass. 444

So, when the facts are that the day was clear and there was a view of one hundred nineteen feet south with nothing to obstruct it except two houses, both some distance back from the tracks, and the operator, when seventy-five feet from the track, looked both ways but never slowed down or stopped, he as matter of law exercised no care in a place of unusual danger.

The conclusion of fact must be that the operator either did not look or he looked carelessly and is guilty of contributory negligence.

(I) Reliance upon Gates or Crossing Tender. 

Although the operator has been misled by open gates and the absence of the gate tender who is regularly stationed at the crossing to raise and lower the gates on which red lanterns are hung at night, yet the operator, after slowing, is not cautious in driving over the crossing when he is familiar with the physical surroundings and knows how the view is obstructed by a fence which, nevertheless, gives opportunity for observation of which he can avail himself, and knows that when ten feet from the rails he can see along the track a train near at hand.

7. As to Street Cars. (See Section 229, page 270.)

An operator of a motor vehicle, to exercise proper care, must look for street cars.

c. Backing Onto Track.

The plaintiff, with several others in his car, backed his auto from a standing position twelve feet into the side of the defendant's car, causing serious personal injury, and damage to the motor vehicle.

The plaintiff had a clear view for four hundred fifty feet in the direction from which the car came but testified he saw nothing although he was constantly looking as he backed. The defendant's car moved one hundred thirty-five feet up grade after the accident. 

Held that the conclusion is irresistible that the negligence of the plaintiffs contributed to their injuries. If any of them had seen the car and given warning, the accident could have been avoided. The record discloses a situation where the plaintiffs, each on his own account. went into a path of known danger in plain sight without rational explanation consistent with due care. 

Pigeon v. Mass. Northeastern St. Ry. Co., 230 Mass. 

392, at 395 and 396

The motor vehicle was just starting from a stationary position on low speed and moving slowly. It could have been stopped almost instantly. The fact of the accident shows that the defendant's car was within the plain field of vision of each one for a sufficient period of time to have enabled the plaintiff to stop his automobile if any one of those with him had seen and spoken of the danger. The fact that none did this is irrefutable evidence of the negligence of each directly contributing to the accident. 

Pigeon v. Mass. Northeastern St. Ry. Co., 230 Mass. 

392, at 396 and cases cited

$295 

Where one in a motor vehicle looked to the rear one hundred thirteen feet and, seeing nothing, backed upon the defendant's tracks colliding with one of its cars, he was held not to be in the exercise of due care. 

The street car must have been in plain sight when the plaintiff backed his car and with any care he must have seen it. If he looked and did not see it he must have looked carelessly and is in no better position than if he did not look at all. 

Birch v. Athol & O. St. Ry. Co., 198 Mass. 257

SECTION 295. 

d. Glaring Headlight of Street Car as Cause of Operator's Collision with Other Vehicle. 

Where a motorman failed to shut off a brilliant headlight, in violation of his employer's rules, although the plaintiff's motor vehicle was in sight more than one thousand feet, a finding of negligence is warranted. 

Bailey v. Worcester Cons. St. Ry., 228 Mass. 477

A failure to apply brakes when another car is a short distance ahead is evidence of negligence, even though the plaintiff was running with his headlights extinguished and only small sidelights burning, did not see a carriage preceding until twenty feet from it, and did not stop then but instead, on looking to the left and seeing an approaching motor vehicle, attempted to pass to the right of the carriage ahead and, misjudging the distance between the carriage and the car track owing to the glare of the headlight, ran into the car, his due care was a question for the jury. It could not be said that the statutory presumption was entirely overcome. 

Bailey v. Worcester Cons. St. Ry., 228 Mass. 477 

8. Operator's. Acts as Affecting Owner's Rights. 

SECTION 296. 

a. Principal and Agent.

$367 

If the operator is the agent of the owner, the negligence of the operator is imputed to the owner and the owner is deprived of recovery because of the contributory negligence of the operator. 

Nash v. Lang, 268 Mass. 407, at 410

As Chief Justice Rugg said in the above cited case, at pages 414 and 415: "Commonly, an injured person may proceed to judgment against any or all who have committed a tort against him. 

The imputation of negligence rests upon the relation of master and servant, principal and agent, the obligation of a custodian to care for an incapable dependent, cooperation in a common enterprise and cases of that nature.” 

SECTION 297. 

b. Bailor and Bailee. 

A bailor, free from personal negligence, may recover for damage to the bailed motor vehicle resulting from negligence of a third person alone or from concurring acts of negligence of the bailee and a third person. 

Anthony v. Boston & Maine R. R., 1931 A. S. 1697, at 1701 

Nash v. Lang, 268 Mass. 407, at 412

The negligence of the bailee, concurring with that of a third person to injure the bailed motor vehicle, is not imputed by law to the innocent bailor nor is he barred from recovery for the wrong done him. 

Nash v. Lang, 268 Mass. 407, at 412

The contributory negligence of a bailee, concurring with that of a third person to injure the bailed property, is not imputed to the bailor. He is free from any negligence. 

Nash v. Lang, 268 Mass. 407, at 412

The owner, if not himself at fault, may recover dam-

$298 

 ages for injury to his property flowing from the negligence of another even though that property be at the moment in the possession of one whose relation to it is that of bailee. 

Nash v. Lang, 268 Mass. 407, at 413

As was said by Chief Justice Rugg in the last cited case, at page 413: "Juristic thought is inclined to the position that the doer of a legal wrong ought to be held to make compensation for its harmful consequences to the person injured unless the latter has himself contributed thereto by his own tortious conduct."

The owner is not prevented from recovering compensation for the injury sustained to his property through the positive neglect of duty owed to him by a third person, even though such neglect may have concurred, with negligence of the bailee of the owner's property, to produce the harm. 

Nash v. Lang, 268 Mass. 407, at 415

SECTION 298. 

(I) Husband and Wife. 

The mere relation of husband and wife does not constitute one the agent of the other nor prevent the existence of the relation between them of bailor and bailee. 

So, a wife who gratuitously lends her automobile to her husband, a physician, in order to enable him to make his professional calls, does not constitute the husband the agent of the wife in driving the automobile. The husband is acting independently in his own right. 

Nash v. Lang, 268 Mass. 407, at 410

The interest of the wife in the professional success of her husband, aided though it may be by the marital obligation to support her, is not sufficient to render the work of the husband a joint enterprise of both. There must be

$369 

 additional factors to establish the relation of principal and agent or master and servant. 

Nash v. Lang, 268 Mass. 407, at 410

In these circumstances, the relation of the wife and her husband with respect to the automobile is that of bailor and bailee. 

Nash v. Lang, 268 Mass. 407, at 410

As was said in Anthony v. Boston and Maine Railroad, 1931 A. S. 1697, at 1701: 

66 the plaintiff Angus S. Anthony [the husband] and his two children were precluded from recovery because of his conduct It does not follow, however. that Leah W. Anthony [the wife] may not recover for damages caused to [her] truck. It could have been found that her husband was not intrusted by her with the control of the truck and that he did not have charge of it within the meaning of G. L. c. 160, s. 232. . . . It also could have been found that the damage to it was the result of the concurring negligence of her husband and the defendant. She was free from any negligence, and none is to be imputed to her because of her husband's use of the truck without her knowledge. She is not responsible for his conduct in the circumstances here disclosed and is not to be deprived of a remedy against one who has damaged her property, although she has no right of action against her husband. That fact, however, presents no reason why she should not have a cause of action against another wrongdoer who has contributed to cause the damage sustained by her. If. the accident was due to the failure of the defendant to give the statutory signals, she is entitled to recover even if the negligence of her husband concurred to produce such damage."

B. PEDESTRIANS. 

SECTION 299.

$299 

Speaking with precise technicality, every traveller upon a highway is bound to exercise the care of the ordinarily prudent and cautious person under all circumstances. The degree of vigilance and continuity of alertness necessary to attain that standard vary with the time and place, surroundings and means of transportation. 

Comm. v. Horsfall, 213 Mass. 232, at 235 

Arnold v. Colbert, 273 Mass. 161 

Barrett v. Checker Taxi Co., 263 Mass. 352

Pedestrians, like all other travellers, have a right to use the public highway at any time of day or night even though the highway is not improved and although it may contain street railway or railroad tracks. 

Pedestrians have a legal right to travel in the highway, or to cross it at any point, and the mere fact that a pedestrian does so does not render him guilty of contributory negligence as matter of law.

However, every pedestrian must exercise reasonable care for his own safety and consider all circumstances existent at the time.

When a pedestrian crosses the highway at a place other than a regular crossing, he may be required to exercise some additional vigilance. 

44 A. L. R. 1299 

9 A. L. R. 1248

But a pedestrian has a right to walk longitudinally in a street or highway and is not, as matter of law, guilty of contributory negligence in so doing. 

Booth v. Meagher, 224 Mass. 472 

67 A. L. R. 109

The law of the road, which requires a traveller in a vehicle upon meeting another vehicle to turn to the right, does not apply to pedestrians. And, generally, the law of the road has no application to travellers upon foot but is confined to travellers in vehicles.

$371 

Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 392 

67 A. L. R. III 

Usually a pedestrian going into a public highway is required to stop, observe the conditions as to safety, and pay attention to warnings or signals of approaching motor vehicles or other travellers.

However, the pedestrian has a right to rely to some extent on the expectation that the operator of the motor vehicle will observe the law and exercise reasonable care to avoid injury to the pedestrian.

The pedestrian has the right to rely in part upon assumption that the operator will not be negligent. 

Cambra v. Santos, 233 Mass. 131, at 133 

Sarmento v. Vance, 231 Mass. 310, at 312 

Emery v. Miller, 231 Mass. 243, at 245 

Gagnon v. Worcester Cons. St. Ry. Co., 231 Mass. 160, at 162 

Dilorio v. Jordan Marsh Co., 211 Mass. 280 

When the plaintiff is lawfully on the highway, he has a right to assume that he will not be run into. 

Bombard v. Worcester Cons. St. Ry. Co., 234 Mass.

I, at 4 

Casey v. Boston & Maine R. R., 231 Mass. 529, at 534 

Burns v. Oliver Whyte Co., 231 Mass. 519, at 521

So, a pedestrian who starts to cross a highway when no vehicles are in sight can assume that the defendant will slow down and give a timely signal of his approach (G. L. c. 90, s. 14, as amended by Acts 1925, c. 305) and that the driver of an approaching vehicle will not alter his course and turn his vehicle toward the plaintiff, but may reasonably believe he can cross the street in safety. 

Martin v. Florin, 273 Mass. 13, at 15 

Seymour v. Dunville, 265 Mass. 78 

Barrett v. Checker Taxi Co., 263 Mass. 252 

Gauthier v. Quick, 250 Mass. 258

$299 

Pedestrian in walking across street may take into account auto driver's duty to reduce speed and duty to exercise proper care. 

Gaulin v. Yagoobian, 261 Mass. 145 

Davicki v. Flanagan, 250 Mass. 379 

Gauthier v. Quick, 250 Mass. 258 

Right to rely on signal from vehicle-in exercise of due care. 

Goulding v. Boston El. Ry., 262 Mass. 47, at 50 and cases collected A pedestrian, whether he sees a motor vehicle or not, has a right to rely to some extent on the expectation that any motor vehicle approaching him will (1) slow down. (2) give a timely signal, and (3) observe the other re quirements of General Laws Chapter 90, Sections 1. 

and 17. 

Barrett v. Checker Taxi Co., 263 Mass. 252, at 254

The plaintiff may be found to be in the exercise of due care even though he does not see the approaching motor vehicle when he looks. 

Davicki v. Flanagan, 250 Mass. 379 

Bishop v. Pastorelli, 240 Mass. 104, at 107 

Kaminski v. Fournier, 235 Mass. 51 

French v. Mooar, 226 Mass. 173

Looking up and down the street and seeing that the street is clear for a reasonable distance, then starting to cross and, when partly across, being struck and injured by a motor vehicle, is not necessarily contributory negligence. 

Moran v. Brodeur, 261 Mass. 120 

Looking straight ahead while walking on a sidewalk may be due care. 

, at 282 (Boy struck by vehicle coming from alley)

$373 

 SECTION 300. 

2. Intoxication. 

See: Section 212, page 240.

Section 324, page 396. 

Where there is evidence of the defendant being under the influence of liquor at the time of the accident, this is violation of a penal law and that violation is in itself evidence of negligence. 

Tripp v. Allen, 226 Mass. 189

Evidence that a pedestrian is intoxicated at the time of his injury does not warrant the direction of a verdict. 

Martin v. Florin, 273 Mass. 13

SECTION 301. 

3. Walking Longitudinally Upon the Highway. 

Where the plaintiff was walking in the street a few feet from the sidewalk when the defendant's automobile struck her, it was held that the plaintiff had a right to walk in the roadway in preference to the sidewalk under such circumstances. While she may not have observed the highest degree of care with regard to automobiles, her due care was for the jury. The plaintiff had a concurrent use of the roadway with the defendant.

Booth v. Meagher, 224 Mass. 472 

Where two girls were walking a little to the left of the center of a sixteen foot road when a street car with a brilliant headlight and an automobile with strong headlights approached from the rear, the latter moving at an excessive speed, so that the girls, becoming alarmed, ran toward the right of the road and were struck by the automobile, although if they had remained where they were they would not have been hit, it was held their due care was for the jury. 

Emery v. Miller, 231 Mass. 243

It cannot be ruled, as matter of law, that failure of a

$302 

 pedestrian upon a main highway to carry a lantern after dark is want of due care, although he is leading horses along the highway. 

Powers v. Loring, 231 Mass. 458 

4. Crossing the Highway.

SECTION 302. 

a. At Public Crossings and Intersections. 

When a pedestrian, before entering upon a crosswalk, looks to the left and to the right and does not see any motor vehicle approaching or moving within a block, and does not hurry, but walks at a normal gait, and keeps on looking to his right until one-half or two-thirds the distance across the street, which is about forty or fifty feet wide, then looks forward to prepare for stepping on the curbing, sees no lights, other than parking lights on a few vehicles, sees no moving traffic, particularly does not see the defendant's vehicle before it strikes him, and he is struck from behind and from the right, the question whether the pedestrian was careless in failing to see the defendant's car before it hit him is not of law but of fact. 

The pedestrian's failure to see the defendant's automobile under these circumstances does not create an instance where he looks and looks negligently. 

Arnold v. Colbert, 273 Mass. 161, at 163 

But see cases contra:

Walsh v. Boston El. Ry., 271 Mass. 477 

Pigeon v. Mass. Northeastern St. Ry., 230 Mass. 392

Collins v. Boston El. Ry., 218 Mass. 284 

Tognazzi v. Milford etc. St. Ry. Co., 201 Mass. 7

Especially is this true when the defendant's vehicle comes from around the corner of a street or passageway.

$375 

44 A. L. R. 1299 

28 A. L. R. 1279 (Stepping into roadway where view obstructed) 9 A. L. R. 1248 

Even though one is mistaken in his estimate of the speed of an approaching automobile as he crosses an intersection, his due care is for the jury. 

Payson v. Checker Taxi Co., 262 Mass. 22 

Fournier v. Zinn, 257 Mass. 575, at 577 

In Barrett v. Checker Taxi Co., 263 Mass. 252, the court said at page 254: "A pedestrian, whether he sees an automobile or not, has a right to rely to some extent on the expectation that any motor vehicle, approaching him, will slow down and give a timely signal and observe the other requirements of Gen. Laws, c. 9, ss. 14, 17."

So, when a pedestrian, arriving at the corner of an intersection of two streets which are level and about eighty to ninety feet wide from curb to curb, stopped, looked both ways, and saw no automobile moving in either direction and then started to cross one of the streets, continuing to look in both directions along that street, his view being unobstructed for several hundred yards in each. direction, looked ahead and to each side several times, and, when about twenty-five or thirty feet from the curb at the farther corner of the streets was struck by the defendant's automobile, did not know what part of the automobile struck him or where it came from and did not see the defendant's automobile until it "loomed up and struck" him, and heard no warning or signal of the approach of the automobile and no such warning or signal was given and the scene of the accident was a well lighted business street, although the night was misty and rainy, it cannot be ruled as matter of law that the burden of proving the plaintiff's contributory negligence had been

$303 

 sustained by the defendant; or, that if the plaintiff looked he must have looked carelessly [even though if the plaintiff had seen the automobile he could have got out of its way].

It also appeared that while the plaintiff was crossing the street and had passed over sixty feet of the distance, the automobile traffic started from the opposite side of the other street and the defendant's automobile was the first in traffic coming from that direction, moving at a speed from twenty to twenty-five miles an hour; that the defendant did not see the plaintiff until the latter was near the bumper of the defendant's automobile, the lights of which were lighted, and there being nothing to obstruct the view of the plaintiff. 

McGuiggan v. Atkinson, 1932 A. S. 251 

The court said in the last cited case at page 252: "However close and difficult the question may have been to determine as matter of fact, it nevertheless was a fact to be decided by the weighing of evidence. . . . Moreover, there... [was] ample space for the defendant to have driven in front of or behind the plaintiff without striking him. 66 The plaintiff might reasonably expect the driver of a motor vehicle to avoid him rather than to hit him." 

Durling v. Lamontain, 1931 A. S. 2429 

Hutchingson v. H. E. Shaw Co., 273 Mass. 51 and cases cited 

Gibb v. Hardwick, 241 Mass. 546 

But see: 

Will v. Boston Elevated Railway, 247 Mass. 250

SECTION 303. 

(I) At Other Points on Highway. 

A pedestrian has a right to cross between sidewalks and between public crossings if he uses due care. Usually such due care should consist of looking in directions from which vehicles are likely to approach.

$377 

Seabut v. Ward Baking Co., 231 Mass. 339 

A pedestrian who, intending to cross the highway, looks in both directions before leaving the sidewalk and sees no vehicle approaching, and none parked on his side of the highway, and who walks to the middle of the trolley car track where he pauses to permit an automobile coming from his right to pass in front of him, and, while walking and pausing, again looks to left and sees no vehicle approaching, and while still waiting is struck by the defendant's truck which comes from his left cannot be ruled to be wanting in due care or guilty of contributory negligence. 

Hutchinson v. Shaw Co., 273 Mass. 51, at 52

SECTION 304. 

b. Duty to Stop, Look and Listen. 

Usually, a pedestrian, to exercise due care, should stop, look and listen before crossing a street or highway in order to become acquainted with traffic conditions and regulate his conduct concerning his own safety.

However, this rule is not absolute and existing conditions may not require the pedestrian to do any of these things. 

What the pedestrian's conduct should be is a question of fact but where all the facts are in evidence and danger exists or reasonably should be anticipated, the pedestrian's conduct may be negligent as matter of law and also it may even be ruled to be as contributive to the pedestrian's injury or damage.

However, even though a pedestrian looks but sees no truck or vehicle coming at any time before he is struck nor does he see the truck operated by the defendant, and hears no warning from it or signal, it does not follow that the defendant sustains the burden of proving contributory negligence. 

Hennessey v. Moynihan, 272 Mass. 165, at 167

$304 

Especially is this so when traffic conditions are confusing and there are a great many people walking and vehicles travelling in and around the highway where the pedestrian is injured. 

Hennessey v. Moynihan, 272 Mass. 165, at 167

Nor does it follow that the pedestrian looked carelessly or in any respect failed to exercise due care. 

Hennessey v. Moynihan, 272 Mass. 165, at 168 

Barrett v. Checker Taxi Co., 263 Mass. 252, at 255 

Pawloski v. Hess, 253 Mass. 478, at 480 

Morrissey v. Boston & Maine R. R., 216 Mass. 5, at 6 

But see: 

Pigeon v. Mass. Northeastern St. Ry. Co., 230 Mass. 393, at 396 (Where plaintiff's negligent conduct is only reasonable explanation of circumstances undisputed or shown by his testimony) 

Gibb v. Hardwick, 241 Mass. 546 

Kaminski v. Fournier, 235 Mass. 51, at 54 

Fitzgerald v. Boston El. Ry., 194 Mass. 242 

Roberts v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R. Co., 175 Mass. 296 Where plaintiff, who could see the road for several hundred feet, left the grass plot and was hit within a distance of eight to ten feet, neither seeing nor hearing the automobile, it was held to be for the jury to say how far away the automobile was when plaintiff looked and whether her negligent conduct contributed to cause the accident. The plaintiff could be found to be in the use of due care even if she did not see the automobile when she looked, and the defendant is not entitled to a ruling that plaintiff could not recover if she did not look, or if she looked and did not see the defendant's automobile.

$379 

 Barrett v. Checker Taxi Co., 263 Mass. 252 

Chaplin v. Brookline Taxi Co., 230 Mass. 155 (Looked both ways, took five or six steps and was struck) 

French v. Boston & Maine R. R., 230 Mass. 163, at 166 (Need not look a second time)

SECTION 305. 

c. Crossing in Front of Approaching Vehicle. 

There is nothing in the law that requires a pedestrian to remain on a sidewalk, or refrain from crossing the highway, just because a motor vehicle is approaching. 

The circumstances are important, particularly the distance between the motor vehicle and the pedestrian at the time of the motor vehicle's approach. 

So, where a motor vehicle is one hundred fifty feet away from a pedestrian and it moves out of line to pass another car in front and the pedestrian, then on the highway, does not stop but continues on and is struck by the motor vehicle, he is not negligent in failing to stop or in continuing on. 

Stafford v. Comm. Co., 263 Mass. 240

However, a pedestrian who, without looking or listening, steps from behind one vehicle in front of another, which injures him, is guilty of contributory negligence, as matter of law. 

Jean v. Nester, 261 Mass. 442 

65 A. L. R. 207

The question of contributory negligence is one of fact, even when a pedestrian who started across the highway passed in front of a parked automobile and, upon reaching the center of the street, stopped and waited for the passing of an automobile going in one direction, and, after again starting, was hit by the defendant's automobile going

$306 

 in the opposite direction, when the pedestrian heard no horn after she stopped to let the first automobile pass and then started to cross again without looking for the defendant's vehicle which she could have seen if she had looked. 

Jean v. Nester, 261 Mass. 442 

65 A. L. R. 210

Where a pedestrian, in order to avoid a rapidly moving automobile approaching him on the side of a country road, jumps in the middle of the road in front of another automobile which approaches without warning, his due care is for the jury. 

Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 392

SECTION 306. 

(I) Newsboys.

Contributory negligence is a question of fact where a newsboy is run over while selling papers in a public square although he suddenly jumps in front of the motor vehicle. 

Rasmussen v. Whipple, 211 Mass. 546 

In the last cited case, the court said: "If he suddenly left the crowd of people and jumped in front of the approaching car, as the defendant testified, or if he had safely crossed in sight of the machine, and then suddenly ran back just in front of it, as the driver said, his conduct would generally be condemned as careless." 

SECTION 307. 

d. Colliding with Side of Vehicle. 

A pedestrian who walks or runs into the side of a motor vehicle because he does not observe the vehicle or because his head is down or for other cause is guilty of contributory negligence and is not in the use of due care.

381 

Cook v. Farnum, 258 Mass. 145 

25 A. L. R. 1513 

So, a boy of eight who, while running and pushing against the motor vehicle, falls and is run over, is not using due care. 

Smith v. Whittal, 257 Mass. 306

SECTION 308. 

e. Crossing Diagonally or at Unusual Places. 

Although a pedestrian is not confined to a particular place in his right to cross the highway, yet he must exercise reasonable prudence and care.

A boy who runs diagonally across a highway after jumping off the rear of a wagon on which he has been riding, without observing conditions or attempting to prevent injury to himself, is not in the exercise of due care but is contributorily negligent and no recovery can be had for his injury or death. 

Mills v. Powers, 216 Mass. 36 

14 A. L. R. 1173 f. 

SECTION 309. 

Obstruction of View. 

The plaintiff, about to cross a street thirty feet wide, stood at a point where a curve prevented her seeing more than fifty feet, waited for two cars to pass, then, seeing nothing in sight, took five or six steps and was knocked down by the defendant's car going twenty-five miles an hour.

The defendant's negligence was admitted and the plaintiff's due care was for the jury. 

Chaplin v. Brookline Taxi Co., 230 Mass. 155

Where the defendant turned his automobile out toward the center of the street to pass a wagon standing next to the curbing, and then, after passing, without blowing his

$310 

 horn, turned to the right at a moderate speed and struck and killed the plaintiff's intestate, a boy of eight, who suddenly ran from the sidewalk in front of the horse of the standing vehicle and was hit by the right front fender of the defendant's automobile, there was no evidence of negligence.

Lovett v. Scott, 232 Mass. 541 

28 A. L. R. 1279

A pedestrian on the highway for a proper purpose, who looked in both directions, the last time a short while before the accident, was not careless because he did not see car as it approached, when in view of the presence of auto trucks, autos and other traffic, etc., it could be found that his view was so obstructed that he could not see the car in time to avoid the accident. 

Goulding v. Boston El. Ry., 262 Mass. 47, at 50 

Johnston v. Bay State St. Ry. Co., 222 Mass. 583, at 587 

SECTION 310. 

g. Compliance with or Violation of Traffic Sig nals.

Neither a compliance with nor a violation of a traffic signal, as matter of law, can be ruled to be due care or contributory negligence.

A compliance with a traffic signal may, under particular conditions, be a lack of due care, such as,-going directly into the path of a motor vehicle that is approaching at a high rate of speed, or where it is apparent that the vehicle cannot stop without striking the pedestrian. 

On the other hand, a violation of a traffic signal, where the conditions on the highway are such that no vehicle is in sight or could jeopardize the safety of the pedestrian, may not be lack of due care or contributory negligence. 

Wilson v. Freeman, 271 Mass. 438, at 440

$383 

(Signal of traffic officer does not authorize operator to make a turn so as to collide with plaintiff)

Margeson v. Town Taxi Inc., 266 Mass. 192 

(Driver saw pedestrian five feet from him while vehicle was stationary but struck pedestrian) 

Donovan v. Mutrie, 265 Mass. 472

h. Towing Vehicles. 

Beaucage v. Mercer, 206 Mass. 492

SECTION 312. 

5. Standing or Sitting in the Highway. 

Plaintiff's intestate, a boy of sixteen, was standing in the street halfway between car tracks watching the operation of a concrete hopper when, the hopper suddenly lowering, to avoid being hit by it, he stepped backward a step or two directly in front of the defendant's automobile then distant five or six feet and travelling thirty miles an hour.

The fact that the intestate did not look back is not conclusive against his due care. He might well think he could step back when he was standing within three feet of the machine and there was ample space in the highway behind him for the automobile to pass without striking him. 

Sarmento v. Vance, 231 Mass. 310

Standing in middle of bridge where workmen, trucks and motor vehicles were passing, and looking a short time before accident, not careless. 

Goulding v. Boston El. Ry., 262 Mass. 47, at 50

7. Crossing Private Driveway.

SECTION 315. 

C. POLICE OR TRAFFIC OFFICERS. 

Where a police officer was standing in the center of car tracks directing traffic on a summer evening, dressed in blue uniform with white gloves and the automobile approached the place with its lights on, the officer turned his head toward it and put up his hand for it to stop and kept his hand up, but the automobile kept going right along and, when officer tried to jump out of its way he was struck by the front part of it and knocked down and the automobile then went more than seventy feet without stopping, the operator was negligent. 

Mathews v. Carr, 271 Mass. 362 

Hartnett v. Tripp, 231 Mass. 382 (Policeman at night struck and knocked down)

CARS. 

1. Walking To. 

SECTION 317. 

See: Section 198, page 230. 

The usual rule of ordinary care does not impose upon pedestrians the burden of being constantly on the lookout to see if their path is free from dangerous defects, or in a state of apprehension of personal injury from other travellers. 

, at 586

The traveller has a right to presume not only that the way is reasonably fitted for his use, but also that those who may be lawfully using it will exercise a proper degree of care.

SECTION 318. 

See: Section 199, page 231.

There is no imperative rule of law generally requiring a pedestrian when lawfully using a public way to be continuously looking or listening to ascertain if motor vehicles are approaching, under the penalty that upon failing to do so, if he is injured, his negligence must be conclusively presumed. 

, at 586 

Robbins v. Springfield St. Ry. Co., 165 Mass. 30

So, where a pedestrian desires to become a passenger on an electric car which is about to pass on the opposite side of the street, and gives the usual signal so that the car stops and the pedestrian starts to walk across, after looking to see if there is any danger but not observing the automobile, nor hearing any signal of its approach sounded because the defendant's automobile is at some distance, it cannot be said that there is a balancing of probabilities by the pedestrian, with a willingness to take a chance of safely getting over before the defendant comes up. 

Hennessey v. Taylor, 189 Mass. 583, at 584 and 585

But see Whitman v. Boston Elevated Railway Com pany, 181 Mass. 138, and cases similar, where in a spirit of apparent indifference a pedestrian voluntarily exposes himself to the chance of serious injury. 

Hennessey v. Taylor, 189 Mass. 583, at 585

$387 

Donovan v. Lynn & Boston R. R., 185 Mass. 533 

Judge v. Elkins, 183 Mass. 229 

Hurley v. West End St. Ry. Co., 180 Mass. 370 

Mathes v. Lowell, L. & H. St. Ry. Co., 177 Mass. 416 

Kelly v. Wakefield etc. St. Ry. Co., 175 Mass. 331 

Creamer v. West End St. Ry. Co., 156 Mass. 320

If the pedestrian sees the defendant's motor vehicle approaching and decides that it is at a sufficient distance to enable him to pass safely, the pedestrian may be found to have exercised due care, though an accident proves that his judgment was erroneous. What is an error of judgment does not usually amount to lack of due care or contributory negligence. 

, at 585 

Coleman v. Lowell, L. & H. St. Ry. Co., 181 Mass. 591 It is usually for the jury to interpret the language of the party or witness, and also to determine how far any failure by the pedestrian to more fully and carefully observe the amount or kind of travel on the highway was indicative of such want of care as ought to bar his recovery. 

Hennessey v. Taylor, 189 Mass. 583, at 585 

3. Alighting.

SECTION 319. 

See: Section 200, page 232.

A passenger of a street car has a right to rely to some extent upon the fact that a motor vehicle will not pass within eight feet of the step or portion of the car from which the passenger is alighting. 

G. L. c. 90, s. 14

When the passenger is struck by the motor vehicle as he comes forth from the car, concurrently with the act of

$320 

 alighting, and before he has passed from the side of the car, the operator of the motor vehicle is negligent and the passenger is in the exercise of due care. 

Ames v. Madonna, 247 Mass. 270 

47 A. L. R. 1256

The passenger is contributorily negligent when he goes to the rear of the street car from which he has alighted and attempts to cross the street and is struck, almost immediately after stepping off the further track of the street railway, by the automobile of the defendant approaching in the opposite direction, and the passenger, as he steps down from the street car does not notice the automobile until it is almost upon him, when he could have seen it. 

The failure to see the approaching automobile sooner than the time when he is struck by it, and in time to avoid the accident, is due to the passenger's own carelessness and a verdict should be directed for the defendant. 

Gibb v. Hardwick, 241 Mass. 546 

47 A. L. R. 1248

But if only a few seconds elapse between the time of alighting from the street car and being knocked down by the motor vehicle, the street car passenger is not necessarily lacking in due care, for his opportunity to get to a place of safety is limited. 

Hartnett v. Tripp, 231 Mass. 382 (Policeman at night struck and knocked down) 

4. Moving From. 

SECTION 320. 

See: Section 201, page 234. 

A street car passenger, in following other passengers who have alighted from a street car, in crossing the street is not as matter of law contributorily negligent, even if a motor vehicle is approaching at thirty-five miles an hour with or without giving any signal of its approach, for the

389 

 street car passenger has a right to rely to some extent on the expectation that the driver will not run into him. 

Hepburn v. Walters, 263 Mass. 139, at 141 

But see:

The burden of showing the street car passenger's contributory negligence is on the operator of the motor vehicle.

SECTION 321. 

F. PERSONS COASTING, SLIDING AND SLED- DING. 

See: Section 210, page 239.

When children are coasting on a public highway on which coasting is prohibited, they are guilty of contributory negligence and cannot recover. 

Brown v. Daley, 273 Mass. 432, at 436

Labay v. Leiken, 252 Mass. 579 

But when it is a question of fact whether the plaintiff children were coasting (as evidence from which it could be found that they were not coasting) the jury can take into account the grade of the place, the condition of the driveway or footway, the absence of any marks at the place, except marks from other vehicles, depth of snow, the ashes or other appearances of the place. 

Brown v. Daley, 273 Mass. 432, at 436

So, where the mitten of the child was not found in the

8321 

 street but near the stone wall, near the private driveway or footway, and part of his sled was in this place where blood was seen, the jury can find that the child was not upon the street but on the driveway or footway when struck. 

Brown v. Daley, 273 Mass. 432, at 436

See: 

Ayers v. Ratshesky, 213 Mass. 589 

The plaintiff, a boy of eleven years of age, and other boys were coasting down hill in Worcester in the center of Parker Street toward an intersecting street called Mason Street. The plaintiff reached the latter street and looked to his right when he saw about forty-five or fifty feet away a truck operated by the defendant coming on Mason Street. The plaintiff did not know whether the truck was coming fast or slow. He "slued" to the left and went up on the embankment at the corner of the two streets. The truck turned to the right a little into Parker 

Street to avoid hitting a boy who was sliding on a sled behind the plaintiff, and then turned back into Mason Street, and in doing this the rear wheel of the truck went over the plaintiff when he was on the embankment about three, four or five feet from the corner, having rolled off the sled. The embankment was five feet high. The plaintiff was in Parker Street when picked up and "it happened at once-it was all very quick." Parker Street was described as a narrow street and when the truck reached it the plaintiff was upon the embankment. The truck when one hundred yards from the intersection of the two streets was travelling at the rate of about forty miles an hour; the driver's head was turned toward a man at his side with whom he appeared to be talking as the truck approached Parker Street. After striking the plaintiff, the truck went about thirty feet before stopping. The plaintiff was off the travelled part of the way when struck but the evidence was somewhat conflicting as to whether he was near it or so far from it as four or five feet. As the

391 

 truck approached the intersection, the corner at the driver's left was described as a "blind one."

If the plaintiff received his injury while coasting upon a street from which coasters were excluded by the ordinance, his violation of law would bar recovery for injuries caused by negligence of the defendant. 

Query v. Howe, 273 Mass. 92, at 95 

Boyd v. Ellison, 248 Mass. 250

The reason for this rule is that the violation of that kind of ordinance is as matter of law a proximate contributing cause of the injury suffered. 

Query v. Howe, 273 Mass. 92, at 95 

Even though the plaintiff was not upon his sled when injured and if it be assumed that he had reached a point outside the limits of the street, his illegal act in sliding upon the street was so intimately connected with his injury as a proximate cause that as matter of law he is barred from recovery on the first count based upon negligence. 

Query v. Howe, 273 Mass. 92, at 96

See: 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, at 157 

Wallace v. Merrimack River Nav. & Exp. Co., 134 

Mass. 95

The defendant in approaching the intersection of the streets at a speed of forty miles per hour, apparently talking to a companion, and in turning the truck into Parker Street and back into Mason Street, as described in the evidence, could be found to be negligent, but the evidence would not justify a finding of wilful, wanton and reckless conduct. He had a right to assume that boys would not be coasting on Parker Street where coasting was prohibited. 

Query v. Howe, 273 Mass. 92, at 96 

Labay v. Leiken, 252 Mass. 579, at 581

8321 

The knowledge or state of mind of the defendant with reference to the probability of injury to another is an important matter to be considered in determining whether his conduct toward the plaintiff is wilful, wanton and reckless. 

Query v. Howe, 273 Mass. 92, at 96 

Foley v. Wesson Meml. Hospital, 246 Mass. 363, at 365 

Prondecka v. Turners Falls Pwr. & Elec. Co., 238 

Mass. 239, at 243

To establish such conduct the plaintiff must prove that the wrongdoer inflicted injury intentionally or was so “utterly indifferent to the rights of others that he acts as if such rights did not exist." 

Query v. Howe, 273 Mass. 92, at 96 

Wentzell v. Boston El. Ry., 230 Mass. 275, at 277

Romana v. Boston El. Ry., 218 Mass. 76 

It did not appear on the evidence that the defendant was wantonly reckless in exposing the plaintiff to danger, nor did his conduct partake of the nature of a wilful, intentional wrong. 

Query v. Howe, 273 Mass. 92, at 96

See: 

Freeman v. United Fruit Co., 223 Mass. 300, at 302

Wanton, wilful and reckless conduct would not be inferred from those movements. Upon all the evidence proof of an essential element required in law to make a wanton, wilful and reckless act was absent. 

Query v. Howe, 273 Mass. 92, at 97

When a child is coasting upon a public highway on which coasting is not permitted by the local authorities and he collides with a stationary automobile which is in one of the ice ruts so that he goes under the automobile and strikes his head against one of its springs causing injuries which result in his death, the immediate cause of

§393 

 the accident is the illegal use made of the street by the intestate and such use is not a condition of an otherwise lawful use, but is a contributing cause without which the accident would not have happened. 

Richards v. Pass, 1931 A. S. 2271, at 2274 

Cook v. Crowell, 273 Mass. 356 

Newcomb v. Boston Protective Dept., 146 Mass. 596, at 603 

SECTION 322. 

G. PERSONS BEING ON PRIVATE PROPERTY. 

The question of contributory negligence was held for the jury where there was evidence that plaintiff was a watchman in a freight yard, and that early in the evening, before dark, he walked in a passageway leading from a public way to the rear of his employer's freight house, and noticed an automobile which he thought did not belong there, while still nearer him he saw the defendant's car, one of the occupants satisfactorily explaining to him the ownership of the other car which he had been on his way to investigate. He then turned round from where he was standing in front of the defendant's car and started to walk toward the office when he was struck and knocked senseless.

There was evidence from which the jury could find that the accident happened in front of a certain freight house and that, almost immediately after the plaintiff had been informed of the ownership of the other automobile, the defendant's car began backing and that no other vehicle could have passed around the corner of the freight yard and struck the plaintiff without first coming into collision with defendant's automobile. 

Noonan v. P. M. Leavitt Co., 238 Mass. 481 

67 A. L. R. 662

H. PERSONS UNDER DISABILITY. 

See: Section 211, page 240.

§323 SECTION 323. 

1. Feeble, Blind, Halt, Deaf or Otherwise Impaired in Capacity.

In Keith v. Worcester and Blackstone Valley Street 

Railway Company, 196 Mass. 478, at 482 and 483, it is said: "The standard of care established by the law is what the ordinarily prudent and cautious person would do to protect himself under given conditions. There is no higher or different standard for one who is aged, feeble, blind, halt, deaf or otherwise impaired in capacity, than for one in perfect physical condition. It has frequently in recent as well as earlier cases, been said, in referring to one under some impediment, that greater caution or increased circumspection may be required in view of these adverse conditions. See, for example, Hamilton v. Boston & N. St. Ry. Co., 193 Mass. 324 

Hawes v. Boston El. Ry., 192 Mass. 324 

Vecchioni v. N. Y. C. & H. R. R. R., 191 Mass. 9 

Hilborn v. Boston & N. St. Ry. Co., 191 Mass. 14 

Hall v. West End St. Ry., 168 Mass. 461 

Winn v. Lowell, I Allen, 177 "These expressions mean nothing more than that a person so afflicted must put forth a greater degree of effort than one acting under any disabilities, in order to attain that standard of care which the law has established for everybody. When looked at from one standpoint, it is incorrect to say that a blind person must exercise a higher degree of care than one whose sight is perfect, but in another aspect, a blind person may be obliged to take precautions, practise vigilance and sharpen other senses, unnecessary for one of clear vision, in order to attain that degree of care which the law requires. It may depend in some slight degree upon how the description of duty begins, where the emphasis may fall at a given moment, but when the whole proposition is stated, the rights of the

395 

 parties are as fully protected in the one way as in the other. It is perhaps more logical to say that the plaintiff is bound to use ordinary care, and that in passing upon what ordinary care demands, due consideration should be given to blindness or other infirmities. 

Neff v. Wellesley, 148 Mass. 487 

Smith v. Wildes, 143 Mass. 556 "But it is also correct to say that in the exercise of common prudence one of defective eyesight must usually as matter of general knowledge take more care and employ keener watchfulness in walking upon the streets and avoiding obstructions than the same person with good eyesight, in order to reach the standard established by the law for all persons alike, whether they be weak or strong, sound or deficient."

Plaintiff's want of hearing made it incumbent upon him to be more alert in the use of his other senses. For him to cross in such a place, where he could not fail to know that passing vehicles were constantly to be expected, in such a state of inattention that he knew nothing of the approach of the car until after he was struck, showed a want of ordinary care. 

Hall v. West End St. Ry., 168 Mass. 461, at 462

If plaintiff was a person of poor sight, common prudence required greater care in walking upon the streets, and avoiding obstructions, than is required of persons of good sight. 

Winn v. Lowell, I Allen, 177, at 180

In determining what was ordinary care, the jury should consider his infirmity of vision and other conditions of physical weakness incident to his age, and all the conditions bearing upon the question, as to what care was reasonably necessary to insure his safety. 

O'Connor v. Hickey, 260 Mass. 110, at 115 (72 years of age, using cane, clouded eyesight,

8324 

 pedestrian on street, runaway horse) 

Mercier v. Union St. Ry. Co., 230 Mass. 397

Hanley v. Boston El. Ry., 201 Mass. 55 

Keith v. Worcester etc. St. Ry., 196 Mass. 478, at 482 

Neff v. Wellesley, 148 Mass. 487, at 495 

Where a woman with defective hearing, walking along the right hand side of a highway on a rainy evening, because the sidewalk is muddy, was struck by an automobile coming from behind, the question whether she exercised the care of an ordinarily prudent person is for the jury. 

Booth v. Meagher, 224 Mass. 472 

67 A. L. R. 117 and 118

The taking of two drinks of whiskey does not necessarily, as matter of law, constitute contributory negligence.

Even being under the influence of intoxicating liquor is not sufficient to bar the plaintiff from recovery, for it must also appear that such condition of the plaintiff contributed to his injury caused by the defendant's negligence.

3. Children. 

See: Section 213, page 240.

SECTION 325. 

a. General Statement. 

The law does not require the conduct of a child to measure up to the care demanded of an adult. 

Milbury v. Turner Center System, 274 Mass. 358, at 363 

Sullivan v. Chadwick, 236 Mass. 130

A child is merely bound to use the care, of a prudent boy or girl of his or her age and experience. 

Milbury v. Turner Center System, 274 Mass. 358, at 363 

Jean v. Nester, 261 Mass. 442 

McNeil v. Boston Ice Co., 173 Mass. 570

A child of tender years, though unattended, may recover for negligence if the child exercised the care required of an adult under like circumstances. 

Sullivan v. Chadwick, 236 Mass. 130, at 134 

Miller v. Flash Chemical Co., 230 Mass. 419 

Wiswell v. Doyle, 160 Mass. 42, at 43 

Collins v. South Boston R. R. Co., 142 Mass. 301

$326 

Whether a child was careless at the time of the accident is usually a question of fact to be determined by the jury and usually cannot be ruled as matter of law. 

Brown v. Daley, 273 Mass. 432, at 435

So, whether a child of tender years, on crossing a street where his father is on the opposite side, fails to use the care of one of his age and experience is generally for the jury. 

Milbury v. Turner Center System, 274 Mass. 358, at 363 (Child-five years of age)

The child may be found to have properly exercised due care when he sees his father in a position to warn him, faces to the right and turns his gaze to the left as soon as he can see anything on the street approaching from that direction. It is a matter of fact rather than of law. 

Milbury v. Turner Center System. 274 Mass. 358, at 363 

Patrick v. Deziel, 223 Mass. 505 (Plaintiff rolling hoop in gutter on right hand side of street, struck from rear by defendant's automobile. His due care for jury. Also for jury the question of whether at time of his injury plaintiff was violating a city ordinance prohibiting the playing of games in the street.) 

b. Effect of Negligence of Parent. 

SECTION 326. 

(I) On Recovery by Child. 

The Due Care Statute, General Laws Chapter 231, Sec tion 85, applies to a child if its parent is not present. 

Sullivan v. Chadwick, 236 Mass. 130, at 134 and 135 

Miller v. Flash Chemical Co., 230 Mass. 419 

Wiswell v. Doyle, 160 Mass. 42, at 43 

Collins v. South Boston R. R. Co., 142 Mass. 301

§ 

399 But the Due Care Statute is inapplicable when the parent is present, for the parent's negligence is imputed to the child. 

Gallagher v. Johnson, 237 Mass. 455

SECTION 327. 

(II) On Recovery by Parent. 

But a parent who is contributorily negligent cannot recover for injury to the child.

A parent is not contributorily negligent in allowing a child 6 years and 5 months old to go upon the sidewalk near her home at a place in view from the dining room. window with instructions to her 8-year-old sister to look out for the younger child. 

Linnane v. Millman, 261 Mass. 491, at 494

It is not careless, as matter of law, for a mother to leave her girl (4 years and 3 months old) and boy (7 years old) at play in the yard of her home while she attends to her household duties, especially if she instructs them not to leave the yard and the highway in front of the house is not much travelled and she sees them in the yard five or six times before the accident.

Coldiron v. Worcester, 253 Mass. 462

Child Leaving Custodian. 

When a boy of six and one-half years of age walking with his sister eight and one-half years old on a public way, comes to a driveway leading across sidewalk to defendant's place of business, with sister on outside of sidewalk and boy on her right hand side, and defendant's truck, travelling from opposite direction, turns into the driveway in such a manner that the sister is compelled to let go of the boy's hand and step back to save herself or both would have been killed, and the boy does not see the truck, the boy is not negligent in view of his tender years and the fact of truck approaching from his side and his sister, holding his hand, is, in a sense, between him and the truck.

$330 

 I. PERSONS IN OR ON VEHICLE. 

See: Sections 218-224, pages 244-255.

SECTION 330. 

A person in or on a motor vehicle is required to exercise due and reasonable care for his own protection and safety. 

Learned v. Hawthorne, 269 Mass. 554, at 560 and 561 

Lambert v. Eastern Mass. St. Ry., 240 Mass. 449

The mere relationship of operator and passenger does not make the operator the agent of the passenger, nor is the negligence of the operator imputed to the passenger. 

An operator of a motor vehicle is not necessarily the agent of the occupant unless such relationship in fact. exists. 

Acts 1928, Chapter 317, Section 1, which states that: 

"Evidence that a motor vehicle was registered in the name of defendant as owner shall be prima facie evidence that it was then being operated by and under the control of the person for whose conduct the defendant was legally responsible," has no application to an action against the owner or operator of another vehicle in which the owner of the first vehicle is the plaintiff. The statute, in terms, applies only to a defendant, and it has no relation to a plaintiff whose motor vehicle is involved in a collision. 

Thompson v. Sides, 275 Mass. 568, at 571

So, a plaintiff who was riding in her own automobile driven by her husband, is not necessarily responsible for the conduct of her husband, and, if she is exercising proper care for her own safety, may recover against a third person who negligently collides with the plaintiff's automobile. 

Thompson v. Sides, 275 Mass. 568, at 571

$407 

While the negligence of the operator of a motor vehicle is not chargeable to a passenger (See: Section 266, page 

313) yet the passenger is bound to exercise such care for his own safety as the exigencies of the situation require. 

Griffin v. Hustis, 234 Mass. 95 Bailey v. Worcester, 228 Mass. 477 Lynch v. Boston El. Ry., 224 Mass. 93 

(A fire department captain, riding on an automobile ladder truck was bound to exercise due care for his own safety) 

Fogg v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R., 223 Mass. 444

As a general rule, attempting to "get on or off a motor vehicle while it is in motion" is not due care. 

England v. Boston & Maine R. R., 153 Mass. 490 Duncan v. Bancroft, 110 Mass. 267 

Gavett v. Manchester etc. R. R. Co., 16 Gray, 501

Lucas v. New Bedford & T. R. R. Co., 6 Gray, 64 

But there "may be circumstances which will relieve the passenger making such an attempt from the imputation of negligence." 

Merritt v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R. Co., 162 Mass. 326, at 329 

Gallagher v. West End Ry., 156 Mass. 157 

See: 

Burnham v. Boston & Maine R. R., 227 Mass. 422

SECTION 331. 

2. Reliance on Operator's Care. 

A passenger is under no duty to anticipate that the operator will be negligent.

Negligence on the part of a passenger which does not contribute to his injury will not bar his recovery.

While the passenger in a motor vehicle approaching a street car line is required to exercise reasonable care, he may trust somewhat to the expectation that the operator

8332 

 of the motor vehicle will act with due regard for his own safety, as well as the safety of the passenger. 

Salisbury v. Boston El. Ry., 239 Mass. 430

One unacquainted with the operation or management of a motor vehicle who is riding with one whom he knows to be an experienced operator, there being no mutuality in a common enterprise between them, cannot be charged with the negligence of such operator. 

Chadbourne v. Springfield St. Ry. Co., 199 Mass. 574

However, if the passenger relies entirely upon the care of the operator, then he in fact makes the operator his agent and the acts of the operator are imputed to the passenger and the passenger's right to recovery is based upon the operator being free from negligence.

The fact that a passenger asks the operator for the time is not as matter of law negligence on the part of the passenger. Particularly is this so when the passenger does not know at the time he makes the inquiry that the operator is wearing a wrist watch and by making the inquiry the passenger has no reason to expect that the operator will abandon all care in the operation of the motor vehicle. 

Kirby v. Keating, 271 Mass. 390, at 393

SECTION 332. 

3. Duty to Observe and Warn of Danger. 

It is no less the duty of the passenger, where he has the opportunity to do so, than of the operator to learn of danger and to avoid it if practicable. 

Salisbury v. Boston El. Ry., 239 Mass. 430

A guest who is sitting in the middle of a seat looking straight ahead of her and watching the way and makes no protest as to speed or manner of operation of the automobile is not necessarily negligent as matter of law. 

Gallup v. Lazott, 271 Mass. 406, at 408

409 

 Haun v. LeGrand, 268 Mass. 582 

Connors v. Cunard S. S. Co., 204 Mass. 310, at 317

It does not show as a matter of law that the guest voluntarily surrendered all care of herself to the caution of the driver so that his negligence may be imputed to her. 

Gallup v. Lazott, 271 Mass. 406, at 409

SECTION 333. 

Occupant Not Required to Take Same Precautions as Operator.

A guest or invitee is not charged with the same strict legal duty of keeping a lookout and being watchful as is the operator.

A person of ordinary prudence riding with another upon his invitation naturally will put a certain trust in his judgment and will rely in some measure on the assumption that he will use care to avoid the ordinary dangers of the road.

This rule is particularly applicable to women guests. 

Pigeon v. Mass. Northeastern St. Ry. Co., 230 Mass. 392 

A passenger or guest should not place his safety entirely in the keeping of the driver, but must exercise due and reasonable care for his own protection and safety. 

Lambert v. Eastern Mass. St. Ry. Co., 240 Mass. 495

SECTION 334. 

b. At Railroad Crossings. 

See: Section 228, page 258. 

Section 287, page 355.

An operator and a passenger were proceeding in a coupe on a wide cement highway upon which they had travelled occasionally, at about four o'clock on a dark and clear morning at a rate of speed of about twenty-five to twenty-eight miles an hour, the highway intersecting at right angles with a single track railroad of the defendant. 

About ten feet away, the operator first saw a freight train

$334 

 crossing the highway without any lights or other signal to indicate its presence there, and collided with the train, not being able to stop his automobile in this distance. 

The passenger, who was looking ahead, did not see the freight train or car, there being no traffic on the highway at the time, although both operator and passenger saw some sparks shooting up in the air to their right some distance before reaching the crossing. It did not occur to them, however, that the sparks came from a locomotive, nor did they see the railroad crossing signs or that the freight train was on the crossing. A moment or two after the collision the train began to move, although the movement had nothing to do with the accident and the headlights of the automobile were in perfect condition so as to cast light 150 feet ahead. The operator and passenger were not in the exercise of due care and as a matter of law the defendant railroad sustained the burden of proving contributory negligence on their part, even though they ran into the freight train on a highway at a grade crossing. 

Mailhot v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R. Co., 273 Mass. 277, at 279 The fact that the freight cars were of the same color and the operator and passenger did not see them is no excuse for their conduct. The immutable fact of the collision and the testimony of the operator and passenger permits only one rational inference and that is that the negligence of the plaintiffs contributed directly to their injury and damage. 

Mailhot v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R. Co., 273 Mass. 277, at 279

SECTION 335. 

Failure to Direct or Warn Operator.

If the passenger sees or hears anything indicating danger that the operator cannot, or probably does not, see or hear, it is the passenger's duty to tell the operator. 

But it is not incumbent upon the passenger to tell the operator of every approaching street car or other vehicle, or of every defect in the highway which is as manifest to the operator as to the passenger. 

Lambert v. Eastern Mass. St. Ry. Co., 240 Mass. 495 In the last cited case, it was said at pages 499 and 500: "If the jury found that in the exercise of common prudence she [the plaintiff] ought to have given warning to her husband of carelessness on his part, which she observed, or ought to have observed in the exercise of due care for her own safety, and that she ought to have warned him that he was driving at too great a rate of speed in view of the condition of the surface of the street or that in the exercise of reasonable care she should have seen the approaching car and directed his attention to it and that she failed to do so, she would not be entitled to recover. "Nor could she recover if she negligently abandoned the exercise of her own faculties and trusted them entirely to the care and caution of her husband and his negli-
