SECTION 337. 

4. Duty to Protest Conduct of Operator. 

A guest who is sitting in the middle of a seat looking straight in front of her and watching the way and makes no protest as to the speed or manner of operation of the automobile is not necessarily negligent as matter of law. 

Gallup v. Lazott, 271 Mass. 406, at 409 

Haun v. LeGrand, 268 Mass. 582 

Connors v. Cunard S. S. Co., 204 Mass. 310, at 317

Nor does her failure to protest amount necessarily to negligence, Gallup v. Lazott, 271 Mass. 406, at 409 especially where, apart from speed, nothing is shown as to the manner in which the automobile was being driven prior to the accident which called for any protest from the passenger. 

Gallup v. Lazott, 271 Mass. 406, at 409 

But see: 

Thorp v. Boston El. Ry., 259 Mass. 415 

The guest is not usually required to give warning or make protest when occurrences at the time of the accident

413

Gallup v. Lazott, 271 Mass. 406, at 409 

Harter v. Boston El. Ry., 259 Mass. 433, at 436

Whether, in order to exercise due care, a passenger is bound to protest against the speed of the automobile before the accident, is a question of fact for the jury. 

Gallup v. Lazott, 271 Mass. 406, at 410 

Lambert v. Eastern Mass. St. Ry. Co., 240 Mass. 495, at 499 Even if there is evidence of negligence on the part of the operator by reason of excessive speed, it is not conclusive that the failure of a passenger to protest, even if amounting to tacit acquiescence, is negligence.

5. Riding in Dangerous or Improper Place or Posi tion.

Plaintiff, while sitting on the floor at the rear end of the wagon, looked over track on which car was approaching, where his view was unobstructed for a long distance, and in passing from the wagon he again looked, but failed in each instance to observe the street car which the jury could find was plainly visible. a. Passenger in Towed Vehicle. 

A guest, riding in a motor vehicle which is being towed,

 who is injured through the defendant's negligence which is twofold: first, in the manner in which the cars are hitched together, and second, in the manner in which the towing car is managed in the way of excessive speed or otherwise, is not barred from recovery if he does not appreciate the danger attached to the manner in which the vehicles are hitched and if he has no means of controlling the speed of the towing car. Any negligence of the driver of the towing vehicle is not imputed to such guest.

SECTION 339. 

6. Duty to Alight or to Leave Vehicle. 

It is usually a question of fact whether a passenger in a motor vehicle is guilty of contributory negligence in failing to change his position in the motor vehicle, or warn the operator of an impending accident, or do anything to avoid it, when he sees the probability of such accident. 

Maidman v. Rose, 253 Mass. 594 

47 A. L. R. 298

So, a passenger in a motor vehicle standing at the curb near a street intersection who is injured by another vehicle which collides with still another vehicle, a truck, at the street intersection, and then collides with the vehicle in which the passenger is sitting, may be guilty of contributory negligence in failing to: a. change his position in the motor vehicle, or b. warn the chauffeur of the impending accident, or c. do anything to avoid it, though he saw the truck and other vehicle which caused the accident when both were forty or fifty feet from the intersection of the street, approaching in such manner that the collision between them was certain. 

Maidman v. Rose, 253 Mass. 594 

47 A. L. R. 298 

Laffey v. Mullen, 275 Mass. 277, at 279

c. Intoxicated.

Where an operator of a motor vehicle is drunk immediately after the accident, a guest who did not reasonably know of the operator's condition before the accident is not necessarily guilty of contributory negligence. 

O'Connell v. McKeown, 270 Mass. 432

So, when the operator is, to a degree, under the influence of liquor and that fact is perceivable when the jaunt begins, or if not then apparent becomes so thereafter, it cannot be ruled as matter of law that the guest is negligent in accepting the invitation to ride with the driver or continuing to ride with him after he knows of his intoxicated condition,

$343 

O'Connell v. McKeown, 270 Mass. 432, at 435 

If the guest knows after the ride begins that the driver is under the influence of intoxicating liquor it is incumbent on the defendant to prove that the plaintiff guest could have left the automobile without peril to his life or limb, and failing so to prove, the defendant is not permitted to shift the consequences of his own folly to the shoulders of the plaintiff. 

O'Connell v. McKeown, 270 Mass. 432, at 435 and 436

O'Connell v. McKeown, 270 Mass. 432, at 436 

Particularly when the plaintiff guest sees no signs of liquor on the driver and in so far as he can tell from the driver's actions he is perfectly sober and when the ride begins the driver shows no signs of anything wrong, the guest is not guilty of negligence in intrusting his safety to the driver at the time they started out on their trip. 

O'Connell v. McKeown, 270 Mass. 432, at 433 and 434

SECTION 343. 

8. Assumption of Risk. 

Where a girl, who had never ridden upon a motorcycle before, continued to ride after the operator of the motor-

417 

 cycle, against the girl's complaint, drove at an unreasonable speed and failed to heed her, although she pounded his back and asked him to go very slowly; and then she was told that the headlights were poor and brakes defective; and was forced by the cold air to keep her head down behind the driver's back so that she could not see the road ahead; and although she had several opportunities to alight and refuse to go farther, which she did not take advantage of and never refused to go on; she assumed the risks of the driver's gross negligence, knowing the speed, the reckless driving, the questionable headlight and doubtful brakes; and she confided her care solely to the operator and did not do what she might have done to secure her safety; it is full acceptance of appreciated risks. 

Laffey v. Mullen, 275 Mass. 277, at 278 

Oppenheim v. Barkin, 262 Mass. 281

J. IMPUTED NEGLIGENCE. 

SECTION 344. 

One who sustains an injury without any fault or negligence of his own, or of some one subject to his control or direction, or with whom he is so identified in a common enterprise as to become responsible for the consequences of his negligent conduct, may look for compensation to any other person whose neglect of duty occasioned the injury, even though the negligence of some third person, with whom the injured person was not identified as above, may have contributed thereto. 

Before the concurrent negligence of a third person can

$344 

 be interposed to shield another whose neglect of duty has occasioned an injury to one who was without fault, it must appear that the person injured and the one whose negligence contributed to the injury sustained such a relation to each other, in respect to the matter then in progress, as that in contemplation of law the negligent act of the third person was, upon the principles of agency, or cooperation in a common or joint enterprise, the act of the person injured. Until such agency or identity of interest or purpose appears, there is no sound principle upon which it can be held that one who is himself blameless, and yet is injured by the concurrent wrong of two persons, shall not have his remedy against one who neglected a positive duty which the law enjoined upon him.. 

Shultz v. Old Colony St. Ry. Co., 193 Mass. 309, at 

316 and 317 and cases collected (Wife riding with husband, struck by street car, husband's negligence not imputable to wife)

Negligence in the conduct of another will not be imputed to a party if he neither authorized such conduct nor participated therein, nor had the right or power to control it. If, however, two or more persons unite in the joint prosecution of a common purpose, the negligence of one in the management thereof, will be imputed to all the others. 

Schultz v. Old Colony St. Ry. Co., 193 Mass. 309, at 

318 and cases cited 

That one cannot recover damages for an injury to the commission of which he has directly contributed is a rule of established law and a principle of common justice. 

And it matters not whether that contribution consists of his participation in the direct cause of the injury, or his omission of duties which, if performed, would have prevented it.

If his fault, whether of omission or commission, has

$419 

 been the proximate cause of the injury, he is without remedy against one also in the wrong. It would seem that the converse of this doctrine would be accepted as sound; that is, when one has been injured by the wrongful act of another, to which he has in no way contributed, he should be entitled to damages from the wrongdoer. 

And such is the generally accepted doctrine, unless a contributory cause of the injury has been the negligence or fault of some person towards whom he sustains the relation of superior or master, in which case the negligence is imputed to him though he may not personally have participated in nor had knowledge of it, and he must bear the consequences. The doctrine may also be subject to other exceptions growing out of the relation of parent and child, or guardian and ward, and the like. 

Shultz v. Old Colony St. Ry. Co., 193 Mass. 309, at 

320 and cases collected

The courts have refused to impute the negligence of the driver to a gratuitous passenger in a private conveyance. 

Shultz v. Old Colony St. Ry. Co., 193 Mass. 309, at 

320 and cases collected

Where an adult person, possessing all his faculties and personally in the exercise of that degree of care which common prudence requires under all the attending circumstances, is injured through the negligence of some third person and the concurring negligence of one with whom the plaintiff is riding as guest or companion, between whom and the plaintiff the relation of master and servant, or principal and agent, or mutual responsibility in a common enterprise, does not in fact exist, the plaintiff being at the time in no position to exercise authority or control over the driver, then the negligence of the driver is not imputable to the injured person, but the latter is entitled to recover against the one through whose wrong his injuries were sustained.

$344 

Disregarding the passenger's own due care, the test whether the negligence of the driver is to be imputed to the one riding, depends upon the latter's control or right of control of the actions of the driver, so as to constitute in fact the relation of principal and agent or master and servant, or his voluntary, unconstrained, non-contractual surrender of all care for himself to the caution of the driver. 

Shultz v. Old Colony St. Ry. Co., 193 Mass. 309, at 322 and 323 It cannot be ruled as matter of law that the plaintiff and defendant were engaged in a common enterprise so that the negligence of the latter can be imputed to the plaintiff.

It could be found that transportation was an implied part of the plaintiff's contract when the patient was at some distance and that the plaintiff was obliged under the contract to accept transportation in the defendant's automobile when it was offered. 

Loftus v. Pelletier, 223 Mass. 63 (Plaintiff nurse in defendant's automobile which while making a sharp turn to take hill at speed of 30 miles an hour skidded, ran on two wheels some distance and turned over, plaintiff being thrown out. While skidding is not evidence of negligence, it was for the jury to say whether it was due to defendant's negligence in driving around a sharp curve at such a speed) 

Four actions of tort, three by two guests and a daughter of G. C. and the fourth by administrator of estate of latter for personal injuries of some of the plaintiffs and for the death of plaintiff's intestate by reason of collision of intestate's automobile with car of defendant. 

No negligence being imputable to these plaintiffs, the presumption of the statute (G. L. c. 231, s. 85) becomes applicable, but this presumption does not extend to pre-

$421 

 sumption of due care of, or control over, agents or chauffeurs. 

Bullard v. Boston El. Ry., 226 Mass. 262

Mercer, 206 Mass. 492, at 499 (Guest riding in motor vehicle which is being towed, injured through defendant's negligence, such negligence of the driver of the towing vehicle not imputed to guest) While a driver's negligence is not imputed to a passenger if the former is not under the direction and control of the latter, the passenger may be found guilty of negligence if her failure to exercise reasonable care for her safety is a contributing cause of her injury, and the same is true if the passenger fails to exercise any care at all by surrendering all care for her safety to the caution of the driver if her failure in this respect is a contributing cause of her injury. But if what took place at the time of an accident discloses that there was nothing that the passenger did or failed to do that contributed to her in-

$347 

 jury, her right of recovery is not defeated, since the negligence of the driver, over whom she had no direction and control, cannot be imputed to her. This was the situation in this case and the jury so found. 

Marcus v. Forcier, 38 Fed. (2d) 8

SECTION 347. 

4. Passengers in Common Enterprise or Joint Ad venture with Operator.

To constitute a common or joint enterprise between two or more persons and thereby make the doctrine of joint enterprise applicable as a branch of imputed contributory negligence, it must appear that such persons have an equal right to direct and control the conduct of the others concerning the acts or omissions which contributed to cause the injury. In such circumstances the negligence of each of such persons is imputed to each of the others. 

Caron v. Lynn Sand & Stone Co., 270 Mass. 340, at 346 In a joint enterprise each is responsible for the conduct of all the participants and the conduct of each participant is imputed to every other participant. 

Donoghue v. Holyoke St. Ry. Co., 246 Mass. 485, at 491 (Fireman on fire apparatus injured in collision with street car) 

If two or more persons participate in a common or joint undertaking and one is injured by the negligence of a third person, the contributing negligence of a joint participant in the enterprise is imputed to the injured person. 

Donoghue v. Holyoke St. Ry. Co., 246 Mass. 485, at 491 

To constitute participation, plaintiff must have:

An equal right with the driver in respect of the control of the motor vehicle;

$429 

Power to control the means; or 

An equal right to direct the conduct of the undertaking. 

Barry v. Harding, 244 Mass. 588, at 592 and 593: "We do not think the acceptance of an invitation to ride in the circumstances disclosed by the evidence constitutes an engagement in a joint enterprise, even if the person accepting has reason to know that the person inviting is acting in so doing without the scope of his authority; because there is lacking with the facts the essential elements which constitute in the law of negligence a joint enterprise; that is, the evidence does not warrant a finding that the plaintiff had an equal right with the driver in respect of the control of the automobile; that it does not warrant a finding that he had power to control the means, or an equal right to direct the conduct of the undertaking; nor does it show a community of interest in the object and purpose to be subserved by the giving and acceptance of the invitation to carry the plaintiff to the place where he might take control of the street car." 

The common purpose of riding together for pleasure does not alone establish a joint enterprise. 

Caron v. Lynn Sand & Stone Co., 270 Mass. 340, at 347 Whether negligence of Smith, if any, should be imputed to him, was therefore properly submitted to the jury. 

Caron v. Lynn Sand & Stone Co., 270 Mass. 340, at 347 

Farr v. Whitney, 260 Mass. 193 

Harter v. Boston El. Ry., 259 Mass. 433 

Donoghue v. Holyoke St. Ry. Co., 246 Mass. 485 

Bullard v. Boston El. Ry., 226 Mass. 262 

Shultz v. Old Colony St. Ry. Co., 193 Mass. 309

The relation of principal and agent must exist in fact in order to bar a recovery, for

$347 

"the law will not create or presume the relation from the mere fact that he accepted the invitation of another to ride in his carriage. If he is but the guest of another, and neither has nor assumes the right to direct or control the conduct of the driver, neither he nor the owner can be regarded as his servant." 

Shultz v. Old Colony St. Ry. Co., 193 Mass. 309, at 317 A mere guest riding in an automobile, without any authority or control over the driver and having no voice in directing and governing the operation of the car, cannot be said to be engaged in a joint enterprise with the driver so that the negligence of the driver will be imputed to the guest, and so bar recovery for injuries sustained by him as against the negligent driver of another whose negligence concurred with that of the driver to produce the injury.

Labatte v. Lavallee, 258 Mass. 527 

Under General Laws, Chapter 260, Section 232, making a railroad company liable to any one injured or killed at a grade crossing by collision with the engines or cars of the railroad company if the railroad company neglected to give signals required by law, unless in addition to mere ordinary care the person injured or the person who had charge of his person or property was, at the time of the collision, guilty of gross or wilful negligence or was acting in violation of the law and such gross or wilful negligence or unlawful act contributed to the injury, it is held even if the driver is not the servant of the occupants of the motor vehicle, he is their associate in driving the car for them and for himself through their assent in the execution of the common purpose of all to be transported to a certain place.

Under these circumstances the occupants of the motor vehicle place the responsibility of safely driving the vehicle

$431 

 upon one of themselves, and in the management of the vehicle he necessarily has charge of it and its occupants within the meaning of said General Laws, Chapter 260, Section 232. 

Lewis v. Boston & Maine R. R., 263 Mass. 87, at 91 and 92 

Chase v. N. Y. C. & H. R. R. R., 208 Mass. 137, at 146 and 147 So long as a joint enterprise is in force, the contributory negligence of one participant would bar the recovery of either from the third person, provided always the negligence is a matter within the scope of the joint agreement. 

Beaucage v. Mercer, 206 Mass. 492, at 498

But although a person may start out on a joint venture in a motor vehicle with the agreement that the expenses should be shared equally, such joint enterprise may be stopped or ended when the motor vehicle becomes disabled so that the owner in telephoning for assistance may be acting in his sole capacity as owner of the vehicle. 

Beaucage v. Mercer, 206 Mass. 492, at 498 

Where two persons suffer personal injuries while they are engaged in a joint enterprise, if the negligence of one of them contributed to the accident which caused their injuries, such negligence is a bar to an action brought by the other against a third person for such injuries, provided such contributory negligence was in a matter within the scope of the joint enterprise. 

Beaucage v. Mercer, 206 Mass. 492

A plaintiff who engages in a joint enterprise with the other occupants of a motor vehicle is responsible for the conduct of all the participants. 

Pendleton v. Boston El. Ry., 266 Mass. 214 

Donoghue v. Holyoke St. Ry. Co., 246 Mass. 485, Stemler v. Cady, 246 Mass. 384 at 491

$347

Skerry v. Rich, 228 Mass. 462 

Beaucage v. Mercer, 206 Mass. 492

The essential elements which constitute, in the law of negligence, a joint enterprise, or an engagement in a joint enterprise, are: 

An equal right with the operator to control the means of operation; or

An equal right to control the conduct of the operation of the motor vehicle. 

Thompson v. Sides, 275 Mass. 568, at 570 

Caron v. Lynn Sand & Stone Co., 270 Mass. 340 

Dumas v. Ward, 251 Mass. 497 

Donoghue v. Holyoke St. Ry. Co., 246 Mass. 485 

Adams v. Swift, 172 Mass. 521

The mere fact that the driver and passenger are related as husband and wife does not by itself warrant the conclusion that they are engaged in a joint enterprise or that the husband's lack of care is imputed to the wife. 

Thompson v. Sides, 275 Mass. 568, at 570

When all that appears is that the husband and wife are on a trip to a certain place to spend the week end with the wife's sister, that is not enough to establish a joint undertaking. The fact that they are riding together for pleasure is not enough to establish a joint enterprise. 

Thompson v. Sides, 275 Mass. 568, at 570

To constitute a joint enterprise the occupant must have an equal right with the driver with respect to the control of the motor vehicle, that is, the power to control the means or an equal right to control the conduct of the undertaking. 

Thompson v. Sides, 275 Mass. 568, at 570 

Barry v. Harding, 244 Mass. 588, at 592 and 593 Where plaintiff was injured by collision with automobile in which defendant, his brother and his nephew were driv-

$433 

 ing, and of which his brother was owner, there being evidence that the brother told his nephew, the driver, who was unlicensed and inexperienced, just before the accident to keep to the right and to look out for the plaintiff, it was held that the jury could find these directions were intended to control or influence the conduct of the driver in properly operating the car. It could also be found on the evidence that the defendant and his relatives were engaged on an excursion for their mutual enjoyment and that in common with his brother he participated in the active management of the car. 

Hutchings v. Vacca, 224 Mass. 269

If when the plaintiff is riding with the operator they are engaged in any business or occupation in which they are jointly interested, the negligence of the operator becomes imputed to the plaintiff. 

Caron v. Lynn Sand & Stone Co., 270 Mass. 340, at 347 When there is no negligence on the part of the operator, the issue whether the plaintiff and the operator were engaged in a joint enterprise is immaterial. 

Caron v. Lynn Sand & Stone Co., 270 Mass. 340, at 347 When the injury has resulted from the negligent act of another the plaintiff may recover if such negligence was the efficient cause. In other phraseology, where the defendant is the doer of a wrong which causes injury to a plaintiff who is free from any contributory negligence, the circumstances that the negligence of a third party also contributed to the injury does not ordinarily bar recovery. 

The injured plaintiff ought not to go remediless against one by whose wrongful act he was harmed. 

Shultz v. Old Colony St. Ry. Co., 193 Mass. 309, at 316 The negligence of the driver of a motor vehicle cannot

$347 

 be imputed to a passenger therein, when the passenger is free from personal negligence, has no control over the driver and has not been guilty of want of due care in selection of the driver. 

Shultz v. Old Colony St. Ry. Co., 193 Mass. 309, at 315 

Murray v. Boston Ice Co., 180 Mass. 165

As to occupants of private conveyances, in case of a person injured by the negligence of one with whom the injured person is riding as guest or companion, such negligence is not imputable to the injured person, although the exception to this rule was recognized, that when the injured person was in a position to exercise authority or control over the driver, or was guilty of negligence, or failed to exercise such care under the circumstances as he could, and should, exercise under the particular circumstances to protect himself, there could be no recovery. 

Shultz v. Old Colony St. Ry. Co., 193 Mass. 309, at 316 There is no enterprise where the plaintiff, a nurse, was hired and paid by a women's club to attend patients (who could not afford a nurse) when called upon to do so by the doctor in charge of such patient, and where it was a common thing for different doctors to take her to their cases when they were making calls, the right to be transported to the patient being an implied term of the plaintiff's contract of employment. Under that contract the plaintiff was bound to accept the doctor's automobile as a method of transportation when it was offered to her. At the time of the accident the plaintiff nurse was being carried under her contract of employment, that is, she was being carried by the defendant doctor for hire. 

Loftus v. Pelletier, 223 Mass. 63, at 66 

Skerry v. Rich, 228 Mass. 462

In Donoghue v. Holyoke Street Railway Company, 246 

Mass. 485, at 491:

$435 

"The plaintiff and the other occupants of the truck were not engaged in a joint enterprise so that each was responsible for the conduct of all the participants. The elements necessary to establish a joint undertaking are lacking. There was uncontradicted evidence that the lieutenant was 'in charge of this piece of apparatus, and the men upon it. The principle that, if two or more persons participate in a common or joint undertaking and one is injured by the negligence of a third person, the contributing negligence of a joint participant in the enterprise is to be imputed to the injured person, has no application in the case at bar. As was said in Barry v. Harding, 244 

Mass. 588, 592, 593, 'the evidence does not warrant a finding that the plaintiff had an equal right with the driver in respect of the control of the automobile . . . it does not warrant a finding that he had power to control the means, or an equal right to direct the conduct of the undertaking." 

There is no common enterprise just because a passenger holds on to a rope by which a horse in the rear of the vehicle is being led. 

Davis v. Boston & Northern St. Ry., 214 Mass. 98 

So, where a guest neither owns nor exercises any control over a motor vehicle, but renders gratuitous assistance in holding on to a rope attached to a horse in the rear of a motor vehicle, but is not in any sense a participant in the performance of any contract to deliver the horse to anyone, for which purpose the operator had undertaken the journey and had asked the guest to accompany him, even if the operator is careless, the guest could be found not to have been at fault, and this is sufficient to enable the guest to recover upon proof of the defendant's negligence. 

Davis v. Boston & Northern St. Ry., 214 Mass. 98, at 99 and 100 (Horse and buggy struck at rear by street car) 

Shultz v. Old Colony St. Ry. Co., 193 Mass. 309

$348 

In Jackson v. Queen, 257 Mass. 515, at 517, it states that while it could be found that the sale having included delivery the plaintiff was on the truck for defendant's benefit and at his request, it could not be ruled as matter of law that plaintiff was a guest or that his transportation was gratuitous.

The journey was not an enterprise in which the parties had equal rights. The plaintiff had no control over the driver to select the route to be taken or to instruct him in the management of the truck. 

G. L. c. 106, s. 31 (1)

When one party takes turns with another party in driving a car, the negligence of each will not be attributed to the other under the rule that they are engaged in a common enterprise. 

Isaacson v. Boston, etc. St. Ry., 1932 A. S. 385, at 396 

Caron v. Lynn Sand and Stone Co., 270 Mass. 340, at 346 The fact that the two occupants take turns in driving a car does not necessarily make the operation of it a joint enterprise. 

Isaacson v. Boston, etc. St. Ry., 1932 A. S. 385, at 396 

SECTION 348. 

5. Husband and Wife.

Even though an automobile collision is caused by the concurrent negligence of the defendant and the husband of the plaintiff, with whom the plaintiff is riding, the husband's negligence is not imputed to the wife if the plaintiff is in the exercise of due care and does not intrust herself in the care, management and operation of the motor vehicle to her husband at the time of the accident and immediately prior thereto, and is in no wise responsible for the husband's lack of due care.

$437 

McDonald v. Levenson, 238 Mass. 479, at 480 (Where wife looking out for own safety when faced with emergency took every precaution which the circumstances permitted) 

Hanley v. Boston El. Ry., 201 Mass. 55, at 58 

Shultz v. Old Colony St. Ry. Co., 193 Mass. 309 

But see: 

Fogg v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R. Co., 223 Mass. 444 (Where the intestate wife either intrusted herself to the care of her husband who was driving the automobile, or did nothing for her own safety, where the accident was due to his carelessness)

Where a passenger is inexperienced in regard to automobiles and the driver, whose guest she is, is skilful and experienced in that regard, she may be found to be in the exercise of due care even if she remains quiet at the time of the danger. 

Chadbourne v. Springfield St. Ry. Co., 199 Mass. 574 In the above cited case, at pages 576 and 577, the court said of such a passenger: "She seems to have conducted herself as an invited guest of the driver of the automobile or other vehicle naturally would do. She trusted him as to the running of the machine; that is, she did not attempt to interfere with his management of the automobile. In view of her inexperience and of what might have been found to be the skill and experience of the driver, the jury might well have thought that this was a wise course on her part. 

Nor was there any relation of agency between her and the driver such as of itself would affect her with negligence on his part. She had no right to control him. There was no mutuality in a common enterprise between them. 

It cannot be said as matter of law that she ought to have warned the driver against turning out from behind the car which he had been following, especially in view of וון

$349 

 the fact that he was turning both in the direction required by statute (G. L. c. 89, s. 2) and in the only direction in which the width of the bridge afforded room for him to pass that car. And she had a right to rely somewhat on the acquaintance with the road which she might presume that he had."

SECTION 349. 

6. Parent and Child. 

See: Sections 238-242, pages 291-296.

Sections 325-329, pages 397-405. 

A child may be a guest of its father so that the negligence of the father will not be imputed to the child. 

Stemler v. Cady, 246 Mass. 384

Peabody v. Haverhill etc. Ry., 200 Mass. 277 

But children of tender years may be so young as to create the father a custodian of the children in which event the father's negligence is imputed to the child. 

Anthony v. Boston & Maine R. R., 1931 A. S. 1697, at 1700 

SECTION 350. 

7. Custodian of Child. 

See Sections 213-217, pages 240-243.

In the case of the death of a child (four years and eight months of age) the evidence may warrant a finding that he was too young to be capable of taking care of himself but that his custodian at all times was in the exercise of due care for her own and for the child's safety. 

Clark v. Martin, 261 Mass. 60, at 62 (Killed while crossing the street at a crosswalk)

Piantedosi v. Bassett, 1932 A. S. 1001 

(Negligence of custodian imputed to child)

439 

There is no abstract principle of law whereby an innocent person in the full possession and exercise of his faculties, and himself using due care, should be prohibited from recovery against a wrongdoer whose tortious act contributes as a proximate cause to his injury. 

It is familiar law that an injured person may recover against one or both of two wrongdoers between whom there is no concert of action, whose concurring act produces the injury even though the act of either alone might not have caused any harm, when "no distinction can be drawn between their acts." 

Shultz v. Old Colony St. Ry. Co., 193 Mass. 309, at 321 

Oulighan v. Butler, 189 Mass. 287, at 293 

Corey v. Havener, 182 Mass. 250

SECTION 351. 

8. Principal and Agent-Master and Servant. 

See: Section 245, page 299.

The negligence of an agent, while engaged in the principal's business, is imputed to the latter, and likewise the negligence of the servant acting within the scope of his employment is imputed to the master. 

But it does not follow that the negligence of the principal is imputed to the agent nor that the negligence of the master is imputed to the servant unless at the time of the accident the respective persons concerned were engaged in a common or joint enterprise so that it could be said that the principal or master was the representative of the agent or servant.

SECTION 352. 

K. MOTORCYCLISTS. 

A motorcyclist who runs into the rear of a wagon that is being driven on a country road without a light, as required by General Laws, Chapter 85, Section 15, is not lacking in due care or guilty of contributory negligence

8353 

 as matter of law but such question is one of fact to be determined by the jury. 

Hallett v. Crowell, 232 Mass. 344. 

Bogert v. Thompson, 260 Mass. 206 (Excessive speed and failure to go to right of intersection-for jury) 

Where motorcyclist, approaching intersection of two streets forty feet wide at fifteen miles an hour, when about fifty feet away reduced speed to eight miles an hour, and saw a taxi approaching from his right at thirty-five miles an hour, did not stop nor look again, nor speed up to avoid collision, as taxi was two hundred feet away, figuring that taxi would slow down and there was evidence taxi proceeded twenty-five feet before stopping, the motorcyclist could be found to be in the exercise of due care. 

Payson v. Checker Taxi Co., 262 Mass. 22, at 24

SECTION 354. 

M. PERSONS IN CHARGE OF ANIMALS. 

See: Sections 202-203, pages 235-236. 

The plaintiff's intestate, a teamster, while leading his horses from a yard to the public way, had his horses by the head and walked backward. Just as he got in the gutter, the defendant's truck came along hugging the gutter and struck and killed him. Held that the evidence sustained the burden under the death statute of showing the plaintiff's intestate was "actively and actually" in the exercise of due care. "It does not appear whether the intestate looked in the direction from which the truck came before taking his position, but as he stood at the head of the horses he was lawfully upon the highway and had the right to assume that he would not be run into and how far his failure to look either forward or backward evinced carelessness was for the jury.”

Burns v. Oliver Whyte Co., 231 Mass. 519 

Plaintiff's intestate without a lantern on a dark night in October was leading two horses along the highway a little to the right of the center of the road when he

$354 

 was hit and killed by the defendant's automobile coming from the rear, going 26 miles an hour. 

It was held it could not be said that the plaintiff's intestate was not using due care even though he was walking on a dark night without a light. There can be no question that it might be found negligent to overtake in a motor car at night and run into a pedestrian travelling continuously in a direct path. 

Powers v. Loring, 231 Mass. 458

CHAPTER XV. 

ACTIONS SECTION 355. 

A. NATURE AND FORM OF ACTION. 

An action for injury or damage caused by the motor vehicle is one of tort and is derived from the common law actions of trespass and trespass on the case. 

An action for death under General Laws, Chapter 229 

is a statutory remedy and the provisions of the statute must be strictly followed. 

Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 392, at 398 and 399 

In Wescott v. Henshaw Motor Company, 275 Mass. 82, the court said at 85: 66 'An action for wrongfully causing the death of another is not a common law action; it is purely a statutory right. 

Where such a right is given, subject to certain conditions, failure to comply with the conditions is fatal to the existence of the right.” 

Bickford v. Furber, 271 Mass. 94, at 96 

Castaline v. Swardlick, 264 Mass. 481 and cases cited at page 483 

An action allowing recovery for death is purely statutory and is now governed by General Laws, Chapter 229, Section 5 (as amended by Acts 1922, c. 439; and Acts 

1925, c. 346, s. 9) which is called "Penalty for Causing

Death Through the Operation of a Motor Vehicle." 

Dzura v. Phillips, 275 Mass. 283

Proof of simple negligence is sufficient in an action for death caused by the motor vehicle. 

Dzura v. Phillips, 275 Mass. 283

$356 

 SECTION 356. 

B. JURISDICTION. 

An action for injury or damage caused by a motor vehicle is transitory and does not differ in character from other actions of tort.

The Superior, Municipal, District and Police Courts have jurisdiction over such actions.

C. VENUE. 

SECTION 357. 

General Laws, Chapter 223, Section 7, provides, in part, that: "An action against a city, town, person, or corporation to recover for injury or damage received in the commonwealth by reason of negligence shall be brought in the county where the plaintiff lives or has his usual place of business, or in the county where the alleged injury or damage was received."

The court said, in Sandler v. Boston Elevated Railway 

Company, 218 Mass. 333, at 334: "The purpose of G. L. c. 223, s. 7 is... to relieve the courts of those counties in which defendants in actions of negligence usually have a place of business from the trial of actions where the act of negligence happened in another county to plaintiffs residing or having a place of business in other counties. If [as is contended by the plaintiff] it were still possible to begin the action [in such cases] by a trustee writ, the purpose of the enactment to a large extent would be nullified. We are of opinion that the Legislature meant what it said when it provided that such actions 'shall be brought' in the county where the plaintiff lives or has his usual place of business, or in the county in which the injury was received, and that R. L. c. 189, ss. I, 2, were to that extent impliedly repealed. See in this connection

$445 Actions 

Kilby Bank, Petnr., 23 Pick. 93 

Merchants Bank v. Cook, 4 Pick. 405"

General Laws, Chapter 223, Section 7 applies in the 

Superior and Supreme Court but does not apply in the Municipal, District or Police Courts, which are governed by General Laws, Chapter 223, Section 2. 

In Hanley v. Eastern Steamship Company, 221 Mass. 

125, at 132 and 133, it is said: "The words 'usual place of business,' as used in this statute, do not include a place where one pursues a ‘trade or calling.""

So, this does not include the place where the plaintiff is employed.

A defendant, by appearing and generally answering to the merits, waives the objection which he might have to claim that the action was brought in the wrong venue. 

Paige v. Sinclair, 237 Mass. 482

D. PARTIES. 

SECTION 358. 

The rules governing parties to civil actions generally are applicable to actions for injury, damage or death caused by motor vehicles.

SECTION 359. 

2. Real Party in Interest.

The action should be brought in the name of the party who has the real interest in the outcome of the case. 

So, the purchaser of a motor vehicle under a contract providing for its conditional sale, who has paid part of its purchase price and is in possession of the property, may maintain an action for injury to such vehicle. 

Downey v. Bay State St. Ry. Co., 225 Mass. 281

$360 

3. Joinder of. a. 

Defendants. 

SECTION 360. 

(I) Owner and Operator of Vehicle. 

The owner of a motor vehicle and the one operating it at the time of a collision, not as agent of the owner, but with his permission, and in his absence, may not be joined as defendants in a single action for injury or damage occasioned by the collision. 

Johnson v. Carroll, 272 Mass. 134 

69 A. L. R. 1244

Nor can the owner and operator be joined as defendants in such an action. 

Popkin v. Goldman, 266 Mass. 531

SECTION 361. 

(II) Joint Tortfeasors. 

Joint tortfeasors should not be joined in an action for death under G. L., c. 229, s. 5. 

Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 392 

Where two or more tortfeasors by concurrent acts of negligence which, although disconnected, yet in combination inflict injury, the plaintiff may sue them jointly or severally, although he can have but one satisfaction in damages. 

Feneff v. Boston & Maine R. R., 196 Mass. 575

If each contributes to the wrong, the proximate cause is the wrongful act in which they concurrently participate, whether the result causes instantaneous death or injuries which the sufferer survives. 

Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 392, at 397

$447 Actions 

D'Almeida v. Boston & Maine R. R., 209 Mass. 81, at 87 

Feneff v. Boston & Maine R. R., 196 Mass. 575 

Doe v. Boston & Wor. St. Ry. Co., 195 Mass. 168, at 171

4. Amendment as to Parties. 

SECTION 362. 

a. 

Substitution. 

In Johnson v. Carroll, 272 Mass. 134, at 136, the court says: "The allowance of the amendment striking out Osborne as the defendant and inserting Carroll as the defendant was an adjudication by the court that the several plaintiffs would thereby be enabled to maintain their actions for the causes for which they were originally intended to be brought. It cannot be set aside if warranted upon the facts. It plainly was warranted. "The cause of action intended to be prosecuted when the writs were sued out was that founded on the negligent operation of the automobile through collision with which they were injured. The facts hitherto recited fully warranted a finding that the cause of action for which each writ was brought was the same as that now being prosecuted." 

Clark v. N. E. Tel. & Tel. Co., 229 Mass. I, at 5 and 6

SECTION 364. 

The introduction of a new party defendant, without notice to him of motion to amend the writ and declaration by inserting his name, is permissible, though to bring him into court he must be served with process. 

Johnson v. Carroll, 272 Mass. 134, at 137

In the last cited case, an action based on the negligent operation of an automobile, it was held that there was no error in allowing the plaintiffs to amend by striking out the original defendant and substituting a new one, without giving the proposed defendant notice, or an opportunity to be heard. It was pointed out that the new defendant had every opportunity to defend himself to the same extent as if he had originally been made the defendant, and that, after the rightful allowance of the amendment and the bringing of the defendant into court by due process, the case stood the same in effect as if he had originally been named as defendant. 

69 A. L. R. 1250

Hearing was given to Osborne, then the party defendant. That was all that was necessary. The introduction of a new party defendant without notice to him of the amendment is permissible. Of course, he could not be brought into court without process.

After the rightful allowance of the amendment and the bringing of the defendant into court by due process, each case stood the same in effect as if he had been originally named as defendant. 

Holmes v. Carraher, 251 Mass. 536, at 538 

69 A. L. R. 1246

The defendant had the right to contest the power of the

$365 

 court, as matter of law, to allow the amendments under the statute and proper practice. For example, he could demonstrate that, as matter of law, it was impossible for the court to find that the cause of action was the same as the one originally intended to be brought. 

Bowen v. Fairfield, 260 Mass. 38 and cases collected 

Sterling v. Leyland & Co., Ltd., 242 Mass. 8 

69 A. L. R. 1246

It was also open to him to contend that the requisite finding was not supported by the evidence, or as inference from established facts. 

Silver v. Jordan, 139 Mass. 280 

69 A. L. R. 1246

There was no legal impediment to the allowance of the amendments provided the court found the essential fact that the plaintiffs originally intended to bring actions for the causes now disclosed on the papers as amended, and that finding was permissible on the facts reported.

G. DEFENSES. 

SECTION 368. 

1. Contributory Negligence. 

If the plaintiff has been negligent and such negligence contributed toward his injury, he is barred from recovery. 

But such contributory negligence of the plaintiff must be set up as matter of defense; otherwise the issue is not open and the plaintiff's due care will be conclusively presumed. 

G. L. c. 231, s. 85

See: Chapters XIII and XIV, pages 329 to 443. 

SECTION 369. 

2. Discharge. 

See: Section 431, page 553. [By release of joint tortfeasor.]

When the plaintiff has no cause of action against a third person for or on account of the alleged tort and there is in fact no claim of negligence on the part of that third person, and no such claim was ever made by the

$370 

 plaintiff, the fact that the plaintiff was paid money by that third person does not make the principle applicable to joint tortfeasors pertinent in a suit of the plaintiff against the defendant for the defendant's negligence. 

Mathews v. Carr, 271 Mass. 362, at 364 (Widow of police officer killed while on duty, paid sum by town, gave release)

Payment made to plaintiff was in the nature of gratuity and not something paid in satisfaction of an injury for which the Commonwealth is or might be liable according to established rules of law. 

Mathews v. Carr, 271 Mass. 362, at 364 

Pickwick v. McCauliff, 193 Mass. 70, at 75

Payment made under policy of accident insurance inadmissible in action of tort against a Railroad Company for its negligence. 

Mathews v. Carr, 271 Mass. 362, at 364 

Gray v. Boston El. Ry., 215 Mass. 143, at 146 

Ridgeway v. Sayre Electric Co., 258 Penn. St. 400, at 406 

SECTION 370. 

3. Lack of Responsibility or Agency. 

Under General Laws, Chapter 231, Section 85A (as amended by Acts 1928, c. 317, s. 1), a presumption is created that the person operating the motor vehicle was the agent of the registrant so that the latter was responsible for the acts of the former. The defense of lack of responsibility, or agency of the operator of the motor vehicle must be specially set up by the defendant in his answer. 

See: Sections 243 through 258, pages 296 to 320. 

4. Res Judicata.

SECTION 371. 

The judgment entered upon agreement of parties for

455 Actions the plaintiff for a substantial sum in a previous action involving the same facts where the parties are reversed is res judicata of negligence, due care and contributory negligence, and bars a subsequent action. 

Biggio v. Magee, 272 Mass. 185, at 187

The doctrine of res judicata applies even though the judgment was entered by consent in an action at law. 

It was an adjudication and settled finally the rights of the parties to the same cause of action. 

Biggio v. Magee, 272 Mass. 185, at 187

It does not matter that the agreement for judgment was signed by the attorney for a company which insured the present plaintiff, and by authority contained in the terms of the insurance policy. 

Biggio v. Magee, 272 Mass. 185, at 189

See: Acts 1932, chapter 130, which provides that a judgment entered by agreement in a case under a motor vehicle policy shall not operate as a bar to an action unless the agreement was signed by the defendant in person. 

Where a plaintiff was insured and had a policy of insurance in a certain company and a summons was served upon him in an action by the present defendant against the plaintiff and the plaintiff turned the summons over to his insurance broker, and did not know what had happened to it afterwards, was not able to find his insurance policy, nor did he ever know or speak to any member of the firm of attorneys which appeared for him, and who were in fact employed by the Insurance Company, and never did he authorize any such attorneys to agree to any judgment against him, and in fact the attorneys agreed for a judgment against him and a further entry of "judgment satisfied," the matter was res judicata that the plaintiff had been negligent and such negligence caused injury to the defendant and contributed to his, the plaintiff's own injury. 

Long v. MacDougall, 273 Mass. 386, at 387

$371 

In the above cited case, the court said, at page 388: "The parties in the action of MacDougall against Long lived in this Commonwealth. The court which rendered the judgment against Long had jurisdiction of the subject matter and of the party defendant in the action perforce of its summons, which the defendant admitted was served upon him. A domestic judgment rendered by a court of general jurisdiction in the absence of fraud is conclusive upon the parties to the writ affected by it, and collaterally cannot be impeached by evidence of want of authority to appear or to act for the defendant or for any other cause." 

Biggio v. Magee, 272 Mass. 185 

Young v. Watson, 155 Mass. 77 

Finneran v. Leonard, 7 Allen 54

The defendant's relief in such a case is found in a proper application for review or writ of error, and in exceptional cases by a bill in equity. 

Long v. MacDougall, 273 Mass. 386 

Joyce v. Thompson, 229 Mass. 106 

Brooks v. Twitchell, 182 Mass. 443 

Hendrick v. Whittemore, 105 Mass. 23

A judgment is a bar to a subsequent action only when either the parties or their privies are the same in both cases. 

Giedrewicz v. Donovan, 1932 A. S. 63, at 64 

In McCarthy v. William H. Wood Lumber Co., 219

Mass. 566, the court said, at page 567, that the doctrine of res judicata is that the determination on its merits of an issue of fact or law "by the judgment of a court of competent jurisdiction, constitutes a bar to any further litigation upon the same matter either by the parties or by their privies." It is only "a judgment in rem or one affecting the status of persons or things" that is "conclusive as to all the world." "A verdict and judgment are conclusive by way of estoppel only as to those facts which were necessarily

§457 Actions involved in them, without the existence and proof or admission of which such a verdict and judgment could not have been rendered. An estoppel is an admission or determination under circumstances of such solemnity that the law will not allow the fact so admitted or established to be afterwards drawn in question between the same parties or their privies . . . When a fact has been once determined in the course of a judicial proceeding, and a final judgment has been rendered in accordance therewith, it cannot be again litigated between the same parties without virtually impeaching the correctness of the former decision, which from motives of public policy the law does not permit to be done.' 

Burlen v. Shannon, 99 Mass. 200, at 202-203 

In Bigelow v. Winsor, I Gray, 299, at 301-302, the court said: "One valid judgment, by a court of competent jurisdiction, between the same parties, upon considerations as well of public policy, is held to be conclusive, except where a review, an appeal, or rehearing in some form, is allowed and regulated by law. No man is to be vexed twice with the same controversy." 

Biggio v. Magee, 272 Mass. 185, at 188

In McAlevey v. Litch, 234 Mass. 440, a judgment for the defendant which was rendered in a case against a corporation for personal injuries caused by negligence in operating an automobile by Litch who was alleged in the plea to be its president, treasurer, manager and one of its directors, was held not to be a bar to an action of tort for the same injuries by the same plaintiff against the officer individually, because the jury may have disbelieved the testimony, and the general verdict did not disclose how the jury found on the question of whether the officer was acting in the scope of his employment, or on what issues the plaintiff failed. 

Where the plaintiff has brought an action against the

8372 

 principal for the injuries and damage sustained by him and the judgment was rendered in that case for the defendant principal, the same is not res judicata in an action against the operator agent or employee for causing the plaintiff's injury and damage unless it appears from the record of that case that the operator agent or servant was at the time of the accident within the scope of his employment for the principal.

But when it appears from the record either by way of an admission in the former trial or otherwise that the operator's employment at the time of the accident causing the plaintiff's injury was conclusively established as being within its proper scope, then the judgment of the former case is res judicata. 

Giedrewicz v. Donovan, 1932 A. S. 63

In the last cited case, the court said at page 68: "As a matter of public policy and in the interest of accomplishing justice, the better rule would seem to be that if it is clearly established in the trial of an action either against the employee or against the principal for damages caused by the employee's negligent conduct, that the employee is not negligent, the judgment in the first. case tried is a bar to a subsequent action by the same plaintiff for the same negligent act of the same employee. 

In principle it would seem to be immaterial whether the first judgment was obtained in an action against the employee provided the only ground for holding the employer is the negligence of the employee and it clearly appears that in the first trial the employee was found to be free from culpability."

SECTION 375. 

Amendment. 

General Laws, Chapter 231, Section 51, authorizes any amendment which will enable the plaintiff to sustain the action for the cause for which it was intended to be brought. 

Pearson v. Bara, 263 Mass. 502, at 504

Allowance of an amendment does not render the proceeding a new suit. 

Pearson v. Bara, 263 Mass. 502, at 504 (Change of plaintiff)

The allowance of an amendment implies a finding by the judge that the action as amended was a proceeding

$461 Actions begun to obtain redress for the cause intended. It is the same suit and not a new one. 

Pearson v. Bara, 263 Mass. 502, at 504 (Substitution of wife as plaintiff; automobile registered in wife's name) 

Johnson v. Carroll, 272 Mass. 134 

McLaughlin v. West End St. Ry., 186 Mass. 150

But the court has no power to allow an amendment in certain instances. 

Bowen v. Fairfield, 260 Mass. 38 

Boston Tow Boat Co. v. Medford Natl. Bank, 228 

Mass. 484 

Church v. Boylston & Woodbury Cafe Co., 218 Mass. 231 

Brooks v. Boston & Northern St. Ry., 211 Mass. 277 

Silver v. Jordan, 139 Mass. 280

The presiding judge, under the authority of General Laws, Chapter 231, Section 51, allowed the plaintiff to amend his declaration "by setting up specifically the making of a new contract between the plaintiff and the defendant on January 31," 1920. ...

The defendants duly excepted to the allowance, and now contend that the allowance of the amendment after the trial of the case on "the alleged right of the plaintiff to demand such credits and securities in his capacity as the assignee operated to deprive these defendants of their property without due process of law as secured by the 14th Amendment to the Federal Constitution—inasmuch as the defendants never had any hearing or trial at all nor any opportunity to be heard in their defence to the said ground of liability upon which the said finding in favor of the plaintiff is based." The amendment allowed sets up no allegations which are not covered by evidence. 

Pizer v. Hunt, 250 Mass. 498, at 504

A party to an action has no vested right to have a case decided and determined upon a form of procedure which

8376 

 may have been inadvisedly or mistakenly chosen. 

The evidence may show a substantial variance between the allegations of the declaration and the proof, and at the same time disclose a legal right which the court in its own discretion may make available and valuable by the allowance of an amendment "in matter of form or substance." 

Pizer v. Hunt, 250 Mass. 498, at 504 and 505 

See also:

G. L. c. 231, s. 51

6. Examination of Parties Before Trial. 

a. 

SECTION 385. 

Admissions of Fact. 

Under Acts 1926, Chapter 381, Section 1, either party may require the other to admit material facts or the execution of documents. 

Butter v. Sovrensky, 275 Mass. 88

SECTION 386. 

b. Interrogatories.

By General Laws, Chapter 231, Sections 61-67, inclu sive, any party may interrogate an adversary party for the discovery of facts and documents admissible in evidence at the trial of the case.

As of right, no more than thirty interrogatories may be filed, except that the court for adequate cause shown may permit a larger number.

Interrogatories to an adversary party are in the nature of an examination designed to obtain declarations of fact admissible in evidence. The field is broad. Whatever facts are material to the issues raised may be developed by interrogatories. 

Goldman v. Ashkins, 266 Mass. 374, at 379

Questions shall be concise and directed to a definite object, not rambling and scattered. 

Goldman v. Ashkins, 266 Mass. 374, at 380

The statute as to interrogatories confers rights which may be asserted in a proper way. 

Goldman v. Ashkins, 266 Mass. 374, at 380

$386 

The determining factor, however, is whether the interrogatories are competent, without repetitions and without diversions into collateral or disconnected matters. If they are competent and not repetitious or verbose, or objectionable in form or substance, they must be answered, although annoying to the interrogated party. 

Goldman v. Ashkins, 266 Mass. 374, at 380 and 381

These sections of the statute enable a party to interrogate his adversary to the same extent as would be permissible if he were called as a witness at the trial. 

Warren v. DeCoste, 269 Mass. 415, at 417 

Goldman v. Ashkins, 266 Mass. 374, at 380 

Cutter v. Cooper, 234 Mass. 307 

Looney v. Saltonstall, 212 Mass. 69

The test in general as to the necessity of making answers to interrogatories is whether they are directed to obtain disclosures of facts admissible in evidence as to which the party interrogated could be required to testify as a witness. 

Warren v. DeCoste, 269 Mass. 415, at 417

The interrogatories must be proper in form and designed to elicit facts within the knowledge of the party and admissible in evidence upon the issue raised by the pleadings. 

Warren v. DeCoste, 269 Mass. 415, at 417

Fundamental rules as to the admission and exclusion of evidence define and limit interrogatories save as otherwise expressly provided. This conclusion follows also from the terms of General Laws, Chapter 231, Section 89, that the "answers of a party to interrogatories filed may be read by the other party as evidence at the trial." 

Warren v. DeCoste, 269 Mass. 415, at 418

The scope of the subjects about which interrogatories may be asked is as broad as the field of inquiry when the

$467 Actions person interrogated is called as a witness to testify orally in the actual trial. 

Cutter v. Cooper, 234 Mass. 307, at 314 and 315

The statute by express terms makes applicable to interrogatories fundamental rules applicable to the presentation of evidence. 

Cutter v. Cooper, 234 Mass. 307, at 315

The words of General Laws, Chapter 231, Section 63 

that in the event of refusal to answer "the court shall, upon motion, order the party interrogated to answer such of the interrogatories as it finds proper," do not vest in the judge an untrammelled discretion upon the subject. They impose the duty to act according to sound principles of law, having regard to all pertinent factors and general rules of evidence. 

Cutter v. Cooper, 234 Mass. 307, at 315 "If a party seasonably files proper interrogatories, he is entitled to be informed of such facts in advance, so as to assist him in preparing for trial; that any error of the court, in refusing to order a disclosure of such facts, is not cured by the introduction of, or opportunity to introduce, testimony on the same point at the trial.” 

Cutter v. Cooper, 234 Mass. 307, at 315 

Baker v. Carpenter, 127 Mass. 226, at 228 

Gunn v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R. Co., 171 Mass. 417, at 421 Whenever, therefore, the rulings of the judge have resulted in a denial of the right to secure disclosure of facts having a substantial relation to the issues involved there is good ground for exception unless it appears that the substantial rights of the excepting party have not been injuriously affected. 

Cutter v. Cooper, 234 Mass. 307, at 315

The principle of trial evidence, to the effect that ordi-

8386 

 narily no exception will be sustained to the refusal to allow a question to be put unless the substance of the answer expected in reply is stated to the court, does not apply to interrogatories. 

Cutter v. Cooper, 234 Mass. 307, at 315 and 316

Interrogatories commonly are propounded to an adversary party for the purpose of ascertaining material facts in advance of the trial. 

Cutter v. Cooper, 234 Mass. 307, at 316

The interrogator may be in utter ignorance of the information likely to be disclosed, and be unable to make any offer of proof.

His right to interrogate does not depend primarily upon the question whether the answers will help or harm him in the ultimate decision of the case. 

Cutter v. Cooper, 234 Mass. 307, at 316

The propriety of the interrogatories must be tested in the light of these principles and issues. 

Cutter v. Cooper, 234 Mass. 307, at 317

The earlier statute confined the rights of each party to inquiries aimed at the discovery of facts and documents material to the support of the contentions set up by his own pleadings. The amendment removes this definite restriction, and permits interrogatories as wide in scope as the issues presented for trial. 

Looney v. Saltonstall, 212 Mass. 69, at 72

The plaintiff may interrogate upon any matter material to the support of his case, and the defendant upon those material to his defense. . . Each party is to be confined to those matters which are material to sustain the case which he sets up by his pleadings; he is to be allowed to obtain, by interrogating his adversary, proofs of his own. case, but not those which establish the case set up against him.

469 Actions 

Looney v. Saltonstall; 212 Mass. 69, at 72

See: 

Davis v. Mills, 163 Mass. 481 

Wetherbee v. Winchester, 128 Mass. 293

Each party is no longer confined to matters strictly in support of his own case. He may inquire as to anything which would be competent in evidence, subject to the narrowing effect of Section 63. 

The result is that Acts 1909, c. 225, has enlarged the time within which interrogatories may be propounded by any party to that intervening between the entry of the action and the opening of the trial on the merits, and that the scope of the questions which may be asked is as broad as the field which would be permitted if the person interrogated was called as a witness to testify orally in the actual trial. 

Looney v. Saltonstall, 212 Mass. 69, at 74 

(I) Right to Propound. 

(A) To Corporation Defendant. 

When interrogatories are propounded to a corporation they must be directed to a particular officer. 

G. L. c. 231, s. 65 

In Wilson v. Webber, 2 Gray, 558, at 561, the court says: "The main purpose of these provisions of the practice act was to substitute, in place of the tedious, expensive, and complex process of a bill in discovery on the equity side of the court, an easy, cheap, and simple mode of interrogatories to an adverse party, as incident to and part of the proceedings in the cause in which the discovery was sought." 

The statute no doubt grew out of and was suggested by the practice which prevailed in equity of making an officer

8386 

 a party in a case where discovery was sought from a corporation. 

Gunn v. N. Y. etc. R. R., 171 Mass. 417, at 419 

Post & Co. v. Toledo, Cinn. & St. Louis R. R., 144 

Mass. 341, at 345

The effect of the statute is to give to the opposite party the same right of interrogating an officer as if he were a party, that is, the corporation itself.

Under the English practice in chancery it is settled that a party may be compelled to answer, not only as to those matters which are within his own personal knowledge, but also as to those respecting which there is information by means of inquiries from his servants, agents, or attorneys fairly within his reach. 

Gunn v. N. Y. etc. R. R., 171 Mass. 417, at 419

Such information is regarded as being in a sense information possessed by him. 

In the above cited case, at pages 419 and 420: "Directors of a company, in answering interrogatories, must not only answer as to their individual knowledge, but in answering for the company they must get such information as they can from other servants of the company who presumably have conducted the transaction in question."

The object of discovery is to obtain information material to the merits of the case of the party seeking it which is within the control or possession of the opposite party, or to compel admissions in respect to material matters. 

Gunn v. N. Y. etc. R. R., 171 Mass. 417, at 420

The fact that the information may be obtained through witnesses does not take away the right of discovery through interrogatories. 

Gunn v. N. Y. etc. R. R., 171 Mass. 417, at 420 

Hubbard v. Hubbard, 6 Gray, 362

471 Actions In the case of an officer of a corporation, the information must be official, that is, derived through his connection with the corporation. 

Gunn v. 

N. Y. etc. R. R., 171 Mass. 417, at 420 

Hancock v. Franklin Ins. Co., 107 Mass. 113, at 115

In any case, where the answers are upon information and belief, it may be so stated. 

Gunn v. N. Y. etc. R. R., 171 Mass. 417, at 420

But an admission is none the less binding because made upon information and belief, and for that reason the party interrogating properly may insist that the party interrogated shall make reasonable inquiries of his servants, agents, and attorneys, who were engaged as such in the transaction in question, for the purpose of ascertaining the facts in relation thereto and answering accordingly. 

Gunn v. N. Y. etc. R. R., 171 Mass. 417, at 420

The interrogatories are addressed to the conscience of the party. They do not require him to set down mere rumors, or simply to state what he has been told. They call for facts, and, in addition to the disclosure of such personal knowledge as he may have, if any, they require such reasonable investigation on his part by means of inquiries from those who are at the time subject to his direction or control as will enable him to state what the facts are. 

Gunn v. N. Y. etc. R. R., 171 Mass. 417, at 421 

In the last cited case, the court says, at page 421: "The party interrogating cannot compel him to get up his case for him, nor to disclose his own case, though the fact that some of the information required by the answers may be material to his own case will not excuse him from answering, if it also is material to that of the party interrogating."

The president stands in the place of the corporation,

8386 

Pub. Sts. c. 167, s. 53, and the corporation, being reputed to have done whatever its servants did in the course of their employment, is supposed to know what they did, and therefore cannot shelter itself under a general profession of personal ignorance on the part of its president. 

Robbins v. Brockton St. Ry., 180 Mass. 51, at 54

Compare: 

Bolchow v. Fisher, 10 Q. B. D. 161, at 171 

Attorney v. Rees, 12 Beav. 50, at 54 and 55

The knowledge of the corporation is a fiction and therefore its obligation to answer is not to be pressed beyond what is reasonable, as was explained in the case cited. 

But if in the case of an accident like the present the servants concerned are still in the employ of the company and within convenient reach, they must be inquired of concerning facts which the plaintiff has a right to know. 

Robbins v. Brockton St. Ry., 180 Mass. 51, at 54 

(II) Requisites of Answers. 

(A) Declarations of Deceased Persons. 

Declarations of deceased persons cannot be ordered answered because it cannot be known before trial what finding the presiding judge might make under the requirements of the statute (G. L. c. 233, s. 65) on 

(1) Good Faith (2) Personal Knowledge 

(3) Before Suit 

Warren v. DeCoste, 269 Mass. 415, at 419

Horan v. Boston El. Ry., 237 Mass. 245 (B) Disclosing Manner in Which Interrogated Party Proposes to Prove Case. 

A party cannot properly be compelled to answer questions which are not competent because they will require the party to disclose the manner in which he proposes to prove his case.

473 Actions 

Wakeley v. Boston El. Ry., 217 Mass. 488, at 491 

Looney v. Saltonstall, 212 Mass. 69 

See, however, Acts 1913, Chapter 815.

So, questions: "Describe fully how the alleged accident happened. State what you were doing, and what happened to you, in the order in which such events took place;" "Please specify in what respect the place where you alighted was unsafe and dangerous as alleged in your declaration," have been held contrary to law,

Wakeley v. Boston El. Ry., 217 Mass. 488, at 491 

for such questions call for a detailed description of precisely how the accident happened.

Wakeley v. Boston El. Ry., 217 Mass. 488, at 491 

Questions or interrogatories which tend to disclose the substance of the case of the adverse party, the means of its proof or the expression of an opinion, need not be answered. 

(C) Disclosure of Names of Witnesses. 

General Laws, Chapter 231, Section 63, provides, in part, that: "The court may compel the party interrogated to disclose the names of witnesses and addresses if practice seems to require it upon such terms and conditions as the court deems expedient." 

McNeil v. Middlesex & Boston St. Ry., 233 Mass. 254, at 258 

Nickerson v. Glines, 220 Mass. 333 

Looney v. Saltonstall, 212 Mass. 69, at 72 

Brooks v. Shaw, 197 Mass. 376

As to denial of names of witnesses, this is discretionary and no exception lies to refusal to give such names.

8386 

McNeil v. Middlesex & Boston St. Ry., 233 Mass. 254, at 258 

Nickerson v. Glines, 220 Mass. 333 

Looney v. Saltonstall, 212 Mass. 69, at 72 

(D) Disclosure of Title to Property. 

No party interrogated shall be compelled to answer a question or produce a document tending to criminate him or disclose his title to any property the title whereof is not material to an issue in the proceeding in the course of which he is interrogated, nor to disclose the names of witnesses, except as stated in the preceding section. 

G. L. c. 231, s. 63 (E) Hearsay.

The interrogated party need not disclose information. which came to him through hearsay.

This statement is subject to limitations respecting relevant information obtained through such inquiry of his agents, servants and attorneys as will enable the party "to make full and true answers to the interrogatories." That is required by G. L. c. 231, s. 62. 

Warren v. DeCoste, 269 Mass. 415, at 417 and 418

To this extent a party may be required to state that which is hearsay and which he could not give as a witness testifying upon the trial. 

Warren v. DeCoste, 269 Mass. 415, at 418

But statements not personal knowledge of agents, servants or attorneys of the interrogated party cannot be asked for when the information was derived wholly from statements made to the party or his agents, servants or attorney by third persons. 

Warren v. DeCoste, 269 Mass. 415, at 418 

(F) Improper and Irrelevant Answers. 

When the answers to interrogatories contain matters which are improper and irrelevant, they furnish good ground for motions to strike out the same.

475 Actions 

Warren v. DeCoste, 269 Mass. 415 (G) Matters of Public Record. 

The interrogated party cannot be required to answer interrogatories as to the contents of a public record. This proof can be made only by a certified copy of the record. 

Warren v. DeCoste, 269 Mass. 415, at 420

Silva v. Fidelity & Casualty Co. of New York, 252 

Mass. 328, at 330 

G. L. c. 46, s. 19 

(H) Opinion. 

The right to interrogate is not a right to abridge the other party's right to try any fairly doubtful fact. Still less is it a right to require him to offer an opinion on the general issue of the case or to state his view of it and to that extent to disclose his defense. 

Robbins v. Brockton St. Ry., 180 Mass. 51, at 55

The defendant is not compelled to disclose in advance its theory of the accident nor state facts upon which it relied to establish its defense. 

Carroll v. Boston El. Ry., 200 Mass. 527, at 532 (I) Personal Signature and Oath of Inter rogated Party.

Under General Laws, Chapter 231, Section 62, the answers must be signed and upon the oath of the party himself and the requirement of the statute is not complied with when the answers are signed and sworn to by an attorney. 

Harding v. Noyes, 125 Mass. 572, at 573 (J) Privileged Communications.

The interrogated party need not reveal private or privileged conversations. or communications but he must claim such privilege as the ground for not answering the interrogatory.

8386 (K) 

Self-Incrimination. 

Although a party is not required to answer matters which would tend to incriminate him yet a question is not incompetent because its answer may tend to incriminate him. That is a privilege which the party interrogated must claim. 

Cutter v. Cooper, 234 Mass. 307, at 308

The privilege against self-incrimination extends only to crimes which may be prosecuted within the jurisdiction where the affiant is examined. 

Republic v. Koukomas, Hale v. Henkel, 201 U. S. 43, at 69

Jack v. State of Kansas, 199 U. S. 372 The Mercantile Trust Co. v. Missouri, Kansas & 

Texas Ry. Co., 161 U. S. 591 

(III) Imperfect Answers. 

(A) Nonsuit or Default.

Where a party merely neglects to answer interrogatories propounded to him within the time alowed by law, the court may enter a nonsuit or default; 

Fels v. Raymond, 139 Mass. 98, at 100 

Harding v. Morrill, 136 Mass. 291 

Harding v. Noyes, 125 Mass. 572 but usually the court does not nonsuit or default without specifying a date at which the nonsuit or default is to be entered, unless answers are filed prior thereto; or, in other instances, the court will enter a conditional nonsuit or default which is to be removed upon the filing of answers on or before a certain date. 

The entry of a nonsuit or default is not the equivalent of a final judgment. The removal of a nonsuit or default before final judgment is within the power of the court. 

Hooton v. G. F. Redmond & Co., 237 Mass. 508, at

Hurnanen v. Gardner Automobile Co., 225 Mass. 189 

513

477 Actions (1) Opportunity to Further Answer.

Questions of great difficulty often arise as to how far a party is bound to answer interrogatories propounded by the adverse party, and it was not the intention of the statute to compel a party to decide such questions at the risk, if he decides erroneously, of a nonsuit or default. 

Fels v. Raymond, 139 Mass. 98, at 101

The interrogating party should file a motion setting forth his objections to the answers, and praying that they be made more full and clear; and it is for the court to determine upon such motion how far the answers are imperfect, and which of the interrogatories require fuller answers. 

Fels v. Raymond, 139 Mass. 98, at 101

If the answers are adjudged to be imperfect, the interrogated party ought to have the opportunity to amend them, after the particulars in which they are insufficient are pointed out.

If he refuses to amend or to answer more fully, according to the order of the court, a nonsuit or default may be entered. 

Fels v. Raymond, 139 Mass. 98, at 101 

Wetherbee v. Winchester, 128 Mass. 293 

Amherst & Belchertown Railroad v. Watson, 8 Gray, 529 But it has never been held that, where a party files answers to interrogatories, it is within the discretion of the court, without further proceedings, to enter a nonsuit or default because the answers are deemed insufficient or evasive; and we are of opinion that the fair construction of the statute does not confer such a discretion or power. 

Fels v. Raymond, 139 Mass. 98, at 100

The defendant was given no opportunity to correct its answers and make them adequate. In this there was error.

8386 

The case is within the authority of Fels v. Raymond, 139

Mass. 98. The point there settled was that after answers to interrogatories are filed, there must be an adjudication that the answers are imperfect and the interrogated party be given an opportunity to amend them, before nonsuit or default can be entered. In the particulars here involved, the present statute is not materially different from that then in force. 

Hooton v. G. F. Redmond & Co., 237 Mass. 508, at 512 

In Downing v. Downing, 227 Mass. 7, after having answered two interrogatories, the trustee was ordered to answer the remaining interrogatories. This was equivalent to an adjudication that the answers made were insufficient and that the other interrogatories must be answered. 

Advantage was not taken of the opportunity thus afforded, because only one of the remaining interrogatories was then answered. Manifestly this was trifling with the order of the court and a default was held to have been entered rightly. 

Nickerson v. Glines, 220 Mass. 333 

Hooton v. G. F. Redmond & Co., 237 Mass. 508, at 512 and 513 

(IV) Evasive and Incomplete Answers. 

(A) As Ground for Motion for Further and Fuller Answers. 

When the answers to interrogatories are evasive or incomplete, they furnish good ground for motions to require the interrogated party to make more complete or fuller answers. 

Warren v. DeCoste, 269 Mass. 415, at 417 

(B) As Evidence of Admission. 

The failure or omission of a party to deny any answer to interrogatories, when he has both the right and oppor-

$479 Actions tunity to develop his whole claim, cannot but tend to create a just belief that the charge in the interrogatories is true. 

Parsons v. Martin, 11 Gray, III, at 115

However, this rule applies only when the fact, or facts, is particularly within the party's own knowledge, and he would naturally and probably avail himself of any and every explanation concerning it which would relieve him · of responsibility. 

Parsons v. Martin, II Gray, III, at 115 (Where stockbroker was charged with having received proceeds of sale)

The conduct of a party in omitting to produce that evidence in elucidation of the subject in dispute which is in his own power, and which is better known to himself than to others, affords occasion for strong presumption against him, since it must raise pregnant suspicions that the truth, if developed, would operate against him. 

Parsons v. Martin, 11 Gray, III, at 115

In D'Addio v. Hinckley Rendering Co., 213 Mass. 465, at 468 (top) and 469 (top), it is said: "The defendant's treasurer does not directly answer

The answer is almost in the nature of confession and avoidance. Under these circumstances the rule applies that when it is in the power of a party to an action to explain things apparently telling against him and he fails to make the explanation, it properly may be presumed that no truthful explanation will help him."
