A. JUDICIAL NOTICE. 

The judge and jurors properly, without the production of evidence, may take cognizance of facts that are generally regarded as forming a part of the common knowledge of all persons of ordinary understanding and intelligence. 

Mady v. Holy Trinity Roman Catholic Polish Church, 

223 Mass. 23, at 26

Within this common knowledge, the following have been held: 

A Dodge automobile is valued at more than fifteen dollars. 

Comm. v. Hosman, 257 Mass. 379

Motor vehicles of one manufacturer are distinguished by a "serial number." 

Wise v. Kennedy, 248 Mass. 83

Automobiles are chattels and commonly bought and sold. 

Clark v. Henshaw Motor Co., 246 Mass. 386

Motor vehicles can be run more quickly and safely over smooth roads with little or no street traffic than over more direct roads involving rough roads and street car traffic. 

Mathewson v. Edison Elec. Illg. Co., 232 Mass. 576, at 581 A larger number of persons are conveyed upon the highways in motor vehicles than in horse drawn vehicles. 

Kelleher v. Newburyport, 227 Mass. 462

$389

Welch v. Boston El. Ry., 226 Mass. 87 

Gasoline is a product of crude petroleum. 

Moeckel v. Cross, 190 Mass. 280

Contracts of insurance are commonly expressed in writing in the form of a policy. 

Emery v. Boston Marine Ins. Co., 138 Mass. 398

Judicial notice will be taken of the usual meaning of words describing ordinary things, such as that a "motor car" does not include a "motorcycle."

B. PRESUMPTIONS. 

SECTION 389. 

Presumptions are of two classes: first, presumptions of fact which are instances where circumstances exist from which an inference of fact may be drawn; and second, presumptions of law which require that certain inferences of fact must be drawn, either prima facie or conclusively, from the existence or non-existence of circumstances or other facts.

A presumption is not evidence of the facts which it assumes, but takes the place of evidence as to those facts, until evidence is introduced to rebut or control it.

$483 Evidence 

In Thomes v. The Meyer Store, Inc., 268 Mass. 587, which involves General Laws, Chapter 231, Section 85A, creating the presumption that a motor vehicle registered in the name of a person is being operated by and under the control of such person or another person for whose conduct the registrant is legally responsible, the court said, at page 589: "It is to be observed that the effect of this statute is to create certain specified facts when proved as prima facie evidence of a further important fact. The statute does not establish a presumption; a presumption is not evidence but a rule concerning evidence and it disappears when the facts are shown." 

Comm. v. Madeiros, 255 Mass. 304, at 316 (Presumption of innocence) 

Comm. v. Orler, 252 Mass. 55 (Letters on the letter head of defendant, addressed to the deceased, and which were found in her effects, raised the rational inference that the letters were received by the deceased and had been opened by her) 

Comm. v. De Francesco, 248 Mass. 9, at 13 

Bagnell v. Boston El. Ry., 247 Mass. 235

In Duggan v. Bay State Street Railway Company, 230 

Mass. 370, at 378: "A presumption ordinarily is not evidence but a rule about evidence. It is no new thing in the history or administration of the law that peculiar and artificial force is given or attributed to particular facts, or a series of facts, as means and instruments of legal proof." 

Hyde Park v. Canton, 130 Mass. 505

Usually a fact or condition is presumed to continue to exist until the contrary is shown. 

Martin v. The Fishing Ins. Co., 20 Pick. 389 a. 

Conflicting Presumptions.

When there are conflicting presumptions, each of which

$390 

 without the other having the force to create prima facie evidence, neither has any force and the case is thrown open to be considered at large upon all the evidence. 

Talbot, Petnr., 250 Mass. 517 

Prudential Trust Co. v. Hayes, 247 Mass. 311 

Fisher v. Drew, 247 Mass. 178 

Chandler v. Prince, 217 Mass. 451

Turner v. Williams, 202 Mass. 500, at 505 

Comm. v. McGrath, 140 Mass. 296, at 297 

Hyde Park v. Canton, 130 Mass. 505

SECTION 390. 

2. Res Ipsa Loquitur.

The doctrine of res ipsa loquitur is applicable when, according to the common experience of mankind, an accident or an event such as is involved in the particular case does not ordinarily happen except through negligence on the part of the person having control of the motor vehicle, and who has charge of it. It is then that an inference from the happening of the accident itself may arise that it was caused by the negligence of the person having control of the motor vehicle, even although it cannot be pointed out or specified in what particulars that negligence exists. That is, if the most reasonable inference to be drawn from the happening of the accident itself is, according to the common experience of mankind, that it happened through the defendant's negligence, then the law permits that inference, unless the accident is otherwise explained, or sufficient cause has been produced for its occurrence. 

Draper v. Cotting, 231 Mass. 51, at 62 

Trim v. Fore River etc. Co., 211 Mass. 593, at 594

This rule has no operation if the cause of the accident is sufficiently explained; 

Draper v. Cotting, 231 Mass. 51, at 62 

Trim v. Fore River etc. Co., 211 Mass. 593, at 594

$485 Evidence however, the jury is not required to believe the explanation, and may rely upon the original inference created by this doctrine. "It was said in Wing v. London General Omnibus Co. (1909) 2 K. B. 652, at pages 663 to 664: The rule of res ipsa loquitur applies only 'when the direct cause of the accident and so much of the surrounding circumstances as was essential to its occurrence, were within the sole control and management of the defendants, or their servants, so that it is not unfair to attribute to them a prima facie responsibility for what happened. An accident in the case of traffic on a highway is in marked contrast to such a condition of things. Every vehicle has to adapt its own behaviour to the behaviour of other persons using the road, and over their actions those in charge of the vehicle have no control. Hence the fact that an accident has happened either to or through a particular vehicle is by itself no evidence that the fault, if any, which led to it was committed by those in charge of that vehicle.'” 

Ellis v. Ellison, 275 Mass. 272, at 276 

Kelley v. Boston Woven Hose & Rubber Co., 275 

Mass. 21

Bartlett v. Town Taxi Inc., 263 Mass. 215 

DiLeo v. Eastern Mass. St. Ry., 255 Mass. 140 

Lamberti v. Neal, 253 Mass. 99

Reardon v. Boston El. Ry., 247 Mass. 124 

Boutlier v. Malden, 226 Mass. 479 and other cases cited by the plaintiff are distinguishable from the present case 

Melvin v. Penn. Steel Co., 180 Mass. 196 

Doyle v. Boston & Albany R. R., 145 Mass. 386 

White v. Boston & Albany R. R., 144 Mass. 404 

But in Bartlett v. Town Taxi, 263 Mass. 215, the rule of res ipsa loquitur was held inapplicable where the only evidence as to the cause of the accident was that the driver of a taxi turned around so abruptly, on a street covered with snow, that he nearly tipped over, and the plaintiff's

$390 

 testatrix, a passenger, was thrown to the floor of the machine. The court stated that the fact that an accident had happened, either to or through a particular vehicle, was by itself no evidence that the fault, if any, which led to it, was committed by those in charge of that vehicle. 

69 A. L. R. 998

The doctrine of res ipsa loquitur is not applicable where the defendant drove his automobile at an excessive speed and struck a bicycle rider travelling in the opposite direction who suddenly turned to his left beyond the center of the road and was struck by defendant's vehicle. 

Ellis v. Ellison, 275 Mass. 272, at 276

The doctrine is not applicable where a radiator cap blew off and steam and hot water scalded pedestrian. 

Randazzo v. Wheaton, 1932 A. S. 563

In reason the principle of res ipsa loquitur is also applicable to the unexplained automatic starting of a motor vehicle from a state of rest into motion, when, according to its mechanical construction, it ought to remain still, this being evidence not only of some defect or want of repair in the machine but also of negligence in failing to discover and remedy such defect or want of repair, even though the details of such defect or want of repair may not be shown by the evidence. 

Glaser v. Schroeder, 269 Mass. 337, at 339 (Auto backed downhill) 

66 A. L. R. 442

This doctrine is applicable to unexplained starting of an automobile when parked and left alone. 

Glaser v. Schroeder, 269 Mass. 337, at 339 

Burns v. Holyoke St. Ry., 253 Mass. 443 

Lonergan v. Am. Ry. Exp. Co., 250 Mass. 30, at 36 

St. Louis v. Bay State St. Ry. Co., 216 Mass. 255, In the common experience of mankind, it is extraordiat 257

$487 Evidence nary, unusual and not a common event for a parked automobile to begin to move and to gain momentum. It would not happen unless there was some fault on the part of the person who left the automobile, in failing to set the brake sufficiently tight or to block the automobile or to rest it against the curb or to chain its wheels or to stop its engine, or in some other particulars to take precautions essential to its security and permanence in position. 

Glaser v. Schroeder, 269 Mass. 337, at 339

The mere happening of a collision on the highway is no evidence of negligence of a defendant and does not warrant the invocation of the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur. 

Glaser v. Schroeder, 269 Mass. 337, at 339 

Bartlett v. Town Taxi Inc., 263 Mass. 215, at 219 

DiLeo v. Eastern Mass. St. Ry., 255 Mass. 140 

Reardon v. Boston El. Ry., 247 Mass. 124, and cases collected 

Curtin v. Boston El. Ry., 194 Mass. 260, at 264 

66 A. L. R. 442

The circumstances in the case at bar are different in nature. The grade of the street demanded caution. What happened was the natural result of leaving the automobile without setting the brakes sufficiently tight or otherwise securing it in a fixed position. There was no error in ruling that the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur was applicable. 

Glaser v. Schroeder, 269 Mass. 337, at 340 

Burns v. Holyoke St. Ry., 253 Mass. 443 

Lonergan v. Am. Ry. Exp. Co., 250 Mass. 30, at 36 

St. Louis v. Bay State St. Ry., 216 Mass. 255, at 257 The doctrine of res ipsa loquitur does not apply to collisions between moving vehicles on a highway. 

Reardon v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 247 Mass. 124 

BUT the unexplained collision of a motor truck with a large stationary excavating machine parked near the

Dorne v. Adams, 243 Mass. 438 (Starting or running of unattended motor vehicle without interference by third person) a. Skidding.

SECTION 391. 

The verb "to skid," when used in connection with the operation of a motor vehicle on the roadway, means that the car when driven slips sidewise on the road, and the rear wheels fail to grip the roadway. 

Correira v. Boston Motor Tours, Inc., 270 Mass. 88 

A jury would be warranted in finding negligence where one operating an automobile in wet car tracks at great speed suddenly turned out of the tracks and skidded.

Mere skidding of a motor car unexplained is not evidence of negligence.

The mere fact that a motor vehicle skids or slips in the road is not evidence of negligence.

The skidding of a motor vehicle is not of itself evidence of negligence. 

Marcienowski v. Sanders, 252 Mass. 65

But where there is further evidence of negligence such as that the street is icy and slippery, that the passage over the way is blocked by an approaching automobile and the

 speed of the car is "fast," then such combined facts justify a finding that the driver should know that the application of the brakes at that time would be likely to cause the vehicle to skid or slip, and constitutes negligence.

Also, where the application of the brakes upon a macadam highway, which is wet and has leaves on it, coupled with an excessive speed, would be likely to cause the car to skid and pass beyond the control of the driver, such skidding is negligence.

Logan v. Reardon, 274 Mass. 83, at 86 

In Hennessey v. Moynihan, 272 Mass. 165, the defendant's truck skidded and struck the plaintiff, who was crossing a public square. The street was wet and slippery. Lonergan v. The defendant was not entitled to the ruling limiting his liability to negligence at the time the emergency arose since his negligence cre- ated the emergency." 

Lambert v. Eastern Mass. St. Ry., 240 Mass. 495, at 499

Rasmussen v. Whipple, 211 Mass. 546, at 548

In Spain v. Oikemus, 1932 A. S. 573, the plaintiff, a pedestrian, was awaiting a trolley car at a regular stopping place. A deep bank of snow three feet in width was at the edge of the sidewalk and automobiles were parked closely both on the right and left of the plaintiff along the side next to the snow so that the plaintiff, standing about two feet away from a parked automobile was about ten feet into the street from the edge of the sidewalk. The street was icy and very slippery. Automobiles were parked so close together that it was impractical to stand anywhere else. A crowd of ten or fifteen people were together, the plaintiff being on the left and nearer the approaching trolley car. The trolley car began to slow down for the stop and the automobile of the defendant kept coming fast (at the rate of 12 to 

15 miles an hour) and not being equipped with chains, when 10 or 15 feet away, its front wheels being in the

$391 

 car track, skidded, crushing the plaintiff against a parked automobile. 

The court said at page 575: "The mere skidding of an automobile is not evidence of the negligence of its driver. But skidding may occur in connection with other actions of omission and commission under such circumstances as to support a finding of negligence." 

Brown v. Daley, 273 Mass. 432, at 434 and 435 

Hennessy v. Moynihan, 272 Mass. 165 

Lonergan v. American Ry. Express, 250 Mass. 30, at 35 Where an automobile, driven by a physician at a speed of more than thirty miles an hour round a sharp curve where the crowned surface of the road was loose and wet, skidded and overturned injuring a nurse whom he was carrying to the house of a patient, the question of his negligence is for the jury. 

Loftus v. Pelletier, 223 Mass. 63

Liability of driver and his employer for death of a pedestrian run into on the sidewalk by an automobile, control of which was lost by reason of bursting of tires when it skidded against the curbstone, where evidence warranted a finding that the skidding and loss of control were due to negligent driving. 

Roach v. Hinchcliff, 214 Mass. 267

Res ipsa loquitur is inapplicable where an automobile, skidding upon tracks of a street railway on a wet street and passing upon the sidewalk, ran into and fatally injured a pedestrian. It is erroneous to instruct the jury that lack of explanation warrants a finding of negligence. 

Williams v. Holbrook, 216 Mass. 239

b. Rear End Collisions.

§391A Evidence A rear end collision does not ordinarily give rise to the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur. However, instances may arise from which negligence may be inferred. So, where the plaintiff's automobile for a substantial distance was in front of an electric car and turned upon its track, a collision caused by the trolley car running into the rear end of the automobile may give rise to an inference that the operator of the trolley car was negligent. 

Guay v. Eastern Mass. St. Ry. Co., 1931 A. S. 2037 

Riley v. Boston El. Ry., 265 Mass. 176, at 178 and cases collected

Glennon v. Boston El. Ry., 251 Mass. 103 

(Where the street car hit an automobile which was crowded in between a tip cart and the street car, causing the automobile in turn to strike the tip cart, the plaintiff was in the tip cart and the operator of the trolley car was negligent.) 

Where the operator of an automobile going slowly passed a street car between it and the curb just as it was starting up, going in the same direction, and proceeded at least 150 feet without looking back, and, at a place where the street narrowed between the tracks and the curb the street car struck the left rear part of the automobile and pushed it onto the sidewalk into a tree, it could be found that the motorman was negligent. 

Riley v. Boston El. Ry., 265 Mass. 176 

In the last cited case, Chief Justice Rugg said at page 178: "A motorman is required to keep the street in front of his moving car constantly within his view. 

Kiley v. Boston El. Ry., 207 Mass. 542 at 544 

Ordinarily a defendant cannot run into from behind another traveler without affording evidence of negligence."

SECTION 393. 

Violation of Statute, Ordinance, Regulation, 

Rule or Custom.

A violation of a statute is some evidence of negligence. 

Dzura v. Phillips, 275 Mass. 283, at 289 

Milbury v. Turner Center System, 274 Mass. 358, at 362 The question as to whether the violation of the statute is one of the direct causes of the collision, is for the jury. 

Newton v. McSweeney, 225 Mass. 402

What effect did this violation have upon the right of either party to recover, when there was an accidental collision between two cars on the highway?

It is universally recognized that the violation of a criminal statute is evidence of negligence on the part of the violator, as to all consequences that the statute was intended to prevent. It has been said in a general way that such violation is evidence of negligence of the violator, and it has sometimes been stated that this would show negligence, that can be availed of as a ground of recovery by one who suffers any kind of an injury from him while this illegality continues; but it is now settled that it is not even evidence of negligence except in reference to matters to which the statute relates. 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, at 166 and 167

$499 Evidence 

Davis v. John L. Whiting & Son Co., 201 Mass. 91, at 96 and cases cited

A criminal statute in the usual form is enacted for the benefit of the public. It creates a duty to the public. 

Every member of the public is covered by the protecting influence of the obligation. If one suffers injury as an individual, in his person or his property, by a neglect of this duty, he has a remedy, not because our general criminal laws are divided in their operation, creating one duty to the public and a separate duty to individuals; but because as one of the public in a peculiar situation, he suffers a special injury, different in kind from that of the public generally, from the neglect of the public duty. 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, at 167 

As was said by Mr. Justice Matthews in Hayes v. 

Michigan Central Railroad, 111 U. S. 228, at 240: "The duty is due not to the city as a municipal body, but the public, considered as composed of individual persons; and each person specially injured by the breach of the obligation is entitled to his individual compensation, and to an action for its recovery." 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, at 167

The fact that the number of punishable misdemeanors has multiplied many times in recent years as the relations of men in business and society have grown complex with the increase of population, is a reason why the violation of a criminal statute of slight importance should not affect one's civil rights, except when this violation, viewed in reference to the element of criminality intended to be punished, has had a direct effect upon his cause of action. 

Our decisions seem to have been tending toward this adoption of such a rule. 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, at 169. 

Chase v. N. Y. C. & H. R. R. R. Co., 208 Mass. 137, Moran v. Dickinson, 204 Mass. 559, at 562 at 157

$393 

Dudley v. Northampton St. Ry., 202 Mass. 443, at 446 

Hall v. Ripley, 119 Mass. 135

Damon v. Scituate, 119 Mass. 66 Steele v. Burkhardt, 104 Mass. 59 

Spofford v. Harlow, 3 Allen, 176 

Welch v. Wesson, 6 Gray, 505 

Parking an automobile unlocked, contrary to statute, is not the proximate cause of a collision due to theft of the auto and the negligence of the thief who is operating. 

Slater v. T. C. Baker Co., 261 Mass. 424

Where it appeared in evidence that the operator of a motor vehicle had no license at the time of the accident the court held that evidence that he never had one was incompetent on the issue of his due care. This issue can be "determined only by his conduct at the time when the accident occurred. If the jury found, upon the facts as shown by the evidence, that his conduct did not contribute to his injury, his previous inexperience would be immaterial." 

Kenyon v. Hathaway, 274 Mass. 47, at 52 

Polmatier v. Newbury, 231 Mass. 307, at 309

In Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, at 171 and 172, where the license of the driver of the defendant's automobile expired by its own limitation the day before the accident, his application for renewal was dated two days before the accident and the new license was issued two days after the date of the accident, and there was evidence that he had driven an automobile forty thousand miles, the court said: "The operating of the automobile in itself is unobjectionable. The illegal element in the act is the failure to have a license. The purpose of the requirement of a license is to secure competency in the operator. If in any case the failure to have a license, looking to those conditions that ordinarily accompany the failure to have it, is a cause contributing directly to an injury, a violator of the law would be legally responsible to another person injured by the failure; or, if he is injured himself, would be precluded from recovery against another person who negligently contributed to the injury.” 

Kenyon v. Hathaway, 274 Mass. 47, at 52 "But we are of opinion that his failure in that respect is only evidence of negligence in reference to his fitness to operate a car, and to his skill in the actual management

$393 

 of it, unless in the case of the plaintiff, it is shown to be a contributing cause to the injury sued for, in which case it is a bar to recovery." 

Kenyon v. Hathaway, 274 Mass. 47, at 52

The jury should have been instructed that the defendant's failure to have a license was only evidence of his negligence as to the management of the car. 

Kenyon v. Hathaway, 274 Mass. 47, at 53 

In Holland v. Boston, 213 Mass. 560, at 561 and 562, the plaintiff, who was driving his own automobile without having a license to operate, sought to recover damages for a defect in the highway, the court, speaking through 

Sheldon, J., said this fact "was not necessarily fatal to his right to recover. It was merely evidence of his negligence in the management of his machine, to be considered by the jury in connection with the other evidence bearing upon that question." 

In Holden v. McGillicuddy, 215 Mass. 563, at 564, the accident occurred in Vermont and the court, assuming the common law of Vermont to be like that of Massachusetts, said: "Under our decisions the illegal conduct of the plaintiff in operating his machine without a license to do so was merely evidence of negligence on his part. But on the whole evidence the jury have found, not only that he was in the exercise of due care, but also that this illegal conduct did not contribute to the injury sued for. Under the common law, therefore, it was not a bar to his recovery." 

Kenyon v. Hathaway, 274 Mass. 47, at 53

In Pigeon v. Massachusetts Northeastern Street Rail way, 230 Mass. 392, at 395, it appeared that the plaintiff, who was driving the automobile, had for several years held an operator's license but at the time of the accident his license had expired and had not been renewed. The

$503 Evidence court there said: [The failure to have a license] “was some evidence of his negligence in operating the car, but it was not conclusive and did not warrant the ordering of a verdict." 

Kenyon v. Hathaway, 274 Mass. 47, at 53 

In McMahon v. Kenyon v. Hathaway, 274 Mass. 47, at 54

These decisions seem to have established two rules: (1) that the violation of the statute forbidding a person to operate a motor vehicle upon a way unless licensed is evidence of negligence of the operator to be considered by the jury with the other evidence tending to prove his negligence; and (2) that the violation of the statute forbidding an owner to allow an unlicensed person to operate his motor vehicle is evidence for the consideration of the jury bearing on the negligence of the owner. 

Kenyon v. Hathaway, 274 Mass. 47, at 55 

In Brown v. In a case where the defendant was licensed in Massachusetts, but the operator had a Rhode Island license and no Massachusetts license, the jury should have been permitted to consider with the other evidence bearing on the defendant's negligence the fact that his agent was driving without a Massachusetts license. It is the law that violation of a statute or ordinance is evidence of negligence.

The causal connection is broken if, between the defendant's negligent act and the plaintiff's injury, there has intervened the negligence of a third person who had full control of the situation and whose negligence was such as the defendant was not bound to anticipate and could not be said to have contemplated, which later negligence resulted directly in the injury to the plaintiff.

4. Proximate Cause. 

If other happenings cause or contribute toward the injury or intervene between the violation and the injury, the mere circumstance that there have intervened, between the wrongful cause and the injurious consequence, acts produced by the volition of animals or of human beings, does not necessarily make the result so remote that no action can be maintained. The test is to be found, not in the number of intervening events or agents, but in their character and in the natural and probable connection between the wrong done and the injurious consequences. 

So long as it affirmatively appears that the mischief is attributable to the negligence as a result which might reasonably have been foreseen as probable, the legal liability continues. 

Milbury v. Turner Center System, 274 Mass. 358, at 361 

Quoting from McDonald v. Snelling, 14 Allen, 290, at 296:

$509 Evidence "This is not an impracticable or unlimited sphere of accountability, extending indefinitely to all possible contingent consequences. An action can be maintained only where there is shown to be, first, a misfeasance or negligence in some particular as to which there was a duty towards the party injured or the community generally; and secondly, where it is apparent that the harm to the person or property of another which has actually ensued was reasonably likely to ensue from the act or omission complained of." 

Milbury v. Turner Center System, 274 Mass. 358, at 362 

Rea v. Checker Taxi Co., 272 Mass. 510

5. Ownership or Control. 

(See Sec. 405, page 528)

The fact that one is insured against liability for damage caused by a motor vehicle is admissible on the issue of ownership and control of that motor vehicle at the time of the accident.

$395 

Marsh v. Beraldi, 260 Mass. 225, at 232 and 233 

Perkins v. Rice, 187 Mass. 28, at 30

Where the plaintiff's evidence upon the question of agency and control showed that the defendant at the time of the accident and long before conducted an ice cream and fruit business; that K, his son-in-law, lived with him and worked in the business and continued to do so for a few months after the accident; that in June preceding the accident, an auto was purchased which was used to sell ice cream and fruit; that this car bore the defendant's name and was insured in his name; and the defendant testified that K bought the car with his own money entirely, registered it in his own name and went into business for himself, the defendant giving up business then; that the defendant's books had been burned in a fire; that he was ignorant that his name was on the auto or that the latter was insured in his name; and that he did not request K to take the occupants of his car for a ride; it was held the jury need not find K was not a servant of defendant.

The fact that K both before and after the accident was in the defendant's employ, that the business was carried on without apparent change except to substitute an auto for a wagon, that the auto bore the name of the defendant, the fact of insurance and even the burning of the books warranted the finding that K was in the defendant's employ.

Upon the question whether at the time of the accident it could be found K was acting in the scope of his employment, the testimony of the plaintiff that K was alone in the automobile which contained an ice cream freezer and candy boxes would warrant a finding that he was engaged in the defendant's business. 

Heywood v. Ogasapian, 224 Mass. 203 As bearing upon the scope of a servant's employment it is competent to introduce rules framed to govern such

$5II Evidence employment in order to show that the act in question is outside that scope.

SECTION 399. 

6. Due Care and Contributory Negligence of Person 

Injured.

General Laws, Chapter 231, Section 85 provides that: 

"In all actions, civil or criminal, to recover damages for injuries to the person or property or for causing the death of a person, the person injured or killed shall be presumed to have been in the exercise of due care, and contributory negligence on his part shall be an affirmative defence to be set up in the answer and proved by the defendant."

The presumption of this statute is co-extensive with the requirement as to due care. 

Burns v. Oliver Whyte Co., Inc., 231 Mass. 519, at

The presumption is commensurate with the degree of 521

$399 

care required for the plaintiff's right to recover. 

Powers v. Loring, 231 Mass. 458, at 460

The statutory presumption is not evidence and it ceases to be of force when any evidence of actual conduct of the plaintiff is introduced. 

Mahoney v. Boston El. Ry., 271 Mass. 274 

Wilmur v. Eastern Mass. St. Ry., 271 Mass. 31

Bagnell v. Boston El. Ry., 247 Mass. 235 

Duggan v. Bay State St. Ry., 230 Mass. 370

The burden of proof is on the defendant to prove that the plaintiff and another were engaged in a joint enterprise. 

Caron v. Lynn Co., 270 Mass. 340, at 346

The presumption created by the statute (G. L. c. 231, s. 85) is not evidence but merely a rule about evidence. 

Duggan v. Bay State St. Ry. Co., 230 Mass. 370, at 378 and 379 The statute does not change the law; but merely shifts the burden of proof. 

Pigeon v. Mass. Northeastern St. Ry. Co., 230 Mass. 392, at 397 

Duggan v. Bay State St. Ry. Co., 230 Mass. 370, at 378 and 379 

Miller v. Flash Chemical Co., 230 Mass. 419

This statute affects procedure only and is applicable to cases brought in this Commonwealth for injuries sustained in a foreign jurisdiction. 

Levy v. Steiger, 233 Mass. 600

Under this statute due care is presumed at the outset of the trial but when evidence is introduced, the presumption disappears and due care is determined from the evidence alone with the burden of proving the plaintiff's lack of due care resting upon the defendant.

$519 Evidence 

Ferris v. Ray Taxi Service Company, 259 Mass. 401 

Duggan v. Bay State St. Ry. Co., 230 Mass. 370, at 377 Even though the plaintiff at the time of the accident was violating the law of the road, the due care statute (G. L. c. 231, s. 85) requires the defendant to prove that the plaintiff's violation contributed to his injury. 

Mullen v. Fallon, 229 Mass. 214 

Bailey v. Worcester Cons. St. Ry. Co., 228 Mass. 477, at 480 a. Agents and Servants.

The presumption of due care under General Laws, Chapter 231, Section 85, applies only to the person injured or killed and not to his servants or agents and not to those under his control. 

Bullard v. Boston El. Ry., 226 Mass. 262, at 267 b. Children. 

The due care statute (G. L. c. 231, s. 85) is not applicable to injuries to children of tender years when received in the presence of their parents. 

Gallagher v. Johnson, 237 Mass. 455

But the statutory presumption does prevail when the children receive injuries in the absence of their parents. 

Sullivan v. Chadwick, 236 Mass. 130

C. Waiver of Statutory Presumption. 

The plaintiff may waive the benefit given to him by the due care statute. 

Grant v. Boston El. Ry., 229 Mass. 219

7. Failure to Properly Register Motor Vehicle. 

The matter of an improper or illegal registration, whether to establish liability or as a defense, places upon the party asserting it the burden of satisfactorily estab-

$400 

 lishing the facts resulting in that conclusion. 

Murray v. Indursky, 266 Mass. 220, at 223 

Conroy v. Mather, 217 Mass. 91 

Doherty v. Ayer, 197 Mass. 241

However, it need not be specially pleaded other than as a claim of contributory negligence. 

Murray v. Indursky, 266 Mass. 220, at 223

It is incumbent upon a defendant to show that a machine is not duly registered. Evidence that a car bore a registration number which had expired three months before an accident, especially when the owner offers no evidence in explanation, may warrant a finding that the car was not registered. 

Feeley v. Melrose, 205 Mass. 329

When the plaintiff claims that the defendant's automobile was a trespasser and nuisance upon the public highway, the burden of proof is on the plaintiff to prove that the defendant's automobile was not properly registered. 

Ducharme v. Coe Motors Inc., 275 Mass. 69, at 72

If at the time of the accident the automobile was not registered in the name of its owner, it was therefore unlawfully upon the highway, and the defendant owed to the plaintiff no other duty than that of abstaining from injuring him by wilfulness, wantonness, or recklessness.

SECTION 401. 

8. Failure to Obtain Proper License to Operate Motor Vehicle. 

In Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, the court said at pages 171 and 172: "Take the provision in St. 1903, c. 473, s. 5, chat: 'no person shall operate an automobile or motor cycle for hire, unless specially licensed by the commission so to do,' and the earlier provision in the same section that no person shall: 'operate an automobile or motor cycle upon any public highway or private way laid out under authority of statute unless licensed so to do under the provision of this act. The operating of the automobile in itself is unobjectionable. The illegal element in the act is the failure to have a license. The purpose of the requirement of a license is to secure competency in the operator. If in any case the failure to have a license, looking to those conditions that ordinarily accompany the failure to have it, is a cause contributing directly to an injury, a violator of the law would be legally responsible to another person injured by the failure; or, if he is injured himself, would be precluded from recovery against another person who negligently contributed to the injury. But we are of opinion that his failure in that respect is only evidence of negligence in reference to his fitness to operate a car, and to his skill in the actual management of it, unless, in the case of the plaintiff, it is shown to be a contributing cause to the injury sued for, in which case it is a bar to recovery.

We think that the operation of a car without a license, while it is a punishable act, does not render the operator a trespasser on the highway, but that the illegal element in the act is only the failure to have a license without operating it, so that if the operation and movement con-

§401 

 tributed to the accident with which the want of a license had no connection, except as a mere condition, they would not preclude the operator as a plaintiff from recovery.

If the illegal quality of the act had no tendency to cause the accident, the fact that the act is punishable because of the illegality, ought not to preclude one from recovery for harmful results to which, without negligence, the innocent features of the act alone contributed. "The difference between this provision of the statute and that involved in the present case [as to operator's license] is in part one of form, but in connection with the form, it is still more the seeming purpose and intent of the legislature as to permitting such machines upon the public ways without adequate means of identifying them and ascertaining their owner, together with the requirement that the machine itself, as a thing of power, shall have its own registration and legalization, the evidence of which it shall always carry with it." 

In Chase v. New York Central and Hudson River Rail road Company, 208 Mass. 137, at 158, is this language: "Under the decisions, the operation of the unregistered automobile is deemed to be unlawful in every feature and aspect of it. Everything in the conduct of the operator that enters into the propulsion of the vehicle is under the ban of the law. . . The operator, in running it there and thus bringing it into collision with the locomotive engine is guilty of conduct which is permeated in every part by his disobedience of the law," etc. 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, at 172 "We are of opinion that the law of these last cases should not be extended to the provision of the statute requiring every operator to have a personal license to operate the car. The jury should have been instructed that the defendant's failure to have a license was only evidence of his negligence as to the management of the car."

$523 Evidence 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, at 172

It is evidence of negligence for one to employ a chauffeur who is unlicensed.

The burden is upon the defendant to prove that an automobile is operated in violation of law. Presumptions of law and fact are always in favor of innocence. 

Conroy v. Mather, 217 Mass. 91

b. Responsibility of Owner for Operation of Motor Vehicle. 

SECTION 404. 

(I) General Statement. 

General Laws, Chapter 231, Section 85A provides that: 

"In all actions to recover damages for injuries to the person or to property or for the death of a person, arising out of an accident or collision in which a motor vehicle was involved, evidence that at the time of such accident or collision it was registered in the name of the defendant as owner shall be prima facie evidence that it was then being operated by and under the control of a person for whose conduct the defendant was legally responsible, and absence of such responsibility shall be an affirmative de-

$525 Evidence fence to be set up in the answer and proved by the defendant." 

Since this statute relates only to evidence and not to substantive rights, it regulates all trials taking place after, even though the cause of action arose before, it went into effect. 

Smith v. Freedman, 268 Mass. 38, and cases there cited The prima facie evidence created by the statute means evidence which, standing alone and unexplained, maintains the proposition and warrants the conclusion to support which it is introduced. 

Thomes v. Meyer Store Inc., 268 Mass. 587, at 588 

Emmons v. Westfield Bank, 97 Mass. 230, at 243 

Coghlan v. White, 236 Mass. 165, at 169

If such evidence is not in any way met or controlled, and relates to the decisive issue in the case, a verdict or finding is required in accordance with its effect. 

Thomes v. Meyer Store Inc., 268 Mass. 587, at 588 

Wakefield v. American Surety Co., 209 Mass. 173, at 176 The inference of the one fact from the proof of the others, as required by the statute, appears to rest upon a rational connection and is not purely arbitrary. 

Thomes v. Meyer Store Inc., 268 Mass. 587, at 589 

Opinion of the Justices, 251 Mass. 569, at 599 

Duggan v. Bay State St. Ry., 230 Mass. 370, at 380 

Opinion of the Justices, 208 Mass. 619, at 623 and 624 

Holmes v. Hunt, 122 Mass. 505, at 516 

McFarland v. American Sugar Refining Co., 241 

U. S. 79, at 86

The statute changes the rule of evidence of the common law of this Commonwealth as to this point.

$404 

 , at 

519 It is rarely that it can be ruled as matter of law that an affirmative defense has been made out or that a prima facie case has been overcome. 

Thomes v. Meyer Store Inc., 268 Mass. 587, at 589 

Lennon v. Cohen, 264 Mass. 414 

Claffey v. Fenelon, 263 Mass. 427, at 430

McDonough v. Metropolitan Life Ins. Co., 228 Mass. 

450, at 452 and cases cited

It is to be observed that the effect of this statute is to create certain specified facts when proved as prima facie evidence of a further important fact. The statute does not establish a presumption; a presumption is not evidence but a rule concerning evidence and it disappears when the facts are shown. 

Thomes v. Meyer Store Inc., 268 Mass. 587, at 589 

Comm. v. De Francesco, 248 Mass. 9, at 13 and 14 

Duggan v. Bay State St. Ry., 230 Mass. 370, at 378 and cases there collected 

See Wigmore on Evidence (2d ed.) ss. 2490 and 2494 The truth and weight of the explanation offered by the defendant, tending to meet nad control the prima facie case made out for the plaintiff under the statute, is for the consideration of the jury. The plaintiff is not bound by them and has the right to go to the jury on proof of the facts establishing the prima facie evidence that the driver of the motor vehicle was the agent of the defendant acting within the scope of his authority. 

Thomes v. Meyer Store Inc., 268 Mass. 587, at 589 and 590 

Eddy v. Johnston, 250 Mass. 299, at 301 

Leary v. William G. Webber Co., 210 Mass. 68, at 74

$527 Evidence Distinguishable from: 

Doyle v. Boston El. Ry., 248 Mass. 89, and cases there collected At most, this raises only a question of fact to be settled by the jury. 

Thomes v. Meyer Store Inc., 268 Mass. 587, at 590 

Walsh v. Feinstein, 251 Mass. 109, at 112 

McDonough v. Vozzela, 247 Mass. 552, at 558 and 559 

Barney v. Magenis, 251 Mass. 268 

Reynolds v. Denholm, 213 Mass. 576 

Proof that the motor vehicle causing damage, injury or death was registered by the defendant at the time of the accident establishes a prima facie case for the plaintiff. 

In other words, a rebuttable presumption or inference arises, from proof of the defendant's registration of the motor vehicle, that at the time of the damage, injury or death, the motor vehicle was in the registrant's control or possession and was being operated by him personally or by his agent or servant under circumstances which would render him liable for his conduct under the doctrine of respondeat superior. 

Ferreira v. Franco, 1931 A. S. 2051, at 2052 

Wilson v. Grace, 273 Mass. 146

But the owner or registrant of a motor vehicle which causes damage, injury or death is not liable merely because he owns the car and permits it to be operated. 

To establish liability, there must be evidence that the driver was the agent of the owner or registrant and at the time engaged in his business and although the statute (G. L. c. 231, s. 85A) creates prima facie presumption of this fact, the burden remains on the plaintiff to show that the operator at the time of the accident was such agent. 

Field v. Evans, 262 Mass. 315 

Dennis v. Glynn, 262 Mass. 233

Arnold v. Brereton, 261 Mass. 238

SECTION 406. 

(III) Agency and Authority of Operator. 

Acts of 1928, Chapter 317, Section 1, added a new sec tion, 85A, to General Laws, Chapter 231, which is set forth in Section 404, page 00.

This section became operative September 1, 1928. Since it is procedural in its nature, it applies to cases where, as here, the cause of action arose before, and the trial took place after, its passage. 

Wilson v. Grace, 273 Mass. 146, at 150 

Haun v. LeGrand, 268 Mass. 582

$529 Evidence 

Thomes v. Meyer Store Inc., 268 Mass. 587 

The case brought by Sophie Wilson being an action "to recover damages for injuries to the person," is within the terms of the statute. 

Wilson v. Grace, 273 Mass. 146, at 151

By force of this statute, the fact that the motor vehicle was registered in the name of the defendant as owner is "prima facie evidence that it was then being operated by and under the control of a person for whose conduct the defendant is legally responsible," and the absence of such responsibility is an affirmative defense to be set up in the answer and proved by defendant. 

Wilson v. Grace, 273 Mass. 146, at 151 

Smith v. Freedman, 268 Mass. 38

This statute does not impose upon the owner of an automobile liability for the negligence of the unauthorized operator, whether or not such operator is a thief or is violating General Laws, Chapter 90, Section 24, as amended by Acts 1926, Chapter 253 by using "a motor vehicle without authority knowing that such use is unauthorized." 

Wilson v. Grace, 273 Mass. 146, at 151

This statute, merely as a matter of trial procedure; (a) puts upon the owner the burden of proving that the automobile was not "being operated by and under the control of a person for whose conduct [he] was legally responsible," with the attendant risk of liability if he does not sustain the burden, Wilson v. Grace, 273 Mass. 146, at 151 

Smith v. Freedman, 268 Mass. 38, at 40 and (b) makes the fact that the automobile was registered in the name of the defendant as owner prima facie evidence (as it was not before the passage of the statute) 

Wilson v. Grace, 273 Mass. 146, at 151

 , at 

519 that the automobile was "being operated by and under the control of" such a person. 

Wilson v. Grace, 273 Mass. 146, at 151 

Even though the defendant sets up in his answer the affirmative defense that the operator of his automobile was not acting as his agent or servant, it usually cannot be ruled as matter of law in accordance with this contention, that the prima facie evidence of agency was overcome and the affirmative defense proved. 

Wilson v. Grace, 273 Mass. 146, at 151

And this is so even if the testimony of the defendant's witness is uncontradicted, and tends to show the operator's lack of authority, and the plaintiff is not bound by their testimony. 

Wilson v. Grace, 273 Mass. 146, at 152

Duggan v. Bay State, 230 Mass. 370, at 378 and cases collected

But the effect of this statute is to create certain specified facts when proved as prima facie evidence of a further important fact, and testimony of plaintiff's or defendant's witnesses raise merely a question of fact to be settled by the jury. 

Thomes v. Meyer Store Inc., 268 Mass. 587, at 589 

SECTION 407. 

c. Responsibility of Guest for Acts of Opera tor. 

A guest is presumed to be in the exercise of due care. 

Bullard v. Boston El. Ry., 226 Mass. 262

$533 Evidence But evidence that the guest exercised some control over the operator is admissible. 

Also evidence that the guest intrusted his safety to the operator and abandoned all care to look out for himself is admissible. 

Such evidence may be by expressed language or implied from conduct. 

Shultz v. Old Colony Ry., 193 Mass. 309 

d. Insurance. 

SECTION 408. 

Before the Compulsory Insurance Law (Acts 1925, Chap. 346) evidence of the fact that the defendant was insured against accident was not admissible as evidence of his negligence or control of the vehicle. 

Anderson v. Duckworth, 162 Mass. 251

But such evidence probably would be admissible now to show the real ownership of the vehicle for which registration was procured.

So, before the statute, evidence that the plaintiff's automobile was insured against theft was inadmissible on the issue of the genuineness of a plaintiff's claim that the car had been stolen. 

Feins v. Ralby, 245 Mass. 228

However, the fact of insurance is admissible to prove ownership. 

Lekarczyk v. Dupre, 265 Mass. 33 

Stevens v. Stewart, 223 Mass. 44, at 46 and 47 

Perkins v. Rice, 187 Mass. 28

It also is admissible to prove that the defendants were partners and were jointly liable. 

Rosseau v. Deschenes, 206 Mass. 469

Also a conversation in which the defendant admits his

$409 

 liability is not to be excluded because the defendant refers to the fact that he is insured against accident, if the jury is instructed that the fact of insurance should be disregarded. 

Anderson v. Duckworth, 162 Mass. 251

A witness may be asked if he is in the employ of the insurance company for whose benefit the action is brought. 

This evidence is not admissible as evidence of negligence but is permissible to show bias. 

Dempsey v. Goldstein Bros. Amusement Co., 231 

Mass. 461, at 464

A report made to an insurance company under the policy is admissible to prove ownership of the team where the ownership is denied. 

Sibley v. Nason, 196 Mass. 125, at 129

Also other material facts stated in such a report make the report admissible. 

Sibley v. Nason, 196 Mass. 125, at 129 e. 

SECTION 409. 

Circumstances and Manner of the Accident. 

The manner of the happening of the accident and all the surrounding circumstances are admissible to show the negligence of the defendant and the due care of the plaintiff and to supply the standard by which the conduct of all the parties concerned should have been governed. 

So, where the motor vehicle of the plaintiff was damaged by the defendant's motor vehicle running into it in the rear, the defendant contended the accident was caused by another motor vehicle belonging to M. & L. The plaintiff asked the defendant on the stand if he had sued M. & L. and the defendant replied that he had not. The defendant was then asked by his counsel what he had done about his claim, but was not permitted to answer. 

The defendant then offered to prove by E. that the de-

535 Evidence fendant wrote to M. & L. and was referred to an insurance company and presented his claim for damages and was told the insurance company wanted to await the outcome of the suit of Foley v. Lord, because it did not want to do anything which might be construed as an admission against M. & L. in any claim which Foley might bring against the latter. It was held that it was the defendant's contention that M. & L. were primarily responsible for the accident. In the absence of this evidence the jury might well infer that this defense was a mere makeshift because the defendant having been sued had taken no steps whatsoever to assert his claim against them if the plaintiff recovered judgment. 

Foley v. Lord, 232 Mass. 368

SECTION 410. 

f. Ability to Avoid the Accident.

The ability of the defendant to avoid the accident and the reasonableness of his conduct in failing to do so are proper subjects to be admitted in evidence. 

g. Physical Conditions at the Place of the Ac cident.

SECTION 411. 

(I) General Statement. 

A jury which views the scene of the accident, the premises, the driveway, the width of the street, and its grade, may determine, without other evidence, the extent to which the view of an operator approaching the place would be obscured. 

Brown v. Daley, 273 Mass. 432, at 435

SECTION 413. 

General Statement. 

The test of excessive speed is found in the statute,

537 Evidence (G. L. c. 90, s. 17) which establishes rates of speed which are prima facie excessive. 

Clark v. Martin, 261 Mass. 60 (25 miles an hour-tire marks-25 feet before vehicle stopped) 

Bogert v. Thompson, 260 Mass. 206

Proof of the fact of excessive speed may be shown by means of photo speed recorder. 

Comm. v. Buxton, 205 Mass. 49 

In Clark v. Martin, 261 Mass. 60, at 63, it is said: "Many people came out of the casino with the intestate, Marjorie and the Soucy girl, and were crossing the street, some from the driveway and some at the crosswalk. There were adults and ‘about a hundred children.' The automobile came from the east, was running twenty-five miles an hour when it turned southerly to avoid the intestate. 

It struck him with the fender, passed over him, and ran twenty-five feet before it stopped. Tire marks on the pavement, due to application of the brakes, extended from a point about thirty-five feet easterly of the crosswalk in a southwesterly direction to the westerly line of the crosswalk."

The driving of a motor vehicle at a speed which prevents the operator from stopping within the length of his vision is negligence as matter of law. 

Morehouse v. Everett, 141 Wash. 399

SECTION 414. 

Opinion or Estimate. 

Usually, anyone may testify as to speed. 

Johnston v. Bay State St. Ry., 222 Mass. 582, at 585 

As was said in Davidson v. Beacon Hill Taxi Service,

Inc., 1932 A. S. 567: 

"It is well settled that proof of speed of a motor vehicle does not depend solely upon expert testimony but that any witness may testify respecting such speed if found by the presiding judge to understand the nature of an oath and to possess sufficient knowledge and intelligence to testify to the point. Much must be left to the discretion of the judge before whom the case is heard. "The undisputed evidence of the witness was to the effect that he ran out of the alley into the street and saw the defendant's taxicab for the first time when it was 15 feet away.

It is inconceivable that he could have had any intelligent opinion as to the speed of the taxicab in these circumstances. His estimate of its speed was too unreliable and untrustworthy to charge the jury upon that question." 

So, a boy nineteen years of age, not an expert, may so testify. 

Creedon v. Galvin, 226 Mass. 140, at 143 

Also a fourteen year old boy may testify as to speed of the defendant's motor vehicle, particularly if he has driven a motor vehicle and his attention was called to the defendant's motor vehicle by seeing its lights when it was about one hundred sixty feet from the point of the accident and he had it in full view until it struck the plaintiff. 

Mahoney v. Gooch, 246 Mass. 567 

70 A. L. R. 545

The owner of a car who has driven for fourteen years is competent to testify that a car travelling fifteen miles. an hour can be stopped in twelve feet.

$539 Evidence 

Foley v. Lord, 232 Mass. 368

In Koch v. Lynch, 247 Mass. 459, it was held that a witness who did not see an automobile “until it had just struck the plaintiff," ought not to be permitted to give his opinion as to its speed, as he could have had no intelligent thought about it, even though he was fifty-seven years of age. 

70 A. L. R. 547

As a matter of law a witness may testify as to the comparison of speeds of vehicles by use of the words "it was going considerably faster."

This testimony is not a mere epithet as descriptive of speed. 

Sax v. Horn, 274 Mass. 428, at 430 

Marcienowski v. Sanders, 252 Mass. 65, at 67 

Whalen v. Mutrie, 247 Mass. 316, at 318 

Selibedea v. Worcester Cons. St. Ry., 223 Mass. 76 

Singer Sewing Machine Co. v. Springfield St. Ry., 216 Mass. 138

While a witness' testimony is not couched in terms of miles per hour, it is a statement of comparison touching the relative speeds of two or more vehicles involved in an accident.

It is or might be material on the issue of the fault of the drivers to determine which automobile was being driven at the higher rate of speed. 

Sax v. Horn, 274 Mass. 428, at 430

But witness may be unable to express a helpful opinion as to the rates of speed of motor vehicles, and yet give an accurate estimate of their relative speeds. Such testimony is entitled to probative value. 

Sax v. Horn, 274 Mass. 428, at 430 

Noyes v. Noyes, 224 Mass. 125, at 129 and 130 

Johnston v. Bay State St. Ry., 221 Mass. 583, at 585

$415 

Welch v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R., 176 Mass. 393

This is especially true where the plaintiff might have been found to be entitled to the right of way across the area constituting the intersection of two streets and where the defendant was approaching it. 

Sax v. Horn, 274 Mass. 428, at 430 

Fournier v. Zinn, 257 Mass. 575 

G. L. c. 89, s. 8 (as amended by Acts 1926, c. 330; 

Acts 1928, c. 357, s. 4; Acts 1929, c. 147, s. I)

An expert only may testify as to the distance in which a motor vehicle stops at different speeds with locked brakes. 

Foley v. Lord, 232 Mass. 368, at 370

SECTION 415. 

(III) Distance Travelled by the Defendant's Vehicle After the Accident. 

Where the defendant vehicle, after striking a pedestrian, went about a hundred feet before it came to a stop, this fact is an indication of its excessive speed. 

Hepburn v. Walters, 263 Mass. 139, at 141

Approaching a group of children in the street at the rate of fifteen to twenty miles an hour and then travelling sixty feet after the child was hurt is evidence of negligence. 

Linnane v. Millman, 261 Mass. 491 

Gaulin v. Yagoobian, 261 Mass. 145, at 147

In determining the speed of the defendant's motor vehicle the damage done to the other vehicle may be considered as well as the position in which the respective vehicles were found after the collision.

SECTION 417. 

(V) Tire Marks. 

A mark observed in the street caused by the defendant's motor vehicle and the effect of the impact of the defendant's motor vehicle with that of the plaintiff has some competency to show its speed, and a jury may infer that in its operation the operator was negligent. 

Barrett v. Checker Taxi Co., 263 Mass. 252, at 254

Evidence is admissible that after the accident there were tire marks on the road which corresponded with the tread of the tires of the defendant's motor vehicle and showed that the vehicle was two feet away from the curbing on the side of the street at the time of the collision. 

Podwapinska v. Teixeira, 1931 A. S. 2397, at 2398 

Also evidence is proper that there was a red paint mark on the street corresponding with the paint on the plaintiff's bicycle, and a mark on the metal of the bumper and also on the middle of the radiator of the defendant's vehicle, showing the point of contact with the bicycle. 

Podwapinska v. Teixeira, 1931 A. S. 2397, at 2398

In Isaacson v. Boston, Worcester and New York Street 

Railway Company, 1932 A. S. 385, the court said at page 393: "The testimony of Ward, the driver of the bus, as to the cause of the accident in its important details corresponds with the testimony of witnesses who on that night were westbound. The brake marks on the roadway bear mute corroboration."

ווה i. Control.

$543 Evidence Any evidence tending to show whether the motor vehicle was or was not under control of the operator is admissible.

SECTION 419. 

j. Intoxication. 

To sustain a conviction for driving under the influence of liquor, the Commonwealth need not prove that the defendant was drunk; the fact that within half an hour after inflicting the injury, he was under the influence of liquor is sufficient. 

Comm. v. Lyseth, 250 Mass. 555, at 558

The presence or absence of other vehicles or travellers in the street is immaterial. 

Comm. v. Lyseth, 250 Mass. 555, at 558

Also the engine of the motor vehicle need not be running. 

Comm. v. Clarke, 254 Mass. 566

The drunkenness of an operator does not necessarily compel the conclusion of fact that he was grossly negligent. 

Bertera v. Cuneo, 273 Mass. 181, at 183 

k. Acts and Conduct. 

(I) 

SECTION 420. 

BEFORE Accident. 

Acts and conduct of the operator and occupants of a motor vehicle shortly before, and not too remote from, the time of the accident, are admissible if they have a

$421 

 direct bearing upon the questions of negligence and due care of the respective parties at the time of the accident. 

So, an operator's failure to sound the horn or pay any attention to a pedestrian, after seeing the pedestrian at a place where the pedestrian might start to cross the street, may be found to be negligent conduct on the part of the operator. 

Barrett v. Checker Taxi Co., 263 Mass. 252, at 254 and 255 

SECTION 421. 

(II) AFTER Accident. 

Acts and conduct of the operator after the accident, and those who were riding with him at the time of the accident, are admissible if they are directly connected with the conditions and circumstances that existed at the time the plaintiff received his injury or damage.

So, the distance that the defendant's vehicle travels after striking the plaintiff may well be considered as some evidence of improper operation. 

Hepburn v. Walters, 263 Mass. 139, at 141

Merely to take the injured person to a hospital and promise the pay for his treatment is not an admission of liability. 

Wilson v. Daniels, 250 Mass. 359, at 364 

1. Conversations, Statements, Declarations. 

SECTION 422. 

(I) BEFORE Accident. 

Conversation between occupants of the plaintiff's motor vehicle immediately preceding a collision is not admissible upon the question of the operator's due care especially where each occupant at the trial has described what was done at the moment. 

Nathan v. Boston El. Ry., 229 Mass. 63

Evidence that passenger in vehicle said to driver "Look out for street cars," is not admissible upon driver's due care.

Nathan v. Boston El. Ry., 229 Mass. 62. 

But distinguish cases where the conduct of two people depends upon the reliance each puts on the other, as in

SECTION 423. 

(II) AT OR NEAR THE TIME of Accident. 

Statements made simultaneously with the accident are considered part of the res gestae and are admissible. 

Conklin v. Consolidated Ry. Co., 196 Mass. 302, at 

306 

Of course, statements of the defendant personally, or those made in his presence, are always admissible as bearing upon his negligence and due care.

The res gestae really becomes important when the statements of a third person such as an agent are offered as evidence. 

O'Connell v. Cox, 179 Mass. 250, at 254 

Cooley v. Norton, 4 Cush. 93 

Richards v. Humphreys, 15 Pick. 133

But a recital as to past conduct or action is not admissible when made by a third person although it may have. some relation to the act which the person may be doing at the time when he makes the declaration.

Rankin v. Brockton Public Market, Inc., 257 Mass. 

6, at II

Haynes v. Rutter, 24 Pick. 242 

Woods v. Clark, 24 Pick. 35

It is competent for the plaintiff to introduce a conversation between the defendant and a passenger in his car, one-half mile from the place of and before the accident, to show that the defendant should have known, and therefore could be found negligent in not knowing that application of the brakes, considering the condition of the highway and the speed of the car, would be likely to cause the car to skid and pass beyond the control of the driver. 

Hiller v. Desautels, 269 Mass. 437, at 438 

Arnold v. Brereton, 261 Mass. 238 

Lambert v. Eastern Mass. St. Ry., 240 Mass. 495

It is also admissible to controvert the contention of the defendant that his act in applying the brakes under the conditions as they existed with respect to the speed of the car and character of the roadway was not negligent conduct because, though unwise, it was induced by an emergency which required action on the "spur of the moment." 

Hiller v. Desautels, 269 Mass. 437, at 438

Evidence between the accident and the conduct of the operator of the omnibus immediately before the accident, and thereby to throw light upon the issue of whether or not the driver exercised the highest degree of care for the safety of the plaintiffs which was consistent with the defendant's undertaking.

(III) AFTER Accident. 

When the owner of a motor vehicle is told that he has killed the deceased who was the sole support of her mother, and the owner said, “Never mind, . . . I am insured and I will take care of her mother," this is an admission of liability. 

Shepherd v. Nirenstein, 273 Mass. 7, at 8 

Also, a reply by the defendant that: "You bring your boy in the hospital and tomorrow and after tomorrow I come in your house, I fix it up everything," is an admission of liability on the part of the defendant and can be found to have been a promise to pay not only the plaintiff's hospital bills but all damages sustained by the plaintiff as the result of his injuries, hence this is evidence of

$425 

 an admission of liability on the part of the defendant. 

Bernasconi v. Bassi, 261 Mass. 26, at 28 and 29 

Jasman v. Meany, 250 Mass. 576 

Dennison v. Swerdlove, 250 Mass. 507

The declaration of the wife of the owner of a motor vehicle to the effect that if the plaintiff had to go to the hospital she would pay the expenses is not an admission of liability of the motor vehicle owner nor of any liability or legal obligation of the wife. 

Kindell v. Ayles, 263 Mass. 244

However, a statement made by a chauffeur after an accident that "the A. G. Co. would take care of the boy" was not made in the performance of his duty and was not binding on the defendant. 

O'Rourke v. A. G. Co., 232 Mass. 129

(I) Consciousness of Liability. 

SECTION 427. 

(A) Conveyance of All Attachable Prop erty.

The voluntary conveyance of all of one's attachable property, after notice of the plaintiff's claim, to avoid an attachment by the plaintiff may be admitted as evidence of consciousness of liability on the part of the defendant as to amount to admission of the plaintiff's claims. 

Wilson v. Grace, 273 Mass. 146, at 155 

Carroll v. Carroll, 262 Mass. 10, at 12 

Portland Gaslight Co. v. Raud, 242 Mass. 272, at 275 

Bennett v. Susser, 191 Mass. 329, at 331 

Banfield v. Whipple, 10 Allen, 27, at 31

The mere fact that, having notice of the plaintiff's claim, the next year after the accident, though continuing to own the automobile, the defendant had it registered in the name of his daughter who was not licensed to operate motor vehicles, does not warrant a finding that the automobile "constituted all of the defendant's attachable property, and was voluntarily conveyed to avoid an attachment by the plaintiff" thereby showing such consciousness of liability on the part of the defendant for the results of the accident as to amount to an admission thereof. 

Wilson v. Grace, 273 Mass. 146, at 155

SECTION 428. 

Condition and Equipment of Motor Vehicle. 

See: Sections 107-117, pages 158-169. 

The plaintiffs were riding in an automobile without skid chains upon an icy and slushy road. At a certain point in the road the car skidded sixty to seventy feet, coming in contact with an electric light pole, lying within a few feet of the gutter and parallel thereto, in such a way that the driver lost steering control and ran into ant electric light pole on the side of the road. The pole in the road had lain there ten days. It was held the jury could find that the position of the pole had not changed during the ten days it was on the ground, that its presence was not helpful or necessary to the prosecution of any remaining work of the defendant, that it was an obstruction and a menace to travel and made the travelled way unsafe unless its presence was justified. It might have been found that the collision with the upright pole was a consequence of the contact with the pole on the ground. 

Whether it was safe under the conditions to operate a car without chains was a question for the jury and not for an expert. 

Reed v. Edison Elec. Illg. Co., 225 Mass. 163

SECTION 431. 

q. Compromise, Settlement or Release. 

A compromise, settlement or release with the defendant, if specially pleaded, is admissible. 

So also a compromise, settlement, release or discharge with a joint tortfeasor of the defendant is admissible. 

O'Neil v. National Oil Co., 231 Mass. 20, at 29

Under this rule, the defendant not being a party to the transaction with a joint tortfeasor can show that the actual agreement with the joint tortfeasor was in effect a full discharge even though the written documents showed that it was merely a covenant not to sue. 

O'Neil v. National Oil Co., 231 Mass. 20, at 29 

Any amount paid by a joint tortfeasor upon a covenant not to sue must be deducted from the damages to be awarded the plaintiff as against the defendant. 

O'Neil v. National Oil Co., 231 Mass. 20, at 29

SECTION 431A. 

(I) Release Distinguished from Covenant not to Sue. 

See Section 369, page 453.

Although the plaintiff has given a written covenant not to sue to another joint tortfeasor and has made a settlement with him, the defendant may show that the real transaction between the plaintiff and that joint tortfeasor was a discharge of liability and not merely a covenant not

$432 

 to sue.

That is, it is open to the defendant to contend that the real transaction was an extinguishment, a complete discharge of the cause of action and not a mere covenant not to sue, and if the defendant successfully shows by the greater weight of the evidence that the transaction was a complete release and discharge, then the plaintiff is barred against the defendant. 

Green v. Hoffarth, 1931 A. S. 2451, at 2453 

O'Neil v. National Oil Co., 231 Mass. 20, at 28 

Matheson v. O'Kane, 211 Mass. 91

So, although the plaintiff testifies in cross examination that she had stated to a third person, that for a given sum she would discharge any claims she had against the joint tortfeasor to whom she consequently gave a written covenant not to sue, yet she may also testify on redirect examination by use of the word "discharge" she meant that she did not intend to bring such joint tortfeasor in to court. 

As was said in Green v. Hoffarth, 1931 A. S. 2451, at 2453 and 2454: "We are of the opinion that [the plaintiff] in saying "yes" to a question in which the word "discharge" was used cannot as of law be held to have intended to use the word in its strict legal sense. In view of her explanation of her understanding of its meaning and the absence of any evidence to show what [the third person was saying and what his authority was to represent the defendant] in the matter, the ruling leaving to the jury the question whether the claim was in fact discharged was sufficiently favorable to the defendant." 

SECTION 432. 

(II) Offers to.

An offer of compromise is not to be given in evidence against the party making it. The rule is founded in

555 Evidence policy that there may be no discouragement to amicable adjustment of disputes by a fear that if not completed, the party amicably disposed may be injured. 

Strauss v. Skurnik, 227 Mass. 173

Grebenstein v. Stone and Webster Engineering Corp., 205 Mass. 431 

Higgins v. Shepard, 182 Mass. 364 

Hill v. Commercial Union Ins. Co., 164 Mass. 406 

Draper v. Hatfield, 124 Mass. 53 

Gay v. Bates, 99 Mass. 263 

Batchelder v. Bates, 2 Allen, 105 

Harrington v. Lincoln, 4 Gray, 567 

Upton v. So. Reading R. R. Co., 8 Cush. 600 

Gerrish v. Sweetser, 4 Pick. 374 (A)

Courts and trial justices shall, upon their own initiative or upon the request of the registrar or his agents, furnish to the registrar the details of all particularly flagrant cases which may be heard before them; and they may make such recommendations to the registrar as to the suspension or revocation of the licenses and certificates of registration of the defendants in such cases as they may deem necessary."

SECTION 436. 

Damage caused to the motor vehicle and reasonable value for the loss of its use are admissible in evidence. 

The damage may consist in the cost of repair or restoration, or, when the injury to the motor vehicle cannot be adequately compensated by the cost of repairs, the measure of recovery may be the difference between its value at the time of the accident and its value in the condition immediately following it. 

Antokol v. Barber, 248 Mass. 393 (Loss of use)

As was said in the above cited case, at page 396: "The allegation of great damage to the automobile of the plaintiff implies not only expense of repair but also loss of use while the harm caused by the collision is being mended. . .. The loss of use of the automobile during the period of repair is as much the natural and necessary consequence of the tortious act of the defendant described in the declaration as is the cost of the repair."

(II) Conscious Suffering. 

A statement made by a deceased may be admissible as an admission against interest in a suit for conscious suffering but is not admissible in a suit for death which is in behalf of next of kin where there is no privity with deceased.

S. 385, the court said, at page 397: "The evidence that he was 'standing up in the centre of the fire' and was groping with his hands is not naturally explainable as reflex movements, but tends to show consciousness and an intelligent attempt to escape from the fire. The nature of the groans as above described to the jury and the sharp intake of breath described cannot be said as matter of law not to indicate the pain and

$561 Evidence suffering of a dying man. Although the case is close upon this issue, we cannot say that the foregoing testimony did not indicate conscious suffering."

In the early case of Townsend v. Pepperell, 99 Mass. 

40, the records of a hospital were properly admitted in evidence to show that there was nothing in the recorded condition or treatment of a certain patient to indicate that she was insane, even though the record was made forty years before, and the person by whom it was made was not identified. The decision was apparently based on the ancient document rule. 

In Cashin v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R., 185 Mass. 543, the court referring to Townsend v. Pepperell, 99 Mass. 40 said that in that case "the record was admitted evidently upon the doctrine that, it being more than thirty years old, there was no need to show the death of the person who made it." Holding that (probably for lack of a

$439 

 proper foundation,) the records were properly excluded, the court said at page 546: "In the case of the books which were offered as records of the respective hospitals, it was not contended that, as to either institution, the records were kept under any requirement of law. They were, therefore, not public records, and were not admissible, unless supported by the testimony of the one who made them, if that person were still alive and capable of being produced to testify.. 

The court may well have found upon the evidence as to each hospital both that the records were imperfect and that there was no reason to suppose that the writers could not be produced."

By Acts 1905, Chapter 330, records of public hospitals were made admissible as evidence as to all matters therein contained; 

Clark v. Beacon Oil Co., 271 Mass. 27, at 29 and Acts 1908, Chapter 269, made admissible records kept before and after 1905. 

Clark v. Beacon Oil Co., 271 Mass. 27, at 29 

Delaney v. Framingham Gas etc. Co., 202 Mass. 359

Under the statute as thus amended, it was held in Raymond v. Flint, 225 Mass. 521, that records of the date of 1896 were admissible in a proceeding which involved the mental capacity of a deceased patient, for the purpose of showing her treatment and medical history while at the hospital. 

The Legislature felt that entries were made which ought not to be taken in evidence, and so enacted Acts 1912, Chapter 442 which amended the earlier statutes of 1905 and 1908 by limiting the requirement to keeping "records of the treatment of the cases under their care and the medical history of the same" (inserting the words here underlined); and by striking out from the enactment giving the records admissibility in evidence the words "as to

$565 Evidence all matters therein contained" and inserting in their place "so far as such records relate to the treatment and medical history of such cases; but nothing therein contained shall be admissible as evidence which has reference to the question of liability." 

Karpowicz v. Seder, 275 Mass. 413

Whipple v. Grandchamp, 261 Mass. 40

Glass v. Metropolitan Life Ins. Co., 258 Mass. 127 

G. L. c. 233, s. 79 

G. L. c. III, s. 70

In practice "the liability" referred to in the statute is liability for damage caused by the happenings which occasioned or attended the patient's presence in the hospital. 

A distinction is, therefore, made between (a) entries which record details of diagnosis, treatment and prognosis with mention of facts helpful to the understanding of the medical or surgical case and (b) those which narrate events or state facts connected with the patient or the occasion for his resort to the hospital but having no reference to his treatment or medical history in the hospital. 

Clark v. Beacon Oil Co., 271 Mass. 27, at 30 

So, a record is inadmissible which recites that: "while patient was running along the road four days ago, she was run over by an automobile producing injuries as per local [left leg]." 

Clark v. Beacon Oil Co., 271 Mass. 27, at 30 

Inangelo v. Petterson, 236 Mass. 439, at 440

Hospital records dealing with the history and treatment of the case were considered upon the question of liability arising in the proceedings.

§439

Beacon Oil Co., 271 Mass. 27, at 30 It was held that too strict a rule was imposed in confining consideration of an entry in a hospital record "Vomited fluid twice resembling coffee grounds and had an odor of whiskey," simply to the treatment and medical history. The fact of the presence of an odor of whiskey in the vomitus of the injured man could be considered in deciding whether the patient had used whiskey shortly before the accident out of which the action arose; and, in substance, decided that facts shown by evidence of entries in hospital records, admissible properly under the statute, may be considered upon any issue to which they are relevant under the rules of law. 

Clark v. Beacon Oil Co., 271 Mass. 27, at 30

Clark v. Beacon Oil Co., 271 Mass. 27, at 28 

Leonard v. Boston El. Ry., 234 Mass. 480

Nor should consideration of these words be limited to being evidence only upon and in connection with the patient's physical condition and excluded as reference in connection with the liability or cause of the accident or as evidence or proof that the patient at the time of the accident was under the influence of liquor. 

Clark v. Beacon Oil Co., 271 Mass. 27, at 30

The improper application of the facts recorded can be prevented by means of suitable instructions to the jury. 

Leonard v. Boston El. Ry., 234 Mass. 480, at 482

w. Expert Testimony.

$440 

 give opinions is not confined to the evidence of experts, testifying on subjects requiring special knowledge, skill or learning, but includes the evidence of common observers, testifying to the results of their observations, made at the time, in regard to common appearances of facts and a condition of things which cannot be reproduced and made palpable to a jury. Nor is it a mere opinion which is thus given by a witness, but a conclusion of fact to which his judgment, observation, and common knowledge has led him in regard to a subject matter which requires no special learning or experiment, but which is within the knowledge of men in general. . . The competency of this evidence rests upon two necessary conditions, first, that the subject matter to which the testimony relates cannot be reproduced or described to the jury precisely as it appeared to the witness at the time; and second, that the facts, upon which the witness is called to express his opinion, are such as men in general are capable of comprehending and understanding The same rule applies to this class of testimony as to the testimony of experts; whether the expert is competent by his study of business, and whether he has qualified himself to testify or had proper opportunity to examine, are preliminary questions for the court."
