Duggan v. Bay State St. Ry., 230 Mass. 370, at 382

An expert cannot be asked to give an opinion "on the evidence in the case" if the evidence is conflicting. 

Connor v. O'Donnell, 230 Mass. 39

As to who is an expert, this is a matter largely in the discretion of the trial judge. 

Old Colony Trust Co. v. DiCole, 233 Mass. 119, at 125 Questions should not be framed on possibilities, Taylor v. Whittier, 240 Mass. 514 

or interpretations of the law, Killam v. St. Oil Co., 248 Mass. 575 or call for matters outside the range of expert opinion. 

Comm. v. Reilly, 248 Mass. I

In a death case if facts are in issue the court may exclude the question, "What caused the death?" 

Comm. v. Williams, 244 Mass. 515, at 521 The same rule applies in all cases. 

Convery v. Eastern Mass. St. Ry. Co., 252 Mass. 418

The remoteness of time of the conditions on which an expert rests his opinion is largely within the court's discretion. 

Goldman v. Regan, 247 Mass. 492

Much is left to the court's discretion, in the examination of medical experts. 

King v. Belmor, 248 Mass. 108

The cross-examination of an expert in tort cases frequently tends to show that an insurance company representing the defendant hired the expert. Such evidence is usually admitted only if necessary to preserve the rights of the party.

$575 Evidence 

Bilodeau v. Fitchburg St. Ry., 236 Mass. 526

The credibility of an expert is for the jury. 

Comm. v. O'Brien, 254 Mass. 86

If a question to an expert as to the distance within which a driver should have stopped his truck does not include all the elements properly to be taken into account to render the opinion competent, it may be excluded. 

Hicks v. H. B. Church Truck Service Co., 259 Mass. 272 

Comm. v. Mara, 253 Mass. 793 

See: Medical Testimony, section 439, page 561. (II) 

Cross-Examination. 

"In the present case the objectionable cross-examination, against the repeated objection and exception of the defendant was continued so that as reported it covers more than five pages of the exceptions. Similar questions were put in different forms as to different treatises, ending with general questions calling for and eliciting answers as to any text books that might agree with the claim of the plaintiff and accompanied by the display of several medical books on the table of the counsel. "As in Kaler v. Builders' Mutual Fire Insurance Co., 120 Mass. 333, at 335, 'the effect, and as may reasonably be supposed the purpose,' of counsel were to bring before the jury the opinions of others who were, it was suggested, persons skilled in such matters, and to lessen the weight of the witness's testimony by showing that their views were different from his. His testimony was not affected and the desired object was not attained unless this effect was produced by use of the incompetent means allowed to be resorted to. We should hesitate to say that even a broad instruction to the jury to disregard wholly the evidence thus obtained would have cured the injury which had been caused to the defendant." 

Allen v. Boston El, Ry., 212 Mass. 191, at 194

8441 

"But no such instruction was given. The incompetent evidence was not stricken out, and the jury were not told to disregard it. They were merely instructed, with emphasis and elaboration it is true, not to consider the opinions expressed by the authors of medical books; and the context abundantly shows that this meant only that they were not to consider such opinions as bearing upon the medical questions raised in the case. All the evidence remained before them, and they were left at full liberty to consider these opinions as differing from those of Dr. 

Baldwin and so bearing upon the weight of his testimony." 

Allen v. Boston El. Ry., 212 Mass. 191, at 194 

See also: 

Comm. v. Homer, 235 Mass. 526, at 534 and 535

D. WEIGHT AND SUFFICIENCY OF EVIDENCE. 

SECTION 441. 

The jury is not obliged to give credence to the testimony of the defendant even if uncontradicted and may disbelieve that part of it tending to exonerate him from blame. 

Tyrrell v. Caruso, 269 Mass. 379, at 380 and 381

The jury may believe as much of the testimony or evidence of a party which is in the nature of an admission and disbelieve such portions as are favorable to him. 

Gordon v. Bedard, 265 Mass. 408, at 411, and cases collected So, where the defendant testified that his son took his truck in his presence but that he forbade his son to take it, the jury could believe that the son in the plaintiff's presence took the truck, but the jury could disbelieve that the defendant forbade his son to take it.

$577 Evidence 

Gordon v. Bedard, 265 Mass. 408, at 411

Where the physical facts are irrefutable they may have a decisive bearing upon the questions of the defendant's negligence and the plaintiff's due care and contributory negligence.

Palombella v. Foss, 1931 A. S. 2049 

Evidence that a pedestrian was intoxicated at the time of his injury does not warrant the direction of a verdict against him. 

Martin v. Florin, 273 Mass. 13

When testimony of a witness is radically inconsistent on direct and cross-examination, it cannot be said that the testimony on cross-examination, as matter of law, has the effect of annuling that given on direct examination. 

Coyle v. Worcester Cons. St. Ry. Co., 273 Mass. 475, at 476 

Haun v. LeGrand, 268 Mass. 582 

Martin v. Boston El. Ry., 262 Mass. 542, at 544 

Sullivan v. Boston El. Ry., 224 Mass. 405

The rule is different where the witness has made two distinct statements touching the same event, and finally adheres to one in preference to the other as being the truth and is therefore bound by it. 

But see: 

Martin v. Boston El. Ry., 262 Mass. 542, at 544 

Sullivan v. Boston El. Ry., 224 Mass. 405

But where the witness has made more or less inconsistent statements in the course of the examination, it is for the jury to say where the truth is. 

Coyle v. Worcester Cons. St. Ry., 273 Mass. 475, at 477 

2. Negligence of Defendant. 

SECTION 442. 

a. General Statement.

$442 

An operator is not liable unless he was careless in acting in an unreasonable manner, and this depends on all the facts. 

The drunkenness of an operator does not necessarily compel the conclusion of fact that he was grossly negligent. 

Bertera v. Cuneo, 273 Mass. 181, at 183

A plaintiff by calling a witness who is adverse on question of control does not waive the prima facie evidence established by Acts 1928, c. 317. 

Haun v. LeGrand, 268 Mass. 582

The prima facie evidence created by the statute will carry a case to a jury in almost all cases regardless of the defendant's evidence. 

Thomes v. Meyer Store Inc., 268 Mass. 587 

Haun v. LeGrand, 268 Mass. 582

In the absence of evidence relative to traffic and other conditions existing, a speed of fifteen miles per hour is not evidence of negligence. 

Franca v. Rubin, 268 Mass. 590

A jury which views the scene of the accident, the premises, the driveway, the width of the street and its grade, may determine, without other evidence, the extent to which the view of an operator approaching the place would be obscured. 

Brown v. Daley, 273 Mass. 432, at 435

Unfavorable road conditions, together with speed of a truck at thirty miles an hour, and inferences of such speed from its "lolling" from side to side of the road, striking a tree with great force, warrant a finding of ordinary negligence. 

Cook v. Cole, 273 Mass. 557, at 562 

Terlizzi v. Marsh, 258 Mass. 156

$579 Evidence

In these days of extensive use of the highways by motor vehicles of various kinds, it is a matter of common knowledge that, to prevent collisions with pedestrians or with other vehicles, the sudden turning or stopping of a motor vehicle is often unavoidable. 

Bartlett v. Town Taxi Inc., 263 Mass. 215, at 217 and 218 The fact that the driver of a taxicab turns the cab around so abruptly that he nearly tips it over and the passenger is thrown to the floor of the taxicab and injured, in the absence of any other evidence to show the circumstances attending the accident, is insufficient to justify a finding of negligence, particularly when there is no evidence to show traffic conditions in the street at the time and place, or whether or not the abrupt turn is reasonably necessary to avoid a more serious accident. 

Bartlett v. Town Taxi Inc., 263 Mass. 215, at 217

The mere occurrence of such an accident is not of itself evidence of negligence. 

Bartlett v. Town Taxi Inc., 263 Mass. 215, at 218, citing Wing v. London General Omnibus Co. 

(1909) 2 K. B. (Eng.) 652, at 663 

Reardon v. Boston El. Ry., 247 Mass. 124, at 126 and 127

Glaser v. Schroeder, 269 Mass. 337, at 340

 c. Agency.

SECTION 444. 

When testimony as to the statement of an agent has been admitted without objection or application for restriction of its use, and no specific ruling on its competency has been sought or made, and no question with respect thereto has been raised by a motion for a directed verdict, such testimony is entitled to its natural probative force as tending to show by a statement of the agent, but not by an admission on the part of the principal, that the agent was driving the automobile within the scope of his employment and for the defendant at the time the plaintiff was injured. 

DuBois v. Powdrell, 271 Mass. 394, at 398

An important question at the trial was whether there was any evidence that Richard P. Whitman was operating the automobile as the servant of his father, at the time of the accident, or only on his own account. The weight of the testimony was that he was using it with his father's permission, solely for his own purposes. SECTION 446. 

3. Proximate. Cause.

$447 

The rule of res ipsa loquitur applies only when the direct cause of the accident, and so much of the surrounding circumstances as is essential to the occurrence, are within the sole control and management of the defendant, or his servants, so that it is not unfair to attribute to them a prima facie responsibility for what happens. 

Bartlett v. Town Taxi Inc., 263 Mass. 215, at 218

An accident in the case of traffic on a highway is in marked contrast to such a condition of things. 

Bartlett v. Town Taxi Inc., 263 Mass. 215, at 218

Every vehicle has to adapt its behaviour to the behaviour of other persons using the road and over their actions those in charge of the vehicle have no control. Hence the fact that an accident has happened either to or through a particular vehicle is by itself no evidence that the fault, if any, which led to it was committed by those in charge of that vehicle and the principle of res ipsa loquitur does not apply. 

Reardon v. Boston El. Ry., 247 Mass. 124, at 126 and 127 

Bartlett v. Town Taxi Inc., 263 Mass. 215, at 218

3. Identity.

The burden of proving the identity of the defendant with, or as the owner of, the motor vehicle, or the existence of such relation between the defendant and the driver that the defendant is liable for the operator's acts, is on the plaintiff; 

Hinds v. Bowen, 268 Mass. 55, at 59 and until such identity is shown, the defendant is under no obligation to be present in court or to introduce evidence; 

Hinds v. Bowen, 268 Mass. 55, at 59 and no inference can be drawn against the defendant because of his absence from court. 

Bishop v. Pastorelli, 240 Mass. 104

Similarity of name by itself is not sufficient evidence to warrant the finding of identity;

Ayers v. Ratshesky, 213 Mass. 589, at 593 and 594 although taken with other evidence of likeness, it may suffice to raise the issue of fact of identity.

SECTION 452. 

4. Joint or Several Liability. 

Where two or more tortfeasors by concurrent acts of negligence which, although disconnected, yet in combination inflict injury, the plaintiff may sue them jointly or severally, although he can have but one satisfaction in damages.

$593 Trial 

Feneff v. Boston & Maine R. R., 196 Mass. 575 

62 A. L. R. 1194

If each contributes to the wrong, the proximate cause is the wrongful act in which they concurrently participate, whether the result causes instantaneous death or injuries which the sufferer survives. 

Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 392, at 397 

Feneff v. Boston & Maine R. R., 196 Mass. 575 

Doe v. Boston & W. St. Ry. Co., 195 Mass. 168, at 171 

Oulighan v. Butler, 189 Mass. 287, at 293 

D'Almeida v. Boston & Maine R. R., 209 Mass. 81, at 87 

In Fraser v. Flanders, 248 Mass. 62, where a pedestrian, while crossing a street, was struck by the rear end of a car which either skidded or was pushed into him by another car, the court stating that how the accident occurred was a question for the jury to determine, and the jury giving the plaintiff a verdict against the defendant who was in fault in not conceding the other defendant the statutory right of way at the crossing; in reply to the contention of counsel for the plaintiff that both defendants should be liable as joint tortfeasors, the court states that, where two or more wrongdoers concurrently contribute to the injury of another, they may be found jointly and severally liable. 

62 A. L. R. 1427 (Joint liability for injury to third person or damage to his property due to concurring negligence of drivers of motor vehicles) 

In Foley v. Lord, 232 Mass. 368, the plaintiff sought to recover for damage done to his automobile when it was standing in the street. He contended that the defendant was responsible, because he so operated his automobile on

8453 

 the street that the driver of a truck, in attempting to pass over a cross street, had to change his course to avoid a collision, and in the operation ran into the plaintiff's car. 

It was held that an instruction was erroneous that a single action could not be brought against the defendant and the owners of the truck. The court held that the defendant and the owners of the truck, though not joint tortfeasors, who might be sued jointly or severally at the plaintiff's election, were separately liable. 

62 A. L. R. 1193

a. 

Under Death Statute. 

Recovery under a death statute against separate defendants whose joint or concurrent acts have caused the death must be brought under separate actions; 

Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 392, at 399

Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 392, at 399 

D'Almeida v. Boston & Maine R. R., 209 Mass. 81

There are no provisions for separate judgments in actions of tort even if death has been caused by the concurrent acts of wrongdoers who have been joined in one suit. 

Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 392, at 399

5. Proximate Cause. 

See: Section 98, page 136. 

A driver of an automobile who turns his machine to the right so that it strikes a tree on the right side of a highway resulting in injury to his person and damage to his automobile, may recover even though there was no physical contact between his automobile and the vehicle of the defendant.

Harrington v. Cudahy Packing Co., 273 Mass. 15 

So the defendant's acts can be the proximate cause of the plaintiff's injury even though there was no physical contact between the defendant's automobile and the plaintiff's vehicle.

6. Negligence. 

SECTION 455. 

a. General Statement. 

See: Section 91, page 112.

Antecedent, simultaneous and subsequent conduct of the operator of a motor vehicle, and the person sought to b held liable for the conduct of the operator, may be the proper subject of inquiry at the trial.

So, as bearing upon recklessness, the operator's conduct after he sees a pedestrian is by no means decisive,

$456 

 for his driving previous to that moment may have been such as to ignore the rights of other travellers, even if he did not see them. 

Antecedent conduct may be found to be reckless, even though all possible care may be exercised after the specific danger is actually discovered.

Indeed, a person might be guilty of reckless driving although no one was upon the street. 

Comm. v. Horsfall, 213 Mass. 232, at 235 

But see:

SECTION 484. 

h. Liability for Acts of Third Persons. 

The defendant was general manager of a chain of lunch rooms and his automobile was used by M., a servant, in connection with the defendant's business and for pleasure. The defendant testified that M. took all orders from him; that M. reported the accident to him; but did not have any collections with him belonging to the company; that he could not tell whether the car was being used for any particular purpose at the time of the accident; that he had no recollection as to what M. was using the car for at the time of the accident except what he might infer from the custom between them. It was held that the plaintiff had failed on this evidence to establish agency on the part of M.

Later the defendant was asked, "Bearing in mind his custom is there any doubt he was using it on your account that night?" to which the defendant replied, "No doubt whatever in my mind but what that is what he was using it for." It was held there was evidence from which in connection with their business relations to each other the jury might find that M. was acting for the defendant in the use of the car.

7. Due Care and Contributory Negligence. 

SECTION 485. 

a. General Statement. 

Contributory negligence in all actions for injury to person or property, or death, is an affirmative defense with the burden resting on the defendant, General Laws 

Chapter 231, Section 85, and, with rare exceptions, presents an issue of fact for the jury. 

Kirby v. Keating 271 Mass. 390 

Gallup v. Lazott, 271 Mass. 406 

O'Connell v. McKeown, 270 Mass. 432, at 435 

Sullivan v. Chadwick, 236 Mass. 130, at 137 

Powers v. Loring, 231 Mass. 458 

Mercier v. Union St. Ry., 230 Mass. 397 

Duggan v. Bay State St. Ry., 230 Mass. 370

The presumption that the plaintiff was in the exercise of due care does not require submission to the jury in a case where there is no evidence explaining the plaintiff's conduct or showing in what manner he acted. 

Mahoney v. Boston El. Ry., 271 Mass. 274, at 277

Wilmur Motors Inc. v. Eastern Mass. St. Ry., 271 

Mass. 31

Bagnell v. Boston El. Ry., 247 Mass. 235 

Pigeon v. Mass. Northeastern St. Ry. Co., 230 Mass. 392 Whether any contributory negligence of the plaintiff has been proved, is usually a question of fact for the jury. 

Margeson v. Town Taxi Inc., 266 Mass. 192 

In deciding whether it can be ruled, as matter of law, that a plaintiff's contributory negligence has been estab-

$607 Trial lished, the testimony introduced in behalf of the defendant must be disregarded. 

Linnane v. Millman, 261 Mass. 491, at 494

Such a ruling can be made only when based upon facts admitted or indisputable or upon evidence by which the plaintiff is bound.

SECTION 505. 

(I) Guest or Occupant. 

An operator of a motor vehicle is not necessarily the agent of the occupant, unless such relationship in fact

$505 

 exists. Acts 1928, Chapter 317, Section I enacts that: 

"Evidence that a motor vehicle was registered in the name of defendant as owner shall be prima facie evidence that it was then being operated by and under the control of the person for whose conduct the defendant was legally responsible." 

This has no application to an action against the owner or operator of another vehicle in which the owner of the first vehicle is the plaintiff. The statute, in terms, applies only to the defendant, and it has no relation to a plaintiff whose motor vehicle is involved in a collision. 

Thompson v. Sides, 275 Mass. 568, at 571

So, a wife who was riding in her own automobile driven by her husband, is not necessarily responsible for the conduct of her husband and, if she is exercising proper care for her own safety, may recover against a third person who negligently collides with her own automobile. 

Thompson v. Sides, 275 Mass. 568, at 571

Where an operator of a motor vehicle is drunk immediately after the accident, a guest, who did not reasonably know of the operator's condition before the accident, is not necessarily guilty of contributory negligence. 

O'Connell v. McKeown, 270 Mass. 432, at 435

So, when the operator is to a degree under the influence of liquor and that fact is perceivable when the jaunt begins, or, if not then apparent, becomes so thereafter, it cannot be ruled as matter of law that the guest is negligent in accepting the invitation to ride with the driver or continuing to ride with him after he knows of his intoxicated condition. 

O'Connell v. McKeown, 270 Mass. 432, at 435 

If the guest knows after the ride begins that the driver is under the influence of intoxicating liquor, it is incum-

$615 Trial bent on the defendant to prove that the plaintiff guest could have left the automobile without peril to his life or limb, and, failing so to do, the defendant is not permitted to shift the consequences of his own folly to the shoulders of the plaintiff. 

O'Connell v. McKeown, 270 Mass. 432, at 435 

Harter v. Boston El. Ry., 259 Mass. 433 

Pitman & Brown v. Eastern Mass. St. Ry., 255 Mass. 292 

Chadbourne v. Springfield St. Ry., 199 Mass. 574 

Krause v. Hall, 195 Wis. 565

So, when the driver's condition as to liquor is not readily observable when the ride begins, and when his condition is observed, the plaintiff directs the driver's attention to the excessive speed of the car, the plaintiff guest is exercising sufficient due care, O'Connell v. McKeown, 270 Mass. 432, at 436 particularly when the plaintiff guest sees no signs of liquor on the driver and insofar as he can tell from the driver's actions he is perfectly sober, and when the ride begins the driver shows no signs of anything wrong, the guest is not guilty of negligence in intrusting his safety to the driver at the time they started out on their trip. 

O'Connell v. McKeown, 270 Mass. 432, at 433 and 434

C. DIRECTING OR ORDERING VERDICT. 

1. For Plaintiff.

SECTION 507. 

It rarely, if ever, can occur that a verdict should be directed for the plaintiff in an action for death, injury or damage caused by a motor vehicle but where the facts creating the defendant's liability are admitted or have the binding effect of conclusiveness, as matter of law, it is proper to direct a verdict for the plaintiff but the question of damage must be left for the jury. 

Loveland v. Epstein Drug Co., 227 Mass. 311

Martin v. International Textbook Co., 221 Mass. I 2. For Defendant. 

SECTION 508. 

Although a trial judge has power to direct a verdict at the close of the opening, Energy Electric Co., Petr., 262 Mass. 534 he is not, as matter of law, obliged to do so. 

Meaney v. Doyle, 1931 A. S. 1471, at 1473

See: 

Farnham v. Lenox Motor Car Co., 229 Mass. 478, at 482 and cases there cited 

Whether so to rule rests in his discretion. 

Meaney v. Doyle, 1931 A. S. 1471, at 1473

When a motion is made to direct a verdict for the defendant, the plaintiff is entitled to a construction of the testimony most favorable to his contention, and is not bound by the testimony of other witnesses even though called by himself.

$617 Trial 

Coyle v. Worcester Cons. St. Ry., 273 Mass. 475, at 477 

Haun v. LeGrand, 268 Mass. 582, at 583

Whatever may be the significance of the circumstance that a witness, asked on the witness stand concerning a material fact, bows his head, the party offering such witness is not bound by that testimony. 

Hirrel v. Lacey, 274 Mass. 431, at 435 

Haun v. LeGrand, 268 Mass. 582, at 583

And in a case without a jury, the judge is not required to find that such conduct by witness contradicted all the other testimony in the case, warranting a finding of the existence of that material fact. 

Hirrel v. Lacey, 274 Mass. 431, at 436 

Haun v. LeGrand, 268 Mass. 582, at 583 

When the question whether the defendant blew his horn is in issue, the trial judge is bound to assume that he did not, for the purpose of deciding to direct a verdict. 

Dzura v. Phillips, 275 Mass. 283, at 288

If there is evidence which will sustain a verdict against the defendant for negligence, then whether that negligence arose simply from the violation of a legal requirement or from other negligent conduct, the plaintiff is entitled to have the jury pass upon the issue, unless the negligent act bore any causal connection to the accident, or unless his own lack of due care contributed to his injury.

The usual rules that govern instructions to the jury in civil cases are applicable to actions involving death, injuries or damages caused by motor vehicles.

2. Requirement of Giving. 

SECTION 510. 

a. General Statement. 

Each party is entitled to a full and clear charge or instruction to the jury upon all the material issues involved in the case. 

Mahoney v. Gooch, 246 Mass. 567, at 571 

O'Brien v. Shea, 208 Mass. 528

Maxwell v. Mass. Title Ins. Co., 206 Mass. 197

623 Trial The judge is not required to deal specifically with requests which relate to certain portions of the evidence. 

Isaacson v. Boston, etc. St. Ry. Co., 1932 A. S. 385, at 397 

SECTION 511. 

b. Effect of Request. 

The trial judge is not required to make rulings or grant requests for instructions relating to fragmentary portions of the evidence, especially when such portions are not vital issues in the case. 

Keyes v. Checker Taxi Co., 275 Mass. 461, at 468 

Coates v. Bates, 265 Mass. 444

McDonough v. Vozzella, 247 Mass. 552 

The trial judge is not required to single out a part of all the evidence and give instructions upon that part. 

Jenkins v. North Shore Dye House, Inc., 1931 A. S., 2299, at 2302 

Selectmen of Wakefield v. Judge of District Court, 

262 Mass. 477, at 484 

Ayers v. Ratchesky, 213 Mass. 589, at 593

C. 

SECTION 512. 

Absence of Request.

Even in the absence of a request therefor, each party is entitled to complete instructions upon the material issues involved in the trial. 

As was said in Mahoney v. Gooch, 246 Mass. 567, at 571: "A judge should instruct the jury fairly, clearly, adequately, and carefully concerning principles that ought to guide and control their action. This duty is not affected by the absence of specific requests by counsel.” 

3. Form and Language.

8513 a. 

SECTION 513. 

General Statement. 

No good exception lies to a refusal to rule with regard to this portion of the evidence. 

Meaney v. Doyle, 1931 A. S. 1471, at 1473 (There is no evidence of excessive or unlawful speed in this case) 

Buckley v. Frankel, 262 Mass. 13, at 15

Although a request may not be strictly accurate it may be sufficient to sustain an exception if it directs the court's attention to an important branch of the case. 

Bogert v. Corcoran, 260 Mass. 206, at 209 

Bilodeau v. Fitchburg etc., 236 Mass. 526, at 539 

Bergeron v. Forest, 233 Mass. 392, at 401 

SECTION 514. 

b. Particular Language of Request. 

The trial judge is not required to grant a request for an instruction in terms even though it is accurate in law provided the subject is adequately covered in the charge. 

Wharmby v. Richards, 1931 A. S. 2041

All that is required is that the judge give sound and reasonably ample instructions touching the particular subject matter referred to in the request. 

Wharmby v. Richards, 1931 A. S. 2041

Although the defendants requested instructions, it was not essential that the court should adopt their exact phraseology. It is sufficient if the principles were rightly stated to the jury and correct rules prescribed to aid them in the decision of the questions in issue. So, it is enough that the substance of the requests for instructions was given to the jury. 

Parsons v. Martin, II Gray, III, at 114

$625 Trial So, it was proper for the judge to refuse requests for instructions which had been covered in his charge. 

Browning-Drake Corp. v. Amer. Tran. Sales Co., 274 Mass. 545, at 549

Even though the requests for instructions state the law correctly, the court is not required to grant the request and to instruct the jury in the language asked. 

Norwood v. Somerville, 159 Mass. 105, at 112 

As was said in Graham v. Middleby, 185 Mass. 349, at 354: "As we have already said, this [request for instruction] stated the law correctly. But no particular or set form of words are recognized by which the principle is to be defined; any language that conveys to a jury the substance of the rule and its application is sufficient, and it is enough to say that the judge was not required to instruct, in the language requested."

SECTION 518. 

No damages can be awarded for future injuries as to which there is no evidence other than testimony that it is possible that a certain condition may result in the future. 

Demoranville v. Martin, 273 Mass. 269, at 271

Demoranville v. Martin, 273 Mass. 269, at 271 (I) 

Decrease in Income.

A plaintiff may be permitted to testify to his average monthly income for the year prior to his injury and for the year following it. 

Hendler v. Coffey, 1932 A. S. 291, at 293

$627 Trial It is a proper instruction that: "Decrease in income is not an element of damage when it is interwoven with profits derived from a business in which capital is employed and to the success of which the service, skill and zeal of other [s] contribute; personal earnings may be considered as damage, but the more or less uncertain profits from a business venture arising from an investment and from ability in employing and managing labor cannot be taken into account; the uncertain profits of a commercial undertaking depending for its success upon other essential factors, besides this plaintiff's personal services, are too remote to be of assistance in assessing the damages in this case." 

Hendler v. Coffey, 1932 A. S. 291, at 294 

Donoghue v. Holyoke St. Ry., 246 Mass. 485, at 493 

Mahoney v. Boston El. Ry., 221 Mass. 116, at 117-8

SECTION 519. 

5. Existence, Weight or Importance of Facts or 

Evidence. 

Under General Laws, Chapter 231, Section 81, a judge is not permitted to comment on the facts or weight of the evidence. 

It is a trial judge's duty to charge the jury with clearness and with force. 

Comm. v. McDonald, 264 Mass. 324 

Whitney v. Wellesley & Boston St. Ry., 197 Mass. 495, at 502 The provision of the constitution that judges shall be "as free, impartial and independent as the lot of humanity will admit," and the provision of General Laws, Chapter 231, Section 81, that "the courts shall not charge juries with respect to matters of fact, but they may state the testimony and the law" are not violated by “calling the attention of the jury to the degree of weight and importance to be attached to particular facts, if they are

$519 

 proved or admitted. To say that certain circumstances deserve to be seriously considered, or are entitled to great weight, is not expressing an opinion as to what facts have been proved, but only instructing the jury with regard to the relative materiality and importance of different portions of the evidence." 

Federal National Bank v. O'Keefe, 267 Mass. 75, at 82 It "is not a violation of the constitutional requirement if the instructions, while judicially fair, are comprehensively strong, rather than hesitatingly barren or ineffective," and, if no error of law appears, neither the tone of a charge nor the form of verbal delivery is of itself ground of exception. 

Federal National Bank v. O'Keefe, 267 Mass. 75, at 82 

Comm. v. McDonald, 264 Mass. 324 

Whitney v. Wellesley & Boston St. Ry., 197 Mass. 495, at 502 "On the other hand the parties to an action are entitled to a fair and unprejudiced submission of the testimony and the issues to the jury, without indication of the opinion of the judge upon the weight or effect of evidence or as to who should prevail upon any issue where a material fact is left in doubt by the testimony or there are inferences to be drawn from the facts in proof, save as such indication may flow from a clear analysis of the evidence and unbiased statements of testimony. Portions of the charge here assailed could not have failed to give the impression that the plaintiff was being held up to scorn and ridicule and to disclose the view of the judge, apart from impartial references to evidence, that the plaintiff ought not to prevail. It is obvious that the jury would so understand and thus be influenced in their subsequent deliberations. A careful study of the entire charge constrains us to the belief that the jury must have perceived

$629 Trial the attitude, the bent of mind of the judge, and that in all human probability they entered upon their final deliberations in a state of mind which was biased and interested. A further study leads us to the conclusion that the effect of the charge on the jury was not removed by any adequate instruction to disregard what had been said to them if it be assumed it were possible to eradicate the impression produced by the entire charge." 

Federal National Bank v. O'Keefe, 267 Mass. 75, at 83 The trial judge is not required to give specific instructions respecting possible findings from particular parts of the evidence upon a single issue. 

Coates v. Bates, 265 Mass. 444, at 448

It is largely a matter of discretion for the presiding judge as to how far he will discuss different phases of the testimony upon a particular subject and give specific instructions each founded upon a part of the testimony bearing upon the subject. 

Coates v. Bates, 265 Mass. 444, at 448 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, at 164 

Brown v. Harrington, 208 Mass. 600, at 602 

Hicks v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R. Co., 164 Mass. 424, at 428 It is the duty of the judge presiding over a jury trial to give full, fair, correct and clear instructions as to the principles of law governing all the essential issues presented so that the jury may understand their duty and be enabled to perform it intelligently. If he does this, it is not necessary that he single out particular facts for emphasis. 

Buckley v. Frankel, 262 Mass. 13, at 15 

Goldsmith v. Grysmish, 238 Mass. 341, at 344 

Herrick v. Waitt, 224 Mass. 415 

Altabilla v. Old Colony Ry., 222 Mass. 322

$519 

Hanley v. Eastern Steamship Corp., 221 Mass. 125, at 135 

Maxwell v. Mass. Title Co., 206 Mass. 197, at 200 

As was said by Knowlton, J., in Hicks v. New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad Company, 164 Mass. 

424, at 428: "If he gives full and sufficient instructions, which enable the jury to understand the law applicable to all branches of the case, it is not a ground of objection that he declines to take each fragment of the testimony and to state a conclusion of law applicable to a possible finding founded on it." 

Buckley v. Frankel, 262 Mass. 13, at 15 and 16 

Mahoney v. Gooch, 246 Mass. 567, at 571 

Ayers v. Ratshesky, 213 Mass. 589, at 593 

Bourne v. Whitman, 209 Mass. 155, at 164 The duties of a judge presiding over a jury trial have been stated in several recent decisions. It was said in 

Whitney v. Wellesley & Boston Street Railway Company, 197 Mass. 495, at 502, with ample citations of authorities, that the judge "may sum up the testimony according to his recollection In any clear analysis of the evidence, however impartial, the attention of the jury necessarily must be directed to the weight and importance of particular facts which they may find to have been proved. 

If an unbiased analytical statement of the testimony and of the law distinctly indicates the party who is entitled to prevail, this furnishes no just reason for the defeated party to complain, either of the method employed or of the adverse verdict. Besides, it is not a violation of the constitutional requirement that judges shall be 'as free, impartial and independent as the lot of humanity will admit, if the instructions, while judicially fair, are comprehensively strong, rather than hesitatingly barren or ineffective, and neither the tone of the charge nor the

$631 Trial form of verbal delivery are of themselves ground of exception, if no error of law appears." 

Buckley v. Frankel, 262 Mass: 13, at 15, 16 and 17

SECTION 520. 

F. WAIVER OF RIGHT TO INSTRUCTIONS. 

When at the conclusion of the charge, the trial judge requests counsel for a particular party to direct his attention to anything else which counsel thinks ought to be said on any particular subject, and no reply is made by that counsel, the party for whom he is counsel has no ground for complaint. Notwithstanding his exception to the denial of his earlier request on that particular subject, counsel should state his objection, if any, to the inadequacy of the charge provided he thinks there is any defect in it, when invited to do so by the judge, otherwise he waives the party's right to have instructions on the particular subject matter. 

Wharmby v. Richards, 1931 A. S. 2041 

McCoubrey v. German American Ins. Co., 177 Mass. 327 

McCart v. Squire, 150 Mass. 484, at 488 

Boutelle v. Dean, 148 Mass. 89

Dubois v. Goldstein, 1931 A. S. 2043, at 2044

2. New Trial. 

a. 

SECTION 523. 

General Statement.

$633 Trial 

A new trial may be granted where "by mistake of parties or counsel . . . a question of fact which is essential to the determination of the rights of the parties has not been tried.”

Comm. v. Madeiros, 257 Mass. I 

In the Matter of Alvah G. Sleeper, 251 Mass. 6, at 22

Comm. v. Morrison, 134 Mass. 189

Matters of right which could have been presented at the trial on the merits cannot be presented as of right upon a motion for a new trial. 

Barry v. Alton Rubber Co., 274 Mass. 18, at 19 

Energy Electric Co., Petnr., 262 Mass. 534, at 538 and cases cited

A judge may grant rehearing on motion for new trial. 

Waucantuck Mills v. Magee Carpet Co., 225 Mass. 31 (I) 

SECTION 524. 

Court's Power to Grant.

By General Laws, Chapter 231, Sections 127 and 128, a verdict shall not be set aside except on written motion by a party to the cause, stating the reasons relied upon in its support, and whenever a new trial is granted the judge shall file a statement setting forth the grounds upon which the motion is granted. 

Wright v. Apikian, 270 Mass. 302, at 304

This regulation is a constitutional exercise of legislative power concerning the right of trial by jury. It restricts the power of the judge existing at common law to set aside of his own motion a verdict for any cause deemed by him to be sufficient, and confines him to the causes set forth in the written motion for a new trial. 

Wright v. Apikian, 270 Mass. 302, at 304

$525 

So, when two cases are tried together a judge cannot set aside the verdict upon any of the grounds not set out in the motion for a new trial. 

Wright v. Apikian, 270 Mass. 302, at 304 (Where the judge ordered a new trial in one case and also in the companion case for the reason that the two were so interrelated that a new trial in one required a new trial in the other but filed only a memorandum in the former where no ground of the motion claimed the interrelationship as reason for the new trial in the companion 

The judge's action was improper.) case.

When the judge does not follow the statute by allowing the motion for a ground not stated in the motion the verdict is not legally effectually set aside. 

Wright v. Apikian, 270 Mass. 302, at 305 

Simmons v. Fish, 210 Mass. 563, at 572 and 573 

Coughlan v. McGarvey, 267 Mass. 49 

Barnett v. Loud, 243 Mass. 510, at 514 

Waucantuck Mills v. Magee Carpet Co., 225 Mass. 31 

Tildsley v. Boston El. Ry., 224 Mass. 117 

Parker v. Lewis J. Bird Co., 221 Mass. 422, at 425 and 426 

McDonnell, Petnr., 197 Mass. 252

(A) When Compulsory. 

When a judge has made a clerical mistake, such matter should be raised by motion for a new trial so that the judge can correct the error before the entry of judgment. 

Duralith Corporation v. Leonard, 274 Mass. 397, at 401 

SECTION 526. 

(II) Statutory Provisions.

$635 Trial "The court may, at any time before judgment, set aside the verdict in a civil action and order a new trial for any cause for which a new trial may by law be granted; but a verdict shall not be set aside except on written motion by a party to the cause, stating the reasons relied upon in its support, filed and heard after notice to the adverse party according to the rules of the court. A verdict shall not be set aside as excessive until the prevailing party has first been given an opportunity to remit so much thereof as the court adjudges is excessive." 

G. L. c. 231, s. 127 "Whenever a verdict is set aside and a new trial granted under the preceding section, the justice granting the motion for the new trial shall file a statement setting forth fully the grounds upon which the motion is granted, which statement shall be a part of the record of the case. 

If it appears from the statement that the sole ground for granting the motion was that the damages awarded were either inadequate or excessive, then the new trial shall be limited to the question of the amount of damages." 

G. L. c. 231, s. 128 "A new trial may be granted, upon motion, for a mistake of law or for newly discovered evidence in a case heard by the court. When a decision has been rendered in such a case, the clerk shall notify the parties, and a motion for a new trial may be filed within three days after receipt of such notice or within such further time as the court allows." 

G. L. c. 231, S. 129 "If a new trial is refused, the court may impose terms upon the moving party, to be taxed as costs." 

G. L. c. 231, S. 130 "Sections one hundred and twenty-two and one hundred and twenty-three shall not limit or effect the power of a trial court to grant a new trial.” 

G. L. c. 231, s. 131

127, are a constitutional regulation of the right of trial by jury.

637 Trial As is said in Davis v. Boston Elevated Railway Company, 235 Mass. 482, at 496 and 497: "It commonly and rightly is said that such a motion is addressed to the discretion of the court. By such expression is implied absence of arbitrary determination, capricious disposition, or whimsical thinking. An exhibition of ungoverned will, or a manifestation of unbridled power is not the use of discretion. The word imports the exercise of discriminating judgment within the bounds of reason.

Discretion in this connection means a sound judicial discretion, enlightened by intelligence and learning, controlled by sound principles of law, of firm courage combined with the calmness of a cool mind, free from partiality, not swayed by sympathy nor warped by •prejudice nor moved by any kind of influence save alone the overwhelming passion to do that which is just.”

As to newly discovered evidence, see: 

Hallett v. Jordan Marsh Co., 240 Mass. 110, at 112 

Flynn v. Johnson, 234 Mass. 36 

Davis v. Custer, 230 Mass. 603, at 604 

Matter of Samuel Carver, 224 Mass. 169, at 171

A party cannot, as matter of right, be heard upon a motion for a new trial on the ground that the finding of the judge was against the evidence and the weight of the evidence. 

O'Grady v. Supple, 148 Mass. 522, at 523

The legislature may regulate (G. L. c. 231, s. 127) but cannot abolish. 

Simmons v. Fish, 210 Mass. 563 

Opinion of Justices, 207 Mass. 606

It is established practice not to grant motion for a new trial on matters which might have been raised by exceptions. 

Comm. v. Dascalkis, 246 Mass. 12, at 25

Existing party may be required to elect between motion for new trial and exceptions. 

Wheeler v. Klaholt, 178 Mass. 141 The court has no power to allow filing of motion for new trial after time set in rule. 

Cram v. Moore, 158 Mass. 276, at 277 

But see: 

Whitney-Spiller Mfg. Co., 218 Mass. 318

$639 Trial 

As to second motion for new trial, see: 

Barry v. Alton Rubber Co., 274 Mass. 18, at 19 See: 

Clark v. McNeil, 246 Mass. 250, at 256 and 257 

Davis v. Boston El. Ry., 235 Mass. 482, at 496 and 497 

Waucantuck Mills v. Magee Carpet Co., 225 Mass. 31, at 33 

Com. v. Ruisseau, 140 Mass. 363, at 365

C. 

Grounds for Granting in Jury Cases. 

SECTION 528. 

(I) Erroneous Ruling During Trial. 

Where without fault party has been deprived of legal right or remedy, Barrowscale v. Royal Bosworth, 98 Mass. 34 to have standing as of right exception must have been duly taken. 

Sullivan v. Boston Bar Assn. of City of Boston, 170 

Mass. 504 

Lynch v. Peabody, 137 Mass. 92 

Caverly v. McOwen, 126 Mass. 222

However, in its discretion court may reconsider such ruling, but in such case no exception will lie to refusal. 

Nagle v. Laxton, 191 Mass. 402 

Robbins v. Brockton St. Ry., 180 Mass. 51 

Garrity v. Higgins, 177 Mass. 414

SECTION 529. 

(II) Verdict Against Evidence or Weight of 

Evidence.

The question of weight of evidence is for the jury exclusively. 

Snow v. Alley, 151 Mass. 14

$529 

This ground raises a question of fact, not of law, and no exception lies. 

Lopes v. Connolly, 210 Mass. 487

Scannell v. Boston El. Ry., 208 Mass. 513 

Stetson v. Medford, 109 Mass. 242

Lowell Gas Light Co. v. Bean, I Allen, 274 

Shea v. Lawrence, I Allen, 167

The court should not set the verdict aside unless in its opinion no reasonable man would have been justified in finding as the jury did. 

Scannell v. Boston El. Ry., 208 Mass. 513 

The mere fact that if the judge would have been deciding the case he would have found differently, does not justify the setting of the verdict aside, for this would in practical effect result in a trial of the facts by the Court instead of by the jury. 

Aiken v. Holyoke St. Ry., 180 Mass. 8 

Reeve v. Dennett, 137 Mass. 315

Cunningham v. Magoun, 18 Pick. 13 

But where the question is purely matter of fact, where there is evidence for the minds of the jury actually and fairly to weigh and balance, where presumptions are to be raised and inferences drawn, and the jury may be presumed fairly to have exercised their judgment a court will not feel at liberty to set a verdict aside, although the same evidence he would have decided the other way. 

Aiken v. Holyoke St. Ry., 180 Mass. 8

To be set aside as being against the weight of the evidence, the verdict must be so obviously against it as to show that the only reasonable inference is that the jury acted under some gross mistake, or misapprehension, or disregard of duty. 

Merwin, Equity, page 5

SECTION 530. 

(III) Verdict Against the Law.

$641 Trial The question of fact or law may be raised: if fact, no exception; if law, there is exception. 

Loveland v. Rand, 200 Mass. 142 

Lufkin v. Hitchcock, 194 Mass. 231 

Coffing v. Dodge, 169 Mass. 459

The Court is not confined to narrow questions of jury's disregard of instructions but may re-examine any law question during the trial. 

Weil v. Boston El. Ry., 218 Mass. 397, at 404 

Loveland v. Rand, 200 Mass. 142

Special findings, whether consistent or inconsistent, may be set aside in whole or in part. 

Randall v. Peerless Motor Car Co., 212 Mass. 352, at 390 

McManus v. Thing, 202 Mass. II

If different parts of verdict are inconsistent, it is the Court's duty to set it aside and grant a new trial. 

Lufkin v. Hitchcock, 194 Mass. 231

The setting aside of general verdict includes special findings. 

Welsh v. Milton Water Co., 200 Mass. 409

SECTION 531. 

(A) Error of Law.

In order to warrant a new trial, the error of law must affect injuriously the substantial rights of the party. 

Simmons v. Fish, 210 Mass. 563, at 567 

G. L. c. 231, s. 132 

When a trial judge denies a motion for a new trial for a cause assigned by him for setting aside the verdict as a rule of law, and that rule of law is error, the Supreme Judicial Court will invalidate the order for a new trial and the case stands as if such order had never been made.

$532 

Dziegel v. Town of Westford, 274 Mass. 291, at 295 So, when a trial judge granting a new trial on the ground that it appeared that in sending out the jury after a separation, and inquiry was not made in the jury room by the jurors themselves as to any prejudicial circumstance which might have arisen during separation, this was error, and his order in granting a new trial was de cided by the Supreme Judicial Court. 

Dziegel v. Town of Westford, 274 Mass. 291, at 295 (Trial judge sending out jury after separation) Questions of law which could have been, but were not, raised at the trial cannot be raised as of right on a motion for a new trial. 

Comm. v. Vallarelli, 273 Mass. 240, at 248 

Comm. v. Cero, 264 Mass. 264, at 275 

Energy Electric Co., Petnr., 262 Mass. 534, at 538 

Comm. v. Clifford, 254 Mass. 390, at 393 

Comm. v. Dascalakis, 246 Mass. 12, at 24 

Comm. v. Morrison, 134 Mass. 189

SECTION 532. 

(B) Unprejudicial Error. 

General Laws, Chapter 231, Section 132, provides that: 

"No new trial shall be granted in any civil action or proceeding on the ground of improper admission or rejection of evidence, or for any error as to any matter of pleading or procedure, if the judge who presided at the trial when application is made by motion for a new trial, or the supreme judicial court when application is made by exceptions or otherwise, deems that the error complained of has not injuriously affected the substantial rights of the parties; and, if it appears to such court that said error affects part only of the matter in controversy or some or one of the parties, the court may direct final

$643 Trial judgment as to part thereof, or some or one only of the parties, and may direct a new trial as to the other part only or as to the other parties." 

(IV) Damages. 

SECTION 533. 

(A) Issues of, as Affecting. 

Ordinarily if the plaintiff's right of recovery is established by a verdict and no reversible error appears except in matters that affect damages, the new trial would be confined to that issue. 

McNulty v. Whitney, 273 Mass. 494, at 505 and 506 

Thomson v. Pentecost, 206 Mass. 505, at 513

SECTION 534. 

(B) Excessive or Inadequate.

The prevailing party must first be given opportunity to remit the excess. 

G. L. c. 231, s. 127

The new trial must be limited to question of damages. 

G. L. c. 231, s. 128

Ordinarily this ground raises a question of, fact to which no exception lies. 

Lopes v. Connolly, 210 Mass. 487 

Phillips v. Soule, 6 Allen, 150

But it may raise a question of law as to whether any reasonable man could have reached the conclusion of the jury. 

Simmons v. Fish, 210 Mass. 563

However, the court is reluctant to interfere where plaintiff's feelings or reputation are involved. 

Lufkin v. Hitchcock, 194 Mass. 231 

Treanor v. Donahoe, 9 Cush. 228

$535 

Shute v. Barrett, 7 Pick. 82 

Clark v. Binney, 2 Pick. 113, at 118 

(V) Intermeddling With, or Misconduct of, Jury.

SECTION 535. 

(A) Intermeddling. 

Further communication of law can only be made in open court, Lewis v. Lewis, 220 Mass. 364 

Munde v. Lambie, 125 Mass. 367

Read v. Cambridge, 124 Mass. 567 

Merrill v. Nary, 10 Allen, 416 

Alger v. Thompson, I Allen, 453 

Sargent v. Roberts et al., I Pick. 337 but judge may inquire whether they have agreed or direct them to go out again and come to an agreement or disagreement. 

Comm. v. Heden, 162 Mass. 521 

Whitney v. Comm., 190 Mass. 531

However, a paper delivered to the jury by accident, and not read by them, is not sufficient. 

Balcom v. Craggin, 5 Pick. 296

Also remarks by court officers to jury, not relative to case, insufficient. 

Damm v. Boylston, 218 Mass. 557 

Leach v. Wilbur, 9 Allen, 212

Conversation between attorney and jurors upon an indifferent subject, and wholly unrelated to case on trial, does not require a new trial. 

Bannon v. Victory Theatre, 264 Mass. 498 

Claffey v. Fenelon, 263 Mass. 427

If improper intermeddling should be of such charac-

$645 Trial ter as to have any tendency to affect the verdict, the actual effect is immaterial. 

Harrington v. Worcester etc. St. Ry. Co., 157 Mass. 579 It is improper for any party to communicate with a jury while a case is pending. 

Weeks v. Hasty, 13 Mass. 218

But an innocent remark to a juror, by a party with no intent to influence the verdict, is not sufficient as matter of law. 

Kelley v. City of Boston, 201 Mass. 86 

Hilton v. McDonald, 173 Mass. 124 

Comm. v. White, 147 Mass. 76 

Cowles v. Merchants, 140 Mass. 377 

Johnson v. Witt, 138 Mass. 79 

Nichols v. Nichols, 136 Mass. 256 

White v. Wood, 8 Cush. 413 

Shea v. Lawrence, 1 Allen, 167

SECTION 536. 

(B) Misconduct of Jury. 

The jury is confined to evidence introduced before them so visiting scene of crime or accident by juror is sufficient to warrant a new trial, but this is discretionary with the judge. 

Collins v. Splane, 230 Mass. 281 

Comm. v. Desmond, 141 Mass. 200 

But see: 

Harrington v. Worcester etc. St. Ry. Co., 157 Mass. 579 Where the jury was sent for and received cider and food, it was held not sufficient. 

Comm. v. Roby, 12 Pick. 496, at 515

Experiments of jury in jury room not sufficient.

$537 

Bradford v. Boston & Maine R. R., 225 Mass. 129

Where after a verdict, which was reached on the way to court room, a juror departed but shortly returned, this is not sufficient to warrant a new trial. 

Chemical Elec. Lt. & Pwr. Co. v. Howard, 150 Mass. 495 Where deliberations by the jury are not conscientious and there is an improper compromise, this is sufficient. 

Simmons v. Fish, 210 Mass. 563

There may be disqualification of juror, but this is not compulsory.

Gray v. Boston El. Ry., 215 Mass. 143 Manning v. Boston El. Ry., 187 Mass. 496 SECTION 537. 

(VI) Surprise, Accident, Inadvertence or Mis take in Trial.

If without fault of moving party, a question of fact, which was essential to the case, was not. tried, the court in its discretion may allow a new trial. 

Noyes v. Noyes, 224 Mass. 125, at 135 

Ellis v. Ginsburg, 163 Mass. 143 

Greene v. Farlow, 138 Mass. 146 

Cutler v. Rice, 14 Pick. 494

SECTION 538. 

(VII) Newly Discovered Evidence-Discre tionary. 

To have effect, it must be- (A) material, Comm. v. Sacco, 259 Mass. 128

Davis v. Boston El. Ry., 235 Mass. 482 

(B) not merely cumulative,

Davis v. Boston El. Ry., 235 Mass. 482

$647 Trial And 

Herrick v. Waitt, 224 Mass. 415 

Barnes v. Loomis, 199 Mass. 578 

Manzigian v. Boyajian, 183 Mass. 125 

Gardner v. Gardner, 2 Gray, 434, at 443 

Parker v. Hardy, 24 Pick. 246 

Gardner v. Mitchell, 6 Pick. 116 (C) could not have been produced at the trial by the exercise of reasonable diligence. 

Davis v. Boston El. Ry., 235 Mass. 482, at 496 

Gardner v. Gardner, 2 Gray, 434, at 444 

Where defendant found receipt afterward,

Bacon v. Williams, II Gray, 222 

verdict for plaintiff. 

Watts v. Howard, 7 Met. 478

SECTION 539. 

d. Limited to Certain Issues. 

Where witness gave false testimony. 

Chatfield v. Lathrop, 6 Pick. 417 

Gardner v. Mitchell, 6 Pick. 114

New trial will not be granted on ground of newly discovered evidence which only goes to impeach credit of witness at trial.

Hopcraft v. Kittredge, 162 Mass. 1, at 13 

Comm. v. Greene, 17 Mass. 514, at 525 

Hammond v. Wadhams, 5 Mass. 353

SECTION 540. 

e. Review of Judge's Action. 

The denial of a motion for a new trial is a matter of discretion and the exercise of such discretion will not be interfered with unless abused. 

Rosenberg v. Rome, 275 Mass. 64, at 68

8541 

1 

Dixon v. Cunningham, 257 Mass. 63

Can only be reviewed in instances where the trial judge has abused his discretion in denying that the motion be allowed. 

Young v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R. Co., 273 Mass. 

567 

Ryan v. Hickey, 240 Mass. 46, at 48 and cases cited

SECTION 541. 

(I) Instances Where Granting New Trial Im proper. 

Where the trial judge ruled that his action in sending the jury out for further deliberation after they had separated was sufficient cause for granting of new trial, as matter of law, it was improper. 

Dziegel v. Town of Westford, 274 Mass. 291, at 296 

SECTION 542. 

(II) Supreme Judicial Court May Order. 

In appropriate instances this court has and will exercise the power to set aside a verdict in order to prevent a miscarriage of justice when a decisive matter has not been raised at the trial. 

Comm. v. McDonald, 264 Mass. 324, at 336

SECTION 543. 

3. Appeal and Error. 

Although the evidence descriptive of the circumstances of the accident cannot be reconciled, yet, if the plaintiff has obtained a verdict, the inferences from the testimony most favorable to him are to be considered in deciding the question of the defendant's liability. 

Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 392, at 396

$649 Trial 

SECTION 544. 

a. New Trial Limited to Certain Issues. 

When it is impossible to determine whether the verdict was based upon one cause of action or another (rescission or false representation) no such limitation of the issues in the new trial will be made. 

McNulty v. Whitney, 273 Mass. 494, at 505 

Coffing v. Dodge, 167 Mass. 231, at 241

I. JUDGMENT. 

1. Upon Default. 

SECTION 545. 

General Laws Chapter 231, Section 58A [Acts 1931, c. 463, s. 1] provides, as follows: "Damages shall not be assessed, except by special order of the court, in an action of tort, the payment of the judgment wherein is secured by a motor vehicle liability policy or a motor vehicle liability bond, both as defined in section thirty-four A of chapter ninety, and wherein the defendant has been defaulted for failure to enter an appearance, until the expiration of four days after the plaintiff has given notice of such default to the company issuing or executing such policy or bond, and has filed an affidavit thereof. Such notice may be given by mailing the same, postage prepaid, to the said company or to its agent who issued or executed such policy or bond."
